translated_text:
Volume Six
Part Two of the Book of the Names and Attributes

Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

Section

The servant’s drawing near to Allah is mentioned in such verses as:

“Prostrate and draw near.”

“Fear Allah and seek the means of drawing near to Him.”

“Those whom they invoke themselves seek the means of drawing near to their Lord.”

“Then, if he is among those brought near.”

It is also mentioned in the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, reporting from his Lord:

“Whoever draws near to Me a handspan, I draw near to him a cubit”—and the rest of the hadith.

And in His words:

“Nothing brings My servant near to Me like fulfilling what I have made obligatory upon him. My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts until I love him”—and the rest of the hadith.

The same applies to an “offering,” as in His words:

“When the two of them presented an offering, and it was accepted from one of them.”

And His words:

“Until he brings us an offering consumed by fire.”

Such drawing near undoubtedly takes place through knowledge the servant acquires and deeds he performs. This involves movement on his part and a transition from one state to another.

original_text:
ثُمَّ لَا يَخْلُو مَعَ ذَلِكَ:
 إمَّا أَنَّ رُوحَهُ وَذَاتَهُ تَتَحَرَّكُ أَوْ لَا تَتَحَرَّكُ: وَإِذَا تَحَرَّكَتْ: فَإِمَّا أَنْ تَكُونَ حَرَكَتُهَا إلَى ذَاتِ اللَّهِ أَوْ إلَى شَيْءٍ آخَرَ وَإِذَا كَانَتْ إلَى ذَاتِ اللَّهِ بَقِيَ النَّظَرُ فِي قُرْبِ اللَّهِ إلَيْهِ وَدُنُوِّهِ وَإِتْيَانِهِ وَمَجِيئِهِ؛ إمَّا جَزَاءً عَلَى قُرْبِ الْعَبْدِ وَإِمَّا ابْتِدَاءً كَنُزُولِهِ إلَى سَمَاءِ الدُّنْيَا.
فَالْأَوَّلُ:
 قَوْلُ 
" الْمُتَفَلْسِفَةِ "
 الَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ: إنَّ الرُّوحَ لَا دَاخِلَ الْبَدَنِ وَلَا خَارِجَهُ وَإِنَّهَا لَا تُوصَفُ بِالْحَرَكَةِ وَلَا بِالسُّكُونِ وَقَدْ تَبِعَهُمْ عَلَى ذَلِكَ قَوْمٌ مِمَّنْ يَنْتَسِبُ إلَى الْمِلَّةِ.
 فَهَؤُلَاءِ عِنْدَهُمْ قُرْبُ الْعَبْدِ وَدُنُوُّهُ إزَالَةُ النَّقَائِصِ وَالْعُيُوبِ عَنْ نَفْسِهِ وَتَكْمِيلُهَا بِالصِّفَاتِ الْحَسَنَةِ الْكَرِيمَةِ حَتَّى تَبْقَى مُقَارِبَةً لِلرَّبِّ مُشَابِهَةً لَهُ مِنْ جِهَةِ الْمَعْنَى وَيَقُولُونَ:
 الْفَلْسَفَةُ التَّشَبُّهُ بِالْإِلَهِ عَلَى قَدْرِ الطَّاقَةِ؛ فَأَمَّا حَرَكَةُ الرُّوحِ فَمُمْتَنِعَةٌ عِنْدَهُمْ.
 وَكَذَلِكَ يَقُولُونَ:
 فِي قُرْبِ الْمَلَائِكَةِ. وَاَلَّذِي أَثْبَتُوهُ مِنْ تَزْكِيَةِ النَّفْسِ عَنْ الْعُيُوبِ وَتَكْمِيلِهَا بِالْمَحَاسِنِ حَقٌّ فِي نَفْسِهِ؛ لَكِنَّ نَفْيَهُمْ مَا زَادَ عَلَى ذَلِكَ خَطَأٌ؛ لَكِنَّهُمْ يَعْتَرِفُونَ بِحَرَكَةِ جِسْمِهِ إلَى الْمَوَاضِعِ الَّتِي تَظْهَرُ فِيهَا آثَارُ الرَّبِّ كَالْمَسَاجِدِ وَالسَّمَوَاتِ وَالْعَارِفِينَ. وَعِنْدَ هَؤُلَاءِ مِعْرَاجُ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ إنَّمَا هُوَ انْكِشَافُ حَقَائِقِ الْكَوْنِ لَهُ كَمَا فَسَّرَهُ بِذَلِكَ ابْنُ سِينَا وَمَنْ اتَّبَعَهُ كَعَيْنِ الْقُضَاةِ 
(١)
 
(*)
 وَابْنِ الْخَطِيبِ فِي 
" الْمَطَالِبِ الْعَالِيَةِ "
.

translated_text:
Beyond this, however, there are only two possibilities: either his soul and his very self move, or they do not. If they move, their movement is either towards Allah Himself or towards something else. If it is towards Allah Himself, there remains the question of Allah’s drawing near to him, His approach, and His coming and arrival—whether in recompense for the servant’s drawing near or on His own initiative, as in His descent to the lowest heaven.

The first position is that of the “philosophers,” who say that the soul is neither inside the body nor outside it, and that it cannot be described as either moving or at rest. Some who profess adherence to Islam have followed them in this.

According to these people, the servant’s drawing near consists in removing deficiencies and faults from his soul and perfecting it with good and noble qualities, until it becomes akin to the Lord, resembling Him in its qualities. They say, “Philosophy is to resemble the Deity as far as one is able.” As for the soul’s movement, they regard it as impossible.

They say the same concerning the angels’ nearness. What they affirm concerning purifying the soul of faults and perfecting it with virtues is true in itself; their error lies in denying anything beyond that. They do, however, acknowledge the movement of the servant’s body towards places where the Lord’s effects are manifest, such as mosques, the heavens, and those who know Him.

According to these people, the Prophet’s ascension, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was nothing more than the realities of the universe being unveiled to him. This is how Ibn Sīnā interpreted it, as did his followers, such as ‘Ayn al-Qudāt (1) (*) and Ibn al-Khatīb in “al-Matālib al-‘Āliyah.”
translated_footnote:
(1) Thus in the original.

(*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd (55) said:
In the footnote, the compiler—may Allah have mercy on him—commented on the expression “ka-‘Ayn al-Qudāt” (such as ‘Ayn al-Qudāt), saying: “This is how it is written in the original.”
This reading is correct: the person meant is ‘Ayn al-Qudāt al-Hamadhānī, as mentioned in al-Fatāwā, 4:62.

الثَّانِي:
 قَوْلُ الْمُتَكَلِّمَةِ الَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ: إنَّ اللَّهَ لَيْسَ فَوْقَ الْعَرْشِ. وَإِنَّ نِسْبَةَ الْعَرْشِ وَالْكُرْسِيِّ إلَيْهِ سَوَاءٌ وَإِنَّهُ لَا دَاخِلَ الْعَالَمِ وَلَا خَارِجَهُ؛
 لَكِنْ يُثْبِتُونَ حَرَكَةَ الْعَبْدِ وَالْمَلَائِكَةِ فَيَقُولُونَ:
 قُرْبُ الْعَبْدِ إلَى اللَّهِ حَرَكَةُ ذَاتِهِ إلَى الْأَمَاكِنِ الْمُشَرَّفَةِ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ وَهِيَ السَّمَوَاتُ وَحَمَلَةُ الْعَرْشِ وَالْجَنَّةُ وَبِذَلِكَ يُفَسِّرُونَ مِعْرَاجَ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَيَتَّفِقُ هَؤُلَاءِ وَاَلَّذِينَ قَبْلَهُمْ فِي حَرَكَةِ بَدَنِ الْعَبْدِ إلَى الْأَمَاكِنِ الْمُشَرَّفَةِ كَثُبُوتِ 
" الْعِبَادَاتِ "
 وَإِنَّمَا النِّزَاعُ فِي حَرَكَةِ نَفْسِهِ. وَيُسَلِّمُ الْأَوَّلُونَ 
" حَرَكَةَ النَّفْسِ "
 بِمَعْنَى تَحَوُّلِهَا مِنْ حَالٍ إلَى حَالٍ؛ لَا بِمَعْنَى الِانْتِقَالِ مِنْ مَوْضِعٍ إلَى مَوْضِعٍ وَاتِّفَاقُهُمْ عَلَى حَرَكَةِ الْجِسْمِ وَحَرَكَةِ الرُّوحِ أَيْضًا عِنْدَ الْآخَرِينَ إلَى كُلِّ مَكَانٍ تَظْهَرُ فِيهِ مَعْرِفَةُ اللَّهِ كَالسَّمَوَاتِ وَالْمَسَاجِدِ وَأَوْلِيَاءِ اللَّهِ وَمَوَاضِعِ أَسْمَاءِ اللَّهِ وَآيَاتِهِ فَهُوَ حَرَكَةٌ إلَى. . . 
(١)
الثَّالِثُ:
 قَوْلُ: 
" أَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ وَالْجَمَاعَةِ "
 الَّذِينَ يُثْبِتُونَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ وَأَنَّ حَمَلَةَ الْعَرْشِ أَقْرَبُ إلَيْهِ مِمَّنْ دُونَهُمْ وَأَنَّ مَلَائِكَةَ السَّمَاءِ الْعُلْيَا أَقْرَبُ إلَى اللَّهِ مِنْ مَلَائِكَةِ السَّمَاءِ الثَّانِيَةِ وَأَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَمَّا عُرِجَ بِهِ إلَى السَّمَاءِ صَارَ يَزْدَادُ قُرْبًا إلَى رَبِّهِ بِعُرُوجِهِ وَصُعُودِهِ وَكَانَ عُرُوجُهُ إلَى اللَّهِ لَا إلَى مُجَرَّدِ خَلْقٍ مِنْ خَلْقِهِ وَأَنَّ رُوحَ الْمُصَلِّي تَقْرُبُ إلَى اللَّهِ فِي السُّجُودِ وَإِنْ كَانَ بَدَنُهُ مُتَوَاضِعًا. وَهَذَا هُوَ الَّذِي دَلَّتْ عَلَيْهِ نُصُوصُ الْكِتَابِ.
translated_text:
The second position is that of the speculative theologians who say that Allah is not above the Throne, that the Throne and the Footstool stand in the same relation to Him, and that He is neither inside the universe nor outside it.

They do, however, affirm the movement of the servant and the angels. They say that the servant’s drawing near to Allah consists in his own movement towards places honoured by Allah: the heavens, the bearers of the Throne, and Paradise. This is how they interpret the Prophet’s ascension, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They and the preceding group agree that the servant’s body moves towards honoured places, just as they affirm “acts of worship.” Their disagreement concerns only the movement of his soul. The first group concedes “the movement of the soul” in the sense of its changing from one state to another, but not in the sense of its moving from one place to another.

The bodily movement on which they agree—and, according to the latter group, the movement of the spirit as well—is towards every place where knowledge of Allah is manifest, such as the heavens, mosques, Allah’s allies, and places where Allah’s names and signs are found. Thus, it is movement towards . . . (1)

The third position is that of “Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah,” who affirm that Allah is upon the Throne; that the bearers of the Throne are nearer to Him than those below them; and that the angels of the highest heaven are nearer to Allah than the angels of the second heaven. They affirm that when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was taken up to heaven, he drew ever nearer to his Lord as he ascended and rose, and that his ascension was to Allah, not merely to one of His creatures. They also affirm that the soul of the person praying draws near to Allah in prostration, even though his body is lowered. This is what the texts of the Quran indicate.

original_text:
ثُمَّ 
" قُرْبُ الرَّبِّ مِنْ عَبْدِهِ "
 هَلْ هُوَ مِنْ لَوَازِمِ هَذَا الْقُرْبِ كَمَا أَنَّ الْمُتَقَرِّبَ إلَى الشَّيْءِ السَّاكِنِ كَالْبَيْتِ الْمَحْجُوجِ وَالْجِدَارِ وَالْجَبَلِ كُلَّمَا قَرُبْت مِنْهُ قَرُبَ مِنْك؟ أَوْ هُوَ قُرْبٌ آخَرُ يَفْعَلُهُ الرَّبُّ كَمَا أَنَّك إذَا قَرُبْت إلَى الشَّيْءِ الْمُتَحَرِّكِ إلَيْك تَحَرَّكَ أَيْضًا إلَيْك فَمِنْك فِعْلٌ وَمِنْهُ فِعْلٌ آخَرُ. هَذَا فِيهِ قَوْلَانِ 
" لِأَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ "
 مَبْنِيَّانِ عَلَى مَا تَقَدَّمَ مِنْ قَاعِدَةِ الصِّفَاتِ الْفِعْلِيَّةِ كَمَسْأَلَةِ النُّزُولِ وَغَيْرِهَا وَقَدْ تَقَدَّمَ الْكَلَامُ فِي ذَلِكَ. وَعَلَى هَذَا فَمَا رُوِيَ مِنْ قُرْبِ الرَّبِّ إلَى خَوَاصِّ عِبَادِهِ وَتَجَلِّيهِ لِقُلُوبِهِمْ كَمَا فِي 
" الزُّهْدِ لِأَحْمَدَ "
 أَنَّ مُوسَى قَالَ: يَا رَبِّ أَيْنَ أَجِدُك؟
 قَالَ:
 
" عِنْدَ الْمُنْكَسِرَةِ قُلُوبُهُمْ مِنْ أَجْلِي أَقْتَرِبُ إلَيْهَا كُلَّ يَوْمٍ شِبْرًا وَلَوْلَا ذَلِكَ لَاحْتَرَقَتْ "
. هَذَا الْقُرْبُ عِنْدَ الْمُتَفَلْسِفَةِ وَالْجَهْمِيَّة هُوَ مُجَرَّدُ ظُهُورِهِ وَتَجَلِّيهِ لِقَلْبِ الْعَبْدِ فَهُوَ قُرْبُ الْمِثَالِ. ثُمَّ الْمُتَفَلْسِفَةُ لَا تُثْبِتُ حَرَكَةَ الرُّوحِ وَالْجَهْمِيَّة تُسَلِّمُ جَوَازَ حَرَكَةِ الرُّوحِ إلَى مَكَانٍ عَالٍ وَأَمَّا أَهْلُ السُّنَّةِ فَعِنْدَهُمْ مَعَ التَّجَلِّي وَالظُّهُورِ تَقْرُبُ ذَاتُ الْعَبْدِ إلَى ذَاتِ رَبِّهِ وَفِي جَوَازِ دُنُوِّ ذَاتِ اللَّهِ الْقَوْلَانِ وَقَدْ بَسَطْت هَذَا فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ.
وَعَلَى مَذْهَبِ 
" الْنُّفَاةِ "
 مِنْ الْمُتَكَلِّمَةِ لَا يَكُونُ إتْيَانُ الرَّبِّ وَمَجِيئُهُ وَنُزُولُهُ إلَّا تَجَلِّيهِ وَظُهُورُهُ لِعَبْدِهِ. إذَا ارْتَفَعَتْ الْحُجُبُ الْمُتَّصِلَةُ بِالْعَبْدِ الْمَانِعَةُ مِنْ الْمُشَاهَدَةِ الْبَاطِنَةِ أَوْ الظَّاهِرَةِ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الَّذِي كَانَ أَعْمَى أَوْ أَعْمَشَ فَزَالَ عَمَاهُ فَرَأَى الشَّمْسَ
translated_text:
Then, does “the Lord’s nearness to His servant” necessarily follow from this nearness, just as, when you approach something stationary—the House visited on pilgrimage, a wall, or a mountain—the nearer you come to it, the nearer it is to you? Or is it a further drawing near that the Lord Himself brings about, just as, when you approach something that is moving towards you, it too moves towards you, so that there is an action on your part and another on its part? Ahl al-Sunnah hold two positions on this, based on the principle concerning attributes of action discussed earlier, as in the question of the descent and other such matters. This has already been discussed.

In light of this, consider the reports concerning the Lord’s nearness to His elect servants and His manifestation to their hearts, such as the report in Ahmad’s al-Zuhd (Asceticism) that Moses said, “My Lord, where shall I find You?” He replied:

“With those whose hearts are broken for My sake. I draw a handspan nearer to those hearts each day; were it not for that, they would burn.”

According to the philosophers and the Jahmiyyah, this nearness is merely His appearing and manifesting Himself to the servant’s heart; it is thus the nearness of an image. The philosophers, however, do not affirm the movement of the soul, whereas the Jahmiyyah concede that the soul may move to a high place. According to Ahl al-Sunnah, alongside this manifestation and appearance, the servant himself draws near to his Lord Himself. As for whether Allah Himself may draw near, there are the two positions mentioned above. I have discussed this at length elsewhere.

According to the “negators” among the speculative theologians, the Lord’s coming, arrival, and descent are nothing more than His manifesting and revealing Himself to His servant when the veils associated with the servant, which prevent inward or outward vision, are lifted. It is like someone who was blind or dim-sighted, whose blindness then departed so that he saw the sun

original_text:
وَالْقَمَرَ فَيَقُولُ:
 جَاءَنِي الشَّمْسُ وَالْقَمَرُ وَهَذَا قَوْلُ 
" الْنُّفَاةِ "
 مِنْ الْمُتَفَلْسِفَةِ وَالْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَالْأَشْعَرِيَّةِ؛ لَكِنَّ الْأَشْعَرِيَّةَ يُثْبِتُونَ مِنْ الرُّؤْيَةِ مَا لَا يُثْبِتُهُ الْمُعْتَزِلَةُ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يُوَافِقُهُمْ فِي الْمَعْنَى الَّذِي قَصَدُوهُ. وَأَمَّا عَلَى مَذْهَبِ 
" أَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ وَالْجَمَاعَةِ "
 مِنْ السَّلَفِ وَأَهْلِ الْحَدِيثِ وَأَهْلِ الْمَعْرِفَةِ وَمَنْ اتَّبَعَهُمْ مِنْ الْفُقَهَاءِ وَالصُّوفِيَّةِ وَالْعَامَّةِ وَأَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ أَيْضًا؛ فَإِنَّ نُزُولَهُ وَإِتْيَانَهُ وَمَجِيئَهُ قَدْ يَكُونُ بِحَرَكَةِ مِنْ الْعَبْدِ وَقُرْبٍ مِنْهُ وَدُنُوٍّ إلَيْهِ وَهُوَ قَدْرٌ زَائِدٌ عَلَى انْكِشَافِ بَصِيرَةِ الْعَبْدِ فَإِنَّ هَذَا عِلْمٌ وَعِنْدَهُمْ يَكُونُ ذَلِكَ بِعِلْمِ مِنْ الْعَبْدِ وَبِعَمَلِ مِنْهُ فَهُوَ كَشْفٌ وَعَمَلٌ. وَلَا يُنْكِرُ الْأَشْعَرِيَّةُ وَنَحْوُهُمْ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ أَنْ يَكُونَ مِنْ الْعَبْدِ حَرَكَةٌ فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ مُمْكِنٌ وَإِنَّمَا قَدْ يُنْكِرُونَ حَرَكَتَهُ إلَى اللَّهِ كَمَا تَقَدَّمَ.
 وَقَدْ شَبَّهَ بَعْضُهُمْ مَجِيءَ اللَّهِ بِقَوْلِهِ:
 
{وَاعْبُدْ رَبَّكَ حَتَّى يَأْتِيَكَ الْيَقِينُ}
 أَيْ الْمُوقَنُ بِهِ مِنْ الْمَوْتِ وَمَا بَعْدَهُ.
 قُلْت:
 هَذَا مِثْلُ قَوْلِهِ: 
{فَإِذَا جَاءَتِ الطَّامَّةُ الْكُبْرَى}
 وَقَوْلِهِ: 
{فَإِذَا جَاءَتِ الصَّاخَّةُ}
 وَقَوْلِهِ: 
{فَقَدْ جَاءَ أَشْرَاطُهَا}
 وَجُعِلَ فِي ذَلِكَ هُوَ ظُهُورَهُ وَتَجَلِّيهِ.
 قُلْت:
 وَلَيْسَ هُوَ مُجَرَّدَ ظُهُورِهِ وَتَجَلِّيهِ وَإِنْ كَانَ مُتَضَمِّنًا لِذَلِكَ؛ بَلْ هُوَ مُتَضَمِّنٌ لِحَرَكَةِ الْعَبْدِ إلَيْهِ ثُمَّ إنْ كَانَ سَاكِنًا كَانَ مَجِيئُهُ مِنْ لَوَازِمِ مَجِيءِ الْعَبْدِ إلَيْهِ وَإِنْ كَانَ فِيهِ حَرَكَةٌ كَانَ مَجِيئُهُ بِنَفْسِهِ أَيْضًا وَإِنْ كَانَ الْعَبْدُ ذَاهِبًا إلَيْهِ وَهَكَذَا
translated_text:
and the moon, and then says, “The sun and moon have come to me.” This is the position of the “negators” among the philosophers, the Mu‘tazilah, and the Ash‘ariyyah. The Ash‘ariyyah, however, affirm concerning vision what the Mu‘tazilah do not, though some of them agree with the Mu‘tazilah in their intended meaning.

According to “Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah”—the early generations, the scholars of hadith, those endowed with spiritual knowledge, and their followers among jurists, Sufis, ordinary people, and speculative theologians as well—His descent, arrival, and coming may involve movement on the servant’s part, his coming near to Him and drawing close to Him. This is something beyond the unveiling of the servant’s inner sight, for that is knowledge; in their view, this involves both knowledge and action on the servant’s part. Thus, it is both unveiling and action. The Ash‘ariyyah and similar speculative theologians do not deny that movement can occur on the servant’s part, since that is possible. What they may deny is his movement towards Allah, as discussed earlier.

Some of them have likened Allah’s coming to His words:

“And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you.”

That is, what is known with certainty: death and what follows it.

I say: This is like His words:

“But when the Greatest Calamity comes,”

and His words:

“But when the Deafening Blast comes,”

and His words:

“For its signs have already come.”

Coming in these instances was taken to mean appearing and becoming manifest.

I say: It is not merely His appearing and manifesting Himself, although it includes that. Rather, it also includes the servant’s movement towards Him. Then, if He is stationary, His coming necessarily follows from the servant’s coming to Him; and if there is movement on His part, then He Himself also comes, even though the servant is going towards Him. The same applies to

مَجِيءُ الْيَقِينِ وَمَجِيءُ السَّاعَةِ 
(١)
، وَفِي جَانِبِ الرُّبُوبِيَّةِ يَكُونُ بِكَشْفِ حُجُبٍ لَيْسَتْ مُتَّصِلَةً بِالْعَبْدِ كَمَا قَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{حِجَابُهُ النُّورُ - أَوْ النَّارُ - لَوْ كَشَفَهُ لَأَحْرَقَتْ سَبَحَاتِ وَجْهِهِ مَا أَدْرَكَهُ بَصَرُهُ مِنْ خَلْقِهِ}
 فَهِيَ حُجُبٌ تَحْجُبُ الْعِبَادَ عَنْ الْإِدْرَاكِ كَمَا قَدْ يَحْجُبُ الْغَمَامُ وَالسُّقُوفُ عَنْهُمْ الشَّمْسَ وَالْقَمَرَ. فَإِذَا زَالَتْ تَجَلَّتْ الشَّمْسُ وَالْقَمَرُ. وَأَمَّا حَجْبُهَا لِلَّهِ عَنْ أَنْ يُرَى وَيُدْرَكَ فَهَذَا لَا يَقُولُهُ مُسْلِمٌ؛ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَخْفَى عَلَيْهِ مِثْقَالُ ذَرَّةٍ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِي السَّمَاءِ.
 وَهُوَ يَرَى دَبِيبَ النَّمْلَةِ السَّوْدَاءِ عَلَى الصَّخْرَةِ الصَّمَّاءِ فِي اللَّيْلَةِ السَّوْدَاءِ وَلَكِنْ يَحْجُبُ أَنْ تَصِلَ أَنْوَارُهُ إلَى مَخْلُوقَاتِهِ كَمَا قَالَ:
 
{لَوْ كَشَفَهَا لَأَحْرَقَتْ سُبُحَاتُ وَجْهِهِ مَا أَدْرَكَهُ بَصَرُهُ مِنْ خَلْقِهِ}
 فَالْبَصَرُ يُدْرِكُ الْخَلْقَ كُلَّهُمْ وَأَمَّا السُّبُحَاتُ فَهِيَ مَحْجُوبَةٌ بِحِجَابِهِ النُّورَ أَوْ النَّارَ. وَالْجَهْمِيَّة لَا تُثْبِتُ لَهُ حَجْبًا أَصْلًا؛ لِأَنَّهُ عِنْدَهُمْ لَيْسَ فَوْقَ الْعَرْشِ وَيَرْوُونَ الْأَثَرَ الْمَكْذُوبَ عَنْ عَلِيٍّ 
" أَنَّهُ سَمِعَ قَصَّابًا يَحْلِفُ لَا وَاَلَّذِي احْتَجَبَ بِسَبْعِ سَمَوَاتٍ فَعَلَاهُ بِالدِّرَّةِ فَقَالَ: يَا أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ أُكَفِّرُ عَنْ يَمِينِي؟ قَالَ لَا؛ وَلَكِنَّك حَلَفْت بِغَيْرِ اللَّهِ "
. فَهَذَا لَا يُعْرَفُ لَهُ إسْنَادٌ وَلَوْ ثَبَتَ كَانَ عَلِيٌّ قَدْ فَهِمَ مِنْ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ أَنَّهُ عَنَى أَنَّهُ مُحْتَجِبٌ عَنْ إدْرَاكِهِ لِخَلْقِهِ فَهَذَا بَاطِلٌ قَطْعًا؛ بِخِلَافِ احْتِجَابِهِ عَنْ إدْرَاكِ خَلْقِهِ لَهُ.
original_footnote: (١) كلمات بالأصل تشيران إلى شيء مفقود من صفحات المجلد
translated_text:
the coming of certainty and the coming of the Hour (1). With regard to lordship, this occurs through the unveiling of veils that are not attached to the servant, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“His veil is light—or fire. Were He to remove it, the radiance of His Face would burn everything in His creation that His sight reaches.”

These veils prevent the servants from perceiving, just as clouds and roofs may conceal the sun and moon from them. When these are removed, the sun and moon become visible. As for these veils obstructing Allah’s sight and perception, no Muslim says this, for not even an atom’s weight in the earth or the heavens is hidden from Allah. He sees the black ant creeping over solid rock on a dark night. Rather, He prevents His lights from reaching His creatures, as he said:

“Were He to remove them, the radiance of His Face would burn everything in His creation that His sight reaches.”

His sight encompasses all creation, whereas the radiance is concealed by His veil of light or fire. The Jahmiyyah affirm no veil for Him whatsoever, because, according to them, He is not above the Throne. They narrate the fabricated report about ‘Alī:

“He heard a butcher swear, ‘No, by Him who has veiled Himself with seven heavens!’ So he struck him with his whip. The man asked, ‘O Commander of the Faithful, must I offer expiation for my oath?’ He replied, ‘No, but you have sworn by other than Allah.’”

No chain of transmission is known for this report. Even if it were established, ‘Alī would have understood the speaker to mean that He is veiled from perceiving His creation. This is unquestionably false, unlike His being veiled from His creatures’ perception of Him.

original_text:
وَيَدُلُّ عَلَى ذَلِكَ الْحَدِيثُ الصَّحِيحُ:
 
{إذَا دَخَلَ أَهْلُ الْجَنَّةِ الْجَنَّةَ نَادَى مُنَادٍ يَا أَهْلَ الْجَنَّةِ: إنَّ لَكُمْ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ مَوْعِدًا يُرِيدُ أَنْ ينجزكموه.
 فَيَقُولُونَ:
 مَا هُوَ؟ أَلَمْ يُبَيِّضْ وُجُوهَنَا. وَيُثَقِّلْ مَوَازِينَنَا وَيُدْخِلْنَا الْجَنَّةَ وَيُجِرْنَا مِنْ النَّارِ؟
 قَالَ:
 فَيُكْشَفُ الْحِجَابُ فَيَنْظُرُونَ إلَيْهِ فَمَا أَعْطَاهُمْ شَيْئًا أَحَبَّ إلَيْهِمْ مِنْ النَّظَرِ إلَيْهِ وَهِيَ الزِّيَادَةُ}
 . وَعِنْدَ مَنْ أَثْبَتَ الرُّؤْيَةَ مِنْ الْمُتَجَهِّمَةِ أَنَّ حِجَابَ كُلِّ أَحَدٍ مَعَهُ وَكَشْفَهُ خَلْقَ الْإِدْرَاكِ فِيهِ لَا أَنَّهُ حِجَابٌ مُنْفَصِلٌ.
 وَأَمَّا إتْيَانُهُ وَنُزُولُهُ وَمَجِيئُهُ بِحَرَكَةِ مِنْهُ وَانْتِقَالٍ:
 فَهَذَا فِيهِ الْقَوْلَانِ لِأَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ مِنْ أَصْحَابِنَا وَغَيْرِهِمْ وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ. وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ وَصَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَى مُحَمَّدٍ وَآلِهِ وَسَلِّمْ تَسْلِيمًا.
translated_text:
This is also indicated by the authentic hadith:

> When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, a caller will proclaim: “O people of Paradise, Allah has made you a promise that He wishes to fulfill.”
>
> They will say: “What is it? Has He not brightened our faces, made our scales heavy, admitted us to Paradise, and protected us from the Fire?”
>
> He said: “Then the veil will be lifted, and they will look upon Him. Nothing He has given them will be dearer to them than looking upon Him. This is the ‘increase.’”

According to those influenced by Jahmī doctrines who affirm that Allah will be seen, each person’s veil is with him, and its removal consists in creating perception within him—not that there is a separate veil.

As for whether His coming, descent, and arrival involve movement on His part and a change of place, there are two views among the adherents of the Sunnah, both our companions and others. Allah knows best.

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. May Allah bless Muhammad and his family and grant them abundant peace.

The Shaykh—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—also said:

Those who define philosophy as making oneself resemble God to the extent of one’s ability—an interpretation found in the writings of a number of people, such as Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī and others like him—do not affirm any real nearness: nearness in its familiar, intelligible sense. Whoever holds that the nearness of His servants who are brought near is not nearness to Him, but only to His reward and bounty, is guilty of negation and falsehood.

For His reward and bounty reach them, and they attain them; each comes into direct contact with the other, as food enters their bodies and clothing envelops them. If they are within His very Paradise, bliss, and reward, how can nearness to His bounty be made the highest goal? Especially since those brought near rank above the righteous companions of the right, whose record is in ‘Illiyyīn:

“What will make you know what ‘Illiyyūn is? A register inscribed, witnessed by those brought near. Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss, reclining on adorned couches, looking on. You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss. They will be given pure, sealed wine to drink, whose seal is musk—so for this let those who compete compete. Its admixture is from Tasnīm, a spring from which those brought near drink.”

Ibn ‘Abbās said concerning “from which those brought near drink”: “They drink it pure, while for the companions of the right it is mixed.”

original_text:
فَقَدْ أَخْبَرَ أَنَّ الْأَبْرَارَ فِي نَفْسِ النَّعِيمِ وَأَنَّهُمْ يُسْقَوْنَ مِنْ الشَّرَابِ الَّذِي وَصَفَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى وَيَجْلِسُونَ عَلَى الْأَرَائِكِ يَنْظُرُونَ فَكَيْفَ يُقَالُ:
 إنَّ الْمُقَرَّبِينَ - الَّذِينَ هُمْ أَعْلَى مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ بِحَيْثُ يَشْرَبُونَ صِرْفَهَا وَيُمْزَجُ لِهَؤُلَاءِ مَزْجًا - إنَّمَا تَقْرِيبُهُمْ هُوَ مُجَرَّدُ النَّعِيمِ الَّذِي أُولَئِكَ فِيهِ؟ هَذَا مِمَّا يُعْلَمُ فَسَادُهُ بِأَدْنَى تَأَمُّلٍ. (الْمَسْأَلَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ فِي 
" قُرْبِهِ "
 الَّذِي هُوَ مِنْ لَوَازِمِ ذَاتِهِ: مِثْلَ الْعِلْمِ وَالْقُدْرَةُ فَلَا رَيْبَ أَنَّهُ قَرِيبٌ بِعِلْمِهِ وَقُدْرَتِهِ وَتَدْبِيرِهِ مِنْ جَمِيعِ خَلْقِهِ لَمْ يَزَلْ بِهِمْ عَالِمًا وَلَمْ يَزَلْ عَلَيْهِمْ قَادِرًا هَذَا مَذْهَبُ جَمِيعِ أَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ وَعَامَّةِ الطَّوَائِفِ إلَّا مَنْ يُنْكِرُ عِلْمَهُ الْقَدِيمَ مِنْ الْقَدَرِيَّةِ وَالرَّافِضَةِ وَنَحْوِهِمْ أَوْ يُنْكِرُ قُدْرَتَهُ عَلَى الشَّيْءِ قَبْلَ كَوْنِهِ مِنْ الرَّافِضَةِ وَالْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ. 
" وَأَمَّا قُرْبُهُ بِنَفْسِهِ مِنْ مَخْلُوقَاتِهِ "
 قُرْبًا لَازِمًا فِي وَقْتٍ دُونَ وَقْتٍ؛
 وَلَا يَخْتَصُّ بِهِ شَيْءٌ:
 فَهَذَا فِيهِ لِلنَّاسِ قَوْلَانِ. فَمَنْ يَقُولُ هُوَ بِذَاتِهِ فِي كُلِّ مَكَانٍ يَقُولُ بِهَذَا وَمَنْ لَا يَقُولُ بِهَذَا لَهُمْ أَيْضًا فِيهِ قَوْلَانِ.
 (أَحَدُهُمَا إثْبَاتُ هَذَا الْقُرْبِ وَهُوَ قَوْلُ طَائِفَةٍ مِنْ الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ وَالصُّوفِيَّةِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ يَقُولُونَ:
 هُوَ فَوْقَ الْعَرْشِ وَيُثْبِتُونَ هَذَا الْقُرْبَ. وَقَوْمٌ يُثْبِتُونَ هَذَا الْقُرْبَ؛ دُونَ كَوْنِهِ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ. وَإِذَا كَانَ قُرْبُ عِبَادِهِ مِنْهُ نَفْسَهُ وَقُرْبُهُ مِنْهُمْ لَيْسَ مُمْتَنِعًا عِنْدَ الْجَمَاهِيرِ مِنْ السَّلَفِ وَأَتْبَاعِهِمْ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْحَدِيثِ وَالْفُقَهَاءِ وَالصُّوفِيَّةِ وَأَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ لَمْ يَجِبْ أَنْ يُتَأَوَّلَ كُلُّ نَصٍّ فِيهِ
translated_text:
He has thus stated that the righteous are immersed in bliss, that they are given the drink Allah Most High has described, and that they sit upon adorned couches, looking on. How, then, can it be said that those brought near—who rank above them, drinking it pure while it is mixed for the others—are brought near merely by receiving the bliss the others already enjoy? The falsity of this becomes apparent with the slightest reflection.

The second issue concerns “His nearness” that is inseparable from His Essence, like knowledge and power. There is no doubt that He is near to all His creation through His knowledge, power, and governance. He has always known them and has always had power over them. This is the position of all Ahl al-Sunnah and most other groups, except those among the Qadariyyah, Rāfidah, and their like who deny His eternal knowledge, or those among the Rāfidah, Mu‘tazilah, and others who deny His power over a thing before it exists.

As for His own nearness to His creatures—a nearness that necessarily obtains at one time rather than another and is not exclusive to any particular thing—people hold two views concerning this. Those who say that He is present in His Essence in every place affirm this nearness. Those who do not hold that view also have two positions concerning it.

The first is to affirm this nearness. This is the position of a group of speculative theologians, Sufis, and others who say that He is above the Throne while also affirming this nearness. Others affirm this nearness without affirming His being upon the Throne.

His nearness is mentioned, on the grounds that such nearness is impossible for Him. Nor does the possibility of His nearness entail that every passage mentioning it refers to His own nearness. Rather, this remains a possibility, and the particular text must be examined: if it indicates one meaning, it is understood accordingly; if it indicates the other, it is understood accordingly. This is like the preceding discussion of the words denoting coming. Although, in their understanding, one passage indicates that He Himself comes, another indicates that He comes with His punishment, as in His words, Most High:

“Then Allah came upon their building at its foundations,”

and His words, Most High:

“So Allah came upon them from where they had not expected.”

Reflect carefully on this, for people frequently err on this point. When those who deny attributes and those who affirm them dispute an attribute and whether a text indicates it, someone may seek to make that expression—wherever it occurs—signify the attribute and bear that apparent meaning.

Then the one who denies the attribute says: “It did not indicate the attribute there, so it does not indicate it here.”

Some who affirm the attribute may say: “It indicated the attribute here, so it must indicate it there.” Indeed, having seen that some texts indicate an attribute, they classify as verses concerning the divine attributes every verse containing something they imagine is ascribed to Allah Most High as an attribute, such as His words, Most High:

“I fell short in my duty towards Allah.”

Groups among both those who affirm attributes and those who deny them fall into this. It is among the gravest errors, for the meaning conveyed in each passage depends on its context and the accompanying verbal and situational indicators.

This also occurs in the case of created beings: in many passages, words denoting their attributes are used to mean something other than those attributes.

I shall give two useful examples of this. The first concerns the attribute of the Face. Affirming this attribute was the position of the people of hadith and the attribute-affirming theologians among the Kullābiyyah, Ash'ariyyah and Karrāmiyyah. Denying it was the position of the Jahmiyyah, including the Mu'tazilah and others, as well as some attribute-affirmers among the Ash'ariyyah and others. Consequently, whenever some people from either side read a verse mentioning the face, they treated it as one of the disputed passages. Those who affirm the attribute regard the verse as referring to an attribute that must not be interpreted away, while those who deny it consider that, if evidence establishes that this verse does not refer to an attribute, the same applies to other verses.

An example is His saying, Most High:

“To Allah belong the east and the west; wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah.”

Groups among both those who affirm attributes and those who deny them included this among the verses concerning the divine attributes. Indeed, “the former,” such as Ibn Khuzaymah, counted it among the passages establishing this attribute, while “those who deny it” used its interpretation as something other than an attribute as an argument for their position in the disputed passages.

Thus, when we gathered at the session that had been convened, I had already said: “I have given everyone who disagrees with me three years. If anyone brings even a single statement from the early generations contradicting anything I have mentioned, he will have established his case, and I will do such-and-such.” My opponents began searching through books and found what al-Bayhaqī mentioned in his book Al-Asmā’ wa-l-Sifāt (The Names and Attributes) concerning His saying, Most High:

“To Allah belong the east and the west; wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah.”

He reported from Mujāhid and al-Shāfi'ī that what is meant is Allah’s direction of prayer. concerning His saying, Most High, ‘To Allah belong the east and the west; wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah’?”

He replied, “Yes.”

I said, “What is meant here is Allah’s direction of prayer.”

He said, “Mujāhid and al-Shāfi‘ī interpreted it figuratively, and they were both among the early generations.”

This objection did not apply to me, for the attribute of the Face was not among the matters over which they had debated me, nor had I affirmed it there. They nevertheless raised it in general terms, whereas my words had been qualified, as in the responses. I did not see fit to press the point against them in that setting. Instead, I said, “This verse is not a verse concerning the divine attributes at all, nor does it fall within the general statement that verses concerning the divine attributes are not to be interpreted figuratively.”

He said, “Does it not mention the face?” When I said, “What is meant here is Allah’s direction of prayer,” he said, “Is this not one of the verses concerning the divine attributes?”

I said, “No. It is not one of the disputed passages. All I concede is that ‘face’ here means the direction of prayer. In Arabic, wajh (‘face’) means ‘direction.’ One says, ‘I headed in this wajh,’ or ‘I travelled in this wajh,’ meaning ‘in this direction.’ This is a common, well-known usage. Thus ‘face’ means ‘direction’: it is what one faces, as in His saying, Most High:

‘Everyone has a direction toward which he turns.’

“That is, a direction that he faces. His words, Most High, ‘a direction toward which he turns,’ are like His words:

‘Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah.’

“The two verses are closely related in both wording and meaning, and both concern the direction of prayer. The ‘face’ or ‘direction’ mentioned in both verses is that toward which we turn—that is, which we face.”

I said, “The context also indicates this, for He says, ‘Wherever you turn.’ The word ‘where’ is an adverb of place, and ‘you turn’ means ‘you face.’ Thus the meaning is: whatever place you face, there is the Face of Allah. He thus places the Face of Allah in the location that a person faces. This follows His saying:

‘To Allah belong the east and the west.’

“These encompass all directions, as in the other verse:

‘Say, “To Allah belong the east and the west. He guides whom He wills to a straight path.”’”

translated_text:
Thus He states that the directions belong to Him, indicating that this attribution denotes special designation and honor—as though He had said, “Allah’s direction and Allah’s direction of prayer.”

Some people, however, concede that what is meant is Allah’s direction—that is, Allah’s direction of prayer—but say that this verse also indicates the attribute and that the servant faces his Lord, as stated in the hadith:

“When one of you stands for prayer, Allah is before his face.”

And likewise in his saying:

“Allah continues to turn His Face toward His servant as long as the servant turns toward Him. When he turns away, He turns His Face away from him.”

They maintain that the verse indicates both meanings. That, however, is a separate matter, which is not our subject here.

The point is that interpreting it as “there is Allah’s direction of prayer” is not the disputed figurative interpretation rejected by those who oppose interpreting verses concerning the divine attributes figuratively. Nor is it something that the affirmers adduce as evidence against them. This meaning is correct in itself, and the verse indicates it. If the verse also indicates the existence of an attribute, that is a separate matter.

There remains the question of how their words, “there is the Face of Allah,” signify “there is Allah’s direction of prayer.” Is the direction of prayer called a “face” because “face” and “direction” have the same meaning? Or is it because whoever faces the Face of Allah thereby faces Allah’s direction of prayer? These questions require discussions for which this is not the place.

(The second example is the word “command.” Allah, Most High, declares:

“His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

And He says:

“Surely, His are creation and command.”

Groups among the early generations cited this verse and others as evidence that the command is uncreated; rather, it is His speech and one of His attributes. Many people consequently began applying this understanding to the word “command” wherever it occurs, treating it as an attribute in order to maintain a uniform interpretation, and regarding its reference to anything other than an attribute as a refutation of that interpretation.

translated_text:
but that is not the case. I have explained in some of my treatises that “command” and other terms denoting attributes sometimes refer to the attribute itself and sometimes to its object. Thus, mercy is an attribute of Allah, while what He creates is also called “mercy.” Power is one of the attributes of Allah Most High, while the object of that power is also called “power,” as is its relation to that object. Creating is one of the attributes of Allah Most High and is termed “creation.” Knowledge is one of Allah’s attributes, while what is known, or what is connected with knowledge, is also called “knowledge.” Thus, sometimes the attribute itself is intended, sometimes its object, and sometimes the relation itself.

“Command” is a verbal noun, so what is commanded is also called a “command.” It is in this sense that Jesus—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was called a “word”: he was brought into existence through the word and came to be through the word. This answers the objection raised by the Jahmiyyah when they said, “Jesus is Allah’s Word, yet he is created; therefore, if the Quran is Allah’s speech, it can only be created.” Jesus is not Allah’s actual word; rather, he was given this name because he was created through the word, contrary to the ordinary manner in which created beings come into existence. The customary course was thus broken in his case: he was told, “Be,” and he was. The Quran, however, is Allah’s actual speech.

Anyone who reflects on what has been transmitted concerning Allah Most High’s names and attributes will recognize that a term’s reference, in certain passages, to Allah’s Essence or to some of His essential attributes does not require it to bear that meaning wherever it occurs. The one affirming the attribute cannot simply apply that meaning uniformly, nor can the one denying it refute it by citing a different usage. Rather, each verse and hadith must be examined individually, in its own context, together with whatever in the Quran and other evidence clarifies its meaning.

This is a great, important, and beneficial principle for understanding the Book and the Sunnah and drawing evidence from them generally. If it is possible for a servant to draw near to his Lord and to bring his Lord near to himself, in either or both of the two senses previously mentioned, then a text may be understood accordingly if it indicates that meaning. some groups hold that they require no reinterpretation, while others consider reinterpretation necessary. I would then say: this verse must refer either to His nearness—glory be to Him—or to the nearness of His angels, as people have differed over this. translated_text:
a verse comparable to the words of the Most High:

“Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private conversations? Yes indeed, and Our messengers are there with them, recording.”

Another example is His saying at the beginning of the surah:

“We certainly know what the earth consumes of them, and with Us is a record that preserves everything.”

On this understanding, there is nothing figurative about the nearness. The question concerns only His words, “And We are nearer,” in which He refers to His angels and messengers, or refers to Himself or His angels, though the nearness of each is appropriate to it. The angels are near to the person at that moment, whereas Allah Most High’s nearness to him is unrestricted.

This is like the second interpretation, in which Allah Most High is intended: “We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.” This brings us back to constant nearness in Himself, concerning which there are two views.

The first affirms this, and is the view of a group of speculative theologians and Sufis.

The second is that the nearness here is through His knowledge, for He says:

“We certainly created man and know what his soul whispers to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.”

The mention of knowledge here indicates nearness through knowledge. Similar to this verse is the hadith of Abū Mūsā:

“You are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. You are calling upon One who hears and is near. The One upon whom you call is nearer to each of you than the neck of his mount.”

Thus, the verse requires no reinterpretation of nearness with respect to Allah Most High except according to this view. In that case, the context itself indicates this meaning. What the context indicates belongs to the apparent meaning of the discourse, so this would not be a point of contention. (The precise answer is as follows:

Either His constant nearness in Himself is possible or it is not. If it is possible, the verse requires no reinterpretation. If it is not possible, the verse is understood according to what its context indicates, namely, His nearness through His knowledge. On this view, either this is the apparent meaning of the discourse indicated by the context, or it is not. If it is the apparent meaning, there is nothing to dispute, since no reinterpretation is involved. If it is not the apparent meaning, then the verse is understood in this way only because Allah Most High has explained in several places in His Book that He is upon the Throne and that He is above. Thus, His repeated statements in His Book that He is above the Throne, together with the mention of knowledge accompanying this verse, indicate that He intended nearness through knowledge. For, on this assumption, what those verses entail conflicts with the apparent meaning of this verse, and an explicit statement takes precedence over an apparent meaning and clarifies it.

Muslims agree that one verse may be explained by the apparent meaning of another, and that discourse may be understood in a sense other than its apparent meaning. None of Ahl al-Sunnah considers this objectionable. Even if it is called reinterpretation and a departure from the apparent meaning, it is supported by the Quran and accords with the Sunnah and the early generations, because it is explaining the Quran by the Quran, not explaining it through personal opinion. What is objectionable is only to divert the Quran from its intended meaning without any indication from Allah, His Messenger, or the earliest Muslims, as explained previously. His discussion of this is more extensive than that of the other renowned imams, whose discussions mostly concern matters of practice, with little on matters of doctrine. Imam Ahmad discusses both doctrinal and practical matters extensively, since this approach is supported by evidence from the Quran and Sunnah. Whoever claims that his position is to reject this has falsely attributed that to him. And Allah knows best.

The discussion of the words of Allah Most High:

“When My servants ask you about Me, I am indeed near. I answer the call of the supplicant when he calls upon Me”

is like the discussion of the Prophet’s words—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“You are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. You are calling upon One who is All-Hearing and near. Indeed, the One upon whom you call is nearer to each of you than the neck of his mount.”

Whoever understands this as His nearness in Himself, whether constant or occasional, leaves nothing to dispute. Whoever says that it means He hears their supplications, answers them, and all that this entails, may say: “The context indicates this, so it does not depart from the apparent meaning.” Alternatively, he may say: “This is indicated by the texts of the Quran and Sunnah which establish that He is above the Throne.” This would be explaining and interpreting the Quran through the Book and Sunnah, and there is nothing objectionable in that.

Know that some people have followed this same approach regarding the very expression “being with.” They say that it is understood according to what the context indicates, even if this differs from its apparent meaning when taken without qualification; or that it is understood contrary to its apparent meaning because the verses indicate that Allah is above the Throne. Thus, they explain one part of the Quran through another. We, however, have explained that there is nothing in the apparent meaning of “being with” that requires this, for we have found that all

Al-Tabarānī and others narrated:

“Some people asked the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—‘Is our Lord near, so that we may address Him quietly, or distant, so that we must call out to Him?’ Allah Most High then revealed: ‘When My servants ask you about Me, I am indeed near. I answer the call of the supplicant when he calls upon Me.’”

May Allah bless Muhammad.

translated_text:
He also said—may Allah have mercy on him:

Section

I have previously written in the second volume of the arranged collection about “the servant’s nearness to his Lord,” his going to Him, “the Lord’s nearness to His servant,” and the Lord’s revealing Himself to him and appearing to him. I discussed what the philosophers acknowledge of these matters, then the speculative theologians, and then the people of the Sunnah, explaining that whatever truth these groups affirm is also affirmed by the people of the Sunnah.

The people of the Sunnah further affirm “things” unknown to the adherents of innovation because of their ignorance and misguidance: they have denied what they did not encompass in knowledge and whose interpretation had not yet come to them. The true meanings that these groups affirm, and in light of which they interpret the texts, are good, sound, and valid. Their error, however, arises from their denial of anything beyond those meanings.

Examples include the philosophers’ affirmation of “the Necessary Existent”; that “the soul is distinct from the body”; that it continues to exist after leaving the body; and that it experiences bliss or torment—spiritual bliss and torment. Likewise, they affirm good and bad faculties of the body and soul. All of this is true. But their claim that the texts mean nothing beyond this, and that there is no truth beyond this

and that “Paradise” and “Hell” refer to this; that the descriptions in the divine scriptures are merely parables intended to convey an understanding of the spiritual afterlife; that “angels” and “jinn” are accidents, namely the soul’s good and corrupt faculties; that the “spirit” does not move, but rather the realities of existence are unveiled to it, and this constitutes its nearness to Allah; and that the Prophet’s ascension belongs to this same category—such negation and denial constitute disbelief.

Likewise, what the speculative theologians affirm—that the servant draws near, in both body and soul, to the “specially favored places” where the Lord’s light appears, such as the heavens and mosques, and that the same applies to the angels—is correct. But their claim that they do not draw near to Allah Himself, and that Allah is not upon the Throne, is false. The correct position is to affirm this, while also affirming what the texts teach concerning the servant’s nearness to his Lord and the Lord’s revealing Himself to His servants by removing the veils attached to them and those separate from them. Such nearness and self-disclosure involve the servant’s knowledge—the truth becoming manifest to him—and the servant’s action—his drawing near to his Lord. I have already discussed the Lord’s drawing near and His nearness, and the disagreement among the people of the Sunnah concerning this.

Yet some professed adherents of the Sunnah and some ignorant people, when they see the truth affirmed by those groups, may recoil from accepting it, even though it does not contradict what those groups dispute with the people of the Sunnah. Rather, all of it is correct. Indeed, acknowledging what is agreed upon may be more important than acknowledging what is disputed, since the former is clearer and more evident, and serves as a foundation for the disputed matter. The reason is that those who affirm remain intent on affirming what the innovators have denied. They feel an aversion to the innovators’ statements because the latter reject and deny the truth; consequently, they turn away from whatever truth the innovators do affirm, recoil from it, or deny it.

This resembles the way some ignorant professed adherents of the Sunnah turn away from certain virtues of ‘Alī and the Prophet’s household when they see the innovators exaggerating them. Indeed, some Muslims display something of this same aversion to the virtues of Moses and Jesus because of the Jews and Christians. It is even related that some ignorant people would revile the Messiah when they heard Christians reviling our Prophet in battle.

[It is also related that an ignorant person said:
“Revile ‘Alī as they reviled your ‘Atīq—
Disbelief for disbelief, and faith for faith.”] (*)

An example of this in the discussion of “the divine attributes” is that when a servant knows and loves his Lord—or even knows, loves, and worships someone other than Allah—the one whom he knows, loves, and reveres remains in his heart and on his tongue. His passion, love, and reverence may become so intense that he is wholly absorbed in his beloved and loses awareness of himself.

Thus, it is related that a man loved another man, and the beloved fell into the sea. The other threw himself in after him. The beloved said, “I fell in, but what made you fall in?” He replied, “I became so lost in you that I lost awareness of myself and thought that you were me.”

This is as the poet said:
“Your image is before my eyes, your remembrance on my lips;
Your dwelling is within my heart—where, then, could you disappear?”

translated_text:
And another said:
“He dwells within the heart and gives it life;
I never forget him, that I should need to recall him.
He is a master with whom I am content;
And my share in him I increase.”

Because of the strength of this connection, some people have claimed that the knower becomes united with what he knows, while others hold that the lover may become united with the beloved. This is either an error or a loose use of language. There is indeed a kind of unity here: unity in the very objects to which their attributes relate—what is sought, loved, commanded, approved, and disapproved—and unity in the kinds of attributes, such as will, love, commanding, forbidding, approval, and displeasure. This resembles the unity between two people who love one another. There are further distinctions to be made here, which we discuss elsewhere.

The point here is simply that certain judgments and true statements apply to the one known and loved in the heart of the knower and lover. Thus Allah Most High says:

“It is He who is God in heaven and God on earth.”

And He Most High says:

“To Him belongs the highest description in the heavens and the earth.”

And He Most High says:

“And exalted is the majesty of our Lord.”

And He says:

“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High.”

Likewise, the opening supplication of prayer says:

“Glory and praise be to You, O Allah. Blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You.”

The hearts of those who know Him experience an abiding establishment and manifestation, which everyone acknowledges. Yet the people of the Sunnah affirm much that the people of innovation do not recognize, just as they affirm His being established above the Throne.

and such words of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) as:

“My servant, I fell ill, but you did not visit Me.” The servant will say, “My Lord, how could I visit You when You are the Lord of all worlds?” He will say, “Did you not know that My servant so-and-so fell ill? Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him.”

He thus stated that He is with His servant and described His servant’s illness as His own. A person may have such love and reverence for a ruler, a scholar, or a place that it dominates his heart. He frequently mentions the object of his devotion and conforms to it in his words and deeds, so that one is said to be the other—as when it is said, “Abū Yūsuf is Abū Hanīfa.”

This resembles, in some respects, the appearance of luminous bodies and other objects in transparent bodies, such as a polished mirror, clear water, and the like. Thus a person sees the sky, the sun, the moon, and the stars in clear water. As someone said:

When the sky falls upon clear water,
Clouded wherever the breeze stirs it,
You see the sky therein, beyond all doubt;
So too the full moon and the stars appear.
So too the hearts of those who witness divine manifestation:
In their purity, Allah the Magnificent is seen.

Likewise, we see in a mirror the image of whatever faces it—the sun, the moon, faces, and other things.

Then another mirror may face that mirror, so that you see in it the image seen in the first, and the process continues from one to another. These reflected images bear a distant resemblance to the appearance of the name of someone loved and revered on paper through writing, whether in ink, by engraving, or otherwise. Here, only the letters of his name appear in a body that has neither sensation nor movement. In polished bodies, his image appears, but the medium in which it appears has neither awareness nor movement. The first is thus a medium in which his name appears, while the second is a medium in which his very self appears.

As for the hearts and souls of servants, the one who is known, loved, and revered, together with his names, appears in the heart that knows and loves him. This kind of appearance is more perfect and exalted than the others; indeed, it has no equal.

To this He alluded in His words:

“He has inscribed faith in their hearts and strengthened them with a spirit from Him.”

It is He who said:

“Whoever rejects faith, his deeds have come to nothing.”

And He said:

“If they believe in the like of what you believe in, then they are rightly guided.”

Likewise, His words:

“There is nothing like unto Him.”

And His words:

“The example of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like that of a grain that produces seven ears.”

Section

No rational person disputes this much, for it is something perceptible and apprehensible. It is the lowest degree of acknowledging Allah—indeed, of acknowledging the existence of anything whatsoever—and the lowest degree of worshipping Him, loving Him, and drawing near to Him. Yet, beyond this, do the heart and the knowing, loving spirit move, or is their only movement a mere transition from one state to another?

The first is the position of Muslims in general and the majority of humankind.

The second is the view of the philosophers and their followers, who hold that the spirit is neither inside the body nor outside it, and neither moves nor remains at rest. The majority, however, acknowledge that it moves toward whatever is loved and sought. Most speculative theologians acknowledge that it moves toward honoured places where the traces and lights of the beloved become manifest, as the hearts and bodies of those who know Allah move toward the heavens, mosques, and similar places. Likewise, these move toward the beloved himself when he is a created being, such as a prophet, an angel, or someone else. Both groups acknowledge the Lord’s self-disclosure and His manifestation to the hearts of those who know Him, which is

As for the movement of the servant’s spirit or body toward the Lord Himself, this is not acknowledged by those Jahmī deniers of the divine attributes who deny that Allah is above the Throne. The early generations declared them to be unbelievers and regarded their innovation as the gravest of all innovations. Some of those early scholars considered them to fall outside the seventy-two sects. These include those who say that He is everywhere, or that He is neither inside the world nor outside it.

Muslims generally, however, the early generations of the Muslim community, and Ahl al-Sunnah from all groups acknowledge this movement. Thus, the servant draws near to his Lord through the movement of his spirit and body. They also affirm that both draw near to honoured places, and that his spirit and body undergo a transition from one state to another.

(The first includes the ascension of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the ascent of the servant’s spirit to his Lord, and his nearness to his Lord in prostration, among other examples.

(The second includes pilgrimage to His House and seeking Him in the mosques.

(The third includes remembering Him, supplicating to Him, loving Him, and worshipping Him while remaining at home. Yet in these latter two cases, they also acknowledge the spirit’s nearness to Allah Himself, thus affirming all these kinds together.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islam Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about someone who says:

“The apparent meanings of the texts consistently indicate what is corporeal or suggest corporeality, whereas reason establishes that the Creator, Almighty and Majestic, is exalted above this. The safest course for the believer is therefore to say: ‘This is ambiguous; none but Allah knows its interpretation.’”

Someone said to him: “There must be a governing criterion for this: a distinction, among the attributes, between what is ambiguous and what is not. Claiming that all the attributes are subject to such interpretation is false and may even lead to disbelief. It would entail that no meaning is known for any of His attributes. There must therefore be a distinction between what is subject to interpretation and what is not.”

He replied: “Whatever rational proof shows to involve ascribing corporeality is ambiguous.”

Is this correct or not? Please explain the matter at length.

He answered:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. This is a major and momentous question concerning which multitudes, both earlier and later, have fallen into confusion since the beginning of the second century after the Prophet’s migration. During the first century, however, there was no confusion among the Muslims concerning this. It arose only at the beginning of the second century, when al-Ja'd ibn Dirham and his associate al-Jahm ibn Safwān appeared, along with the Mu'tazilīs and others who followed them in denying the divine attributes.

translated_text:
Thus arose the doctrine of the Jahmīs who denied the divine attributes. They said:

“Affirming the attributes entails likening Allah to His creation and ascribing corporeality to Him, whereas Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is far above that. For the ‘attributes’—knowledge, power, will, and the like—are accidents and qualities that subsist in something other than themselves. An accident subsists only in a body, and Allah, exalted is He, is not a body. For bodies are never devoid of accidents that come into being, and whatever is never devoid of things that come into being must itself have come into being.”

They said: “This is how we established that bodies came into being. If this argument is invalidated, the proof that bodies came into being is invalidated; consequently, the proof that the world came into being is invalidated, and thus the proof for affirming the attributes is invalidated.”

They said: “Furthermore, if accidents—that is, attributes—subsist only in a body, then that body is composed of parts, and what is composite depends on something other than itself. It cannot be independent of all else and necessarily existent in itself, whereas Allah, exalted is He, is independent of all else and necessarily existent in Himself.”

They said: “Moreover, a body is bounded and finite. If He had attributes, He would therefore be bounded and finite. There would then necessarily have to be something determining why He had one magnitude rather than another. Whatever depends on such a determinant cannot be independent of all else, beginningless, and necessarily existent in itself.”

They said: “Moreover, if attributes subsisted in Him, He would be a body; and if He were a body, He would be like all other bodies. Whatever is possible for them would therefore be possible for Him, and whatever is impossible for them would be impossible for Him. That is impossible with respect to Allah, exalted is He.”

translated_text:
Jahm, along with extremists among the Qarāmitah and the philosophers, went further along these lines, saying:

“He has no name such as ‘thing,’ ‘living,’ ‘knowing,’ or the like. For if He had any such name, He would necessarily possess the quality it signifies, such as life or knowledge. A derived term can apply truly only if the meaning from which it is derived also applies. This would entail attributes subsisting in Him, which is impossible. Moreover, if He were given these names, they are names also given to others, whereas Allah is far above resembling anything else.”

Others went still further in their extremism, saying:

“He is to be designated neither affirmatively nor negatively. One must not say that He is existent or non-existent, living or non-living. For affirmation likens Him to existing things, while negation likens Him to non-existent things. All of this amounts to likening Him to something else.”

When these Jahmīs appeared, the early generations and the imams condemned and refuted their doctrine, meeting it with the religious condemnation it deserved. It remained obscure until it emerged openly and the Jahmīs grew powerful toward the end of the “first century” and the beginning of the “second,” during the reigns of al-Rashīd’s sons. They subjected people to the well-known inquisition, in which they called upon them to profess that the Quran was created, along with the implications of that position, such as denying that Allah will be seen and denying His attributes. This was based on the premise that the Quran is an accident: if it subsisted in Allah’s essence, accidents would subsist in Him, which would entail likening Him to His creation and ascribing corporeality to Him.

Alongside the Jahmīs, there arose people who likened Allah, exalted is He, to His creation, treating His attributes as being of the same kind as the attributes of created beings. The early generations and the imams therefore condemned both the Jahmīs who denied the divine attributes and those who likened Allah to His creation and made Him resemble it.

The leader of the Muʿtazilah, Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, and others like him who denied the attributes said: “This entails His being a body, whereas Allah, exalted is He, is far above that.”

“He possesses attributes, but these attributes are not accidents, for they are eternal and enduring: they neither arise nor pass away. However, He is not described as performing acts that subsist in Him, such as movements, because these arise and pass away.”

Ibn Karrām and his followers said:

“Rather, He possesses attributes, even if they are called accidents, and He performs acts that subsist in Him, even if they come into being.”

When they were told, “This entails His being a body,” [they replied: “Yes, He is a body like other bodies.”] (*) They maintained that this is not invariably impossible; what is impossible is for Him to resemble created beings with respect to what is necessary, possible, or impossible. Some of them said, “He used the term ‘body,’ but did not intend its meaning.” These speculative theologians engaged in lengthy debates, which have been treated exhaustively elsewhere.

As for the early generations and the imams, they did not join any faction in its innovated negations or affirmations. Rather, they held firmly to the Book and the Sunnah, regarding this as consonant with clear reason. They therefore regarded every expression concerning His names and attributes found in the Book and the Sunnah as true and obligatory to believe in, even if the reality of its meaning is not known. As for any expression introduced by people, which some affirm and others deny, we are not obliged to affirm or deny it without qualification until we understand what the speaker intends. If

translated_text:
what he intends is true and accords with what the messengers brought and with the Book and the Sunnah, whether in negation or affirmation, we accept it. But if it is false and contradicts what the Book and the Sunnah teach, whether in negation or affirmation, we prohibit saying it.

They held that the approach presented in the Quran accords with clear reason and authentic revelation, and that it is the approach of the prophets and messengers. The messengers—may Allah’s blessings be upon them—brought general negation and detailed affirmation. Hence He, glorified and exalted, says:

“Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they ascribe to Him. And peace be upon the messengers. And praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds.”

He thus declared Himself far above what those who oppose the messengers ascribe to Him, and pronounced peace upon the messengers because their statements were free of deficiency and fault. The messengers’ approach is the one presented in the Quran: Allah Most High affirms His attributes in detail in the Quran, while denying, in general terms, that anything resembles Him or is His equal.

In the Quran, He states that He knows all things and has power over all things; that He is Almighty, All-Wise, All-Forgiving, Most Merciful; that He is All-Hearing, All-Seeing; that He is All-Forgiving, Most Loving; and that He, exalted in the greatness of His essence, loves the believers and is pleased with them, while He is angry with the disbelievers and displeased with them. He states that He created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rose over the Throne; that He spoke directly to Moses; and that He manifested Himself to the mountain and made it crumble—and other such statements.

By way of negation, He says:

“There is nothing like Him.”

“Do you know of any equal to Him?”

“So do not draw comparisons with Allah.”

“Say: He is Allah, One.”

“Allah, the Self-Sufficient, upon whom all depend.”

“He neither begets nor is born.”

“And there is none comparable to Him.”

Thus He affirms His attributes and denies any likeness to created beings.

translated_text:
The approach of the early generations was to describe Allah as He described Himself and, at times, as His Messenger described Him, without distortion or denial, and without specifying how His attributes are or likening Him to created beings.

Those who oppose the messengers describe Him through negations: “He is not this; He is not that.” When they are told, “Then affirm what He is,” they say, “He is absolute existence,” or, “An essence without attributes.” Yet clear reason establishes that what is absolute on condition of absoluteness exists only in the mind, not in concrete reality. What is absolute without any condition does not exist externally as an absolute, but only as a determinate particular. In their account, the Lord has no reality distinct from created beings. Rather, they either deny Him altogether or make Him the existence of created beings, a part of them, or an attribute of them.

As for ambiguous expressions, they withhold judgment on their meaning. Thus, when some people say, “Allah is in a direction or a spatial location,” and others say, “Allah is neither in a direction nor in a spatial location,” they ask each speaker what he intends, since the terms “direction” and “spatial location” are ambiguous and have multiple meanings.

They say: Nothing exists except the Creator and creation. Allah Most High is transcendent and separate from His creatures. He, glorified be He, created them separate and distinct from Himself, outside His essence. Nothing of His essence is within His creatures, and nothing of His creatures is within His essence. Were He not separate from them, He would either be intermingled with them, indwelling in them, or a locus in which they dwell. Allah Most High is far above that. Alternatively, if He were neither separate from them nor intermingled with them, He would be nonexistent. Allah Most High is far above that.

this; at other times, they make statements that entail denial and the negation of His attributes. Thus, those among them who deny worship nothing, while those who affirm worship everything. It is also said: Since nothing exists except the Creator and creation, the Creator is separate from creation.

If someone says, “He is in a direction,” or, “He is not in a direction,” he is asked: “Does ‘direction’ refer to something existent or nonexistent?” If it is something existent, then—since nothing exists except the Creator and creation, and the Creator is separate from creation—the Lord is not within an existent, created direction. If direction is something nonexistent, in that what lies beyond the world is called a direction, then if the Creator is separate from the world, and what lies beyond the world is called a direction without being something existent, Allah would be in a nonexistent direction in this sense.

Yet there is no difference between saying, “He is within something nonexistent,” and saying, “He is not within anything other than Himself,” for all rational people agree that what is nonexistent is not a thing.

There is no doubt that by the word “direction” they sometimes mean something existent and sometimes something nonexistent. Indeed, a single speaker may combine both meanings in his discourse. Once the ambiguity is removed, the truth of the matter becomes clear. If someone says, “If He were in a direction, that direction would be coeternal with Him,” he is told: “That would follow if ‘direction’ meant something existent other than Him. Allah is not in a direction in this sense.”

If he says, “If He could be seen, He would be in a direction, and that is impossible,” he is told: “If you mean that He would be in an existent direction, then that is impossible. For something existent can be seen even if it is not within another existent thing. The world, for example, has a surface that can be seen, yet it is not within another world.”

He is asked: “Why, then, do you say that His being in a direction in this sense would be impossible?”

If he replies, “Because whatever is separate from the world and can be seen must be a body or spatially located,” the discussion returns to the terms “body” and “spatially located,” just as it returned to the term “direction.”

He is then told: “The term ‘spatially located’ may refer to something encompassed by something else, or to something distinct from something else—and thus spatially separate from it. If you intend the former meaning, He—glory be to Him—is not spatially located, for He is separate from created things and nothing else encompasses Him. If you intend the latter, He—glory be to Him—is distinct and separate from created things; He neither inheres in them nor is united with them.”

These distinctions remove confusion and misrepresentation. Otherwise, anyone who denies any of the names or attributes calls whoever affirms them a corporealist who maintains that Allah is spatially located and in a direction. Thus, the Mu'tazilah and others like them call those who affirm the attributes—who say that Allah Most High is living by virtue of life, knowing by virtue of knowledge, powerful by virtue of power, hearing by virtue of hearing, seeing by virtue of sight, and speaking by virtue of speech—corporealists, anthropomorphists, and Hashwiyyah. Those who affirm the attributes include the early generations, the imams, and all the groups that affirm the attributes, such as the Kullābiyyah, Karrāmiyyah, Ash'ariyyah, Sālimiyyah, and other groups within the Muslim community.

Those who deny the attributes among the Jahmiyyah, the Mu'tazilah, and a group of philosophers said to these affirmers: “If you affirm life, power, and speech for Him, these are accidents, and accidents can subsist only in a body. If you say that He can be seen, vision can only be of something directly beheld in a direction, and this entails corporealism.”

If the Ash'arīs and their followers say, “We affirm these attributes but do not call them accidents, because an accident is something that occurs in its subject, whereas these attributes endure and do not cease,” the deniers reply: “This is a verbal dispute. This is what the Hākimī Bātinī Qarmatians and others have done. They said: “If you say that He is existent, knowing, living, and powerful, this amounts to advocating anthropomorphism, corporealism, and the views of the Hashwiyyah, since it makes Him resemble other, created beings. Moreover, no existent, living, knowing, powerful being can be conceived of except as a body, and these names necessarily entail attributes, while attributes necessarily entail corporealism.”

translated_text:
If a man is among those who deny the names and attributes—as do the extreme Jahmiyyah, the Qarmatians, and the philosophers—he must nevertheless affirm that He exists. The deniers then say to him: “You are a corporealist, an anthropomorphist, and a Hashwī! For if He exists, other beings share with Him in the meaning of existence, and that constitutes resemblance; moreover, nothing existent can be conceived of except as a body or something subsisting in a body.”

He would then have to say: “He is neither existent nor non-existent, neither living nor dead,” or: “He is neither existent nor not existent, neither living nor not living.” This entails denying both sides of a contradiction, as well as opposites equivalent to contradictories. This is among the most manifest absurdities according to self-evident reason. Moreover, the logic of their position entails likening Him to impossibilities, for that which is neither existent nor non-existent can have no reality whatsoever—neither existent nor non-existent. Rather, it is merely something conceived in the mind, with no realization in external reality. All this is in addition to the outright disbelief to which he has committed himself.

Even if he were to deny necessary, beginningless existence altogether, then, besides committing the disbelief that is the root of all disbelief, he would be obstinately rejecting self-evident truths. For we observe existing things and know that every existent is either beginningless or originated, and either necessarily existent in itself or contingent in itself and existent through another. Everything originated and contingent in itself exists through another, and thus necessarily requires something beginningless and necessarily existent in itself. Existence therefore necessarily entails affirming a beginningless existent.

Some existence is contingent and originated, as we observe in originated things such as animals and plants. Thus, once it is known by rational necessity that among existing things there is that which is beginningless and necessarily existent in itself, and that which is originated and contingent in itself, these two existents share in what is denoted by the term

 أَنَّ مَنْ نَفَى الصِّفَاتِ مِنْ الْجَهْمِيَّة وَالْمُعْتَزِلَةِ وَالْقَرَامِطَةِ الْبَاطِنِيَّةِ وَمَنْ وَافَقَهُمْ مِنْ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ يَقُولُونَ؛ إذَا قُلْتُمْ؛ إنَّ الْقُرْآنَ غَيْرُ مَخْلُوقٍ وَإِنَّ لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى عِلْمًا وَقُدْرَةً وَإِرَادَةً فَقَدْ قُلْتُمْ بِالتَّجْسِيمِ؛ فَإِنَّهُ قَدْ قَامَ دَلِيلُ الْعَقْلِ عَلَى أَنَّ هَذَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى التَّجْسِيمِ؛
 لِأَنَّ هَذِهِ مَعَانِيَ لَا تَقُومُ بِنَفْسِهَا:
 لَا تَقُومُ إلَّا بِغَيْرِهَا سَوَاءٌ سُمِّيَتْ صِفَاتًا أَوْ أَعْرَاضًا أَوْ غَيْرَ ذَلِكَ.
translated_text:
Section

With this premise established, it becomes clear that the statement, “Anything that rational proof establishes as implying corporeality is ambiguous,” is an answer that neither settles the dispute nor yields any benefit, nor distinguishes the sound from the unsound or the deviant from the upright.

For everyone who denies any of the names and attributes claims to possess rational proof that what he denies implies corporeality and is therefore ambiguous. This would require treating all the names and attributes as ambiguous. In turn, this would entail complete negation: no meaning could be understood from Allah’s names and attributes, nor could any distinction be drawn between the meanings of the Ever-Living, the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, the Most Merciful, the Compeller, and the Source of Peace; nor between creation and rising over, on the one hand, and causing death and giving life, on the other; nor between coming and arrival, on the one hand, and pardon and forgiveness, on the other.

To explain: those who deny the attributes among the Jahmiyyah, the Mu‘tazilah, the esoteric Qarmatians, and the philosophers who agree with them say:

“If you say that the Quran is uncreated and that Allah Most High possesses knowledge, power, and will, then you have ascribed corporeality to Him. For rational proof has established that this implies corporeality, since these are properties that do not subsist independently, but only in something else—whether they are called attributes, accidents, or anything else.”

قَالُوا:
 وَنَحْنُ لَا نَعْقِلُ قِيَامَ الْمَعْنَى إلَّا بِجِسْمِ فَإِثْبَاتُ مَعْنًى يَقُومُ بِغَيْرِ جِسْمٍ غَيْرُ مَعْقُولٍ.

 قَالَتْ الْمُثْبِتَةُ:
 الرِّضَا وَالْغَضَبُ وَالْوَجْهُ وَالْيَدُ وَالِاسْتِوَاءُ وَالْمَجِيءُ وَغَيْرُ ذَلِكَ: فَأَثْبِتُوا هَذِهِ الصِّفَاتِ أَيْضًا وَقُولُوا: إنَّهَا تَقُومُ بِغَيْرِ جِسْمٍ.

translated_text:
They say:
“We can conceive of a property subsisting only in a body. Thus, affirming a property that subsists in something other than a body is inconceivable.”

If someone who affirms these attributes says:
“Rather, these properties can subsist in something other than a body, just as both we and you can affirm a knowing, powerful being who is not a body,”

then those who affirm pleasure, anger, the Face, the Hand, rising over, coming, and other such attributes say:
“Affirm these attributes as well, and say that they subsist in something other than a body.”

If they say:
“We can conceive of pleasure and anger only as subsisting in a heart, which is a body; and we can conceive of a face and a hand only as parts of a body,”

they are told:
“Nor can we conceive of knowledge or power except as subsisting in a body; nor can we conceive of hearing, sight, or speech except as subsisting in a body. Why, then, have you distinguished between like things? You say, ‘These can subsist in something other than a body, whereas those can subsist only in a body,’ although both are alike from the standpoint of reason.”

If they say:
“Anger is the boiling of the heart’s blood in pursuit of vengeance, and the face is that which has a nose, two lips, a tongue, and a cheek,” or something similar,

they are told:
“If you mean the servant’s anger and face, the corresponding argument against you would be: sight is conceivable only through an eyeball, hearing only through an ear canal, speech only through two lips and a tongue, and will only for securing a benefit or warding off harm. Yet you affirm hearing, sight, speech, and will for the Lord in a manner unlike the servant’s attributes. If what you affirm resembles the servant’s attributes, you are committed to likening Him to creation in all these attributes. But if you affirm them in a manner befitting the majesty of Allah Most High, without any resemblance to the attributes of created beings, then affirm them all in this specified manner. There is no distinction between one attribute and another, for what you have denied
