Either you deny all the attributes—which is impossible—or you liken Him to created beings—which is impossible—or you affirm them all in a manner unique to Him, in which none resembles Him. In that case, there is no distinction between one attribute and another. Distinguishing between them by affirming one and denying another to avoid likening Him to creation and attributing corporeality to Him is a false position: it distinguishes between like things and renders the two claims contradictory.”

If someone says:
“Rational evidence establishes one but not the other—as when it is said that it establishes life, knowledge, and will, but not pleasure, anger, and similar attributes.”

The answer has several aspects:

(First: The absence of evidence does not entail the absence of what it would establish. Suppose that reason does not establish one of these attributes; neither reason nor revelation establishes its negation either. It therefore cannot be denied. Rather, it must be affirmed if evidence establishes it; otherwise, judgment must be suspended.

(Second: It may be said that rational evidence can be adduced for His love, hatred, wisdom, mercy, and other attributes, just as it can for His will, as has been explained elsewhere.

(Third: It may be said that revelation establishes these attributes, while reason does not negate them. Evidence free of any countervailing proof must therefore be accepted.

If he then says:
“Rather, reason does negate them, because these attributes necessarily entail attributing corporeality to Him, and reason rules that out.”

He is told:

translated_text:
attributing corporeality to Him, so does the other; and if it does not entail attributing corporeality to Him, neither does the other. To claim a distinction between them on the grounds that one entails likening Him to creation or attributing corporeality to Him while the other does not is to distinguish between like things and combine contradictions. For what he denies in one, he affirms in the other, and what he affirms in one, he denies in the other. Thus he combines contradictions.”

For this reason, scholars of thorough understanding have said:

“Whoever denies any of the names and attributes established by the Quran and Sunnah inevitably contradicts himself. The very argument he uses to deny what he denies applies equally to what he affirms. If the rational argument for denial is valid, all must be denied; if it is not, none of them need be denied. Affirming something while denying its like is an invalid contradiction.”

If the Mu‘tazilī says:

“The attributes imply corporeality, because attributes are accidents that can subsist only in a body. This is why I interpret the texts concerning the attributes figuratively, but not those concerning the names.”

He is told:

“The same consequence follows for you regarding the names. The very argument by which you infer that one possessing life, knowledge, and power can only be a body is used by your opponent to infer that the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, the Ever-Living can only be a body.”

You are therefore told:

“Affirming One who is living, knowing, and powerful must either entail attributing corporeality to Him or not. If it does, you must affirm that He is a body; thus He would not be bounded with respect to being seen, on either supposition. If it does not, it may equally be said that affirming knowledge, power, and will does not entail attributing corporeality to Him. If the one does not entail it, neither does the other; and if the one entails it, so does the other. There is therefore no distinction between them. To distinguish between them is a manifest contradiction.”

“You cannot deny all names, for your mind must refer to what you affirm, and your tongue must express it. If you say, ‘real, existent, actual, known, eternal, necessarily existent’—whatever you say, you have named Him. Suppose you do not speak at all: either you affirm in your mind an eternal, necessarily existent being, or you do not. If you do not, existence would be devoid of an eternal, necessarily existent Originator. All existing things would then have come into being and would be contingent. Yet it is known of necessity that whatever comes into being and is contingent can exist only through an eternal, necessarily existent being. Your denial of Him thus entails affirming Him. Moreover, this is outright disbelief and negation, which no rational person would profess.”

If you say:

“I do not entertain this question in my mind, nor do I speak of it.”

You are told:

“Your mind’s refusal to know and your tongue’s refusal to speak do not overturn realities or cause existing things to cease to exist. For whatever is true, existent, and established within yourself remains so, whether you know it or are ignorant of it, remember it or forget it. This amounts only to ignorance of Allah Most High, heedlessness of His remembrance, turning away from Him, and disbelief in Him. It does not mean that He is not, in Himself, real and existent, possessing the most beautiful names and the most exalted attributes.”

There is no doubt that this is the ultimate outcome for the Qarmatian esotericists and the eternalist deniers: they remain in the darkness of ignorance and the error of disbelief, neither knowing Allah nor remembering Him. They have no evidence for denying Him or His names and attributes, for that would be a categorical denial, whereas they make no such categorical assertion and have no evidence for denial. They have turned away from His names and signs and have become ignorant of Him, disbelieving in Him and heedless of His remembrance—their hearts dead to knowing Him, loving Him, and worshipping Him.

Then, if they do this, claiming that it is to avoid “likening Allah to creation and attributing a body to Him,” they are told:

“What you have fled to is worse than what you have fled from. Acknowledging the Creator, in whatever manner, is better than denying Him.

“Moreover, if this observable world, including the heavens and the earth, is eternal and necessarily existent in itself, then you have made observable bodies eternal and necessarily existent in themselves. This is worse than what you sought to escape. If, however, it is not eternal and necessarily existent in itself, it must have a Creator who is eternal and necessarily existent in Himself. It then becomes clear that knowing Him and speaking of Him—affirming the Lord in heart and speech—is undoubtedly true, according to both revelation and reason. If this necessarily entails what you call likening Him to creation and attributing a body to Him, then whatever necessarily follows from truth is itself true. If it does not entail this, you can affirm Him without such language.”

Thus, the inconsistency of those who negate the attributes becomes evident, however the proofs are brought to bear against them. So too does the inconsistency of those who affirm some attributes but not others.

If the “negators” say, “We denied the attributes only because our proof that the world came into being and that the Creator exists also demonstrated that these attributes must be denied. We established the Creator’s existence through the world’s having come into being; we established that the world came into being only by establishing that bodies came into being; and we established that bodies came into being only through the coming into being of attributes, which are accidents.”

Or they say:

“We established that bodies came into being only through the coming into being of actions, which are motions, and through the fact that whatever admits them is never without them, while whatever is never without things that come into being must itself have come into being. They are answered as follows:

The reply has several aspects:

(First: The invalidity of this particular proof does not entail the invalidity of all proofs. There are many ways to establish the Creator’s existence, whose details cannot all be encompassed, even though their general categories can be.

Second: None of the Companions, the Successors, or the leading scholars of the Muslims used this proof. If knowing the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and believing in Him depended upon it, this would entail that they neither knew Allah nor believed in Him. By the consensus of the Muslims, this is among the gravest forms of disbelief.

Third: The Prophets and Messengers did not command anyone to follow this path. If knowledge of Allah depended upon it—and such knowledge is obligatory—then following this path would be obligatory. If such knowledge were recommended, following this path would be recommended. Had it been obligatory or recommended, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have prescribed it. Had it been prescribed, the Companions would have transmitted it.

translated_text:
Chapter: An Overview of the Doctrines of the Various Groups and Their Sources

Regarding the divine attributes and Allah’s oneness, denial of the attributes is, broadly speaking, the position of “the philosophers, the Muʿtazila, and other Jahmīs,” although there are certain differences between the philosophers and the Muʿtazila. Likewise, the Baghdad and Basra schools differ concerning hearing and sight—whether they constitute knowledge or a perception distinct from knowledge—and concerning will.

This is the doctrine that the early generations call “the position of Jahm,” because he was the first to propagate it within Islam. Elsewhere, I have explained the chain through which he received it: it derives from the Sabian philosophers, the polytheist Brahmins, and the Jewish sorcerers.

Affirmation of the attributes, broadly speaking, is the doctrine of “those who affirm the attributes”: the Kullābīs, Ashʿarīs, Karrāmīs, scholars of hadith, the majority of Sufis and Hanbalis, most Mālikīs and Shāfiʿīs apart from rare exceptions among them, and many—or most—Hanafīs. It is also the position of [the Salafiyya] (*). However, taking affirmation to the point of likening Allah to His creation is the position of extremists among the Rāfida, ignorant adherents of hadith, and certain others who have deviated. Between the denial of the Jahmīs and the affirmation of those who liken Allah to His creation, there are varying degrees.
translated_footnote: (*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd (p. 257) said: Perhaps the correct reading is “the view of the Sālimiyya.”

translated_text:
“As for the Ash'arīs,” some of them agreed with them concerning the attributes known through transmitted reports, and the majority agreed with them concerning the attributes reported in hadith. Regarding the attributes mentioned in the Quran, however, they hold two positions: al-Ash'arī, al-Bāqillānī, and their early adherents affirm them, while some acknowledge only some of them.

Yet they also exhibit Jahmī tendencies in another respect. Al-Ash'arī absorbed the speculative theology of al-Jubbā'ī, the leading Mu'tazilī scholar, and both his followers and others acknowledge his theological affiliation with him. Ibn al-Bāqillānī is the foremost in affirming the attributes after al-Ash'arī in his “al-Ibāna” (The Elucidation). After Ibn al-Bāqillānī comes Ibn Fūrak, who affirmed some of the attributes mentioned in the Quran.

“As for al-Juwaynī” and those who followed his approach, they inclined toward the Mu'tazilī doctrine. Abū al-Ma'ālī read Abū Hāshim’s books extensively but had little knowledge of transmitted reports; these two factors combined to influence him. Al-Qushayrī was a student of Ibn Fūrak. Thus, from that time onward, al-Ash'arī’s school grew harsher, and estrangement arose between it and the Hanbalis after they had previously been on friendly terms, or at least at peace with one another.

And “as for the Hanbalis, Abū 'Abd Allāh ibn Hāmid was firm and earnest in affirming the attributes, with a particular inclination toward questions concerning the attributes known through transmitted reports. His companion, Judge Abū Ya'lā, followed his approach, but was milder than he and less inclined to go beyond bounds in affirmation. As for Abū 'Abd Allāh ibn Batta, his approach was purely that of the hadith scholars, such as Abū Bakr

translated_text:
al-Ājurrī in “al-Sharī'a” (The Sacred Law), and al-Lālakā'ī in al-Sunan (The Traditions). Al-Khallāl likewise followed an approach close to his, and Shaykh Abū Muhammad and the later hadith scholars incline toward his approach.

[“As for the Tamīmīs,” such as Abū al-Hasan, Ibn Abī al-Fadl, and Ibn Rizq Allāh] (*), they are less inclined toward affirmation, more disposed to agree with others, and more accommodating toward them. Hence the Sufis follow them, and distinguished Ash'arīs, such as al-Bāqillānī and al-Bayhaqī, incline toward them. Indeed, the account of Ahmad’s creed written by Abū al-Fadl is the one upon which al-Bayhaqī relied. Nevertheless, these men follow the Sunnah.

As for Ibn 'Aqīl, if he deviates, a strong Mu'tazilī strain enters his discussions of the divine attributes, divine decree, and the miraculous gifts granted to Allah’s righteous servants—to the point that al-Ash'arī’s statements are sounder than his and closer to the Sunnah.

Al-Ash'arī professed allegiance solely to the school of the hadith scholars, whose imam, in his view, was Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Abū Bakr 'Abd al-'Azīz and others made statements in their debates indicating that they regarded him as one of the speculative theologians among the hadith scholars, rather than as someone separate from them. In earlier times they were close to one another, although some of them criticized him for things they might likewise criticize in one of their own who ventured into speculative theology, because of the religious innovation involved. Nevertheless, the foundations of his doctrine do not conform to the pure Sunnah; rather, they fall short of it in well-known ways.

In what they affirm of the Sunnah, the “Ash'arīs” are dependent upon the Hanbalis, just as the speculative theologians among the Hanbalis are dependent upon them for the rational analogies they use as arguments. The division arose only because of the turmoil surrounding al-Qushayrī.

" الْإِرْشَادِ "
 مَعَ أَنَّهُ قَدْ يَزِيدُ فِي الْإِثْبَاتِ لَكِنْ مَعَ هَذَا فَمَذْهَبُهُ فِي الصِّفَاتِ قَرِيبٌ مِنْ مَذْهَبِ قُدَمَاءِ الْأَشْعَرِيَّةِ والْكُلَّابِيَة فِي أَنَّهُ يُقِرُّ مَا دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ الْقُرْآنُ وَالْخَبَرُ الْمُتَوَاتِرُ وَيَتَأَوَّلُ غَيْرَهُ؛ وَلِهَذَا يَقُولُ بَعْضُ الْحَنْبَلِيَّةِ أَنَا أُثْبِتُ مُتَوَسِّطًا بَيْنَ تَعْطِيلِ ابْنِ عَقِيلٍ وَتَشْبِيهِ ابْنِ حَامِدٍ. وَالْغَزَالِيُّ فِي كَلَامِهِ مَادَّةٌ فَلْسَفِيَّةٌ كَبِيرَةٌ بِسَبَبِ كَلَامِ ابْنِ سِينَا فِي 
" الشفا "
 وَغَيْرِهِ؛ 
" وَرَسَائِلِ إخْوَانِ الصَّفَا "
 وَكَلَامِ أَبِي حَيَّانَ التَّوْحِيدِيِّ. وَأَمَّا الْمَادَّةُ الْمُعْتَزِلِيَّةُ فِي كَلَامِهِ فَقَلِيلَةٌ أَوْ مَعْدُومَةٌ كَمَا أَنَّ الْمَادَّةَ الْفَلْسَفِيَّةَ فِي كَلَامِ ابْنِ عَقِيلٍ قَلِيلَةٌ أَوْ مَعْدُومَةٌ
translated_text:
There is no doubt that the Ash'arīs of Khurasan had deviated toward negating the divine attributes, while many Hanbalis went too far in affirming them. The judge Abū Ya'lā composed his book Ibtāl al-Ta'wīl (Refutation of Figurative Interpretation) in response to Ibn Fūrak, al-Qushayrī’s teacher. The caliph and others were sympathetic to Abū Ya'lā. When the Qushayriyya gained ascendancy through the Seljuks, that turmoil broke out. In that dispute, the Farrā'iyya had most of the truth on their side, along with some falsehood, whereas the Qushayriyya had some truth on their side, along with much falsehood.

The Mu'tazilī element entered Ibn 'Aqīl’s writings through his teachers, the two Mu'tazilīs Abū 'Alī ibn al-Walīd and Abū al-Qāsim ibn al-Tabbān. Thus, in his book Ithbāt al-Tanzīh (Affirmation of Divine Transcendence) and elsewhere, he makes statements resembling those of al-Marīsī and others like him. Yet he also has many sound statements affirming the divine attributes, and this was the position upon which he ultimately settled in his book al-Irshād (Guidance), although he may at times go too far in affirmation. Nevertheless, his position on the attributes is close to that of the early Ash'arīs and Kullābīs: he accepts what is indicated by the Quran and mass-transmitted reports, while interpreting other texts figuratively. Hence some Hanbalis say, “I affirm the attributes, taking a middle course between Ibn 'Aqīl’s negation and Ibn Hāmid’s likening Allah to His creation.”

Al-Ghazālī’s writings contain a substantial philosophical element derived from Ibn Sīnā’s discussions in al-Shifā' (The Healing) and elsewhere, the Rasā'il Ikhwān al-Safā' (Epistles of the Brethren of Purity), and the writings of Abū Hayyān al-Tawhīdī. The Mu'tazilī element in his writings, however, is slight or nonexistent, just as the philosophical element in Ibn 'Aqīl’s writings is slight or nonexistent.

translated_text:
And most of what he says in al-Ihyā’ (The Revival) is sound, but it contains corrupt elements drawn from philosophy, speculative theology, Sufi nonsense, and fabricated hadiths. He and Ibn ‘Aqīl share a tendency toward contradictory statements concerning the divine attributes: regarding one of the attributes, he may condemn as unbelief the very position he champions in another work. When he writes according to a particular group’s approach, its doctrine tends to dominate his thinking.

As for Ibn al-Khatīb, he is exceedingly inconsistent and never settles on a position. His writings are nothing but inquiry and disputation, like someone searching who has not found what he seeks. Abū Hāmid, by contrast, often does settle on a position.

The Ash‘arīs are predominantly Murji’īs concerning religious designations and rulings, and Jabrites concerning divine decree. Regarding the divine attributes, however, they are not outright Jahmīs, though they exhibit a degree of Jahmī doctrine.

The Mu‘tazilīs are Wa‘īdīs concerning religious designations and rulings, Qadarīs concerning divine decree, and outright Jahmīs. The later Shi‘a followed them in this, adding their teachings on the imamate and superior merit, but differing from them concerning divine threats of punishment. They also advocate rebellion against rulers.

The Ash‘arīs, however, do not advocate taking up the sword, agreeing in this with the people of hadith. Overall, they are the speculative theologians closest to the doctrine of the people of the Sunnah and hadith. The Kullābīs, and likewise the Karrāmīs, also have some affinity with the people of the Sunnah and hadith, although each of these positions contains elements contrary to their teachings.

original_text:

، بَلْ الْحَقُّ أَنَّ الْجَلِيلَ مَنْ كُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْ الصِّنْفَيْنِ

translated_text:
As for the “Sālimiyya,” they and the Hanbalīs are virtually one and the same, except on certain points comparable to the differences among the Hanbalīs themselves. They also have a Sufi tendency. Those among our companions who declare these people innovators likewise regard adopting the Hanbalī label or similar labels in matters of creed as an innovation. They hold that, in matters of creed, one should identify only with the Book and the Sunnah. This is “a sound approach,” but it is a matter in which independent scholarly judgment is permissible. For scarcely any group agrees on the finer points of creed; were it otherwise, the early generations—the Companions and the Successors—would not have disagreed over some of them. Something may warrant censure in one situation but not another, or in the case of one person but not another.

The underlying principle is what I have mentioned elsewhere: doctrinal matters may stand on the same footing as practical matters. Even though the former are called “fundamental matters” and the latter “subsidiary matters,” this terminology is a later innovation, a classification introduced by some jurists and speculative theologians. It is more prevalent among speculative theologians and legal theorists, especially when they discuss questions of judging views correct or mistaken.

The majority of accomplished jurists and Sufis, however, consider actions more important and more deserving of emphasis than disputed doctrinal positions. The jurists’ discussions concern actions, and they often dislike discussing any question that has no practical implications, as Mālik and others among the scholars of Medina state (1). Rather, the truth is that the weighty questions in either category are “fundamental matters,” while the finer points are “subsidiary matters.”

 وَأَمَّا الْأَعْمَالُ الْوَاجِبَةُ:

Thus, knowing that obligatory duties—such as the five pillars of Islam—are obligatory, and that the manifest prohibitions established by mass transmission are forbidden, is like knowing that Allah has power over all things and knowledge of all things, that He is All-Hearing, All-Seeing, that the Quran is Allah’s speech, and other such manifest truths established by mass transmission. Hence, whoever denies those practical rulings upon which there is consensus disbelieves, just as whoever denies these doctrinal truths disbelieves. Affirming practical rulings may be more obligatory than affirming doctrinal propositions. Indeed, this is generally the case, for doctrinal propositions require only an affirmation of the broad fundamentals: belief in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, resurrection after death, and divine decree, both its good and its evil.

Obligatory actions, however, must be known in detail, because acting upon them is impossible without first knowing them in detail. Hence, the Muslim community accepts without reservation those who expound them in detail, namely the jurists, even though it may censure those who discuss the details of broad doctrinal propositions. This is because there is a pressing need to explain obligatory actions in detail, whereas there is no need to elaborate upon the fundamentals in which belief in general terms is obligatory.

Our statement that doctrinal matters may stand on the same footing as practical matters entails several points: (among them, that they comprise both matters of certainty and matters of probability.

And (among them, that although only one person is correct, someone who errs may be pardoned, may incur sin, may be defiantly disobedient, or may be like someone who errs concerning practical rulings

Yet because practical rulings have numerous ramifications and require detailed elaboration, people have become reconciled to disputes and differences concerning them, unlike doctrinal matters. Disagreement is a harm that should be tolerated only to avert something worse. Thus, when necessity called for elaborating the rulings governing actions and their numerous ramifications—which inevitably gives rise to disputes—people became reconciled to disagreement concerning them.

Doctrinal matters are different: agreement has already been reached on their broad fundamentals. If their details can be explained without dispute, that is good. But if disputes arise over those details, this constitutes harm for which there is no compelling need. Hence the censure of those given to desires and contention, and of those who engage in disputation and controversy over these matters: it brings evil and corruption without any compelling need.

Nevertheless, this does not preclude explaining these matters in detail, knowing their subtleties and essentials, and discussing them on the basis of knowledge, provided no harm results. Nor does it warrant declaring everyone who errs concerning them an unbeliever, unless the conditions for declaring him an unbeliever are fulfilled in his case. All this, by my life, concerns disagreement involving genuine contradiction. As for other forms of disagreement—such as differences of variety, perspective, or wording—these are a minor matter, and they account for much, or most, of the disagreement over doctrinal questions.

A related point is that belief in doctrinal matters may be obligatory, or obligatory in some circumstances but not others, and for some people but not others. It may also be recommended rather than obligatory, or recommended for a particular group or in particular circumstances—just as with deeds. Knowledge of these matters may even harm some people, in which case it is not permissible to teach them such matters. As ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“Tell people what they can understand, and leave aside what they would reject. Would you like Allah and His Messenger to be disbelieved?”

Ibn Mas‘ūd, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“No man tells people something beyond their understanding without its becoming a trial for some of them.”

Likewise, when Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about the verse containing the words of the Most High:

“Allah is the One who created seven heavens,”

Both statements are sound and do not contradict one another, yet stating them together may harm both groups. He therefore presents them together only to those whom this will not harm.

Since these matters may be definitive or open to scholarly judgment, the same grounds that allow scholarly judgment in matters of practice allow it here. Much of Quranic commentary, or even most of it, falls into this category: many disagreements in Quranic commentary concern questions of knowledge and what is reported, rather than questions of practice. Yet personal desires may intrude into major questions just as they may intrude into practical matters.

One proponent may condemn another’s position so strongly that he declares him a disbeliever or a sinful innovator deserving to be shunned, even though he does not deserve this. This, too, is an exercise of scholarly judgment. Such severity may be justified with certain individuals or in certain circumstances, because of the manifest clarity of the Sunnah whose contravention constitutes disbelief, and because of the harm inherent in the opposing view, on account of which its proponent is deemed an innovator. These are matters that a discerning person should understand.

For when a true statement is uttered, its necessary, intrinsic characteristic is that it corresponds to the reality reported. But whether the hearer knows it, considers it probable, or is ignorant of it; whether it is certain or conjectural for him; whether accepting it is obligatory or forbidden; and whether the person who denies it becomes a disbeliever or does not—these are practical rulings that vary according to individuals and circumstances.

فَإِذَا رَأَيْت إمَامًا قَدْ غَلَّظَ عَلَى قَائِلِ مَقَالَتِهِ أَوْ كَفَّرَهُ فِيهَا فَلَا يُعْتَبَرُ هَذَا حُكْمًا عَامًّا فِي كُلِّ مَنْ قَالَهَا إلَّا إذَا حَصَلَ فِيهِ الشَّرْطُ الَّذِي يَسْتَحِقُّ بِهِ التَّغْلِيظَ عَلَيْهِ وَالتَّكْفِيرَ لَهُ؛ فَإِنَّ مَنْ جَحَدَ شَيْئًا مِنْ الشَّرَائِعِ الظَّاهِرَةِ وَكَانَ حَدِيثَ الْعَهْدِ بِالْإِسْلَامِ أَوْ نَاشِئًا بِبَلَدِ جَهْلٍ لَا يَكْفُرُ حَتَّى تَبْلُغَهُ الْحُجَّةُ النَّبَوِيَّةُ. وَكَذَلِكَ الْعَكْسُ إذَا رَأَيْت الْمَقَالَةَ الْمُخْطِئَةَ قَدْ صَدَرَتْ مِنْ إمَامٍ قَدِيمٍ فَاغْتُفِرَتْ؛ لِعَدَمِ بُلُوغِ الْحُجَّةِ لَهُ؛ فَلَا يُغْتَفَرُ لِمَنْ بَلَغَتْهُ الْحُجَّةُ مَا اُغْتُفِرَ لِلْأَوَّلِ فَلِهَذَا يُبَدَّعُ مَنْ بَلَغَتْهُ أَحَادِيثُ عَذَابِ الْقَبْرِ وَنَحْوِهَا إذَا أَنْكَرَ ذَلِكَ وَلَا تُبَدَّعُ عَائِشَةُ وَنَحْوُهَا مِمَّنْ لَمْ يَعْرِفْ بِأَنَّ الْمَوْتَى يَسْمَعُونَ فِي قُبُورِهِمْ؛ فَهَذَا أَصْلٌ عَظِيمٌ فَتَدَبَّرْهُ فَإِنَّهُ نَافِعٌ. وَهُوَ أَنْ يَنْظُرَ فِي 
" شَيْئَيْنِ فِي الْمَقَالَةِ "
 هَلْ هِيَ حَقٌّ؟ أَمْ بَاطِلٌ؟ أَمْ تَقْبَلُ التَّقْسِيمَ فَتَكُونُ حَقًّا بِاعْتِبَارِ بَاطِلًا بِاعْتِبَارِ؟ وَهُوَ كَثِيرٌ وَغَالِبٌ؟ . ثُمَّ النَّظَرُ الثَّانِي فِي حُكْمِهِ إثْبَاتًا أَوْ نَفْيًا أَوْ تَفْصِيلًا وَاخْتِلَافِ أَحْوَالِ النَّاسِ فِيهِ فَمَنْ سَلَكَ هَذَا الْمَسْلَكَ أَصَابَ الْحَقَّ قَوْلًا وَعَمَلًا وَعَرَفَ إبْطَالَ الْقَوْلِ وَإِحْقَاقَهُ وَحَمْدَهُ فَهَذَا هَذَا وَاَللَّهُ يَهْدِينَا وَيُرْشِدُنَا إنَّهُ وَلِيُّ ذَلِكَ وَالْقَادِرُ عَلَيْهِ.
translated_text:
Thus, if you see that an imam has dealt severely with the proponent of a view, or declared him a disbeliever on account of it, this should not be regarded as a general ruling concerning everyone who holds that view, unless the condition warranting such severity and a declaration of disbelief is fulfilled in that person. Someone who denies any of Islam’s manifest prescriptions, but has only recently embraced Islam or grew up in a land of ignorance, is not deemed a disbeliever until the proof conveyed by the Prophet has reached him.

The converse also applies: if you find that an earlier imam expressed an erroneous view and was excused because the proof had not reached him, someone whom the proof has reached is not excused as the former was. Thus, someone who receives the hadiths concerning punishment in the grave and similar matters, yet denies them, is deemed an innovator; whereas ‘Ā’ishah and others like her, who did not know that the dead hear in their graves, are not deemed innovators. This is a fundamental principle of great importance, so reflect upon it, for it is beneficial.

It consists in examining “two considerations concerning a statement.” Is it true, false, or does it admit distinctions, being true in one respect and false in another—as is very frequently the case? The second consideration concerns the ruling on it—whether that ruling is affirmed, denied, or qualified—and how people’s circumstances differ in relation to it.

Whoever follows this approach will arrive at the truth in both word and deed, and will know when a statement should be refuted, upheld, or commended. Such, then, is the matter. May Allah guide us and direct us aright; He is the One who grants this and has power over it.

original_text:
فَصْلٌ:
قَدْ عُرِفَ أَنَّ الْأَشْيَاءَ لَهَا وُجُودٌ فِي 
" الْأَعْيَانِ "
 وَوُجُودٌ فِي 
" الْأَذْهَانِ "
 وَوُجُودٌ فِي 
" اللِّسَانِ "
 وَوُجُودٌ فِي 
" الْبَنَانِ "
 وَهُوَ: الْعَيْنِيُّ وَالْعِلْمِيُّ وَاللَّفْظِيُّ وَالرَّسْمِيُّ.
 ثُمَّ قَالَ:
 مَنْ قَالَ: إنَّ الْوُجُودَ الْعَيْنِيَّ وَالْعِلْمِيَّ لَا يَخْتَلِفُ بِاخْتِلَافِ الْأَعْصَارِ وَالْأَمْصَارِ وَالْأُمَمِ؛ بِخِلَافِ اللَّفْظِيِّ وَالرَّسْمِيِّ فَإِنَّ اللُّغَاتِ تَخْتَلِفُ بِاخْتِلَافِ الْأُمَمِ كَالْعَرَبِيَّةِ وَالْفَارِسِيَّةِ وَالرُّومِيَّةِ وَالتُّرْكِيَّةِ. وَهَذَا قَدْ يَذْكُرُهُ بَعْضُهُمْ فِي 
" كَلَامِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى "
 أَنَّهُ هُوَ الْمَعْنَى الَّذِي لَا يَخْتَلِفُ بِاخْتِلَافِ الْأُمَمِ دُونَ الْحُرُوفِ الَّتِي تَخْتَلِفُ؛ كَمَا هُوَ قَوْلُ الْكُلَّابِيَة وَالْأَشْعَرِيَّةِ وَيَضُمُّونَ إلَى ذَلِكَ أَنَّ كُتُبَهُ إنَّمَا اخْتَلَفَتْ لِاخْتِلَافِ لَفْظِهَا فَقَطْ؛
 فَكَلَامُهُ بِالْعِبْرِيَّةِ هُوَ التَّوْرَاةُ وَبِالْعَرَبِيَّةِ هُوَ الْقُرْآنُ كَمَا يَقُولُونَ:
 إنَّ 
" الْمَعْنَى الْقَدِيمَ "
 يَكُونُ أَمْرًا وَنَهْيًا وَخَبَرًا؛ فَهَذِهِ صِفَاتٌ عَارِضَةٌ لَهُ؛ لَا أَنْوَاعٌ لَهُ. وَيَذْكُرُ بَعْضُهُمْ هَذَا الْقَوْلَ مُطْلَقًا فِي 
" أُصُولِ الْفِقْهِ "
 فِي مَسَائِلِ اللُّغَاتِ وَيَذْكُرُهُ بَعْضُهُمْ فِي مَسْأَلَةِ الِاسْمِ وَالْمُسَمَّى وَأَسْمَاءِ اللَّهِ الْحُسْنَى كَأَبِي حَامِدٍ.
translated_text:
Section

It is known that things have an existence in “external reality,” an existence in “minds,” an existence on “the tongue,” and an existence through “the fingers”—that is, external, cognitive, verbal, and written existence.

Some have then said that external and cognitive existence do not vary with differences of times, places, and nations, unlike verbal and written existence, since languages differ among nations, as with Arabic, Persian, the language of the Romans, and Turkish.

Some invoke this distinction when discussing “the speech of Allah Most High,” maintaining that it is the meaning that does not vary among nations, rather than the letters, which do vary. This is the position of the Kullābīs and Ashʿarīs. They add that His scriptures differ only in their wording: His speech in Hebrew is the Torah, and in Arabic it is the Quran. Likewise, they say that the “eternal meaning” can be a command, a prohibition, or a statement: these are incidental attributes of it, not distinct kinds of it.

Some state this view without qualification in works on the principles of jurisprudence, in discussions of languages. Others, such as Abū Hāmid, mention it when discussing the name and the thing named, and Allah’s Most Beautiful Names.

original_text:
قُلْت:
 وَهَذَا الْقَوْلُ فِيهِ نَظَرٌ وَبَعْضُهُ بَاطِلٌ؛ وَذَلِكَ أَنَّ أَلْفَاظَ اللُّغَاتِ (مِنْهَا مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِ كَالتَّنُّورِ وَكَمَا يُوجَدُ مِنْ الْأَسْمَاءِ الْمُتَّحِدَةِ فِي اللُّغَاتِ.
 وَمِنْهَا:
 مُتَنَوِّعٌ كَأَكْثَرِ اللُّغَاتِ وَاخْتِلَافُهَا اخْتِلَافَ تَنَوُّعٍ لَا تَضَادَّ؛ كَاخْتِلَافِ الِاسْمَيْنِ لِلْمُسَمَّى الْوَاحِدِ. وَكَذَلِكَ مَعَانِي اللُّغَاتِ؛ فَإِنَّ 
" الْمَعْنَى الْوَاحِدَ "
 الَّذِي تَعْلَمُهُ الْأُمَمُ؛ وَتُعَبِّرُ عَنْهُ كُلُّ أُمَّةٍ بِلِسَانِهَا؛ قَدْ يَكُونُ ذَلِكَ الْمَعْنَى وَاحِدًا بِالنَّوْعِ فِي الْأُمَمِ؛ بِحَيْثُ لَا يَخْتَلِفُ كَمَا يَخْتَلِفُ اللَّفْظُ الْوَاحِدُ بِالْعَرَبِيَّةِ.
 وَقَدْ يَكُونُ تَصَوُّرُ ذَلِكَ الْمَعْنَى مُتَنَوِّعًا فِي الْأُمَمِ مِثْلَ:
 أَنْ يَعْلَمَهُ أَحَدُهُمْ بِنَعْتِ وَيُعَبِّرَ عَنْهُ بِاعْتِبَارِ ذَلِكَ النَّعْتِ وَتَعْلَمُهُ الْأُمَّةُ الْأُخْرَى بِنَعْتِ آخَرَ وَتُعَبِّرُ عَنْهُ بِاعْتِبَارِ ذَلِكَ النَّعْتِ كَمَا هُوَ الْوَاقِعُ فِي أَسْمَاءِ اللَّهِ وَأَسْمَاءِ رَسُولِهِ وَكِتَابِهِ وَكَثِيرٍ مِنْ الْأَسْمَاءِ الْمُعَبَّرِ بِهَا عَنْ الْأَشْيَاءِ الْمُتَّفَقِ عَلَى عِلْمِهَا فِي الْجُمْلَةِ 
" فَتُكْرِي وَخَدَّايَ وَنَسَتْ شَكَّ "
 وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ. وَإِنْ كَانَتْ أَسْمَاءَ لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى فَلَيْسَ مَعْنَاهَا مُطَابِقًا مِنْ كُلِّ وَجْهٍ لِمَعْنَى اسْمِ اللَّهِ؛ وَكَذَلِكَ 
" بيغنير وَبِهَشِمِ "
 وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ. وَلِهَذَا إذَا تَأَمَّلْت الْأَلْفَاظَ الَّتِي يُتَرْجَمُ بِهَا الْقُرْآنُ - مِنْ الْأَلْفَاظِ الْفَارِسِيَّةِ وَالتُّرْكِيَّةِ وَغَيْرِهَا - تَجِدْ بَيْنَ الْمَعَانِي نَوْعَ فَرْقٍ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ مُتَّفِقَةً فِي الْأَصْلِ كَمَا أَنَّ اللُّغَتَيْنِ مُتَّفِقَتَانِ فِي الصَّوْتِ وَإِنْ اخْتَلَفَتَا فِي تَأْلِيفِهِ؛ وَقَدْ تَجِدُ التَّفَاوُتَ بَيْنَهَا أَكْثَرَ مِنْ التَّفَاوُتِ بَيْنَ الْأَلْفَاظِ 
" الْمُتَكَافِئَةِ "
 - الْوَاقِعَةِ بَيْنَ الْمُتَرَادِفَةِ وَالْمُتَبَايِنَةِ - كَالصَّارِمِ وَالْمُهَنَّدِ؛ وَكَالرَّيْبِ وَالشَّكِّ وَالْمَوْرِ وَالْحَرَكَةِ وَالصِّرَاطِ وَالطَّرِيقِ.
translated_text:
I say:

This view calls for scrutiny, and part of it is false. Expressions in different languages include shared words, such as tannūr (oven), and other names that are identical across languages. Others vary, as is generally the case with languages. Their differences are differences of variety, not opposition, like two names for the same thing.

The same applies to the meanings expressed in different languages. The “single meaning” known to different nations, which each nation expresses in its own language, may be the same in kind across those nations, without varying as a single Arabic expression may vary.

Yet different nations may conceive of that meaning differently. For example, one nation may know something by one attribute and express it with that attribute in view, while another nation knows it by another attribute and expresses it accordingly. This occurs with the names of Allah, His Messenger, and His Book, and with many names used to express things that are generally known to all. Thus, although “Futukrī, Khaddāy, and Nasat Shakk” and similar expressions are names for Allah Most High, their meanings do not correspond in every respect to the meaning of the name Allah. The same applies to “Bīghnīr and Bihashim” and similar expressions.

Hence, if you examine the Persian, Turkish, and other expressions used to translate the Quran, you will find some difference between their meanings, although they agree in their basic sense—just as two languages share sounds, although they differ in how those sounds are combined. You may even find greater differences between these meanings than between “equivalent” expressions—which fall between synonyms and expressions with distinct meanings—such as “a keen-edged sword” and “an Indian-made sword”; “misgiving” and “doubt”; “surging” and “movement”; and “path” and “way.”

original_text:
وَتَخْتَلِفُ اللُّغَتَانِ أَيْضًا فِي قَدْرِ ذَلِكَ الْمَعْنَى وَعُمُومِهِ وَخُصُوصِهِ؛ كَمَا تَخْتَلِفُ فِي حَقِيقَتِهِ وَنَوْعِهِ وَتَخْتَلِفُ أَيْضًا فِي كَيْفِيَّتِهِ وَصِفَتِهِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ. بَلْ النَّاطِقَانِ بِالِاسْمِ الْوَاحِدِ بِاللُّغَةِ الْوَاحِدَةِ يَتَصَوَّرُ أَحَدُهُمَا مِنْهُ مَا لَمْ يَتَصَوَّرْ الْآخَرُ حَقِيقَتَهُ وَكَمِّيَّتَهُ وَكَيْفِيَّتَهُ وَغَيْرَ ذَلِكَ؛ فَإِذَا كَانَ الْمَعْنَى الْمَدْلُولُ عَلَيْهِ بِالِاسْمِ الْوَاحِدِ لَا يَتَّحِدُ مِنْ كُلِّ وَجْهٍ فِي قَلْبِ النَّاطِقِينَ؛ بَلْ وَلَا فِي قَلْبِ النَّاطِقِ الْوَاحِدِ فِي الْوَقْتَيْنِ؛ فَكَيْفَ يُقَالُ إنَّهُ يَجِبُ اتِّحَادُهُ فِي اللُّغَاتِ الْمُتَعَدِّدَةِ. يُوَضِّحُ ذَلِكَ أَنَّ مَا تَعْلَمُهُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ مِنْهُ لَيْسَ عَلَى حَدِّ مَا يَعْلَمُهُ الْبَشَرُ وَمَا يَعْلَمُهُ اللَّهُ فِيهِ لَيْسَ عَلَى حَدِّ مَا تَعْلَمُهُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ؛ لَكِنَّ الِاخْتِلَافَ اخْتِلَافُ تَنَوُّعٍ لَا تَضَادَّ.
 وَأَمَّا قَوْلُ مَنْ قَالَ:
 إنَّ مَعَانِيَ الْكُتُبِ الْمُنَزَّلَةِ سَوَاءٌ فَفَسَادُهُ مَعْلُومٌ بِالِاضْطِرَارِ فَإِنَّا لَوْ عَبَّرْنَا عَنْ مَعَانِي الْقُرْآنِ بِالْعِبْرِيَّةِ وَعَنْ مَعَانِي التَّوْرَاةِ بِالْعَرَبِيَّةِ لَكَانَ أَحَدُ الْمَعْنَيَيْنِ لَيْسَ هُوَ الْآخَرَ بَلْ يُعْلَمُ بِالِاضْطِرَارِ تَنَوُّعُ مَعَانِي الْكُتُبِ وَاخْتِلَافُهَا اخْتِلَافَ تَنَوُّعٍ أَعْظَمَ مِنْ اخْتِلَافِ حُرُوفِهَا؛ لِمَا بَيْنَ الْعَرَبِيَّةِ وَالْعِبْرِيَّةِ مِنْ التَّفَاوُتِ؛ وَكَذَلِكَ مَعَانِي الْبَقَرَةِ لَيْسَتْ هِيَ مَعَانِي آل عِمْرَانَ. وَأَبْعَدُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ جَعْلُ الْأَمْرِ هُوَ الْخَبَرُ.

 إنَّهَا وَاحِدَةٌ مَعَ تَنَوُّعِهَا: فَكَذَلِكَ اللُّغَاتُ سَوَاءٌ بَلْ اخْتِلَافُ الْمَعَانِي أَشَدُّ.

translated_text:
The two languages also differ in the extent of that meaning and in its generality and specificity, just as they differ in its nature and kind. They also differ in its manner, attributes, and other respects. Indeed, even when two speakers use the same name in the same language, one may conceive of aspects of its nature, quantity, manner, and so forth that the other does not. If the meaning conveyed by a single name is not identical in every respect in the minds of different speakers—or even in the mind of the same speaker at two different times—how can it be said that it must be identical across different languages? This is further illustrated by the fact that what the angels know of it is not of the same extent as what human beings know, nor is what Allah knows of it of the same extent as what the angels know. These differences, however, are differences of variety, not opposition.

As for the claim that the meanings of the revealed Books are identical, its falsity is self-evident. If we expressed the meanings of the Quran in Hebrew and the meanings of the Torah in Arabic, the meanings of the one would still not be those of the other. Indeed, it is self-evident that the meanings of the Books vary, and that these differences of variety are greater than the differences between their letters, given the disparity between Arabic and Hebrew. Likewise, the meanings of al-Baqarah are not those of Āl ʿImrān. Still more far-fetched is the claim that a command is the same as a statement.

It is not denied that these different things may share some common reality, just as languages share some common reality. If they may be called one despite their variety, then the same applies to languages. Indeed, the differences in meaning are greater.

As for the claim that one is a real attribute and the other a conventional one, that is not so.

One indication that the way of Ahl al-Sunnah in following the prophets leads to the truth, unlike the way of the philosophers and speculative theologians who oppose them, is this: the aim is knowledge, and the means to it is evidence. The prophets brought detailed affirmation and comprehensive negation, affirming Allah’s attributes in detail and denying that He has any equal.

The “philosophers,” however, offer detailed negation: He is not this, nor that. When it comes to affirmation, they affirm only an unspecified existence and fall into confusion over “the very first questions concerning His existence”: whether His existence is identical with His essence, an essential attribute of it, or an accidental attribute—and other such conceptual and verbal disputes.

It is well known that negation has no existence of its own, and that negation and nonexistence can be known only after knowledge of what is real and existent. Indeed, a group of speculative theologians denied that the nonexistent could be known unless it were regarded as a thing, because knowledge, they claimed, must relate to a thing.

The truth is that knowledge of nonexistence is obtained through knowledge of what exists. Thus, when we know that “there is no god but Allah,” we conceive of an existing deity and know that what we have conceived is not found in anything other than Allah. Likewise, whatever else we negate, we must first conceive of it and then negate it; and we can conceive of it only

The mind cannot otherwise originate a wholly novel conception of something nonexistent that bears no relation whatsoever to existing things, whether this belongs to theoretical or scientific knowledge—as when an agent conceives of what he will do before doing it. This is, in fact, a conception of something nonexistent that is to be brought into existence. Other conceptions likewise concern something nonexistent, whether possible or impossible, which may or may not come into existence. Thus, whether related to action or not, the human mind cannot originate a conception of something nonexistent without material drawn from what exists, just as human power cannot produce anything without existing material. Origination from nothing belongs exclusively to divine lordship. The manner of knowing and acting is a separate subject.

This makes clear that knowledge of what exists and its attributes is the foundation, while knowledge of nonexistence, whether absolute or qualified, is secondary and dependent upon it. Moreover, knowledge of nonexistence benefits the knower only insofar as it completes knowledge of what exists or serves the perfection of the existent itself. Merely conceiving of “nothing” does not confer any attribute of perfection upon the knower. Knowing, however, that an existent is free of deficiencies, for example, is knowledge of its perfection. Likewise, knowing that it has no partners is knowledge of its oneness, which is an aspect of perfection. Similarly, conceiving of what one intends to do leads to performing the action, while conceiving of what one intends to refrain from leads to abstention: the absence of an evil whose absence perfects the existent.

What I have said here concerning knowledge and speech applies equally to intention and action. Intention is directed primarily towards something existent—namely, the action—and only secondarily towards nonexistence—namely, abstention—in order to ward off harm from the intended existent.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—was asked the following.

The questioner said:

We ask the scholars of Islam and its eminent leaders—may Allah reward them generously and grant them an honourable welcome and final abode—to lift the veil of generality and dispel the obscurity surrounding a “premise” upon which all adherents of religions and doctrines agree and upon which they base their views, except those who obstinately dispute the truth and deny Allah’s lordship.

The premise is this:

“This is an attribute of perfection, so it must be affirmed of Allah; and this is an attribute of deficiency, so it must be denied of Him.”

They disagree, however, over how this premise applies to particular attributes and over which attributes belong to each of these two categories.

Thus, Ahl al-Sunnah say: Affirming hearing, sight, life, power, knowledge, speech, and the other “attributes known through revelation”—such as the Face, the two Hands, the two Eyes, anger, and pleasure—as well as the “attributes of action”—such as laughter, descent, and istiwā—is to affirm attributes of perfection; their opposites are attributes of deficiency.

 يَقُولُونَ: لَوْ قَامَتْ بِذَاتِهِ صِفَاتٌ وُجُودِيَّةٌ لَكَانَ مُفْتَقِرًا إلَيْهَا وَهِيَ مُفْتَقِرَةٌ إلَيْهِ فَيَكُونُ الرَّبُّ مُفْتَقِرًا إلَى غَيْرِهِ؛ وَلِأَنَّهَا أَعْرَاضٌ لَا تَقُومُ إلَّا بِجِسْمِ. وَالْجِسْمُ مُرَكَّبٌ وَالْمُرَكَّبُ مُمْكِنٌ مُحْتَاجٌ وَذَلِكَ عَيْنُ النَّقْصِ.
 وَيَقُولُونَ أَيْضًا:
 لَوْ قَدَّرَ عَلَى الْعِبَادِ أَعْمَالَهُمْ وَعَاقَبَهُمْ عَلَيْهَا: كَانَ ظَالِمًا وَذَلِكَ نَقْصٌ.
 وَخُصُومُهُمْ يَقُولُونَ:
 لَوْ كَانَ فِي مُلْكِهِ مَا لَا يُرِيدُهُ لَكَانَ نَاقِصًا. 
" والْكُلَّابِيَة وَمَنْ تَبِعَهُمْ "

" وَطَائِفَةٌ مِنْهُمْ "

 وَهَكَذَا نَفْيُهُمْ أَيْضًا لِمَحَبَّتِهِ لِأَنَّهَا مُنَاسِبَةٌ بَيْنَ الْمُحِبِّ وَالْمَحْبُوبِ وَمُنَاسَبَةُ الرَّبِّ لِلْخَلْقِ نَقْصٌ:
 وَكَذَا رَحْمَتُهُ لِأَنَّ الرَّحْمَةَ رِقَّةٌ تَكُونُ فِي الرَّاحِمِ وَهِيَ ضَعْفٌ وَخَوَرٌ فِي الطَّبِيعَةِ وَتَأَلُّمٌ عَلَى الْمَرْحُومِ وَهُوَ نَقْصٌ. وَكَذَا غَضَبُهُ لِأَنَّ الْغَضَبَ غَلَيَانُ دَمِ الْقَلْبِ طَلَبًا لِلِانْتِقَامِ. وَكَذَا نَفْيُهُمْ لِضَحِكِهِ وَتَعَجُّبِهِ لِأَنَّ الضَّحِكَ خِفَّةُ رُوحٍ تَكُونُ لِتَجَدُّدِ مَا يَسُرُّ وَانْدِفَاعِ مَا يَضُرُّ. وَالتَّعَجُّبُ اسْتِعْظَامٌ لِلْمُتَعَجَّبِ مِنْهُ.
translated_text:
“The philosophers” say: If His possession of these attributes entails perfection for Him, then He would have attained perfection through something other than Himself and would therefore be deficient in Himself. If it entails deficiency for Him, these attributes cannot be ascribed to Him.

“The Muʿtazilah” say: If attributes possessing real existence subsisted in His essence, He would depend on them, while they would depend on Him. The Lord would thus depend on something other than Himself. Moreover, these attributes are accidents, which can subsist only in a body. A body is composite, and whatever is composite is contingent and dependent; that is deficiency itself.

They also say: If He decreed His servants’ deeds and punished them for those deeds, He would be unjust, and that is a deficiency.

Their opponents say: If anything occurred within His dominion that He did not will, He would be deficient.

“The Kullābiyyah and their followers” deny His attributes of action, saying: If these subsisted in Him, He would be a locus for temporal occurrences. If such an occurrence entailed perfection for Him, He would have lacked that perfection before it, which is a deficiency. If it did not entail perfection for Him, it could not be attributed to Him.

“A group among them” deny His attributes known through revelation, on the grounds that these entail composition, which in turn entails need and dependence.

Likewise, they deny His love, on the grounds that love involves an affinity between the lover and the beloved, and that an affinity between the Lord and creation is a deficiency.

They similarly deny His mercy, because mercy is a tenderness in the one who shows mercy: a weakness and frailty of constitution, and distress over the one shown mercy—and that is a deficiency. Likewise, they deny His anger, because anger is the boiling of the heart’s blood in pursuit of vengeance.

They also deny His laughter and amazement, because laughter is a lightness of spirit arising from the occurrence of something pleasing and the removal of something harmful, while amazement consists in regarding its object as something extraordinary.

translated_text:
And “those who deny prophethood” say: Creation is not of such standing that He should send a messenger to them, just as people on society’s margins are not worthy of having a sovereign send them an envoy.

“The polytheists” say: The Lord’s greatness and majesty require that He be approached only through an intermediary and a chamberlain. To approach Him directly, without intercessors and intermediaries, detracts from His exalted dignity.

Yet those who uphold this “premise” neither accept its implications nor apply it consistently. If they were asked, “Which is more perfect: an essence possessing all forms of perception, including smell, taste, and touch, or an essence not possessing them all?” they would answer that the former is more perfect. Nevertheless, they do not attribute all these forms of perception to the Creator.

And (in sum), perfection and deficiency are relative matters and relational concepts. An attribute may be a perfection for one essence and a deficiency for another. Eating, drinking, and marriage, for example, are perfections for created beings but deficiencies for the Creator. Conversely, self-exaltation, pride, and self-praise are perfections for the Creator but deficiencies for created beings. If this is so, perhaps the attributes you describe as perfections are perfections only in relation to what is observable. It does not necessarily follow that they are perfections for what is unseen, as has been explained—especially given the dissimilarity between the two essences.

If you say, “We set aside the entity to which the attribute pertains and consider the attribute itself: is it a perfection or a deficiency?” then, for that very reason, we consider it impossible to judge it to be either, since it may be a perfection for one essence and a deficiency for another, as mentioned.

translated_text:
It is remarkable that a “premise” upon which there is consensus should itself be the source of disagreement and dispute. May Allah be pleased with whoever gives us an explanation that heals the ailing and combines knowledge of the judgment with a clear account of its proof. Indeed, He Most High hears supplication and is worthy of our hope. He is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.

He replied—may Allah be pleased with him:

Praise be to Allah. The answer to this question rests upon “two premises.”

The first is to know that perfection is affirmed for Allah. Indeed, what is affirmed for Him is the utmost perfection possible: every perfection free of deficiency is affirmed for the Lord Most High, who is entitled to it by virtue of His own holy essence. Affirming this necessarily entails negating its opposite: affirming life entails negating death; affirming knowledge entails negating ignorance; and affirming power entails negating incapacity. This perfection is established for Him by rational evidence and conclusive proofs, alongside the evidence of revelation.

The Quran provides evidence for matters in two ways:

The first is Allah’s truthful report. Whatever Allah and His Messenger have reported is true, just as Allah has reported it.

The second is the Quran’s demonstration through comparisons and its exposition of rational proofs establishing the point at issue. This evidence is both scriptural and rational. It is “scriptural” because revelation points to it and directs us to it, and “rational” because its validity is known through reason. It must not be said that it is known solely through a report.

 هُوَ الْمُسْتَحِقُّ لِلْكَمَالِ وَهُوَ السَّيِّدُ الَّذِي كَمُلَ فِي سُؤْدُدِهِ وَالشَّرِيفُ الَّذِي قَدْ كَمُلَ فِي شَرَفِهِ وَالْعَظِيمُ الَّذِي قَدْ كَمُلَ فِي عَظَمَتِهِ وَالْحَكَمُ الَّذِي قَدْ كَمُلَ فِي حُكْمِهِ وَالْغَنِيُّ الَّذِي قَدْ كَمُلَ فِي غِنَاهُ وَالْجَبَّارُ الَّذِي قَدْ كَمُلَ فِي جَبَرُوتِهِ وَالْعَالِمُ الَّذِي قَدْ كَمُلَ فِي عِلْمِهِ وَالْحَكِيمُ الَّذِي قَدْ كَمُلَ فِي حِكْمَتِهِ وَهُوَ الشَّرِيفُ الَّذِي قَدْ كَمُلَ فِي أَنْوَاعِ الشَّرَفِ وَالسُّؤْدُدِ وَهُوَ اللَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى. وَهَذِهِ صِفَةٌ لَا تَنْبَغِي إلَّا لَهُ لَيْسَ لَهُ كُفُؤٌ وَلَا كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ. وَهَكَذَا سَائِرُ صِفَاتِ الْكَمَالِ وَلَمْ يُعْلَمْ أَحَدٌ مِنْ الْأُمَّةِ نَازَعَ فِي هَذَا الْمَعْنَى؛ بَلْ هَذَا الْمَعْنَى مُسْتَقِرٌّ فِي فِطَرِ النَّاسِ؛ بَلْ هُمْ مَفْطُورُونَ عَلَيْهِ فَإِنَّهُمْ كَمَا أَنَّهُمْ مَفْطُورُونَ عَلَى الْإِقْرَارِ بِالْخَالِقِ؛ فَإِنَّهُمْ مَفْطُورُونَ عَلَى أَنَّهُ أَجَلُّ وَأَكْبَرُ وَأَعْلَى وَأَعْلَمُ وَأَعْظَمُ وَأَكْمَلُ مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ.
translated_text:
When Allah reports something and establishes it through rational evidence, it is demonstrated both by His report and by the rational proof through which it is known. It is thus established by revelation and reason alike. Both are encompassed by the Quran’s evidence, which is called “scriptural evidence.”

The Quran establishes the “meaning of perfection” through various expressions conveying meanings that encompass it. Its affirmation that praise belongs to Him, its detailed account of His praiseworthy attributes, its declaration that His is the highest description, its affirmation of the meanings of His names, and other such statements all establish this meaning.

The word “perfect” is also attested in the report transmitted by Ibn Abī Talhah from Ibn ‘Abbās concerning the explanation of:

“Say, ‘He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge.’”

He explained that “the Eternal Refuge” is the One entitled to perfection: the Master whose mastery is perfect; the Noble whose nobility is perfect; the Great whose greatness is perfect; the Judge whose judgment is perfect; the Self-Sufficient whose self-sufficiency is perfect; the Compeller whose might is perfect; the Knowing whose knowledge is perfect; and the Wise whose wisdom is perfect. He is the Noble whose nobility and mastery are perfect in every respect. He is Allah, glorified and exalted is He. This description befits Him alone: He has no equal, and nothing is like Him.

The same applies to all the other attributes of perfection. No one in the Muslim community is known to have disputed this meaning. Rather, it is firmly rooted in people’s innate nature; indeed, they are innately disposed to it. Just as they are innately disposed to acknowledge the Creator, they are also innately disposed to acknowledge that He is more majestic, greater, higher, more knowing, more magnificent, and more perfect than everything else.

وَقَدْ بَيَّنَّا فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ أَنَّ الْإِقْرَارَ بِالْخَالِقِ وَكَمَالِهِ يَكُونُ فِطْرِيًّا ضَرُورِيًّا فِي حَقِّ مَنْ سَلِمَتْ فِطْرَتُهُ وَإِنْ كَانَ مَعَ ذَلِكَ تَقُومُ عَلَيْهِ الْأَدِلَّةُ الْكَثِيرَةُ وَقَدْ يَحْتَاجُ إلَى الْأَدِلَّةِ عَلَيْهِ كَثِيرٌ مِنْ النَّاسِ عِنْدَ تَغَيُّرِ الْفِطْرَةِ وَأَحْوَالٍ تَعْرِضُ لَهَا. وَأَمَّا لَفْظُ

" الْإِجْمَاعُ "
 وَأَنَّ نَفْيَ الْآفَاتِ وَالنَّقَائِصِ عَنْهُ لَمْ يُعْلَمْ إلَّا بِالْإِجْمَاعِ وَجَعَلُوا الطَّرِيقَ الَّتِي بِهَا نَفَوْا عَنْهُ مَا نَفَوْهُ إنَّمَا هُوَ نَفْيُ مُسَمَّى الْجِسْمِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ؛ وَخَالَفُوا مَا كَانَ عَلَيْهِ شُيُوخُ مُتَكَلِّمَةِ الصفاتية؛ كَالْأَشْعَرِيِّ وَالْقَاضِي أَبِي بَكْرٍ وَأَبِي إسْحَاقَ وَمَنْ قَبْلَهُمْ مِنْ السَّلَفِ وَالْأَئِمَّةِ فِي إثْبَاتِ السَّمْعِ وَالْبَصَرِ وَالْكَلَامِ لَهُ بِالْأَدِلَّةِ الْعَقْلِيَّةِ وَتَنْزِيهِهِ عَنْ النَّقَائِصِ بِالْأَدِلَّةِ الْعَقْلِيَّةِ.
 وَلِهَذَا صَارَ هَؤُلَاءِ يَعْتَمِدُونَ فِي إثْبَاتِ هَذِهِ الصِّفَاتِ عَلَى مُجَرَّدِ السَّمْعِ وَيَقُولُونَ:
 إذَا كُنَّا نُثْبِتُ هَذِهِ الصِّفَاتِ بِنَاءً عَلَى نَفْيِ الْآفَاتِ وَنَفْيُ الْآفَاتِ إنَّمَا يَكُونُ بِالْإِجْمَاعِ الَّذِي هُوَ دَلِيلٌ سَمْعِيٌّ وَالْإِجْمَاعُ إنَّمَا يَثْبُتُ بِأَدِلَّةِ سَمْعِيَّةٍ مِنْ الْكِتَابِ
translated_text:
We have explained elsewhere that acknowledging the Creator and His perfection is innate and self-evident for those whose innate nature remains sound, although abundant evidence also establishes it. Many people may need such evidence when their innate nature has been altered or affected by various conditions.

As for the word “perfect,” al-Ash‘arī reported that al-Jubbā’ī objected to calling Allah perfect, saying that what is perfect has parts joined together. If this dispute concerns the meaning, it is invalid; if it concerns the wording, it is merely verbal. The point here is that His perfection and His freedom from deficiencies can be known through reason.

“A group of speculative theologians,” including Abū al-Ma‘ālī, al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī, and others, claimed that this can be known only through transmitted evidence, specifically “consensus,” and that His freedom from defects and deficiencies is known only through consensus. Their method for denying of Him what they denied consisted solely in denying that He falls under the designation “body,” and the like. They thus departed from the leading theologians who affirmed the divine attributes—such as al-Ash‘arī, Judge Abū Bakr, and Abū Ishāq—and from the early generations and leading scholars before them, who used rational evidence to affirm His hearing, sight, and speech, and to establish His freedom from deficiencies.

Consequently, these later theologians came to rely exclusively on transmitted evidence to affirm these attributes. They say:

If we affirm these attributes on the basis of His freedom from defects, and His freedom from defects is established only through consensus, which is a form of transmitted evidence, while consensus itself is established only through transmitted evidence from the Book

" مُجْمَلٌ "

" مُشْتَرِكٌ "
 وَأَنَّ الْمُسَمَّى بِهَذِهِ الْأَسْمَاءِ لَا يَجِب أَنْ يُمَاثِلَهُ غَيْرُهُ وَلَا أَنْ يَثْبُتَ لَهُ خَصَائِصُ غَيْرِهِ؛

translated_text:
and the Sunnah, they say:

“The texts affirming hearing, sight, and speech are far stronger than the verses establishing the authority of consensus. It is therefore more appropriate and fitting to establish these attributes directly through transmitted evidence, namely the Quran.”

Their basis for denying attributes—denying that He falls under the designation of occupying space and the like—is not only a religious innovation unsupported by the Book, the Sunnah, or any report from the Companions and Successors; it is also rationally inconsistent and untenable. For whenever someone denies something for fear that it would entail that the one possessing it is a body, the same objection can be raised against what he affirms, and the same answer he gives concerning what he affirms can be given concerning what he denies.

For example, the Muʿtazilah affirmed that He is Living, All-Knowing, and All-Powerful, yet said:

“He is not described as possessing life, knowledge, power, or attributes, because these are accidents, which can be attributed only to a body. No subject possessing attributes can be conceived except a body.”

They were answered:

“Yet you have described Him as Living, All-Knowing, and All-Powerful. Nothing can be described as knowing, living, and powerful unless it is a body, and nothing possessing these attributes can be conceived except a body. Whatever answer you give concerning the names is our answer concerning the attributes. If it is permissible to say, ‘Rather, these names may designate one who is not a body,’ then it is likewise permissible to say, ‘These attributes may describe one who is not a body,’ and to say, ‘These attributes are not accidents.’

“If it is said that the term ‘body’ is ambiguous or has several distinct meanings, and that the One designated by these names need not be like anything else or possess the distinctive characteristics of anything else, then it is permissible to say: ‘The One described by these attributes need not be like anything else or possess the distinctive characteristics of anything else.’”

original_text:
وَكَذَلِكَ إذَا قَالَ نفاة الصِّفَاتِ الْمَعْلُومَةِ بِالشَّرْعِ أَوْ بِالْعَقْلِ مَعَ الشَّرْعِ كَالرِّضَا وَالْغَضَبِ وَالْحُبِّ وَالْفَرَحِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ:
 هَذِهِ الصِّفَاتُ لَا تُعْقَلُ إلَّا لِجِسْمِ.
 قِيلَ لَهُمْ هَذِهِ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الْإِرَادَةِ وَالسَّمْعِ:
 وَالْبَصَرِ وَالْكَلَامِ فَمَا لَزِمَ فِي أَحَدِهِمَا لَزِمَ فِي الْآخَرِ مِثْلُهُ.
 وَهَكَذَا نفاة الصِّفَات مِنْ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ وَنَحْوِهِمْ إذَا قَالُوا ثُبُوتُ هَذِهِ الصِّفَاتِ يَسْتَلْزِمُ كَثْرَةَ الْمَعَانِي فِيهِ وَذَلِكَ يَسْتَلْزِمُ كَوْنَهُ جِسْمًا أَوْ مُرَكَّبًا قِيلَ لَهُمْ:
 هَذَا كَمَا أَثْبَتُّمْ أَنَّهُ مَوْجُودٌ وَاجِبٌ قَائِمٌ بِنَفْسِهِ وَأَنَّهُ عَاقِلٌ وَمَعْقُولٌ وَعَقْلٌ وَلَذِيذٌ وَمُلْتَذٌّ وَلَذَّةٌ وَعَاشِقٌ وَمَعْشُوقٌ وَعِشْقٌ وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ.
 فَإِنْ قَالُوا:
 هَذِهِ تَرْجِعُ إلَى مَعْنًى وَاحِدٍ قِيلَ لَهُمْ: إنْ كَانَ هَذَا مُمْتَنِعًا بَطَلَ الْفَرْقُ وَإِنْ كَانَ مُمْكِنًا أَمْكَنَ أَنْ يُقَالَ فِي تِلْكَ مِثْلُ هَذِهِ فَلَا فَرْقَ بَيْنَ صِفَةٍ وَصِفَةٍ. وَالْكَلَامُ عَلَى ثُبُوتِ الصِّفَاتِ وَبُطْلَانِ أَقْوَالِ الْنُّفَاةِ مَبْسُوطٌ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ.
 وَالْمَقْصُودُ هُنَا:
 أَنْ نُبَيِّنَ أَنَّ ثُبُوتَ الْكَمَالِ لِلَّهِ مَعْلُومٌ بِالْعَقْلِ وَأَنَّ نَقِيضَ ذَلِكَ مُنْتَفٍ عَنْهُ فَإِنَّ الِاعْتِمَادَ فِي الْإِثْبَاتِ وَالنَّفْيِ عَلَى هَذِهِ الطَّرِيقِ مُسْتَقِيمٌ فِي الْعَقْلِ وَالشَّرْعِ؛ دُونَ تِلْكَ خِلَافَ مَا قَالَهُ هَؤُلَاءِ الْمُتَكَلِّمُونَ.
وَجُمْهُورُ أَهْلِ الْفَلْسَفَةِ وَالْكَلَامِ:
 يُوَافِقُونَ عَلَى أَنَّ الْكَمَالَ لِلَّهِ ثَابِتٌ بِالْعَقْلِ وَالْفَلَاسِفَةُ تُسَمِّيهِ التَّمَامَ وَبَيَانُ ذَلِكَ مِنْ وُجُوهٍ:
translated_text:
Likewise, when those who deny the attributes known through revelation, or through reason together with revelation—such as pleasure, anger, love, joy, and the like—say:

“These attributes can only be conceived of as belonging to a body,”

they are answered:

“These are no different from will, hearing, sight, and speech. Whatever consequence follows in one case follows equally in the other.”

Similarly, when the philosophers and others who deny the attributes say, “Affirming these attributes entails a multiplicity of meanings in Him, which entails His being a body or a composite,” they are answered:

“This is no different from your affirming that He exists, necessarily exists, and subsists by Himself; that He understands, is understood, and is intellect; that He is delightful, experiences delight, and is delight; that He loves, is loved, and is love; and so forth.”

If they say, “These all amount to a single meaning,” they are answered:

“If this is impossible, the distinction collapses. If it is possible, the same can be said of those attributes as of these. Thus, there is no distinction between one attribute and another.”

The affirmation of the attributes and the refutation of those who deny them have been discussed at length elsewhere.

The purpose here is to explain that Allah’s perfection is known through reason, and that its opposite is excluded from Him. Relying on this approach, rather than the other, in affirmation and negation is sound according to both reason and revelation, contrary to what these speculative theologians have said.

Most philosophers and speculative theologians agree that Allah’s perfection is established through reason. The philosophers call it completeness. This may be explained in several ways:

One is to say:

It has been established that Allah is beginningless in Himself, necessarily existent in Himself, self-subsisting, and a Creator in His own right, among His other distinctive attributes. The familiar argument establishing necessary existence applies to all these meanings.

Thus, to say, “Existence is either necessary or contingent, and contingent existence requires necessary existence; therefore, necessary existence is established in either case,” is like saying: A being is either beginningless or originated, and an originated being requires a beginningless being; therefore, a beginningless being is established in either case. A being is either self-sufficient or dependent, and a dependent being requires a self-sufficient being; therefore, a self-sufficient being exists in either case. A being is either self-subsisting or not self-subsisting, and whatever is not self-subsisting requires one that is; therefore, a self-subsisting being is established in either case. A being is either created or uncreated, and a created being requires an uncreated Creator; therefore, an uncreated Creator is established in either case. There are many similar arguments.

It is then said:

Either this necessary, beginningless Creator can possess the perfection, free of deficiency, that a contingent being can possess, or He cannot. The latter is impossible, because such perfection is possible for an originated, dependent, contingent being. It must therefore be all the more possible for the necessary, self-sufficient, beginningless Being, since both exist. What is under discussion is perfection whose existence is possible and which involves no deficiency. If such perfection is possible for the lesser being, it must be all the more possible for the greater. It is therefore impossible for what is inferior in every respect to possess exclusively a perfection that does not belong to what is superior in every respect. Rather, whatever such perfection belongs to the inferior, the superior is more entitled to possess; it must therefore belong to the superior with all the more reason. Moreover, the creature acquires that perfection only from the Creator, and the One who makes another perfect is more entitled to perfection than that other. Thus, He who grants another power is more entitled to power; He who imparts knowledge to another is more entitled to knowledge; and He who gives another life is more entitled to life.

The philosophers agree with this and say:

“Every perfection in an effect derives from its cause, and the cause is more entitled to that perfection.”

Once it is established that such perfection is possible for Him, whatever of this potentially existent perfection is possible for Him belongs to Him necessarily, without depending on anything else. For if it depended on something else, He would possess it only through that other. If that other were His creation, this would entail the impossible “circular causal dependence,” since whatever exists in that other derives from Him. It is impossible for each of two things to be the cause of the other: this is “circular causal dependence.” Since a thing cannot be its own cause, it is all the more impossible for it to be the cause of its own cause.

Likewise, it is impossible for each of two things to produce that which enables the other to act as a cause. Nor can each of two things bestow perfection upon the other, for the giver of perfection is more entitled to perfection. This would require each to be more perfect than the other, which is intrinsically impossible. It would mean that this one is superior to that one, while that one is superior to this one. Yet the superiority of either precludes the other from being its equal, and therefore all the more certainly precludes the other from being superior to it.

Moreover, if His perfection depended on that other, it would follow that His perfection depended on His bringing that other into being and on that other’s assistance in perfecting Him. Yet that other’s assistance in perfecting Him depends on Him, since both its being brought into existence and its actions depend on the Originator’s action and require no one else. It therefore follows that His perfection does not depend on anyone else.

Thus, to say that His perfection depends on His creation entails that it does not depend on His creation. Whatever entails its own negation is inherently false. Furthermore, every perfection possessed by that other comes from Him, and He is more entitled to perfection than it is. Even if His perfection were said to depend on it, His perfection would depend only on what comes from Himself; and that depends on Him, not on anyone else.

If it is said, “That other is not created, but is another necessarily existent being, eternal in its own right,” the reply is: If one of these two is the giver, and not the other way round, then that one is the Lord and the other is His servant.

If it is said, “Rather, each gives perfection to the other,” this entails “circularity in causation,” which is impossible. This is “circular dependence involving causal priority,” not “simultaneous, correlative dependence.” For the first cannot be perfect until the other makes it perfect, while the other cannot make it perfect until it is itself perfect, since whoever makes something perfect is more entitled to perfection. Yet the other cannot be perfect until the first makes it perfect. Necessarily, therefore, neither can be perfect. For if it were said that something cannot be perfect until it makes itself perfect, and cannot make itself perfect until it is perfect, that would be impossible. How much more so if it were said that it cannot be perfect until it makes perfect that which makes it perfect!

of efficient causes,” which is self-evidently invalid, as all rational people agree.

For positing an endless series of causes, none of which acts independently, does not entail the existence of any one of them, of them all, or of their combination. The Originator of existing things must necessarily exist. Thus, if this one were assumed to be perfect, its perfection would come not from itself but from another, and so on. It would follow that none of these things possessed any perfection. Yet assuming the first to be perfect would entail affirming two contradictories together.

If His perfection is intrinsic and does not depend on another, then perfection is intrinsically necessary for Him, and He cannot lack any perfection possible for Him. Rather, whatever perfection is possible for Him is necessary for Him, as the majority of jurists, hadith scholars, Sufis, theologians, philosophers, and others have acknowledged. Indeed, this holds even for the effects He produces: whatever He wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be, being impossible either in itself or because of another.

Thus, there is only that which exists necessarily, either in itself or through another, or that which does not exist, either on account of its own nature or on account of another. If the complete cause of a contingent thing is present, it becomes necessary through another; otherwise, it is impossible because of another. What is contingent in itself is therefore either necessary through another or impossible because of another.

Allah, glorified be He, has made clear that He is more entitled to perfection than anyone else, and that no one else equals Him in perfection, in such statements as His saying, Most High:

“Is He who creates like one who does not create? Will you not then take heed?”

He has thus made clear that creating is an attribute of perfection, that one who creates is superior to one who does not create, and that whoever equates the two has committed injustice.

He thus makes clear that being owned and powerless is a deficiency, whereas power, ownership, and beneficence are attributes of perfection, and that the two are not alike. These perfections belong to Allah, while those deficiencies belong to what is worshipped besides Him.

And He, Most High, says:

“Allah sets forth another parable: two men, one of whom is mute, unable to do anything, and a burden on his master. Wherever he sends him, he brings back no good. Is he equal to one who commands justice and follows a straight path?”

This is another parable. The first represents one who is incapable of speech or action and has no power over anything. The other speaks, commands justice, and follows a straight path: he is just in his commands and upright in his actions. He thus makes clear that superiority lies in speech that embodies justice and in upright action. For speech and action in themselves may be either praiseworthy or blameworthy. What is praiseworthy is that for which a person deserves praise; such a person is not equal to one who is incapable of speech and action.

And He, Most High, says:

“He sets forth for you a parable drawn from your own lives: do you have, among those whom your right hands possess, any partners who share equally in what We have provided for you, so that you fear them as you fear one another? Thus do We explain the signs for people who reason.”

He, Most High, is saying: If you yourselves are unwilling for a slave to share equally with his owner, because of the deficiency and injustice this entails, how can you accept that for Me, when I am more entitled to perfection and self-sufficiency than you?

This shows that He, Most High, is more entitled to every perfection than anyone else. This is like His saying:

“When one of them is given news of a daughter, his face darkens as he suppresses his grief.”

“He hides himself from his people because of the bad news he has received. Should he keep her in humiliation or bury her in the dust? Evil indeed is their judgment!”

“Those who do not believe in the Hereafter have evil attributes, whereas Allah has the highest attributes. And He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

“If Allah were to take people to task for their wrongdoing, He would not leave a single living creature on earth. But He grants them respite until an appointed time. When their time comes, they can neither delay it for a moment nor bring it forward.”

“They assign to Allah what they themselves dislike, and their tongues falsely claim that the best reward will be theirs. Without doubt, theirs will be the Fire, and they will be abandoned there.”

For they used to say, “The angels are Allah’s daughters,” yet they disliked any one of them having a daughter, regarding this as a deficiency and a disgrace. The Lord, Most High, has a greater right than you to be declared free of every fault and deficiency, for His are “the highest attributes.” Thus, every perfection established for a created being belongs more rightly to the Creator, provided that it is free of deficiency. And every deficiency or fault from which a created being is held to be free is something from which the Creator has an even greater right to be declared free.

And He, Most High, says:

“Are those who know equal to those who do not know?”

This shows that one who knows is more perfect than one who does not know.

And He, Most High, says:

“The blind and the seeing are not equal,”

“nor are darkness and light,”

“nor shade and scorching heat.”

He thus makes clear that one who sees is more perfect, that light is more perfect, and that shade is more perfect. Accordingly, one endowed with such perfection is more worthy. “And to Allah belong the highest attributes.”

And He, Most High, says:

“After Moses had departed, his people made from their ornaments a calf—a body that lowed. Did they not see that it neither spoke to them nor guided them to any way? They took it for worship and were wrongdoers.”

that not speaking or giving guidance is a deficiency, and that one who speaks and guides is more perfect than one who neither speaks nor guides. The Lord has the greatest right to perfection.

And He, Most High, says:

“Say, ‘Can any of your partners guide to the truth?’ Say, ‘Allah guides to the truth.’ Is one who guides to the truth more worthy of being followed, or one who cannot find guidance unless he is guided? What is the matter with you? How do you judge?”

Thus, on the basis of what is firmly established in people’s innate nature, He, glorified be He, makes clear that one who guides to the truth is more worthy of being followed than one who cannot find guidance unless someone else guides him. It follows that the one who guides independently is the one who is perfect, unlike the one who finds guidance only through another. Since there must be a guide for anyone who cannot find guidance independently, that guide is the more perfect.

And He, Most High, says in another verse:

“Did they not see that it did not respond to them and had no power to harm or benefit them?”

This indicates that one who responds and has power to harm and benefit is more perfect than it.

And Abraham said to his father:

“O my father, why do you worship something that neither hears nor sees, nor benefits you in any way?”

This indicates that one who hears, sees, and is self-sufficient is more perfect, and that the one who is worshipped must possess these qualities. There are many similar passages in the Quran describing idols as lacking “attributes of perfection,” such as speech, action, life, and the like. These passages make clear that anything characterized by such deficiencies is deficient and flawed, like all other inanimate things, and that these attributes are absent only from something deficient and flawed.

translated_text:
As for the “Lord of creation,” who is more perfect than every other existent being, He has the greatest right to the attributes of perfection. One who possesses the attributes of perfection is not equal to one who does not. He also points out that inanimate things are ordinarily incapable of possessing these attributes. Whoever holds that the Necessary Existent cannot possess such attributes has therefore placed Him in the same category as the lifeless idols that Allah, Most High, condemned, along with their worshippers. This is why the “esoteric Qarmatians” were among those most deeply engaged in associating partners with Allah and worshipping others besides Him: they did not believe that their god heard, saw, or could benefit them in any way.

Allah, glorified be He, did not mention these passages merely to establish His attributes of perfection. Rather, He mentioned them to show that He alone deserves worship. Thus He established (the two foundations through which monotheism is complete: affirming the attributes of perfection, in refutation of those who deny Allah or His attributes; and explaining that He alone deserves worship—none has the right to be worshipped but Him—in refutation of the polytheists.

Associating partners with Allah is more widespread in the world than denial. Establishing “monotheism,” which excludes associating partners with Allah, does not necessarily invalidate the position of the deniers. Nor does mere affirmation that invalidates the deniers’ position refute the polytheists without a further explanation. The Quran sometimes refutes the deniers, as in its refutation of Pharaoh and others like him. It also refutes the polytheists, and this occurs more frequently, because the Quran is a cure for what is in people’s hearts, and the disease of associating partners with Allah is more prevalent among people than the disease of denial. Moreover, Allah, glorified be He,

has declared that all praise belongs to Him, that He is Praiseworthy and Glorious, that all praise belongs to Him in this world and the Hereafter, and that judgment belongs to Him, along with other expressions of praise.

“Praise is of two kinds”: praise for His kindness to His servants, which is a form of gratitude; and praise for the attributes of perfection for which He is intrinsically deserving of praise. This latter praise is only for what is intrinsically praiseworthy, and only one endowed with attributes of perfection deserves it. These are positive realities, for mere absences contain nothing praiseworthy, good, or perfect.

It is well known that whatever is praised is praised only for the attributes of perfection it possesses. Every quality for which created beings are praised comes from the Creator, and the One from whom those praiseworthy qualities come is more deserving of praise. It is thus established that He deserves perfect praise, that He is more deserving of praise than any other who is praised, and of perfection than any other who possesses perfection. This is what was to be demonstrated.
