translated_text:
Section

As for the “second premise,” we say that two conditions must be considered:

First, the perfection must be possible.

Second, it must be free of imperfection, for imperfection is impossible for Allah. Some people, however, may call something an imperfection when it is not. Such a person should be told: What must be affirmed is whatever perfection can possibly exist and is free of imperfection. If you call this an imperfection, and suppose that its absence is impossible, then removing it would not constitute a possible perfection. Nor, even for someone who calls it an imperfection, would it be an imperfection that could possibly be absent.

If it is said, “Creating all created things from eternity is an attribute of perfection and must therefore be affirmed of Him,” the reply is: It is impossible for all created things—or any one of them that entails all temporal events or even a single such event—to exist from eternity. It is impossible for successive temporal events all to exist at a single instant, whether that instant is assumed to be in the past or the future, let alone to be eternal. Whatever entails successive temporal events cannot exist at a single instant, let alone be eternal. This, then, is not even possible, much less a perfection.

Yet bringing events about one after another is more perfect than being devoid of such action, such that He brings nothing into existence that did not previously exist. For an agent capable of acting is more perfect than an agent incapable of acting.

translated_text:
Thus, if it is said, “He cannot bring events about; rather, what He produces is inseparable from His essence,” this would be an imperfection compared with one who has the power to act and does one thing after another.

Likewise, if it is said, “Making one and the same thing moving and motionless, existent and nonexistent, is an attribute of perfection,” the reply is: This is intrinsically impossible.

Likewise, if it is said, “Bringing into being something eternal whose existence is necessary in itself is an attribute of perfection,” the reply is: This is intrinsically impossible. For its being brought into being entails that its existence is not necessary in itself, but necessary through another. To say that it necessarily exists through itself, yet was brought into existence only through another, is to affirm two contradictories together.

Likewise, if it is said, “As for the acts subsisting in Him and the effects distinct from Him: if His being characterized by them is an attribute of perfection, then He lacked them from eternity; and if it is an attribute of imperfection, then He must be characterized by imperfections,” the reply is: It is impossible for each of the acts dependent on His will and power to be eternal.

Moreover, their existence from eternity need not be an attribute of perfection. Rather, perfection consists in their existing when wisdom requires their existence.

Furthermore, if they were eternal, they would not come into existence one after another. Thus, to say of things whose proper mode of existence is to come into being one after another, “They ought to exist from eternity,” is to affirm two contradictories together. There are many similar examples.

This is why we said, “perfection whose existence is possible.” Whatever is intrinsically impossible has no reality, let alone can it be said to exist or to be a perfection of an existent being.

 كَانَ نَاقِصًا عَنْ الْقَابِلِ لِهَذَا الْكَمَالِ؛ لَكِنَّ هَذَا يَسْتَلْزِمُ حَاجَةَ الْآكِلِ وَالشَّارِبِ إلَى غَيْرِهِ وَهُوَ مَا يَدْخُلُ فِيهِ مِنْ الطَّعَامِ وَالشَّرَابِ وَهُوَ مُسْتَلْزِمٌ لِخُرُوجِ شَيْءٍ مِنْهُ كَالْفَضَلَاتِ وَمَا لَا يَحْتَاجُ إلَى دُخُولِ شَيْءٍ فِيهِ أَكْمَلُ مِمَّنْ يَحْتَاجُ إلَى دُخُولِ شَيْءٍ فِيهِ وَمَا يَتَوَقَّفُ كَمَالِهِ عَلَى غَيْرِهِ أَنْقَصُ مِمَّا لَا يَحْتَاجُ فِي كَمَالِهِ إلَى غَيْرِهِ فَإِنَّ الْغَنِيَّ عَنْ شَيْءٍ أَعْلَى مِنْ الْغَنِيِّ بِهِ. وَالْغَنِيُّ بِنَفْسِهِ أَكْمَلُ مِنْ الْغَنِيِّ بِغَيْرِهِ. وَلِهَذَا كَانَ مِنْ الكمالات مَا هُوَ كَمَالٌ لِلْمَخْلُوقِ وَهُوَ نَقْصٌ بِالنِّسْبَةِ إلَى الْخَالِقِ وَهُوَ كُلُّ مَا كَانَ مُسْتَلْزِمًا لِإِمْكَانِ الْعَدَمِ عَلَيْهِ الْمُنَافِي لِوُجُوبِهِ وقيوميته أَوْ مُسْتَلْزِمًا لِلْحُدُوثِ الْمُنَافِي لِقِدَمِهِ أَوْ مُسْتَلْزِمًا لِفَقْرِهِ الْمُنَافِي لِغِنَاهُ.
translated_text:
As for the other condition, expressed in our words, “perfection that entails no imperfection”—to use the accurate formulation—or “perfection that entails no imperfection whose absence is possible,” in the terminology of those who regard as imperfection what is not in fact imperfection: this excludes what constitutes perfection for some created beings but not others, yet is an imperfection in relation to the Creator because it entails imperfection. Eating and drinking are examples. A healthy animal with an appetite for food and drink is more perfect than a sick one without such an appetite, because its continued existence depends on eating and drinking.

If it were assumed to lack the capacity for this, it would be less perfect than one capable of this perfection. Yet this entails that the one who eats and drinks needs something other than itself, namely the food and drink that enter it. This, in turn, entails that something must leave it, such as waste. A being that needs nothing to enter it is more perfect than one that does, and a being whose perfection depends on another is less perfect than one that needs no other for its perfection. For one who has no need of a thing is superior to one whose sufficiency depends upon it, and one who is sufficient in himself is more perfect than one whose sufficiency comes from another.

Thus, some perfections constitute perfection for a created being but imperfection in relation to the Creator. These include anything that entails the possibility of His nonexistence, which is incompatible with His necessary existence and self-subsistence; anything that entails His having come into existence, which is incompatible with His beginninglessness; or anything that entails His need, which is incompatible with His self-sufficiency.

Once this is clear, it becomes evident that what the “Messenger” brought is the truth to which reason points, and that those with the strongest claim to the truth are those who follow him most closely and conform most fully to his teachings—“namely, the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars”—who affirmed the attributes indicated by the Book and the Sunnah and declared Allah free of any likeness to created beings.

Life, knowledge, power, hearing, sight, and speech are attributes of perfection whose possibility is self-evident and which involve no imperfection. Whoever possesses these attributes is more perfect than one who does not. Imperfection lies in their absence, not their presence. A being capable of possessing them, such as an animal, is more perfect than one incapable of possessing them, such as an inanimate object.

Those who affirm the attributes say to those who deny them: “If He did not possess these attributes, He would possess their opposites: ignorance, muteness, blindness, and deafness.”

Those who deny the attributes reply: “These attributes stand in the opposition of privation and possession, not that of negation and affirmation. Those who affirm the attributes reply:

“This is false for several reasons. First, existing things are of ‘two kinds’: those capable of possessing perfection, such as living beings, and those incapable of it, such as inanimate objects. It is well known that whatever is capable of possessing attributes of perfection is more perfect than whatever is incapable of them.

“Thus, if the Lord were incapable of possessing attributes of perfection, it would follow that He lacks them, and that a being capable of them—namely, a blind, deaf animal that cannot possess hearing or sight—would be more perfect than He. For a being capable of hearing and sight, even while lacking them, is more perfect than one incapable of them. How much more so, then, is one that actually possesses them! Their position would therefore entail that He is devoid of the attributes of perfection and that possessing them is impossible for Him.

“You have fled from likening Him to living beings, only to liken Him to inanimate objects! You claim to declare Him free of imperfections, yet you have described Him in terms of the greatest imperfection.

‘Those they invoke besides Allah create nothing, while they themselves are created.’

‘They are dead, not alive, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.’

translated_text:
The third reason is as follows:

The very absence of these attributes is an imperfection, even if no positively existing opposite is posited. We know necessarily that a being that is living, knowing, powerful, speaking, hearing and seeing is more perfect than one that is not, even if the latter, like an inanimate object, is described as neither hearing nor deaf. Since possessing these attributes is itself a perfection, and lacking them is itself an imperfection, they must be affirmed of Allah, Exalted is He. For this is a perfection possible for an existing being, involving no imperfection whatsoever; rather, the imperfection lies in its absence.

Likewise, suppose we consider two beings possessing these attributes: one can act himself—coming, going, descending, ascending and performing other such acts that subsist in him—whereas the other is incapable of this, so that none of these acts can proceed from him. The one capable of performing these acts is more perfect than the one for whom they are impossible.

If it is said, “For these acts to subsist in Him entails that temporally originated events subsist in Him,” this is like saying, “For attributes to subsist in Him entails that accidents subsist in Him.”

The terms “accidents” and “temporally originated events” are both ambiguous. If what is intended is what speakers of the language understand by them, namely illnesses and afflictions—as when one says, “So-and-so has been afflicted with a severe illness,” or “So-and-so has committed a grave offense,” as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Beware of newly introduced matters, for every newly introduced matter is an innovation, and every innovation is misguidance.”

 مِنْ أَهْلِ الْقِبْلَةِ: كَالرِّبَا وَالسَّرِقَةِ وَشُرْبِ الْخَمْرِ. وَيُقَالُ فُلَانٌ بِهِ عَارِضٌ مِنْ الْجِنِّ وَفُلَانٌ حَدَثَ لَهُ مَرَضٌ. فَهَذِهِ مِنْ النَّقَائِصِ الَّتِي يُنَزَّهُ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا. وَإِنْ أُرِيدَ بِالْأَعْرَاضِ وَالْحَوَادِثِ اصْطِلَاحٌ خَاصٌّ فَإِنَّمَا أَحْدَثَ ذَلِكَ الِاصْطِلَاحَ مَنْ أَحْدَثَهُ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكَلَامِ وَلَيْسَتْ هَذِهِ لُغَةَ الْعَرَبِ وَلَا لُغَةَ أَحَدٍ مِنْ الْأُمَمِ؛ لَا لُغَةَ الْقُرْآنِ وَلَا غَيْرِهِ؛ وَلَا الْعُرْفِ الْعَامِّ وَلَا اصْطِلَاحِ أَكْثَرِ الْخَائِضِينَ فِي الْعِلْمِ؛
 بَلْ مُبْتَدِعُو هَذَا الِاصْطِلَاحِ:
 هُمْ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ المحدثين فِي الْأُمَّةِ الدَّاخِلِينَ فِي ذَمِّ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ.
 وَبِكُلِّ حَالٍ فَمُجَرَّدُ هَذَا الِاصْطِلَاحِ وَتَسْمِيَةُ هَذِهِ أَعْرَاضًا وَحَوَادِثَ:
 لَا يُخْرِجُهَا عَنْ أَنَّهَا مِنْ الْكَمَالِ الَّذِي يَكُونُ الْمُتَّصِفُ بِهِ أَكْمَلَ مِمَّنْ لَا يُمْكِنُهُ الِاتِّصَافُ بِهَا. أَوْ يُمْكِنُهُ ذَلِكَ وَلَا يَتَّصِفُ بِهِ. وَ 
" أَيْضًا "
 فَإِذَا قُدِّرَ اثْنَانِ أَحَدُهُمَا مَوْصُوفٌ بِصِفَاتِ الْكَمَالِ الَّتِي هِيَ أَعْرَاضٌ وَحَوَادِثُ عَلَى اصْطِلَاحِهِمْ؛
 كَالْعِلْمِ وَالْقُدْرَةِ وَالْفِعْلِ وَالْبَطْشِ وَالْآخَرُ يَمْتَنِعُ أَنْ يَتَّصِفَ بِهَذِهِ الصِّفَاتِ الَّتِي هِيَ أَعْرَاضُ وَحَوَادِثُ:
 كَانَ الْأَوَّلُ أَكْمَلَ كَمَا أَنَّ الْحَيَّ الْمُتَّصِفَ بِهَذِهِ الصِّفَاتِ: أَكْمَلُ مِنْ الْجَمَادَاتِ.
translated_text:
and he said:

“Allah has cursed whoever commits an offense or shelters an offender.”

He also said:

“If any one of you enters a state of ritual impurity, he must not pray until he performs ablution.”

The jurists say: Purification is of “two kinds”: purification from ritual impurity and purification from physical impurity. The speculative theologians say: People have differed concerning “those guilty of offenses” among those who face the qiblah—offenses such as usury, theft, and drinking wine. People also say, “So-and-so suffers from an affliction caused by the jinn,” and “So-and-so has developed an illness.” These are imperfections from which Allah is exalted far above.

If, however, “accidents” and “temporally originated events” are intended in a particular technical sense, that terminology was introduced only by those speculative theologians who coined it. It is neither the language of the Arabs nor that of any other nation; neither the language of the Quran nor of anything else; neither common usage nor the terminology of most who engage in scholarly inquiry. Rather, the inventors of this terminology are among those who introduce religious innovations into the Muslim community and fall under the Prophet’s condemnation, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

In any event, merely adopting this terminology and calling these attributes “accidents” and “temporally originated events” does not prevent them from being perfections whose possessor is more perfect than one who cannot possibly possess them, or who can possess them but does not.

“Furthermore,” suppose there are two beings: one possesses attributes of perfection which, according to their terminology, are accidents and temporally originated events—such as knowledge, power, action, and the exercise of force—while the other cannot possibly possess these attributes, which they call accidents and temporally originated events. The first would be more perfect, just as a living being possessing these attributes is more perfect than inanimate objects.

original_text:
وَكَذَلِكَ إذَا قُدِّرَ 
" اثْنَانِ "
 أَحَدُهُمَا يُحِبُّ نُعُوتَ الْكَمَالِ وَيَفْرَحُ بِهَا وَيَرْضَاهَا وَالْآخَرُ لَا فَرْقَ عِنْدَهُ بَيْنَ صِفَاتِ الْكَمَالِ وَصِفَاتِ النَّقْصِ؛
 فَلَا يُحِبُّ لَا هَذَا وَلَا هَذَا وَلَا يَرْضَى لَا هَذَا وَلَا هَذَا وَلَا يَفْرَحُ لَا بِهَذَا وَلَا بِهَذَا:
 كَانَ الْأَوَّلُ أَكْمَلَ مِنْ الثَّانِي. وَمَعْلُومٌ أَنَّ اللَّهَ تَبَارَكَ وَتَعَالَى يُحِبُّ الْمُحْسِنِينَ وَالْمُتَّقِينَ وَالصَّابِرِينَ وَالْمُقْسِطِينَ وَيَرْضَى عَنْ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ وَهَذِهِ كُلُّهَا صِفَاتُ كَمَالٍ.
 وَكَذَلِكَ إذَا قُدِّرَ اثْنَانِ:
 أَحَدُهُمَا بِبَعْضِ الْمُتَّصِفِ بِضِدِّ الْكَمَالِ كَالظُّلْمِ وَالْجَهْلِ وَالْكَذِبِ وَيَغْضَبُ عَلَى مَنْ يَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ وَالْآخَرُ لَا فَرْقَ عِنْدَهُ بَيْنَ الْجَاهِلِ الْكَاذِبِ الظَّالِمِ وَبَيْنَ الْعَالِمِ الصَّادِقِ الْعَادِلِ لَا يُبْغِضُ لَا هَذَا وَلَا هَذَا وَلَا يَغْضَبُ لَا عَلَى هَذَا وَلَا عَلَى هَذَا: كَانَ الْأَوَّلُ أَكْمَلَ. وَكَذَلِكَ إذَا قُدِّرَ اثْنَانِ أَحَدُهُمَا يَقْدِرُ أَنْ يَفْعَلَ بِيَدَيْهِ وَيُقْبِلَ بِوَجْهِهِ.
 وَالْآخَرُ لَا يُمْكِنُهُ ذَلِكَ:
 إمَّا لِامْتِنَاعِ أَنْ يَكُونَ لَهُ وَجْهٌ وَيَدَانِ وَإِمَّا لِامْتِنَاعِ الْفِعْلِ وَالْإِقْبَالِ عَلَيْهِ بِالْيَدَيْنِ وَالْوَجْهِ: كَانَ الْأَوَّلُ أَكْمَلَ.
 فَالْوَجْهُ وَالْيَدَانِ:
 لَا يُعَدَّانِ مِنْ صِفَاتِ النَّقْصِ فِي شَيْءٍ مِمَّا يُوصَفُ بِذَلِكَ وَوَجْهُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ بِحَسَبِ مَا يُضَافُ إلَيْهِ وَهُوَ مَمْدُوحٌ بِهِ لَا مَذْمُومٌ كَوَجْهِ النَّهَارِ وَوَجْهِ الثَّوْبِ وَوَجْهِ الْقَوْمِ وَوَجْهِ الْخَيْلِ وَوَجْهِ الرَّأْيِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ؛ وَلَيْسَ الْوَجْهُ الْمُضَافُ إلَى غَيْرِهِ هُوَ نَفْسُ الْمُضَافِ إلَيْهِ فِي شَيْءٍ مِنْ مَوَارِدِ الِاسْتِعْمَالِ سَوَاءٌ قُدِّرَ الِاسْتِعْمَالُ حَقِيقَةً أَوْ مَجَازًا.
translated_text:
Likewise, suppose there are “two beings”: one loves attributes of perfection, rejoices in them, and is pleased with them; the other makes no distinction between attributes of perfection and attributes of imperfection, neither loving, being pleased with, nor rejoicing in either. The first would be more perfect than the second. It is well known that Allah, blessed and exalted, loves those who do good, the God-fearing, the patient, and the just, and is pleased with those who believe and do righteous deeds. All these are attributes of perfection.

Likewise, suppose there are two beings: one [hates] those characterized by the opposite of perfection, such as injustice, ignorance, and lying, and becomes angry with those who do such things. The other makes no distinction between the ignorant, lying wrongdoer and the knowledgeable, truthful, just person, neither hating nor becoming angry with either. The first would be more perfect.

Likewise, suppose there are two beings: one can act with his two hands and turn toward something with his face, while the other cannot—either because it is impossible for him to have a face and two hands, or because acting with two hands and turning with a face are impossible for him. The first would be more perfect.

Thus, a face and two hands are not considered attributes of imperfection in anything described as possessing them. The face of each thing is appropriate to that to which it is ascribed, and possessing it is a matter of praise, not disparagement. Examples include the use of “face” for the beginning of the day, the face of a garment, the foremost among a people, the foremost among horses, the aspect of an opinion, and so forth. In no instance of usage is the “face” ascribed to something identical with the thing to which it is ascribed, whether that usage is regarded as literal or figurative.

original_text:
" فَإِنْ قِيلَ "
: مَنْ يُمْكِنُهُ الْفِعْلُ بِكَلَامِهِ أَوْ بِقُدْرَتِهِ بِدُونِ يَدَيْهِ أَكْمَلُ مِمَّنْ يَفْعَلُ بِيَدَيْهِ.
 قِيلَ:
 مَنْ يُمْكِنُهُ الْفِعْلُ بِقُدْرَتِهِ أَوْ تَكْلِيمِهِ إذَا شَاءَ وَبِيَدَيْهِ إذَا شَاءَ: هُوَ أَكْمَلُ مِمَّنْ لَا يُمْكِنُهُ الْفِعْلُ إلَّا بِقُدْرَتِهِ أَوْ تَكْلِيمِهِ وَلَا يُمْكِنُهُ أَنْ يَفْعَلَ بِالْيَدِ. وَلِهَذَا كَانَ 
" الْإِنْسَانُ "
 أَكْمَلَ مِنْ الْجَمَادَاتِ الَّتِي تَفْعَلُ بِقُوَى فِيهَا كَالنَّارِ وَالْمَاءِ فَإِذَا قُدِّرَ اثْنَانِ أَحَدُهُمَا لَا يُمْكِنُهُ الْفِعْلُ إلَّا بِقُوَّةِ فِيهِ وَالْآخَرُ يُمْكِنُهُ الْفِعْلُ بِقُوَّةِ فِيهِ وَبِكَلَامِهِ فَهَذَا أَكْمَلُ. فَإِذَا قُدِّرَ آخَرُ يَفْعَلُ بِقُوَّةِ فِيهِ وَبِكَلَامِهِ وَبِيَدَيْهِ إذَا شَاءَ فَهُوَ أَكْمَلُ وَأَكْمَلُ وَأَمَّا صِفَاتُ النَّقْصِ فَمِثْلَ النَّوْمِ فَإِنَّ الْحَيَّ الْيَقْظَانَ أَكْمَلُ مِنْ النَّائِمِ وَالْوَسْنَانِ. وَاَللَّهُ لَا تَأْخُذُهُ سِنَةٌ وَلَا نَوْمٌ وَكَذَلِكَ مَنْ يَحْفَظُ الشَّيْءَ بِلَا اكْتِرَاثٍ أَكْمَلُ مِمَّنْ يَكْرُثُهُ ذَلِكَ؛ وَاَللَّهُ تَعَالَى وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَلَا يَئُودُهُ حِفْظُهُمَا.
 وَكَذَلِكَ مَنْ يَفْعَلُ وَلَا يَتْعَبُ:
 أَكْمَلُ مِمَّنْ يَتْعَبُ. وَاَللَّهُ تَعَالَى خَلَقَ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا فِي سِتَّةِ أَيَّامٍ وَمَا مَسَّهُ مِنْ لُغُوبٍ. وَلِهَذَا وُصِفَ الرَّبُّ بِالْعِلْمِ دُونَ الْجَهْلِ وَالْقُدْرَةِ دُونَ الْعَجْزِ وَالْحَيَاةِ دُونَ الْمَوْتِ وَالسَّمْعِ وَالْبَصَرِ وَالْكَلَامِ دُونَ الصَّمَمِ وَالْعَمَى وَالْبُكْمِ وَالضَّحِكِ دُونَ الْبُكَاءِ وَالْفَرَحِ دُونَ الْحُزْنِ.
translated_text:
If it is said, “One who can act through his speech or power without using his two hands is more perfect than one who acts with his two hands,” the reply is:

One who can act through his power or speech whenever he wills, and with his two hands whenever he wills, is more perfect than one who can act only through his power or speech and cannot act with a hand. For this reason, the human being is more perfect than inanimate things, such as fire and water, which act through forces within them. Suppose there are two beings: one can act only through a force within him, while the other can act both through a force within him and through his speech. The latter is more perfect. If we then suppose another who acts through a force within him, through his speech, and with his two hands whenever he wills, he is more perfect still.

As for attributes of imperfection, sleep is one example: a living being who is awake is more perfect than one who is asleep or drowsy. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Allah. Likewise, one who preserves something without being burdened is more perfect than one who is burdened by doing so. Allah Most High—His Kursī (Footstool) encompasses the heavens and the earth, and preserving them does not burden Him.

Likewise, one who acts without growing weary is more perfect than one who grows weary. Allah Most High created the heavens and the earth and all that is between them in six days, and no weariness touched Him. Thus, the Lord is described in terms of knowledge, not ignorance; power, not inability; life, not death; hearing, sight, and speech, not deafness, blindness, and muteness; laughter, not weeping; and joy, not sorrow.

original_text:
وَأَمَّا الْغَضَبُ مَعَ الرِّضَا وَالْبُغْضُ مَعَ الْحُبِّ فَهُوَ أَكْمَلُ مِمَّنْ لَا يَكُونُ مِنْهُ إلَّا الرِّضَا وَالْحُبُّ دُونَ الْبُغْضِ وَالْغَضَبُ لِلْأُمُورِ الْمَذْمُومَةِ الَّتِي تَسْتَحِقُّ أَنْ تُذَمَّ وَتُبْغَضَ.
 وَلِهَذَا كَانَ اتِّصَافُهُ بِأَنَّهُ يُعْطِي وَيَمْنَعُ وَيَخْفِضُ وَيَرْفَعُ وَيُعِزُّ وَيُذِلُّ:
 أَكْمَلَ مِنْ اتِّصَافِهِ بِمُجَرَّدِ الْإِعْطَاءِ وَالْإِعْزَازِ وَالرَّفْعِ؛ لِأَنَّ الْفِعْلَ الْآخَرَ - حَيْثُ تَقْتَضِي الْحِكْمَةُ ذَلِكَ - أَكْمَلُ مِمَّا لَا يَفْعَلُ إلَّا أَحَدَ النَّوْعَيْنِ وَيُخِلُّ بِالْآخَرِ فِي الْمَحَلِّ الْمُنَاسِبِ لَهُ وَمَنْ اعْتَبَرَ هَذَا الْبَابَ وَجَدَهُ عَلَى قَانُونِ الصَّوَابِ وَاَللَّهُ الْهَادِي لِأُولِي الْأَلْبَابِ.
translated_text:
As for anger alongside pleasure and hatred alongside love, one who possesses these attributes is more perfect than one who shows only pleasure and love, without hatred or anger toward blameworthy things that deserve condemnation and hatred.

For this reason, His being described as giving and withholding, lowering and raising, honoring and humiliating is more perfect than His being described merely as giving, honoring, and raising. For one who also performs the opposite action—when wisdom calls for it—is more perfect than one who performs only one of the two kinds of action and fails to perform the other where it is fitting. Whoever reflects on this subject will find it in accord with sound judgment. And Allah guides those endowed with understanding.

original_text:
فَصْلٌ:
وَأَمَّا قَوْلُ مَلَاحِدَةِ 
" الْمُتَفَلْسِفَةِ "
 وَغَيْرِهِمْ: إنَّ اتِّصَافَهُ بِهَذِهِ الصِّفَاتِ إنْ أَوْجَبَ لَهُ كَمَالًا فَقَدْ اُسْتُكْمِلَ بِغَيْرِهِ فَيَكُونُ نَاقِصًا بِذَاتِهِ وَإِنْ أَوْجَبَ لَهُ نَقْصًا لَمْ يَجُزْ اتِّصَافُهُ بِهَا.
 فَيُقَالُ:

As for the claim made by the heretical “philosophers” and others: “If His possessing these attributes entails perfection for Him, then He has been perfected by something other than Himself and is therefore deficient in Himself. But if it entails deficiency for Him, He cannot possess them.”

The answer is this: It has already been explained that the perfection in question is a perfection whose existence is possible and which involves no deficiency. Thus, if someone’s statement that He would be deficient in Himself means that He would be deficient without these attributes, this is true. Yet this is precisely what we sought to avoid, and we established that He must possess the attributes of perfection; otherwise, He would be deficient. If, however, the intended meaning is that He is perfect only through the attributes He possesses, and would therefore not be perfect in His essence stripped of these attributes, then the first response is as follows:

This objection would hold only if an essence devoid of these attributes could exist, or if a perfect essence devoid of these attributes could exist. If either of these is impossible, His perfection without these attributes is impossible—so how much more so if both are impossible? For the existence of a perfect essence without these attributes is impossible. We necessarily know that an “essence” which is not living, knowing, powerful, hearing, seeing, and speaking is not more perfect than an essence which is not living, knowing, hearing, seeing, and speaking. And if sound reason judges that an essence deprived of these attributes is not equal to

If it is then said, “His essence can be free of deficiency and deprivation of perfection only through these attributes,” the reply is:

Perfection without these attributes is impossible, and the absence of what is impossible is no deficiency. Deficiency consists only in the absence of what is possible. Moreover, once it is established that He can possess perfection, and that whatever attributes He possesses are necessary to Him, His essence cannot be devoid of these attributes. Thus, supposing His essence to be separate from these attributes is an impossible supposition.

If an impossible supposition is made concerning the essence, and it is said that the essence is deficient without it, this indicates the impossibility of that supposition, not the impossibility of its opposite. It is like saying, “If He were to die, He would be deficient”: this entails that He must be living. Likewise, if supposing His essence to be devoid of these attributes entails that it would be deficient, this necessarily entails that He possesses these attributes.

Furthermore, the claim that “He became perfect through something other than Himself” is not conceded. For we do not say of His attributes either that they are other than Him or that they are not other than Him. This is the position of the “imams of the early generations,” such as Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others. It is also the position chosen by accomplished scholars among those who affirm the attributes, such as Ibn Kullāb and others.

Some of them say: “I do not say of the attributes that they are not Him, nor do I say that they are not other than Him. Nor do I combine the two negations by saying: ‘They are neither Him nor other than Him.’” This is the position chosen by a group of those who affirm the attributes, such as al-Ashʿarī. I think that Abū al-Hasan al-Tamīmī’s position is this, or something similar.

Others permit both negations to be stated together, such as al-Qādī Abū Bakr and al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā. This disagreement arises because the term “other” may mean something distinct from a thing, or simply something not identical to it. Using ambiguous expressions without qualification can suggest erroneous meanings.

We offer a precise answer: When someone says, “He attains perfection through something other than Himself,” does he mean something separate from Him, or an attribute inseparable from His essence? The former is impossible; the latter is true. His essence cannot exist without its inseparable attributes, just as they cannot exist without Him. This is perfection through Himself, not through something separate from Himself.

The imams—such as Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others—and the leading scholars who affirm the attributes, such as Abū Muhammad ibn Kullāb and others, explicitly stated that when someone says, “Praise be to Allah,” “I called upon Allah and worshipped Him,” or “By Allah,” the name Allah encompasses His essence endowed with His attributes. His attributes are not additional to what His most beautiful names designate.

If it is asked, “Are His attributes additional to His essence or not?” the answer is: If by ‘essence’ one means the bare essence acknowledged by those who deny the attributes, then the attributes are additional to it. But if one means the essence that exists in external reality, that essence cannot exist except with its inseparable attributes. The attributes are not additional to the essence endowed with attributes, although they are additional to an essence hypothetically conceived as devoid of attributes.

As for the claim, “If real attributes subsisted in Him, He would depend upon them, while they would depend upon Him; thus the Lord would depend upon something other than Himself,” this is of the same kind as the first objection.

The first response is that the statement, “If real attributes subsisted in Him, He would depend upon them,” presupposes the possibility of a substance in which attributes subsist, and the possibility of an essence in which no attributes subsist. If either were impossible, this statement would be invalid; how much more so if both were impossible? For an essence stripped of all attributes can be conceived only in the mind, not in external reality—just as one may conceive of absolute existence that is not individuated in external reality.

The word dhāt is the feminine form of dhū (“possessing”), which is used only in a genitive construction with another word. Thus they say, “So-and-so possesses knowledge and power,” using dhū, and “A soul possesses knowledge and power,” using dhāt. Wherever dhū or dhāt occurs in the Quran or in the Arabic language, it occurs only in a genitive construction, as in His words:

“So fear Allah and set right the relations between yourselves,”

and His words:

“Knowing what is within the breasts.”

And in the words of Khubayb, may Allah be pleased with him:

“And that is for Allah’s sake . . .”

But when speculative thinkers began discussing this subject, they said that one describes it as dhāt ʿilm wa-qudra (“possessing knowledge and power”). They then detached this word from the genitive construction and made it definite, saying “al-dhāt” (“the essence”). This is a later coinage, not an expression belonging to pristine Arabic. For this reason, a group of scholars, including Abū al-Fath ibn Burhān, Ibn al-Dahhān, and others, objected to it, saying, “This word is not Arabic.” Others, including al-Qādī, Ibn ʿAqīl, and others, rebutted them.

(The decisive answer is that it does not belong to pristine Arabic, but is a later coinage, like the terms al-mawjūd (“the existent”), al-māhiyya (“quiddity”), al-kayfiyya (“modality”), and the like. This word therefore implies the existence of attributes to which dhāt is joined in a genitive construction: one says “possessing knowledge,” “possessing power,” and “possessing speech.” The underlying meaning is likewise so: nothing self-subsisting can exist in external reality without any positive attribute whatsoever. Indeed, positing such a thing in external reality is like positing an accident that subsists in itself rather than in something else. Thus, positing a self-subsisting accident that has no attribute is like positing an attribute that does not subsist in something else; both are impossible. Whatever subsists in itself must have an attribute, and whatever is an attribute must have something self-subsisting that is characterized by it.

For this reason, the disputants concede that they know of nothing self-subsisting that has no attribute, whether they call it a substance, a body, or something else. They say: “The existence of a substance stripped of all

How much more so when it is known to be impossible outside the mind! Everything said by those who deny the attributes implies that such a thing cannot exist and can only be supposed mentally. The mind conceives it within itself just as it conceives impossibilities whose existence, or even possibility, in reality is inconceivable.

Moreover, if “the Lord Most High” can possess the attributes of perfection—and whatever is possible for Him is necessary for Him—then He cannot be devoid of those attributes. To posit His essence without the attributes necessarily inseparable from Him is therefore to posit an impossibility.

Since supposing their absence is impossible, both in general and in particular, the statement, “He would be dependent on them, and they would be dependent on Him,” is intelligible only with respect to two things each of which can exist without the other. When this is impossible, that supposition is invalid.

He should then be asked: What do you mean by dependence? Do you mean that the essence produces and originates the attributes, or the reverse? Or do you mean mutual inseparability—that neither can exist without the other? If you mean the dependence of an effect upon its agent, this is false. The Lord does not produce His inseparable attributes. Indeed, no particular act of His, nor any particular thing He produces, is inseparable from Him. How, then, can you regard His attributes as things He produces, when His attributes are inseparable from His essence and are not among the things He produces? But if you mean mutual inseparability, that is true.

translated_text:
This is like saying: He cannot exist unless He is eternal and necessarily existent in Himself, nor can He be knowing and powerful unless He is living.

If His attributes are inseparable from His essence, this represents greater perfection than if the two could be separated. For if He could exist without the attributes of perfection, perfection would not be necessary for Him, but merely possible. He would then depend on another for those attributes to be established in Him. That would be an imperfection, which is impossible for Him, as previously explained.

It is thus clear that the mutual inseparability of His essence and the attributes of perfection is the very height of perfection.

Section

As for someone who says, “They are accidents that can subsist only in a composite body, and whatever is composite is contingent and dependent—which is imperfection itself,” those who affirm the divine attributes take three approaches to applying the term “accident” to His attributes:

Some deny that they are accidents, saying instead, “They are attributes, not accidents.” This is the position of al-Ash‘arī and many jurists among the followers of Ahmad and others.

Others apply the term “accidents” to them, such as Hishām, Ibn Karrām, and others.

Still others refrain from either affirming or denying this designation, as they do with the term “other,” and likewise refrain from doing so with the term “body” and similar expressions. For saying “Knowledge is an accident” is an innovation, and saying “It is not an accident” is an innovation, just as saying “The Lord is a body” is an innovation, and saying “He is not a body” is an innovation.

Likewise, in ordinary Arabic usage, the term “body” means the physical body or bodily frame, as stated by al-Asma‘ī, Abū Zayd, and other Arabic lexicographers.

As for the speculative theologians, some mean by it a composite entity and apply it to the indivisible atom

As for the “philosophers,” they may be told: According to you, the eternal is not indwelt by temporally originated events, yet it has always been a locus of such events. Thus, in your view, eternity does not preclude this. Indeed, you regard this as the “possible perfection” beyond which no other is possible. They deny it of the Necessary Existent only because they think He is not characterized by it. The invalidity of their position on this has already been indicated, particularly since whatever is the locus of successive temporally originated events cannot derive its existence from an eternal, complete cause that necessarily produces its effect. For the effect of a complete, necessitating cause—or any part of that effect—cannot come after the cause. Whenever any part of its effect comes after it, it is a cause of that effect potentially, not actually; and its becoming an actual cause requires another cause.

If it is He Himself who brings it from potentiality into actuality, then there is something potential in Him, and He is the one who actualizes it. This entails that He is receptive or active, which they disallow because they hold attributes—which they call composition—to be impossible. If someone other than Him brings Him into actuality, that is necessarily impossible, as all agree, because it contradicts necessary existence and entails “simultaneous circular dependence” and an “infinite regress of efficient causes.”

If He became the agent producing a particular thing after not having been its agent, He could not be an eternal, complete cause. Thus, the eternity of anything in the world would entail His being a complete cause from eternity. That, in turn, would entail that nothing temporally originated could proceed from Him, whether through an intermediary or without one. This contradicts what is observed.

translated_text:
Secondly, in refuting the claim that the occurrence of temporally originated events is impossible, it may be said:

This rests on the renewal of these matters through the renewal of relations, states, and privations, for people agree that these matters undergo renewal. Al-Āmidī distinguished between the two verbally, saying: “These are temporally originated events, while those are renewals.” Verbal distinctions, however, do not affect substantive truths.

It may therefore be said: If the renewal of these things confers perfection on Him, then He previously lacked that perfection, which is a deficiency. If it confers deficiency on Him, He cannot be characterized by it.

Thirdly, it may be said:

The perfection with which He must be characterized is that whose existence is possible. As for what is impossible, it is not a perfection with which any existing being can be characterized. It is impossible for the temporally originated events connected with His power and will to exist all together from eternity. Their absence from eternity is therefore not a deficiency, because the absence of what is impossible is no deficiency.

Fourthly, it may be said:

If we posit a being that performs one act after another and is itself capable of acting, and another being that cannot itself do anything, but is like an inanimate object incapable of movement, the former is more perfect than the latter. The absence of these acts is therefore necessarily a deficiency, whereas their existence, insofar as it is possible, is perfection.

Fifthly, it may be said:

We do not concede that their absence is, without qualification, either a deficiency or a perfection, nor that their existence is, without qualification, either a deficiency or a perfection. Rather, their existence at the time determined by His will and power

Their absence when wisdom requires their absence is perfection, and their existence when wisdom requires their existence is perfection. Since the existence of one and the same thing may sometimes be a perfection and sometimes a deficiency, and likewise its absence, this unqualified dichotomy is invalid.

Similarly, something may be a mercy to creation when they need it, as with rain, yet a punishment when it harms them. Sending it down to meet their need is therefore mercy and beneficence, and the One who is beneficent and merciful is characterized by perfection. Not sending it down when it would harm them is no deficiency; rather, this too is mercy and beneficence. Thus, He is beneficent by granting it when its presence is a mercy, and by withholding it when its absence is a mercy.

translated_text:
Section

As for the denial of particular “attributes known through revelation” on the grounds that they entail composition, which in turn entails need and dependence, an argument of this kind has already been answered.

If “composition” means what is understood by it in the language, in common usage, or in the usage of certain people—something assembled by another, something previously separate that then came together, something combining indivisible atoms or matter and form, or something whose parts can be separated from one another—then we do not concede the first premise. We do not concede that affirming the Face and Hand entails composition in this sense.

If, however, it means inseparability, while one thing is intrinsically distinct from another, so that this is not that, then the same consequence is binding upon them regarding the qualitative attributes known through reason, such as knowledge, power, hearing, and sight. None of these attributes is identical to another; rather, each is intrinsically distinct from the other, even though the two are inseparable and characterize one and the same being. We understand this in the attributes of created things, as with the sun’s parts and accidental properties.

Furthermore, if by need and dependence it is meant that He cannot exist without something distinct from Him, this is not conceded. But if it means that whatever is included in what His name designates must exist, and that the Necessary Existent cannot exist without those things included in what His name designates,

then it is clear that He cannot exist without His own self; all the more, then, He cannot exist without what is included in it.

If it is said, “He depends upon His own self,” this does not mean that His self brings itself into being. The same applies to what is included in it. The expression, however, is misleading and ambiguous; once its meaning is explained, the difficulty disappears.

It may also be said: We do not apply the term “other” to this, so it does not follow that He needs something other than Himself. This concerns the use of language. As for demonstrative proof, the evidence establishes the existence of a self-existent being, with no agent or efficient cause bringing Him into being, and that He is, in Himself, independent of everything distinct from Him.

As for an existence that has no attribute, and whose name includes no positive meaning within its designation—if someone claims that this is what is meant by necessary existence and self-sufficiency, he is told: But this meaning is not what the evidence establishes. Rather, you have assumed that this is what the name designates. Making the term evidence for this meaning will not help you unless that meaning is established as true in itself. You have no evidence for that; indeed, the evidence establishes its opposite.

These people took the terms “the Self-Sufficient,” “the Eternal,” and “the Necessary Existent in Himself” and began interpreting them in senses that entail further meanings incompatible with affirming the attributes. They stretched the language, then imagined that what they had done was what rational and other evidence necessarily required. This is an error on their part.

" الْمُتَكَلِّمِ "
 وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْأَسْمَاءِ وَلَوْ فُعِلَ
translated_text:
What rational evidence entails cannot be derived from mere wording, while what revealed evidence entails must be understood according to the speaker’s customary usage, not newly devised definitions.

No one, therefore, may claim that the words found in the Quran have been assigned certain meanings and then seek to explain Allah’s intent through those meanings. This is the practice of those who deviate from the truth and fabricate lies. They adopted meanings they supposed to be established and made them the meanings of “the One,” “the Necessary Existent,” “the Self-Sufficient,” “the Eternal,” and the denial of any likeness to Him. They then turned to the Quran and Sunnah, where Allah Most High is described as Unique, One, Most High, and in similar terms denying that He has any likeness or equal. They said: “This indicates the meanings to which we have assigned these names.” This is among the gravest fabrications against Allah.

Likewise, the “philosophizers” took such terms as “Creator,” “Agent,” “Maker,” and “Originator” and assigned them a meaning they had invented. They divided origination into two kinds: essential and temporal. By essential origination, they meant that what is subject to the Lord exists alongside the Lord from eternity and forever. Yet the term is not known to bear this meaning in the language of any people. Had they merely adopted this as their own terminology, you would not dispute it with them. But their purpose was to mislead people and to be able to say: “We affirm that the world originated and that Allah is its Creator, the One who brings it about, and its Maker,” and other expressions whose meanings necessarily and self-evidently entail that what is produced comes after its producer. Such expressions do not apply to something that is beginningless as the Lord is beginningless, existing alongside Him from eternity and forever.

 .

translated_text:
Thus He denied that these people were alike, although they shared a common humanity. How, then, can it be said that the Arabic language requires everything that can be pointed to to be like everything else that can be pointed to?

Allah Most High says:

“Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with ‘Ād—
Iram, of the pillars—
the like of which was never created in the lands?”

He thus states that its like was never created in the lands, although both are cities. How, then, can it be said that, in the Arabic language, every body is like every other body, so that His words,

“There is nothing like Him,”

should be understood on that basis?

The poet said:

“None is like the young man Zuhayr.”

And another said:

“No human being among mankind is like them.”

The poet did not intend thereby to deny the existence of any body whatsoever.

Likewise, the term “resemblance” does not mean “being alike” in the language. Allah Most High says:

“And they will be given it in similar form.”

And He Most High says:

“Similar and dissimilar.”

He did not mean thereby that these things are alike in the linguistic sense. The issue here is not whether substances are alike according to reason or not; that is discussed at length elsewhere. Rather, the point is that speakers of the language in which the Quran was revealed do not regard this alone as sufficient grounds for calling things alike, nor do they regard the denial of likeness as a denial of this. To interpret the Quran on that basis is therefore to attribute a falsehood to it.

translated_text:
Section

The term “affinity” has several possible meanings. It may refer to descent and kinship: one says, “This man is so-and-so’s relative,” or “He is related to him,” when they share a kinship based on birth and human descent. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is far above that.

It may also mean likeness: one says, “This corresponds to that,” meaning that it is like it. Yet Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is One, the Self-Sufficient. He neither begets nor is born, and there is none comparable to Him.

It may also mean agreement in some respect, the opposite of which is disagreement. “Affinity” in this sense is indeed established. For the allies of Allah Most High agree with Him concerning what He commands, so they do it; concerning what He loves, so they love it; concerning what He forbids, so they refrain from it; and concerning what He gives, so they receive it.

Allah is One and loves what is odd-numbered; He is Beautiful and loves beauty; All-Knowing and loves knowledge; Pure and loves cleanliness; Good to His creation and loves those who do good; Just and loves those who act justly—and likewise with other such qualities.

Indeed, glorified is He, He rejoices at the repentance of the repentant person more than a man rejoices upon finding his lost mount, carrying his food and drink, in a deadly wilderness after he has despaired of finding it. Allah rejoices more at His servant’s repentance than this man rejoices at recovering his mount, as is established in the authentic hadith collections from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

translated_text:
Thus, if “affinity” means this and similar things, then such affinity is real and is an attribute of perfection, as indicated earlier. For one who loves attributes of perfection is more perfect than one who makes no distinction between attributes of deficiency and perfection, or who does not love attributes of perfection.

Suppose there are two beings: one loves knowledge, truthfulness, justice, benevolence, and similar things; the other makes no distinction between these things and ignorance, falsehood, injustice, and the like, neither loving the former nor hating the latter. The one who loves those things is more perfect than the other. This shows that if someone strips Him of “attributes of perfection and existence,” denying Him knowledge so that He is like an inanimate object, then a being who knows would be more perfect than Him. It is also well known that one who loves what is praiseworthy and hates what is blameworthy is more perfect than one who loves both or hates both.

The foundation of “this issue” is the distinction between Allah’s love, pleasure, anger, and displeasure, on the one hand, and His will, on the other. This is the position of the early generations, the jurists, and most of those who affirm divine decree, whether among Ahl al-Sunnah or others. Some of the Qadariyyah and some of those who affirm divine decree, however, have held that there is no distinction between them.

The “Qadariyyah” then said: He does not love disbelief, wickedness, or disobedience, nor does He will them. Thus, what He does not will occurs, and He wills what does not occur.

The “affirmers of divine decree” said: Whatever He wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur. Therefore, He has willed disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience, but has not willed them as religion; or He has willed them on the part of the disbeliever but has not willed them on the part of the believer

translated_text:
and therefore He loves disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience, though He does not love them as religion; He loves them on the part of the disbeliever but not on the part of the believer.

Both positions are erroneous and contrary to the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars. They agree that whatever Allah wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur, and that nothing occurs except by His will. They also unanimously agree that He does not love corruption, that He is not pleased with disbelief for His servants, and that the disbelievers devise by night words of which He does not approve. Those who denied His love based their position on this false premise.

translated_text:
Section

As for the claim, “Mercy is weakness and frailty in one’s nature, and distress over the one shown mercy,” this is false.

First, weakness and frailty are blameworthy in human beings, whereas mercy is praiseworthy. Allah Most High says:

“And they counsel one another to patience and counsel one another to mercy.”

Allah has forbidden His servants to lose heart or grieve, saying:

“Do not lose heart or grieve, for you will have the upper hand, if you are believers.”

Yet He has encouraged them to show mercy. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“Mercy is taken away only from one who is wretched.”

He also said:

“Whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy.”

And he said:

“The Most Merciful shows mercy to those who are merciful. Show mercy to those on earth, and the One in heaven will show you mercy.”

It is inconceivable that he would say, “Weakness and frailty are taken away only from one who is wretched.” Rather, because mercy is accompanied by weakness and frailty in many people—as with the mercy shown by women and the like—the mistaken person supposed that this was invariably true of mercy.

 وَالْآخَرُ قَدْ اسْتَوَى عِنْدَهُ هَذَا وَهَذَا وَلَيْسَ عِنْدَهُ مَا يَقْتَضِي جَلْبَ مَنْفَعَةٍ وَلَا دَفْعَ مَضَرَّةٍ:

translated_text:
Furthermore, even if mercy necessarily entailed such weakness in created beings, it would not follow that it necessarily entailed the same in Allah Most High. Likewise, our knowledge, power, hearing, sight and speech entail imperfections and needs from which Allah must be declared free. Similarly, our “existence” and “subsistence in ourselves” entail our need for a Creator who brings us into existence, whereas Allah’s existence is free of the needs inherent in ours. We, our attributes and our acts are bound up with dependence on another. Need is intrinsic to us, and we can never be free of it. He, glorified be He, is the Self-Sufficient; His freedom from need is intrinsic to Him and can never cease. In Himself, He is Ever-Living, All-Sustaining and necessarily existent, whereas in ourselves we are needy and dependent.

Thus, although our essence, attributes and acts, and the perfections we possess—such as knowledge, power and the like—are bound up with need, having come into existence and contingency, this does not require denying Allah an essence, attributes or acts, or denying Him power and knowledge, merely because these things are inseparable from need in us. The same applies to “mercy” and other attributes: even supposing that they are inseparable from need and weakness in us, it does not follow that they must be inseparable from these in Allah.

Furthermore, we know self-evidently that if we suppose two beings, one of whom shows mercy to another, bringing him benefit and warding off harm from him, while the other is indifferent to both and has nothing within him that calls for bringing benefit or warding off harm, then the former is more perfect.

translated_text:
Section

As for the statement, “Anger is the boiling of the heart’s blood in pursuit of revenge,” this is not correct even with regard to us. Anger may arise to ward off something harmful before it occurs, in which case there is no revenge at all.

Furthermore, anger accompanies the boiling of the heart’s blood; anger itself is not simply that boiling. Likewise, modesty accompanies a reddening of the face, and fear accompanies a paling of the face, but neither is identical to the accompanying change. This is because, when the soul is moved to repel something harmful, if it senses that it has the power to do so, the blood surges outward, giving rise to anger. If it senses its own inability, the blood retreats inward, causing the face to grow pale, as happens to someone who is sorrowful.

Moreover, even supposing that this were the true nature of our anger, it would not follow that Allah Most High’s anger must be like ours, just as the reality of Allah’s essence is not like ours. He resembles neither our essence nor our souls, and His attributes are like His essence in this respect.

We know self-evidently that if we suppose two beings, one possessing a strength by which he wards off corruption, while the other is indifferent to righteousness and corruption, the one possessing that strength is more perfect.

 فَيُقَالُ:
 كُلُّ مَا سِوَى اللَّهِ مَخْلُوقٌ مُنْفَعِلٌ وَنَحْنُ وَذَوَاتُنَا مُنْفَعِلَةٌ فَكَوْنُهَا انْفِعَالَاتٍ فِينَا لِغَيْرِنَا نَعْجِزُ عَنْ دَفْعِهَا: لَا يُوجِبُ أَنْ يَكُونَ اللَّهُ مُنْفَعِلًا لَهَا عَاجِزًا عَنْ دَفْعِهَا وَكَانَ كُلُّ مَا يَجْرِي فِي الْوُجُودِ فَإِنَّهُ بِمَشِيئَتِهِ وَقُدْرَتِهِ لَا يَكُونُ إلَّا مَا يَشَاءُ وَلَا يَشَاءُ إلَّا مَا يَكُونُ لَهُ الْمُلْكُ وَلَهُ الْحَمْدُ.
translated_text:
For this reason, someone who feels no protective jealousy in the face of indecency—such as a man who tolerates sexual immorality within his family—is condemned. So too is someone who lacks the zeal to defend the oppressed against injustice. By contrast, someone whose protective jealousy wards off indecency and whose zeal repels injustice is praised. It is recognized that the latter is more perfect than the former.

This is why the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, attributed superior perfection to the Lord in this respect, saying in an authentic hadith:

“No one has greater protective jealousy than Allah. For this reason, He has forbidden indecencies, both open and hidden.”

He also said:

“Are you astonished at Sa'd’s protective jealousy? I have greater protective jealousy than he does, and Allah has greater protective jealousy than I do.”

As for the assertion, “These are reactions of the soul,” the response is:

Everything other than Allah is created and subject to influence; we ourselves, in our very being, are subject to influence. The fact that, in us, these are reactions caused by things outside ourselves, which we are unable to ward off, does not entail that Allah is subject to them and unable to ward them off. Indeed, everything that takes place in existence occurs by His will and power. Nothing occurs except what He wills, and nothing He wills fails to occur. To Him belongs dominion, and to Him belongs all praise.

translated_text:
Section

The assertion that “laughter is lightness of spirit” is incorrect, although the two may occur together. If, by “lightness of spirit,” the speaker means a blameworthy quality, this applies when one laughs at something one ought not to laugh at. Otherwise, laughter in its proper place is a praiseworthy quality and an attribute of perfection. If we suppose two living beings, one of whom laughs at what merits laughter while the other never laughs at all, the first is more perfect than the second.

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The Lord looks upon you in your despair and continues to laugh, knowing that your relief is near.”

Abū Razīn al-ʿUqaylī said to him, “O Messenger of Allah, does the Lord laugh?”

“Yes,” he replied.

He said, “We will never lack goodness from a Lord who laughs.”

Thus, by virtue of his sound innate disposition, this intelligent Bedouin took His laughter as evidence of His kindness and bounty. This indicates that this attribute is associated with praiseworthy beneficence and is an attribute of perfection. A grim-faced person who never laughs is blamed for this. Indeed, the Day of severe punishment is described as:

“a grim and distressful Day.”

translated_text:
It has also been related that the angels said to Adam:

“May Allah grant you life and gladden you”—that is, make you laugh.

The human being is an animal endowed with speech and laughter. What distinguishes human beings from beasts is an attribute of perfection. Just as speech is an attribute of perfection, so too is laughter. One who speaks is more perfect than one who does not, and one who laughs is more perfect than one who does not. If laughter in us necessarily involves some imperfection, Allah is far exalted above that. Such imperfection is, for the most part, particular rather than universal: laughter as such is not inherently associated with imperfection. Likewise, our essences and attributes are associated with imperfection, as is our existence. Nor does it follow that the Lord is an originator and that He has no essence.

This is where the extremist Qarmatians went astray, including the author of al-Iqlīd (The Key) and others like him. They sought to deny of Him everything the heart knows and the tongue expresses, whether by negation or affirmation. They said, “We do not say ‘existent’ or ‘not existent,’ nor ‘possessing attributes’ or ‘not possessing attributes,’” because, they claimed, this would involve likening Him to creation. Yet this entails that His existence is impossible—the consequence of likening Him to what cannot exist.

The resemblance that is impossible for Allah is that He should share any property exclusive to created beings—such as coming into being, death, passing away, and contingency—or resemble them in any of His attributes, such as life, knowledge, and power. For although He is described by these attributes, the Creator’s attribute does not resemble the creature’s attribute.

Section

As for his statement:

“Amazement means regarding its object as something momentous,”

The response is: Yes. It may be accompanied by ignorance of the cause of what occasions the amazement, or it may arise because something stands apart from comparable things. Allah Most High knows all things, so He cannot be unaware of the cause of that at which He marvels. Rather, He marvels because it stands apart from comparable things, regarding it as momentous. Allah Most High regards as great that which is great, whether because of the greatness of its cause or its own greatness. He has described certain good things as great, and certain evils as great. Thus, He Most High says:

“Lord of the mighty Throne.”

And He says:

“We have certainly given you the seven oft-repeated verses and the mighty Quran.”

And He says:

“Had they done what they were admonished to do, it would have been better for them and would have strengthened them more firmly.”

“And then We would have granted them from Us a great reward.”

And He says:

“Why, when you heard it, did you not say, ‘It is not for us to speak of this. Glory be to You! This is a tremendous slander’?”

And He says:

“Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a tremendous wrong.”

Hence His words:

“Rather, I marvel, while they mock,”

according to the reading with a u-vowel. Here, He marvels at their disbelief despite the clarity of the evidence.

The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said to the man who, together with his wife, had given their guest preference over themselves:

“Allah has indeed marveled.”

In another wording in the Sahīh:

“Allah indeed laughed tonight at what the two of you did last night.”

He also said:

“Indeed, the Lord marvels at His servant when he says, ‘My Lord, forgive me, for none forgives sins but You.’ He says, ‘My servant knows that none forgives sins but Me.’”

And he said:

“Your Lord marvels at a young man free of youthful waywardness.”

And he said:

“Your Lord marvels at a shepherd atop a mountain crag who gives the call to prayer and the call to begin it. Allah then says, ‘Look at My servant.’”

Or words to that effect. There are other similar reports.

Section

As for one person’s statement:

“If there were anything in His dominion that He did not will, that would be an imperfection,”

and another’s statement:

“If He decreed and punished, that would be injustice, and injustice is an imperfection,”

the reply is as follows:

The first statement is clear. If it were supposed that there existed within His dominion something He did not will, over which He had no power, and which He neither created nor brought into being, that would constitute an imperfection in several respects.

First, for anything to bring things into being independently of Him would constitute an imperfection even if it were supposed to be outside His dominion. How much more so within His dominion? For we know that, if we posit two beings—one upon whom everything depends, while he depends on nothing, and another upon whom some things depend, while others have no need of him—the first would be more perfect. Thus, the mere fact that anything should fall outside His power and creative activity would constitute an imperfection.

These are proofs of divine oneness, for sharing entails an imperfection in each of the two partners, and absolute perfection lies only in oneness. We know that one who has power in his own right is more perfect than one who needs a helper; one who accomplishes everything by himself is more perfect than one who has a partner and helper in accomplishing some of it; and one upon whom everything depends is more perfect than one of whom some things have no need.

Another consideration is this: being the Creator of everything and having power over everything is more perfect than being the Creator of only some things and having power over only some things. The “Qadariyyah” do not acknowledge Him as the Creator of everything or as having power over everything. Those who espouse philosophy and hold that He is a final cause are worse than them. They do not acknowledge Him as the Creator of any events arising in the world—neither the motions of the celestial spheres nor any other moving things—nor as the Creator of what comes about through them. Nor do they acknowledge that He has power over any of this or knows its details. Yet Allah, glorified and exalted is He, says:

“It is Allah who created seven heavens, and of the earth their like. His command descends among them so that you may know that Allah has power over all things and that Allah encompasses all things in knowledge.”

These people examine the world, yet do not know that Allah has power over all things or that Allah encompasses all things in knowledge.

Another consideration is that, if we suppose two sovereigns—one who wills something that does not come to pass, while what he does not will does come to pass; and another whose every will comes to pass, and nothing comes to pass except what he wills—we know necessarily that the latter is more perfect.

In short, the position of “those who affirm divine power” entails that He is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of everything, that He has power over all things, and that whatever He wills comes to pass. It thus entails the perfection of His creative activity, power, and will. The “deniers of divine decree” deny Him these perfections.

‘Your Lord has prescribed mercy for Himself.’

‘O My servants, I have forbidden oppression for Myself and have made it forbidden among you, so do not oppress one another.’”

They also say:

“If saying that He does whatever He wills and decrees whatever He intends serves to explain His power—that nothing can hinder Him, and that no other can prevent what He wills or cause Him to will—then this is more perfect than the condition of one who has an obstacle preventing what he wills and a helper without whom he can neither will nor carry out what he wills.

“But if ‘doing whatever one wills’ means acting without regard to what knowledge and wisdom require, indeed acting foolishly, whereas another does whatever he wills but his will is joined with knowledge and wisdom, then the second is more perfect.”

The crux of the matter is that perfect power is an attribute of perfection, and a will that takes effect without needing a helper or encountering any obstacle is likewise an attribute of perfection. But a “will” that does not distinguish between one object of willing and another, treating all kinds alike, is not an attribute of perfection. Rather, the will that distinguishes between one object and another—as knowledge and wisdom require—is the will characterized by perfection.

Whoever diminishes His power, His creating, or His will has not esteemed Him as He deserves. And whoever diminishes His wisdom or His mercy has not esteemed Him as He truly deserves. The perfection that is His due requires affirming both.

Section

As for “those who deny prophethood” and their assertion that people are unworthy of Allah sending them a messenger, just as people of lowly standing are unworthy of a ruler sending them a messenger—this betrays clear ignorance concerning both the creature and the Creator. Among the things for which kings are most highly praised is personally addressing the weakest of their subjects, let alone sending them a messenger.

As for the Creator, glorified is He, He is more merciful to His servants than a mother is to her child, and His power accompanies His perfect mercy. Since His power and mercy are perfect, what could prevent Him from sending them a messenger as a mercy from Him? As He, Most High, says:

“We have sent you only as a mercy to the worlds.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I am but a mercy bestowed as a gift.”

Moreover, this is part of His kindness to creation: teaching and guiding them, and explaining what benefits them and what harms them. As He, Most High, says:

“Allah has certainly bestowed a great favor upon the believers by sending among them a Messenger from among themselves, reciting His verses to them, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom.”

Thus He, Most High, has made clear that this is among His favors to His believing servants.

translated_text:
Section:

As for “the polytheists’ claim” that His greatness and majesty require that He be approached only through an intermediary and a barrier, and that approaching Him without these detracts from His exalted dignity, this is false on several grounds.

One is that someone who can be approached only through intermediaries and a barrier is either able to hear his soldiers’ words and meet their needs without those intermediaries and that barrier, or he is not. If he is not able, this is a deficiency. Allah Most High, however, is characterized by perfection. He must therefore hear His servants’ words without intermediaries, answer their supplications, and show them kindness without any need for a barrier. If a king can conduct his affairs without a barrier and dispenses with it out of kindness and mercy, that is an attribute of perfection.

Furthermore, the claim that this detracts from His dignity applies only to someone whom others can harm and who depends on them for his own benefit. Given His perfect power, His complete independence of them, and His immunity to any harm they might cause Him, their drawing near to Him does not detract from His dignity. Indeed, if there are two people, one of whom brings the weak close to him out of kindness toward them and has no fear of them, while the other does not do so, whether out of fear, arrogance, or some other reason, the first is more perfect than the second.

Moreover, this objection does not apply when the one in authority has commanded it. If he permits people to approach him and enter his home, doing so is neither disrespectful to him nor demeaning to his dignity. Such censure therefore applies to those who worship Him in ways He has not prescribed. For this reason, Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of good news, and a warner”

“and as one who calls to Allah by His permission.”

And He Most High says:

“Or do they have partners who have prescribed for them in religion what Allah has not authorized?”

Section

As for the statement:

“If they were asked, ‘Which is more perfect: a being characterized by every kind of perception, including taste, smell, and touch, or a being not characterized by them?’ they would answer, ‘The former is more perfect,’ yet they do not ascribe these to Him.”

Those who affirm the divine attributes reply:

There are three well-known positions concerning these kinds of perception.

The first is to affirm these kinds of perception for Allah Most High, just as hearing and sight are ascribed to Him. This is the position of the judge Abū Bakr and Abū al-Maʿālī, and I believe it is also the position of al-Ashʿarī himself. Indeed, it is also the position of the Basran Muʿtazilites who ascribe these kinds of perception to Him.

These scholars and others also hold that He can be perceived through all five senses, just as He can be seen. The judge Abū Yaʿlā agreed with them on this in al-Muʿtamad and elsewhere.

The second position is to deny these three kinds of perception, as do many who affirm the divine attributes, both among the Sifātiyya and others. This is the position of groups of jurists among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, and of many followers of al-Ashʿarī and others.

The third position is to affirm perception by touch but not by taste, because taste pertains only to what is eaten: only one who eats can possess the sense of taste, and only something eaten can be its object.

and Allah, glorified is He, is far above eating. Touch, by contrast, is comparable to sight. Most scholars of hadith ascribe touch to Him, as do many followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others, but they do not ascribe taste to Him.

The reason for this is that the Muʿtazilites who deny the divine attributes said to those who affirm them:

“If you say that He can be seen, then say that He can be perceived through all the other senses. And if you say that He is All-Hearing and All-Seeing, then ascribe all five kinds of perception to Him.”

All those who affirm the divine attributes replied:

“We describe Him as One who can be seen and whose speech can be heard, as the scriptural texts state. We likewise describe Him as One who hears and sees.”

The majority of the scholars of hadith and the Sunnah said:

“We also ascribe perception by touch to Him, because it is a perfection involving no deficiency, and the scriptural texts indicate it. Perception by taste, however, necessarily entails eating, which in turn entails deficiency, as explained earlier.”

A group of speculative theologians who affirm the divine attributes ascribed all five kinds of perception to Him in both respects: as perceiver and as the object of perception.

Some of them said that He could be the object of these kinds of perception, just as He can be seen, because they believed that existence is what makes something capable of being seen. They did not, however, say that He possesses these kinds of perception.

Most of those who affirm that He can be seen did not hold that mere existence is what makes something capable of being seen. Rather, they said that the basis for this consists of positive, existent realities—not that everything that exists can be seen. There is a difference between the two claims: the latter entails that every existent thing can be seen, whereas the former does not. If what makes something capable of being seen consists of positive, existent realities, without requiring any conditions involving nonexistence, then the more fully something possesses existence and the further it is from nonexistence, the stronger the grounds for its being capable of being seen.

Others among them denied everything apart from hearing and sight in both respects: perceiving and being perceived.

Section

As for the statement, “Perfection and deficiency are relative matters,” we have explained that the perfection befitting the Lord is that which involves no deficiency whatsoever, and that it is the perfection possible for an existent being. Such perfection can never be absent from Allah. Relative perfection, however, entails deficiency: it is perfection in one respect but not another. Eating, for example, is a perfection for someone who is hungry, but a deficiency for someone who is full, because it is not pure perfection; rather, it is accompanied by deficiency.

Self-exaltation, self-magnification, self-praise, commanding people to worship Him, call upon Him, and turn to Him with longing, and other such things exclusive to lordship are praiseworthy perfections in the Lord, blessed and exalted is He, but blameworthy deficiencies in a created being. The same applies to statements concerning what is exclusive to lordship, such as His saying:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me.”

And His saying, exalted is He:

“Call upon Me; I will respond to you.”

And His saying:

“Whether you reveal what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it.”

And His saying:

“Or do those who commit evil deeds think they can escape Us?”

And His saying:

“Indeed, you have no authority over My servants.”

And His saying:

“Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers and those who believe, both in the life of this world and on the Day when the witnesses stand forth.”

These and similar statements, in which the Lord speaks of certain attributes exclusive to Him and truthfully describes Himself with attributes of perfection, are themselves part of His perfection. His explaining these matters to His servants and making them known to them is also part of His perfection. Anyone else who made such claims about himself would be a liar and a fabricator, and lying is among the greatest faults and deficiencies.

When a created being speaks truthfully about himself, however, this is not unconditionally blameworthy. Indeed, it may be praiseworthy if it serves a beneficial purpose, as in the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“I am the foremost of Adam’s descendants, and I say this without boasting.”

If, however, this causes harm that outweighs or equals its benefit, he is blamed for doing something harmful, not for lying. The Lord, exalted is He, does nothing for which He is blameworthy. Rather, all praise belongs to Him in every circumstance, and every act of His is good, beautiful, and praiseworthy.

This is evident according to those who hold that injustice on His part is intrinsically impossible. According to the majority among Ahl al-Sunnah and the Qadariyyah, He acts only in accordance with wisdom and justice. Thus, all His reports, statements, and actions are good and praiseworthy, proceeding with the perfection for which He deserves praise. He possesses qualities exclusive to Him, blessed and exalted is He, by virtue of which He deserves supreme greatness and majesty. His supreme greatness and majesty are thus like His being living, self-subsisting, beginningless, and necessarily existent in His own right; His knowing all things and having power over all things; His being the Almighty, who cannot be assailed; and His being the Subduer of everything besides Him.

translated_text:
All these, then, are attributes of perfection that belong to Him alone. How could something that belongs to Him alone constitute perfection in anyone else, when no one else possesses it? Whoever claims it is a fabricator who contests the exclusive prerogatives of Lordship. As established in an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘Majesty is My lower garment, and supreme greatness is My cloak. Whoever contests either of them with Me, I shall punish him.’”

In short, no one else has any share in the perfection exclusive to Lordship. This affirms that He possesses a perfection in which no one else has any share. Such perfection cannot belong to anyone else; claiming it therefore amounts to contesting His Lordship and fabricating a lie against Allah. It is well known that prophethood is a perfection in a prophet. Yet when impostors—such as Musaylimah and his like—claim it, this constitutes a deficiency in them, not because prophethood is a deficiency, but because claiming it without possessing it is itself the deficiency. Likewise, anyone who claims knowledge, power, or righteousness without possessing them is blameworthy and detestable.

This entails that the Lord Most High possesses perfection that cannot belong to a created being. This does not contradict the principle that whatever constitutes perfection for an existent being simply insofar as it exists is something of which the Creator is all the more deserving. Rather, it means that when a created being is described with a perfection in the manner proper to it, and the Creator is described with that perfection in the manner proper to Him, what belongs to the created being neither equals nor even approaches what belongs to the Creator.

This is true: the Lord Most High deserves perfection and possesses it uniquely, in a manner in which nothing resembles Him. He has neither peer nor equal, whether the perfection is one of which nothing belongs to created beings—such as Lordship over His servants, absolute self-sufficiency, and the like—or one of which a kind is found in created beings;
