 فَإِنْ قُلْتُمْ نَحْنُ نَقْطَعُ النَّظَرَ عَنْ مُتَعَلِّقِ الصِّفَةِ وَنَنْظُرُ فِيهَا هَلْ هِيَ كَمَالٌ أَمْ نَقْصٌ؟ وَكَذَلِكَ نُحِيلُ الْحُكْمَ عَلَيْهَا بِأَحَدِهِمَا؛ لِأَنَّهَا قَدْ تَكُونُ كَمَالًا لِذَاتٍ نَقْصًا لِأُخْرَى عَلَى مَا ذَكَرَ.
 فَيُقَالُ:
 بَلْ نَحْنُ نَقُولُ الْكَمَالُ الَّذِي لَا نَقْصَ فِيهِ لِلْمُمْكِنِ الْوُجُودَ هُوَ كَمَالٌ مُطْلَقٌ لِكُلِّ مَا يَتَّصِفُ بِهِ. وَأَيْضًا فَالْكَمَالُ الَّذِي هُوَ كَمَالٌ لِلْمَوْجُودِ - مِنْ حَيْثُ هُوَ مَوْجُودٌ - يَمْتَنِعُ أَنْ يَكُونَ نَقْصًا فِي بَعْضِ الصُّوَرِ؛
 لِأَنَّ مَا كَانَ نَقْصًا فِي بَعْضِ الصُّوَرِ تَامًّا فِي بَعْضٍ:
 هُوَ كَمَالٌ لِنَوْعِ مِنْ الْمَوْجُودَاتِ دُونَ نَوْعٍ فَلَا يَكُونُ كَمَالًا لِلْمَوْجُودِ مِنْ حَيْثُ هُوَ مَوْجُودٌ.
 وَمِنْ الطُّرُقِ الَّتِي بِهَا يُعْرَفُ ذَلِكَ:
 أَنْ نُقَدِّرَ مَوْجُودَيْنِ: أَحَدُهُمَا مُتَّصِفٌ بِهَذَا وَالْآخَرُ بِنَقِيضِهِ فَإِنَّهُ يَظْهَرُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ أَيُّهُمَا أَكْمَلُ وَإِذَا قِيلَ هَذَا أَكْمَلُ مَنْ وَجْهٍ وَهَذَا أَنْقَصُ مِنْ وَجْهٍ لَمْ يَكُنْ كَمَالًا مُطْلَقًا. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ وَصَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَى سَيِّدِنَا مُحَمَّدٍ وَآلِهِ وَسَلَّمَ.
translated_text:
for the kind of perfection that belongs to the Creator surpasses what belongs to the created being by more than the highest of created beings surpasses the lowest. “The upshot of this” is that a created being is blameworthy for arrogance, domineering pride, and, at times, self-praise, and similar things.

As for the questioner’s statement:

“If you say, ‘We set aside the subject to which the attribute pertains and consider whether the attribute is a perfection or a deficiency,’ we likewise deem it impossible to judge it to be either, since it may be a perfection for one being and a deficiency for another, as mentioned.”

The reply is:

Rather, we say that a perfection involving no deficiency for a contingently existing being is an absolute perfection for everything that possesses it. Moreover, a perfection that constitutes perfection for an existent being—simply insofar as it exists—cannot constitute a deficiency in some instances. For whatever constitutes a deficiency in some instances and a perfection in others is a perfection for one kind of existent being but not another. It therefore cannot be a perfection for an existent being simply insofar as it exists.

One way to establish this is to suppose two existent beings, one possessing this attribute and the other its opposite. It then becomes apparent which of them is more perfect. If it is said, “This is more perfect in one respect but less perfect in another,” then it is not an absolute perfection.

Allah knows best. All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds. May Allah bless our master Muhammad and his family, and grant them peace.

translated_text:
He also said:

Section

Allah Most High says:

“To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names.”

He Most High also says:

“Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.”

He Most High also says:

“Allah—there is no deity except Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names.”

He Most High also says:

“He is Allah, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner. To Him belong the most beautiful names.”

Al-husnā (“most beautiful”) denotes what surpasses al-hasanah (“beautiful”); its singular form is al-ahāsin (“most beautiful”). There are three positions here:

One may say that His names are exclusively the most beautiful, and that He may be invoked only by such names.

Alternatively, one may say that He may be invoked only by the most beautiful names, although He may be named by other permissible names, even if they are not among the most beautiful. These are two well-known positions.

Or one may say that such names may be used both in invoking Him and in speaking about Him.

For in His words:

“To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them,”

and His words:

“Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names,”

He affirms that the most beautiful names belong to Him and commands that He be invoked by them. The apparent meaning of this is that all the most beautiful names belong to Him.

translated_text:
It may also be said that the reference is to “the most beautiful names” as a category: these must not be denied of Him, as the disbelievers did. He commanded that He be invoked by them and addressed using them, contrary to the polytheists’ practice of forbidding people to invoke Him by His name “the Most Merciful.”

Thus, it may be said that His words, “Call upon Him by them,” command that He be invoked by the most beautiful names and not by others. Similarly, His words, “Call them by their fathers’ names,” prohibit calling them by names attributing them to anyone other than their fathers.

A distinction is drawn between invoking Him and speaking about Him. He is to be invoked only by the most beautiful names. When speaking about Him, however, no bad designation may be used, but a good designation may be used, or one that is not bad even if it is not judged to be good. Examples include “thing,” “essence,” and “existent,” when the last means that which has real existence. If, however, it means “the One who is present in times of hardship,” then it is among the most beautiful names. Likewise, “the One who wills” and “the One who speaks” are not among the most beautiful names, since willing and speaking may be either praiseworthy or blameworthy. This is unlike “the All-Wise,” “the Most Merciful,” “the Truthful,” and similar names, which can only be praiseworthy.

The same distinction applies to the Messenger, concerning whom He said:

“Do not address the Messenger among yourselves as you address one another.”

He thus commanded them to say, “O Messenger of Allah” and “O Prophet of Allah,” just as Allah addressed him by saying, “O Prophet” and “O Messenger.” One should not say, “O Muhammad,” “O Ahmad,” or “O Abū al-Qāsim,” even though, when speaking about him—as in the call to prayer and the like—they would say, “I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.” Likewise, Allah Most High said:

“Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.”

He also said:

“And bringing good tidings of a messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad.”

And He said:

“Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah.”

translated_text:
Thus He, glorified be He, addressed Muhammad only by titles of honour, such as “the Messenger,” “the Prophet,” “the Enwrapped One,” and “the Cloaked One,” whereas He addressed the other prophets by their names, even though He sometimes mentions Muhammad’s name when speaking about him. He, glorified be He, thus distinguished between these two forms of discourse concerning the Messenger and commanded us to observe that distinction in his case. This also accords with people’s customary understanding: when addressing eminent rulers, scholars, shaykhs, and leaders, they address and call them only by honourable names. Yet when speaking about one of them, they may say that he is a human being, a rational animal, a body, a being brought into existence, a creature, one subject to a Lord, a fashioned being, someone born of a woman, and someone who eats food and drinks.

But every name and attribute mentioned when speaking about him is used when addressing him privately and speaking to him directly. Although some designations of created beings indicate their imperfection and their having come into existence, Allah’s names indicate neither imperfection nor His having come into existence. Rather, they include the most beautiful names, which indicate perfection, and these are the names by which He is invoked. When speaking about Him, however, one may use a good designation, or one that does not negate goodness without necessarily being good in itself (1).

As for the names handed down in revelation, every one of them conveys a good meaning. This should therefore be carefully considered with regard to supplication and statements about Him, whether transmitted or not transmitted. Such untransmitted statements have been formulated out of necessity because opponents arose—to distinguish between supplication and statements about Him, and to distinguish the transmitted wording that is used—or to acquaint them with what they did not know. Accordingly, not every designation mentioned in one context is to be mentioned in another; rather, the contexts must be distinguished.

He also said:

Section: The Great and Momentous Principle Concerning “Questions of Attributes and Actions”

Regarding their beginninglessness, their necessity or possibility, the terms derived from them, or the necessity of the kind as such and the possibility of particular instances.

We say:

Ascriptions to Allah, glorified be He, in the Quran and Sunnah—whether joining one noun to another in a possessive construction, attributing a verb to a noun, or predicating one noun of another—fall into three categories.

The first is the ascription of an attribute to the one who possesses it, as in His words, exalted be He:

“They encompass nothing of His knowledge.”

And His words:

“Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of strength.”

In the hadith of istikhāra:

“O Allah, I ask You to choose for me by Your knowledge and to grant me ability by Your power.”

And in another hadith:

“O Allah, by Your knowledge of the unseen and Your power over creation.”

These are examples of ascription through a possessive construction.

As for ascription through a verbal form, examples include His words:

“Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves.”

And His words:

“He knew that you would not be able to keep it up, so He turned to you in mercy.”

And as for predication in the form of a nominal sentence, examples include His words:

“Allah has knowledge of all things.”

“Allah has power over all things.”

This is because an expression describing an entity is either a sentence or a non-sentential expression. A sentence may be nominal, as in His words:

“Allah has knowledge of all things.”

Or verbal, as in His words:

“He knew that you would not be able to keep it up.”

A non-sentential expression necessarily involves ascribing the attribute, either explicitly or implicitly, as in His words:

“Anything of His knowledge.”

And His words:

“He is mightier than they in strength.”

Or it involves placing the one possessing the attribute in a possessive construction, as in His words:

“The Possessor of strength.”

And (the second category: the ascription of created things, as in His words:

“Allah’s she-camel and her right to drink.”

And His words:

“Purify My House for those who circle it.”

And His words:

“The Messenger of Allah,”

and:

“The servants of Allah.”

And His words:

“The Possessor of the Throne.”

And His words:

“His Kursī extends over the heavens and the earth.”

Muslims do not disagree that the things belonging to this category are created, just as Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah have not disagreed that the attributes belonging to the first category are beginningless and uncreated. Some speculative theologians have disagreed with them concerning the existence of the attributes, not the judgments concerning them. Some have disagreed with them concerning the beginninglessness of knowledge, and some have affirmed that it came into being. The purpose here is not to discuss this in detail.

(The third—which is the subject of discussion here—is that which involves the meaning of both an attribute and an action, as in His words:

“Allah spoke directly to Moses.”

And His words:

“His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

And His words:

“Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord…”

And His words:

“They wish to change the words of Allah.”

“A group of them used to hear the words of Allah.”

And His words:

“Indeed, Allah decrees whatever He wills.”

“He does whatever He wills.”

Those who disagree with them on this say: The proof that the world has a beginning is that it cannot be free of temporal events and does not precede them. If, however, it could precede them, their subsistence in it would not indicate that it has a beginning.

(*) The act of creation is an attribute subsisting in His essence, whereas the created thing is the entity brought into existence. This is based on our principle that He is described from pre-eternity by the attributes arising from acts, even though the things brought about by those acts originate in time. He said: This is the correct view.

Regarding rising over, descending, coming, and other kinds of acts that fall within the general category of motion, they adopt one of two views. Either they regard these as mere “relations” and “relational ascriptions,” meaning that Allah created the Throne as something below Him and thereby became established over it; that He removes the veils between Himself and His creation and thereby comes to them; and other such explanations. They likewise hold that speaking consists only in making the addressee hear. This is the view held by the adherents of this position who belong to Ahl al-Sunnah among the Hanbalīs, and by the Ashʿarīs and others who agree with them on all or part of it.

Alternatively, they say that these are “mere acts” occurring in created things, without any relational ascription or relation. Their disagreement, then, concerns whether these relations and relational ascriptions are affirmed for Allah, despite the general agreement that “relations” and “relational ascriptions” involving Allah Most High must arise in time, such as His being with His creation and the like.

Ibn ʿAqīl calls these relations “states” of Allah. These are not the “states” disputed by the theologians, such as being knowing and being powerful; rather, it is these relations and relational ascriptions that he calls states. He says that the arising of these states is not the arising of attributes, for these states are relations between Allah and creation, and this does not entail the existence of a reality subsisting

translated_text:
in the one to whom the relation is ascribed. For example, a person climbs towards a roof, which is above him, and then sits on it, so that it is beneath him. The roof is thus described at one time as being above and higher, and at another as being beneath and lower, without any attribute coming to subsist in it or any change occurring in it. Likewise, when a child is born to a man, his brother becomes a paternal uncle, his father a grandfather, his son a brother, and his wife’s brother a maternal uncle. These relations and relational ascriptions apply to them without any change occurring in them.

The second view—held by the Karrāmiyyah, many Hanbalīs, most scholars of hadith, and their followers among the jurists, Sufis, and the general body of Muslims—is that these attributes of action and similar attributes ascribed to Allah constitute a “third category.” Most statements of the early generations and of those who have described their position, even al-Ashʿarī, indicate this view. These attributes are neither created things separate from Him, nor are they on a par with His essence and the pre-eternal, necessary attributes that are not subject to His will, whether in their kinds or their individual instances.

Those holding this view may say that He speaks when He wills and is silent when He wills, and that He has always been One who speaks—meaning that He has always spoken when He wills and been silent when He wills. His speech is from Him; it is not created.

They likewise say that, although He has a pre-eternal will, He wills when He wishes, becomes angry, and abhors.

These scholars, or most of them, affirm the apparent meaning of the scriptural texts, such as His saying:

“Then He rose over the Throne,”

meaning that He rose over it after not having been established over it

translated_text:
and that He draws near to His servants, comes close to them, descends to the lowest heaven, and comes on the Day of Resurrection after not having been coming.

Some of these scholars may say that “temporally originated events” subsist in His essence. Others refrain from using this expression, either because it has not been transmitted in the religious reports, or because it may suggest a false meaning: that this resembles the inherence of “accidents” in created beings. Similarly, most theologians refrain from calling His attributes accidents, even though they are attributes subsisting in the one described by them, as accidents do.

Ibn al-Khatīb maintained that most schools and rational thinkers acknowledge this position in reality, even if they deny it verbally—including the philosophers, the Muʿtazilah, and the Ashʿarīs.

As for the “philosophers,” they hold that relations exist in external reality, and Allah exists with every temporally originated thing. This “being with” is a temporally originated attribute in His essence. Abū al-Barakāt al-Baghdādī, author of al-Muʿtabar, explicitly affirmed that particular instances of knowledge and will originate in His particular essence. He said that acknowledging Him as the God of this world is inconceivable without affirming this. He then said: “He must be exalted above such exaltation, and declared transcendent above such declarations of transcendence.”

As for the “Muʿtazilah,” the Basrans, such as Abū ʿAlī and Abū Hāshim, maintain that things seen and heard come into existence, and that thereby the qualities of being one who hears and sees arise for Allah. Abū al-Husayn al-Basrī maintains that new instances of knowledge arise in His essence as new objects of knowledge arise.

The Ashʿarīs likewise maintain that nonexistent things were neither heard nor seen, but became heard and seen after coming into existence. Yet hearing and sight, in their view, are not merely relations; rather, they are attributes subsisting in the essence of the All-Hearing,

the All-Seeing. They may also be held to this consequence on the basis of their statement that abrogation is the lifting or termination of a ruling, their affirmation of His knowledge of particulars, and likewise the cessation of the relation of His power and will.

The truth of the matter is that explicit disagreement over this principle exists among most schools; it is not confined to the people of hadith. As for “the deniers,” it may be said that this position follows necessarily from their views if they affirm attributes of Allah that are not eternal; this principle would then become a matter of agreement. They may, however, offer answers to these implications: sometimes valid answers, in which case the conclusion does not follow from their position, and sometimes invalid ones, in which case it does. There is no doubt about this.

As for the texts of the Quran and Sunnah, there is no doubt that their apparent meaning accords with this position. Those holding the former view may, however, reinterpret them or leave the matter to Allah. Those holding this position say that some of these texts admit of no reinterpretation, while those that do are accompanied by contextual indications and corroborating evidence (1) (*) establishing with certainty that Allah and His Messenger intended that meaning, or that this is what is understood from them.

They say that the deniers have no reliable proof: all they have is uncritical adherence to their predecessors, coupled with vilification and intimidation directed at listeners unfamiliar with the subtleties of theological argument. They also say that this is the position of most adherents of religious traditions and of Allah’s elect servants, and that only the innovators within those traditions have opposed it. Those holding the former view may say: “This contradicts consensus; this is disbelief; this entails change and temporal origination.” I have seen astonishing things from people concerning this principle.

Imam Ahmad said in the section containing “The Refutation of the Jahmiyyah and the Heretics”: “Likewise, Allah spoke as He willed, without our speaking of an internal cavity, a mouth, or lips.”

He said further on: “Rather, we say that Allah has always spoken whenever He wills. We do not say that He existed without speaking until [speech] was created.” His discussion of this is lengthy.

He said:

“Chapter: The Jahmiyyah’s Denial That Allah Spoke to Moses

We asked: ‘Why do you deny this?’ They replied: ‘Allah has not spoken and does not speak. He merely brought something into being which spoke on His behalf, and created a sound which He caused Moses to hear.’ They claimed that speech can only come from an internal cavity, a tongue, and lips.

We asked: ‘Can anything brought into being, other than Allah, say: “O Moses, indeed I am your Lord”? Or say:

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance”?’

Whoever claims that this was someone other than Allah has attributed lordship to that being. If, as the Jahmī claims, Allah had brought something into being, that created thing would have said: ‘O Moses, Allah is the Lord of all worlds.’ It could not rightly say:

‘Indeed, I am Allah, the Lord of all worlds.’

Allah—exalted be His praise—has said:

‘And Allah spoke to Moses directly.’

He also said:

‘When Moses came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him.’

And He said:

‘I have chosen you above the people through My messages and My speaking to you.’

Khaythamah, from ‘Adī ibn Hātim al-Tā’ī, who reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘There is not one of you but that his Lord will speak to him, with no interpreter between them’?

As for their claim that speech can only come from an internal cavity, a mouth, lips, and a tongue, we say: Did Allah not say to the heavens and the earth:

‘Come, willingly or unwillingly.’ They said: ‘We come willingly.’

Do you suppose that they spoke with an internal cavity, a mouth, lips, and a tongue? He also said:

‘And We subjected the mountains to glorify Us along with David.’

Do you suppose that they glorified Him with an internal cavity, a mouth, a tongue, and lips? Rather, Allah caused them to speak however He willed. Likewise, Allah spoke however He willed, without our speaking of an internal cavity, a mouth, lips, or a tongue.

When the arguments left him no escape, he said: ‘Allah did speak to Moses, but His speech is other than Him.’ We asked: ‘And whatever is other than Him is created?’ He replied: ‘Yes.’ We said: ‘This is the same as your original claim, except that you are trying to shield yourselves from condemnation.’

There is also the report of al-Zuhrī, who said: ‘When Moses heard his Lord’s speech, he said: “My Lord, was what I heard Your speech?” He said: “Yes, Moses, it was My speech. I spoke to you only with the strength of ten thousand tongues. I possess the strength of all tongues, and I am more powerful still. I spoke to you only to the extent that your body could bear. Had I spoken to you with more than that, you would have died.”’ He continued: ‘When Moses returned to his people, they said to him: “Describe your Lord’s speech to us.” He replied: “Glory be to Allah! How could I describe it to you?” They said: “Then give us a comparison.” He said: “Have you heard the sounds of approaching thunderclaps, with the sweetest sound you have ever heard? It was something like that.”’”

They said: “Allah brings something into being, and it speaks on His behalf, just as He brought it into being and it spoke to Moses.”

We said: “Then who says:

‘We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers.’

‘Then We will surely recount to them with knowledge’?

Is it not Allah who does the questioning?”

They said: “In all these cases, He merely brings something into being, and it speaks on Allah’s behalf.”

We said: “You have fabricated a monstrous lie against Allah by claiming that He does not speak. You have thereby likened Him to the idols worshipped besides Allah, for idols neither speak nor move nor pass from one place to another.”

When the argument prevailed against him, he said: “Allah may indeed speak, but His speech is created.”

We said: “You have likened Allah to His creation by claiming that His speech is created. According to your doctrine, there was a time when He did not speak. Likewise, the children of Adam existed without speaking until He created speech for them. You have thus combined disbelief with likening Allah to His creation. Exalted is Allah far above such a description!

“Rather, we say that Allah has always spoken whenever He wills. We do not say that He existed without speaking until He created speech. Nor do we say that He once did not know until He created knowledge. Nor do we say that He once existed without power until He created power for Himself. Nor do we say that He once had no light until He created light for Himself. Nor do we say that He once existed without greatness until He created greatness for Himself.”

He then spoke at length affirming the divine attributes and explaining that they do not contradict Allah’s oneness.

translated_text:
A related question concerns the attributes involving movement, such as coming, arrival, and descent: are they to be interpreted as meaning the coming of His power and His command? Two positions are reported:

The first is that they mean the coming of His power. This is Hanbal’s report concerning the ordeal.

The second is that they are to be accepted as they have come, like the other attributes. This is the apparent position of the school, well known among our scholars. Some held that Hanbal had erred; others said that Ahmad had said this to argue against his opponents on their own premises. Still others, such as Ibn al-Zāghūnī, treated it as a report confined to this particular case, whereas Ibn ‘Aqīl extended it to all the other attributes.

This principle has ramifications for most questions concerning the divine attributes, especially speech, will, and the attributes connected with His will, such as descent and rising over the Throne. It was the cause of the dispute between the imam of imams, Muhammad ibn Ishāq ibn Khuzaymah, and a group of his distinguished companions.

Section

The judge said:

“Ahmad said in Hanbal’s report: ‘Allah has always been speaking, knowing, and forgiving.’ In ‘Abd Allāh’s report, he said: ‘Allah has always spoken whenever He wills.’

I found this in al-Mihnah (The Ordeal), as narrated by Hanbal, when ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Ishāq, al-Mu‘tasim’s judge, questioned and reproached him, saying: ‘What do you say about the Quran?’

He said: ‘I replied, “What do you say about knowledge?” He fell silent. I then said to ‘Abd al-Rahmān, “The Quran is part of Allah’s knowledge. Whoever claims that Allah’s knowledge is created has disbelieved in Allah.”’

He said: ‘I questioned ‘Abd al-Rahmān, but he gave me no answer. ‘Abd al-Rahmān said to me, “Allah existed when there was no Quran.” I replied, “Did Allah exist without knowledge?” He refrained from answering. Had he claimed that Allah existed without knowledge, he would have disbelieved in Allah.’

Then Abū ‘Abd Allāh said: ‘Allah has always been knowing and speaking. Allah is worshipped through His attributes, which are neither delimited nor known except as He has described Himself. We refer the Quran to the One who knows it—to Allah, for He knows it best. From Him it began, and to Him it will return.’

In another passage, he said: ‘I heard Abū ‘Abd Allāh say, “Allah has always been speaking. The Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated in every respect. Allah is not to be described with anything beyond that with which He has described Himself.”’”

Abū Bakr ‘Abd al-‘Azīz, in the first volume of the “Book of the Sunnah” within al-Muqni‘, was presented with the objection: “If you say that He has always been speaking, that would be purposeless.” He replied:

“Our scholars hold two views. The first is that He has always been speaking, just as He has always been knowing, because the opposite of speech is muteness, just as the opposite of knowledge is ignorance.”

He said: “Some of our scholars say: ‘He has affirmed that He is the Creator, yet He cannot be creating at all times. Rather, we say that He creates when He wills to create. His not creating at all times does not invalidate His being the Creator. Likewise, His not speaking at all times does not invalidate His being one who speaks. Rather, He speaks and creates, even though He is not creating at all times or speaking at all times.’”

When this question was put to Judge Abū Ya‘lā in his book Īdāh al-Bayān fī Mas’alat al-Qur’ān (Clarifying the Explanation Concerning the Quran), he said: “We say that He has always been speaking, without being spoken to or addressed, and without commanding or forbidding. Ahmad explicitly stated this in Hanbal’s report.” He continued his discussion until he cited from Abū Bakr what the latter had related in al-Muqni‘. He then said: “Perhaps the scholar among our companions who holds this view follows Ahmad ibn Hanbal’s statement in ‘Abd Allāh’s report: ‘He has always spoken whenever He wills.’”

He said: “Whoever holds this view holds that the Quran came into being. We have already interpreted Ahmad’s words, ‘He speaks whenever He wills,’ at the beginning of this discussion. This is not analogous to His being described as creating and providing, because those attributes

must be understood with that qualification; for if we supposed the act to have existed from eternity, this would entail the eternity of the world. Speech, however, is like knowledge.”

The judge said at the beginning of the discussion:

“Ahmad’s statement, ‘He has always been forgiving,’ establishes that all the attributes are eternal, whether they are derived from an act, such as forgiveness, creation and provision, or are not so derived. His statement, ‘He has always been speaking whenever He wills,’ means: whenever He wills to make it heard.”

I say: This approach of the judge is also that of his followers, their followers and others, such as Ibn ‘Aqīl and Ibn al-Zāghūnī. Most hadith scholars among Ahmad’s followers and others, as well as many speculative theologians, disagree with him on this matter. Regarding the act, they hold one of two views:

The first—which is the judge’s other view and the one regarded as correct by our scholars—is that the act is eternal, while what it produces is created. This is just as we concede to them regarding the will and the word that brings things into being: the will is eternal, while what is willed comes into being. Likewise, the opposing disputant says: “Bringing into being is eternal, whereas what is brought into being is created.”

(The second is that, in their view, the act itself and speech are both uncreated, even though they occur at one time and not at another; for they subsist in Allah, whereas whatever is created must be separate from Allah.

They say that Ahmad’s statement agrees with what we have said, for he said: “He has always been speaking whenever He wills.”

 الَّذِي فِيهِ نِزَاعٌ وَهُوَ يُشْبِهُ الْعِلْمَ مِنْ حَيْثُ هُوَ وَصْفٌ قَائِمٌ بِهِ لَا يَتَعَلَّقُ بِالْمَخْلُوقِ وَيُشْبِهُ الْمَغْفِرَةَ مِنْ حَيْثُ هُوَ مُتَعَلِّقٌ بِمَشِيئَتِهِ كَمَا فَسَّرَهُ فِي الْمَوْضِعِ الْآخَرِ فَعُلِمَ أَنَّ قِدَمَهُ عِنْدَهُ: أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَزَلْ إذَا شَاءَ تَكَلَّمَ وَإِذَا شَاءَ سَكَتَ لَمْ يَتَجَدَّدْ لَهُ وَصْفُ الْقُدْرَةِ عَلَى الْكَلَامِ الَّتِي هِيَ صِفَةُ كَمَالٍ كَمَا لَمْ يَتَجَدَّدْ لَهُ وَصْفُ الْقُدْرَةِ عَلَى الْمَغْفِرَةِ. وَإِنْ كَانَ الْكَمَالُ هُوَ أَنْ يَتَكَلَّمَ إذَا شَاءَ وَيَسْكُتَ إذَا شَاءَ. وَأَمَّا قَوْلُ الْقَاضِي إنَّ هَذَا قَوْلٌ بِحُدُوثِهِ فَيُجِيبُونَ عَنْهُ بِجَوَابَيْنِ. أَحَدُهُمَا أَلَّا يُسَمَّى مُحْدَثًا وَأَنْ يُسَمَّى حَدِيثًا؛ إذْ الْمُحْدَثُ هُوَ الْمَخْلُوقُ الْمُنْفَصِلُ وَأَمَّا الْحَدِيثُ فَقَدْ سَمَّاهُ اللَّهُ حَدِيثًا وَهَذَا قَوْلُ الكَرَّامِيَة وَأَكْثَرِ أَهْلِ الْحَدِيثِ وَالْحَنْبَلِيَّةِ.
 وَالثَّانِي:
 أَنَّهُ يُسَمَّى مُحْدَثًا كَمَا فِي قَوْلِهِ: 
{مِنْ ذِكْرٍ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ مُحْدَثٍ}
 وَلَيْسَ بِمَخْلُوقِ. وَهَذَا قَوْلُ كَثِيرٍ مِنْ الْفُقَهَاءِ وَأَهْلِ الْحَدِيثِ وَالْكَلَامِ
translated_text:
and he did not say, “He has always been addressing others whenever He wills.” According to those who hold that speech is eternal and necessary, what depends on His will is only His addressing others—a contingent act—not His speaking.

This is clarified by Ahmad’s statement elsewhere—may Allah be pleased with him:

“Allah has always been speaking, knowing and forgiving.”

He thus mentioned three attributes: the attribute that is eternal and necessary, namely knowledge; and the attribute that is contingent and dependent on His will, namely forgiveness. There is agreement concerning these two. He also mentioned speaking, the third category, concerning which there is disagreement. It resembles knowledge insofar as it is an attribute subsisting in Him that does not relate to created beings, and it resembles forgiveness insofar as it depends on His will, as he explained elsewhere.

It is therefore clear that, for Ahmad, its eternity means that Allah has always been such that, if He wills, He speaks, and if He wills, He remains silent. He did not newly acquire the ability to speak, which is an attribute of perfection, just as He did not newly acquire the ability to forgive—although perfection consists in speaking when He wills and remaining silent when He wills.

As for the judge’s statement that this amounts to saying that His speech comes into being, they offer two replies.

The first is that it should not be called muhdath (newly originated), but should be called hadīth (discourse), since muhdath denotes something created and separate from Allah, whereas Allah Himself has called His speech hadīth. This is the position of the Karrāmiyya and most hadith scholars and Hanbalīs.

The second is that it may be called muhdath, as in His words:

“a new reminder from their Lord”

without being created. This is the position of many jurists, hadith scholars and speculative theologians

translated_text:
such as Dāwūd ibn Alī al-Asbahānī—the founder of the school. However, Ahmad is reported to have denounced this, and his denunciation may be cited in support of one of the two views held by our companions.

Al-Marwadhī reported that Abū Abd Allāh said:

“Who is Dāwūd ibn Alī al-Asbahānī? May Allah grant him no relief! I received a letter from Muhammad ibn Yahyā al-Naysābūrī stating that Dāwūd al-Asbahānī had falsely declared that the Quran is newly originated.”

Abū Bakr al-Khallāl recorded this report in his Book of the Sunnah.

Abd Allāh ibn Ahmad said: “Dāwūd sought permission to visit my father, who said, ‘Who is this? Dāwūd? May Allah’s love never mend his heart, and may Allah fill his grave with worms!’ He subsequently died infested with worms.”

Unqualified expressions may suggest something other than the intended meaning. One should therefore say:

“If, by ‘newly originated,’ you mean that it is something created and separate from Allah, as the Jahmiyya, Mu'tazila and Najjāriyya maintain, then this is false, and we do not affirm it. But if you mean that it is speech which Allah uttered by His will after not having uttered that particular speech—although He had uttered other speech before it, and has always spoken whenever He wills—then we do affirm this.”

This is what the Quran and Sunnah indicate, and it is the position of the early generations and the hadith scholars. The opposing position was an innovation introduced by the Kullābiyya and Ash'ariyya. Those who affirm the former position, however, hold two views.

The first is that He began speaking after not having spoken, although He had been capable of speech—just as He created the heavens and the earth after not having created them, although He had been capable of creating them. This is the position of the Karrāmiyya and others who say that newly occurring events come to subsist in Him after not having subsisted in Him. The statement that His speech is ‘newly originated’ can bear this meaning, and Ahmad’s denunciation can be understood as directed at it.

translated_text:
The second is that He has always been One who speaks, speaking whenever He wills. This is the position held by those hadith scholars who affirm this view.

Those who hold this position may say that His speech is eternal, neither newly occurring nor newly originated. By this they mean speech as a kind, since He has always spoken whenever He wills, although He utters particular speech whenever He wills. Someone who says, “Newly occurring events do not subsist in His essence,” may intend this meaning, on the basis that speech as a kind did not newly arise in how His essence is characterized.

Abū Abd Allāh ibn Hāmid said in his Usūl:

“Among the things that must be believed and affirmed is that Allah speaks; that His speech is eternal; and that He has always been One who speaks, being characterized by this at all times. His speech is eternal, not newly originated, like His knowledge and power. The school’s position may also allow that speech is an attribute of One who has always been characterized by it and who speaks whenever He wills and when He wills. We do not say that He is silent at one time and speaking at another, beginning with the origination of speech.

“The evidence establishing that He speaks in the manner we have described is the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Prophet, and the consensus of the people of truth, apart from the misguided faction—the Muʿtazila—and other speculative theologians, who refused to affirm that Allah speaks.”

He then mentioned some evidence from the Book and the Sunnah. After that, he said:

translated_text:
“Section

There is no disagreement in what is reported from Abū Abd Allāh that Allah spoke the Quran before He created creation and existed before all created beings; and that Allah has always spoken however He wills and as He wills. When He wills, He sends down His speech, and when He wills, He does not send it down. The Muʿtazila rejected this, saying: ‘It originated after created beings came into existence.’”

I say: Ibn Hāmid, too, has thus reported both positions, although he mentions agreement concerning Abū Abd Allāh’s position that Allah has always spoken however He wills and as He wills. Yet, under either position, he rejected saying: “He is silent at one time and speaking at another.” He affirmed that one may say: “He speaks whenever He wills and when He wills,” but not that He is silent at any time. Likewise, the Karrāmiyya say that He is not described as having been silent or descending from eternity. Yet there is a difference between his statement and theirs, as I shall relate.

Abū Abd Allāh ibn Hāmid said concerning “the attributes of action”:

 قَالَ ابْنُ حَامِدٍ:
 فَإِذَا تَقَرَّرَ هَذَا الْأَصْلُ فِي نُزُولِ ذَاتِهِ مِنْ غَيْرِ صِفَةٍ وَلَا حَدٍّ
translated_text:
Section

Among the matters that believers must affirm is that the True One, glorified be He, descends to the lowest heaven every night and descends on the Day of Arafah, without specifying how, positing an equal, setting bounds, or drawing any likeness.

He said: “This is our imam’s explicit statement.”

Yūsuf ibn Mūsā said: “I asked Abū Abd Allāh: ‘Does Allah descend to the lowest heaven however He wills, without description?’ He replied: ‘Yes.’”

On the question of rising over the Throne, he said, as Hanbal reported from him: “Our Lord is upon the Throne, without limit or description.”

In al-Marwadhī’s report, he was asked concerning Ibn al-Mubārak: “Is Allah known to be upon the Throne with a limit?” He replied: “That has reached me,” and he approved of it.

Then Abū Abd Allāh said:

“Are they waiting for anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds?”

He also said:

“And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank.”

Ibn Hāmid said: “The school’s position, as we have explained, admits of no disagreement: His Essence descends. I have seen some of our companions report that Abū Abd Allāh said concerning His coming: ‘He comes in His Essence.’”

He said: “This amounts to supposition on the part of the person saying it, and attributing it to him is an error, as is clear from the explicit statement we have established from him.”

Ibn Hāmid said: “Once this principle has been established concerning the descent of His Essence, without description or limit,

“Among the things that must be believed and accepted is His coming to the gathering on the Day of Resurrection, just as He descends to His heaven. This is indicated by His words:

‘And your Lord comes, with the angels in rows upon rows.’

And the Most High says:

He said: “This indicates that when He comes to them and sits upon His Footstool, the whole earth will shine with His lights.”

As for ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Yahyā al-Kinānī, the author of al-Hayda (The Evasion) and al-Radd ʿalā al-Jahmiyya wa-l-Qadariyya (Refutation of the Jahmiyya and the Qadariyya), his statements in al-Hayda and his refutation of the Jahmiyya admit of that interpretation. For the substance of al-Hayda is that he refuted Bishr al-Marīsī’s appeal to His words:

“Allah is the Creator of all things,”

and His words:

“Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Quran.”

He then advanced three arguments against al-Marīsī:

(The first was that he said: “If it is created, then you must say either that He created it within Himself, that He created it within something other than Himself, or that He created it as something subsisting independently in and of itself.”

and nothing created can exist within Him, nor can He be deficient such that something is added to Him when He creates it—exalted, majestic and supremely great is Allah, far above that.

If he says, ‘He created it within something other than Himself,’ then reflection and analogy necessarily commit him to saying that every utterance Allah creates within another is Allah’s speech; no distinction can be drawn between the two. Is poetry, then, to be considered Allah’s speech? Is filthy speech to be considered Allah’s speech? Are obscenity and disbelief to be considered Allah’s speech? Is every utterance that Allah has condemned, along with the one who uttered it, to be considered Allah’s speech? This is impossible. There is no way for him to establish or maintain it, given the manifest enormity, disgrace and disbelief it entails for anyone who says it.

If he says, ‘He created it as something subsisting independently in and of itself,’ this is an impossible falsehood that cannot be maintained on the basis of analogy, reflection or reason. Speech can only proceed from a speaker, just as will can only proceed from one who wills, knowledge from one who knows, and power from one who possesses power. No one has ever seen, nor will anyone ever see, speech subsisting independently and speaking by itself. Since its being created is impossible in all three of these ways, it is established that it is an attribute of Allah, and all of Allah’s attributes are uncreated.”

translated_text:
ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said:

I said, “You are right: He brought them into existence by His power, which has always existed. Do you not say that He has always been powerful?”

He replied, “Yes.”

I asked him, “Do you then say that He has always been acting?”

He replied, “I do not say that.”

I said to him, “Then you must necessarily say that He created by an act proceeding from His power. The act is not the power itself, for power is an attribute of Allah, and it is not said that an attribute of Allah is Allah, nor that it is other than Allah.”

Bishr said, “You too must say that Allah has always been acting and creating. If you say that, it follows that created things have always existed alongside Allah.”

I replied, “You have no right to pass judgment on me, impose on me a conclusion that does not follow from what I say, or attribute to me something I have not said. I did not say that the Creator has always been creating and the Doer has always been acting, such that you could impose the conclusion you mentioned. I only said that He has always been the Doer who would act and the Creator who would create, for acting is an attribute of Allah: He has the power to act, and nothing prevents Him from doing so.”

Bishr said, “I say that He brought things into existence by His power. You may say whatever you wish.”

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said:

I said, “Commander of the Faithful, Bishr has acknowledged that Allah existed when nothing else existed, and that He brought things into existence by His power after they had been nothing. I said: if He brought them into existence by His command and His speech, through His power, then, Commander of the Faithful, the first thing Allah created must have been created by a word He spoke, a will He willed, or a power He determined. Whichever of these it was, it is established that there is a will, one who wills, and an object of that will; a word, one who speaks, and one addressed; and a power, one who possesses power, and an object of that power

, and all of this precedes the Creator. Whatever precedes the Creator is not part of creation.”

I say:

By “before creation,” he means the One who wills, speaks, and has power, together with His will, speech, and power. As for the object of His will and power, to which He speaks, either he means its being established in knowledge through His saying to it, “Be,” or it was not included in the wording. This statement implies that … (1)

He also said, “He has always been One who would act,” and explained this in terms of His action, as noted above.

In his History of Nishapur, in the biography of Imam Muhammad ibn Ishāq ibn Khuzaymah, Abū ‘Abd Allah al-Hākim gave a lengthy account of the dispute between him and some of his companions, including Abū ‘Alī al-Thaqafī, Abū Bakr Ahmad ibn Ishāq al-Duba‘ī, Abū Bakr ibn Abī ‘Uthmān the ascetic, and Abū Muhammad ibn Mansūr the judge. He mentioned that a group reported to the imam that some of his companions had begun opposing him without his knowledge, and that they followed the doctrine of the Kullābiyyah. Imam Abū Bakr was firmly opposed to the Kullābiyyah.

Al-Hākim said: Abū Bakr Ahmad ibn Yahyā, the speculative theologian, related to me:

“One night we gathered at the home of a scholar, and the subject of Allah’s speech arose: is it eternal, having always existed, or is it established when He, exalted is He, reports that He has spoken it? We entered into a discussion of this.

“Some of us said, ‘The Creator’s speech is eternal and has always existed.’ Others said, ‘His speech is eternal, but it is established only through His reporting His speech.’

translated_text:
So I went early to Abū ‘Alī al-Thaqafī and told him what had happened. He said, ‘Whoever denies that it has always existed has thereby adopted the belief that Allah’s speech originated in time.’ “This issue” spread throughout the city, and Mansūr al-Tūsī went with a group to Abū Bakr Muhammad ibn Ishāq and informed him of it. Mansūr went so far as to say, ‘Did I not tell the shaykh that these men hold the doctrine of the Kullābiyyah? This is their doctrine!’ Abū Bakr gathered his companions and said, ‘Have I not repeatedly forbidden you to engage in speculative theology?’ He said nothing more to them that day.”

He then mentioned that Abū Bakr subsequently came out to his companions, that he wrote a refutation of them, and that they contradicted him and accused him of holding Jahm’s view that the Quran originated in time, while he classed them as Kullābīs.

Al-Hākim said:

I heard Abū Sa‘īd ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Ahmad al-Muqri’ say: I heard Abū Bakr Muhammad ibn Ishāq say:

“What I hold is that the Quran is Allah’s speech, His revelation, and what He has sent down, uncreated. Whoever says of the Quran, any part of it, or His revelation and what He has sent down that it is created; or says that Allah does not speak after what He spoke in pre-eternity; or says that Allah’s actions are created; or says that the Quran originated in time; or says that any of Allah’s attributes—His attributes of essence—or any of Allah’s names is created: such a person, in my judgment, is a Jahmī who must be called upon to repent. If he repents, well and good; otherwise, I would strike off his head, and he would be cast onto one of the rubbish heaps. This is my position and that of the scholars devoted to the transmitted reports whom I have met in the East and the West.

“Whoever attributes anything contrary to this to me is a liar and a slanderer. Anyone who examines my scholarly writings will clearly see that the Kullābiyyah—may Allah curse them—are lying when they attribute to me views contrary to my foundational position and religious convictions. on Allah’s oneness, divine decree, and the foundations of religious knowledge as I have. Those who attribute to me anything contrary to what is in my books are liars and evildoers.”

He also related that Ibn Khuzaymah said:

“Some of these ignorant men who have emerged in recent years claim that Allah does not repeat His speech. They do not understand Allah’s Book! Allah has explicitly stated in several passages of the Book that He created Adam and commanded the angels to prostrate before him. He repeated this account in more than one place, repeatedly mentioned His speaking to Moses, mentioned Jesus son of Mary in several places, and praised Himself in several places, saying:

‘All praise is for Allah, who has sent down the Book to His servant’;

and ‘All praise is for Allah, who created the heavens and the earth’—to the end of the verse;

and ‘All praise is for Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth.’

He repeated more than thirty times:

‘Then which of your Lord’s favors will you both deny?’

“I never imagined that a Muslim would suppose that Allah does not say something twice. This is the position of someone who claims that Allah’s speech is created and imagines that one cannot say, ‘Allah created the same thing twice.’”

Al-Hākim said:

translated_text:
opponents of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd and his followers, such as al-Hārith and others.” The discussion between him and Abū ʿAlī on this matter continued at length.

I said, “I have compiled the foundations of our positions in a document.” I brought out the document for him and said, “Examine these issues that I have compiled and explained in my own handwriting. If there is anything in them that you reject, explain your objection to us so that we may abandon it.” He took the document from me and continued examining and studying it until he had understood its contents. Then he raised his head and said, “I see nothing here that I do not affirm. All of it is my position, and it is what I found my teachers adhering to.” I asked him to record in his own handwriting, at the end of that statement, that this was his position.

Then Abū So-and-so, So-and-so, and So-and-so went to him and said, “The master did not carefully examine what he wrote in his own handwriting. They have deceived you and misrepresented the situation.”

Al-Hākim said:

Here is a copy of the written statement. Abū Bakr Ahmad ibn Ishāq and Yahyā ibn Mansūr state:

“Allah’s speech is an attribute of His essence. No part of Allah’s speech is creation or a created thing, an act or the product of an act, something newly originated, an event, or events. Whoever claims that any part of it is created or newly originated, or claims that speech is an attribute of action, is a misguided Jahmī and an innovator.

“And I say: Allah has always spoken and will always speak. Speech is an attribute of His essence. Nothing in the speech of His creation resembles His speech, and His speech can never be exhausted. Our Lord, with His speech, His knowledge, His power, and the attributes of His essence, has always been One; He has always been and will always be. Our Lord spoke to His prophets and spoke to Moses. It is Allah who said to him:

‘Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me

so worship Me.’ He will speak to His devoted servants on the Day of Resurrection and greet them with a spoken salutation of peace in His abode of eternal residence. He will call out to His servants, saying:

‘What answer did you give the messengers?’

And He will say:

‘To whom belongs sovereignty today? To Allah, the One, the All-Prevailing.’

He will address the inhabitants of the Fire with rebuke and punishment, saying to them:

‘Remain despised therein, and do not speak to Me.’

The Compeller will speak privately to every one of His creatures, with no interpreter between Him and any of them, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said. ‘Our Lord will speak to Hell, saying to it, “Are you filled?” He will cause it to speak, and it will say, “Is there any more?”’

Whoever claims that Allah spoke only once, and spoke only what He spoke, after which His speech came to an end, has disbelieved in Allah. Rather, Allah has always spoken and will always speak. Nothing is like His speech, for it is one of the attributes of His essence. Allah has denied that anything is like His speech, just as He has denied that anything is like Him. He has denied that His speech can be exhausted, just as He has denied that He can perish. He says:

‘Everything will perish except His Face.’

And He says:

‘Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord were exhausted.’

Allah’s speech is not separate from Allah. It is neither something besides Him, nor other than Him, nor He Himself. Rather, it is one of the attributes of His essence, like His knowledge, which is one of the attributes of His essence. Our Lord has always been knowing and will always be knowing; He has always spoken and will always speak. He is thus the One described by the attributes

“He is the Most Subtle, the All-Aware.”

He spoke to Moses, saying to him:

“Indeed, I am your Lord.”

Whoever claims that someone other than Allah spoke to him has disbelieved in Allah.

For Allah descends every night to the lowest heaven and says: “Is there anyone calling upon Me, that I may answer him? Is there anyone repenting, that I may accept his repentance?” Whoever claims that it is His knowledge or His command that descends has gone astray. Rather, the One who descends to the lowest heaven is the One who is worshipped—glory be to Him—to whom people say, “O Most Compassionate, O Most Merciful!” He speaks to His servants without specifying how.

“The Most Compassionate rose over the Throne”—without specifying how, not as the Jahmiyyah claim, that He took possession of sovereignty or gained mastery. Rather, He rose over His Throne, without specifying how. He is Allah, to whom belong the most beautiful names. Whoever claims that any of His names is created or newly originated is a Jahmī.

Allah addresses His servants repeatedly, recounting His narratives and reiterating His commands and prohibitions to them, generation after generation. Whoever claims that Allah does not address His servants or repeatedly recount His narratives and reiterate His commands and prohibitions to them is astray and an innovator. Rather, Allah, with all the attributes of His essence, is One, and has always been and will always remain so. Anything ascribed to Allah among His attributes of action that is not separate from Him is uncreated. Everything ascribed to Allah that is separate from Him and other than Him is created.

And I say: All the actions of His servants are created.

And I say: Faith consists of speech and action; it increases and decreases. The best of people after the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is Abū Bakr, then ʿUmar, then ʿUthmān, then ʿAlī.

And I say: Those who commit major sins are subject to Allah’s will when they die: if He wills, He punishes them and then forgives them; and if He wills, He forgives them without punishment. Solitary reports are accepted when transmitted by upright narrators and must be acted upon, while concordant reports establish knowledge and must be acted upon.

The text in Imam Ibn Khuzaymah’s handwriting reads:

“Muhammad ibn Ishāq says: Abū Bakr Ahmad ibn Ishāq and Abū Muhammad Yahyā ibn Mansūr affirmed before me the contents of this document. I approve of all of it and consider it correct.”

Al-Hākim said:

I heard the ascetic Abū al-Hasan ʿAlī ibn Ahmad al-Būshanjī say, in the course of a longer account:

“When news reached us of the disagreement that had arisen among the scholars of Nishapur, I left my homeland and travelled to Nishapur. A group gathered around me, asking about those questions, but I said nothing whatsoever about them.

“Then I wrote: ‘The position is that stated by Abū ʿAlī.’ I went to Rayy and visited ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Abī Hātim. I told him what had happened in Nishapur between Abū Bakr and his companions. He said: ‘What business does Abū Bakr have with speculative theology? It is more fitting for us and for him not to speak about what we do not know.’

“I left him and went to see Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Fulānī, who explained those questions to me clearly and said: ‘One of the speculative theologians belonging to the Qadariyyah had come to Muhammad ibn Ishāq, and his words had found acceptance with him.’

 مِنْ غَدٍ ذَلِكَ الْيَوْمَ إنِّي رَأَيْت الْبَارِحَةَ فِي الْمَنَامِ كَأَنَّ أَحْمَد بْنَ السَّرِيِّ الزَّاهِدَ الْمَرْوَزِي لَكَمَنِي بِرِجْلِهِ ثُمَّ قَالَ: كَأَنَّك فِي شَكٍّ مِنْ أُمُورِ هَؤُلَاءِ الْكُلَّابِيَة قَالَ: ثُمَّ نَظَرَ إلَى مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ إسْحَاقَ فَقَالَ: 
{هَذَا بَلَاغٌ لِلنَّاسِ وَلِيُنْذَرُوا بِهِ وَلِيَعْلَمُوا أَنَّمَا هُوَ إلَهٌ وَاحِدٌ وَلِيَذَّكَّرَ أُولُو الْأَلْبَابِ}
.
translated_text:
Then he mentioned that he had presented those questions to the jurists and speculative theologians he found in Baghdad. They agreed with Abū al-ʿAbbās’s position and sought advantage for Abū Bakr ibn Ishāq in what he had made known. He also mentioned that Abū ʿAmr al-Najjār subsequently arrived from Nishapur and wrote on behalf of Abū Bakr Muhammad ibn Ishāq to a group of scholars concerning those questions, and that they would report anyone who disagreed with Abū Bakr ibn Khuzaymah to the ruler.

Al-Hākim said: I heard Abū ʿAlī Muhammad ibn Ishāq al-Abyūrdī say:

“I was present in such-and-such a village for a greeting to a young one among its followers (1). ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hamshād, of such-and-such a clan, and a number of the town’s notables attended. Ishāq ibn Abī al-Fard, the governor of Nishapur, was also present. He had us read Hamawayh ibn ʿAlī’s letter to him, instructing him to carry out Abū Bakr Muhammad ibn Ishāq ibn Khuzaymah’s orders concerning them: exile, beating, and imprisonment.”

He said:

“ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hamshād then rose from that gathering and said: ‘Blessed are they if what is being said about them is falsely attributed to them.’”

Abū ʿAlī said: The following day, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Hamshād said to me:

“Last night I saw in a dream that the ascetic Ahmad ibn al-Sarī al-Marwazī struck me with his foot and then said: ‘You seem to be in doubt about the affairs of these Kullābiyyah.’”

He said: Then he looked at Muhammad ibn Ishāq and said:

“This is a message for mankind, that they may be warned by it, that they may know that He is but One God, and that those of understanding may take heed.”

Al-Hākim related:

I heard Abū Muhammad al-Anmātī, the righteous servant of Allah, say:

“When that conflict intensified, so that no ten people could gather in the town without quarrelling over it, and most ordinary people began exchanging blows over it, Abū ʿAmr al-Hīrī travelled to Rayy, where the martyred emir was then staying, to secure letters to his deputy. One letter was addressed to Abū Bakr ibn Ishāq, instructing him to banish from the town the four men who had opposed Abū Bakr.”

He then mentioned that they convened a session for them.

Shaykh al-Islām Abū Ismāʿīl ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muhammad al-Ansārī said in The Creed of Ahl al-Sunnah and the Matters upon Which the People of Truth in the Muslim Community Have Reached Consensus:

Chapter: Concerning the Quran

“Know that Allah speaks and utters words, and praises Himself for speaking, for He censured the idols and the calf for their inability to speak. He speaks whenever He wills, with no one to prevent or compel Him. The Quran is His speech; He Himself spoke it.”

Ibn ʿAqīl interpreted Shaykh al-Islām’s words in much the same way that al-Qādī interpreted Ahmad’s words.

He said:

“This is another travesty in religion, offending many an eye. Abū Bakr ibn Ishāq al-Lanjarūdī, Ibn Khuzaymah, became alert to it. Nishapur was then the home of transmitted reports: people craned their necks towards it, undertook journeys to it, and brought knowledge back from it. What, then, do you think of gatherings from which al-Thaqafī and al-Dubaʿī were excluded, despite their combined knowledge of hadith and jurisprudence, truthfulness, piety, eloquence, careful verification, stature, and public prominence? They took no pleasure in speculative theology or even a whiff of its adherents. Ibn Khuzaymah was in one house, Muhammad ibn Ishāq al-Sarrāj in another, and Abū Hāmid ibn al-Sharqī in another.”

Shaykh al-Islām said:

“That imam, Abū Bakr, sprang into action against this tribulation. He continued loudly exposing its ugliness and writing refutations of it, like someone warning of an approaching army, until the following was recorded in books, firmly established in hearts, taught in elementary schools, and engraved in prayer niches: Allah speaks; if He wills, He speaks, and if He wills, He remains silent. May Allah richly reward that imam and those illustrious men for defending His religion and honouring His Prophet.”

I say:

In the hadith narrated by Salmān from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“What is lawful is what Allah has made lawful in His Book, and what is unlawful is what Allah has made unlawful in His Book. Whatever He has remained silent about is among the things He has pardoned.”

Narrated by Abū Dāwūd.

And in the hadith narrated by Abū Thaʿlabah from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah has prescribed obligations, so do not neglect them; He has set limits, so do not overstep them; and He has forbidden things, so do not violate those prohibitions. He has remained silent about certain things out of mercy for you, not forgetfulness, so do not ask about them.”

translated_text:
And jurists say, concerning the implications of what is stated and what is left unstated—that is, what the Lawgiver, Allah and His Messenger, has stated and what has been left unstated—that sometimes the unstated case has a stronger claim to the ruling than the stated case: this is concordant implication. Sometimes its ruling differs: this is contrary implication. Sometimes it resembles the stated case: this is pure analogy.

Thus, the Sunnah and consensus establish that Allah is described as being silent. Silence, however, sometimes means refraining from speaking, and sometimes means refraining from making speech manifest and known. Thus, in the two Sahīh collections, Abū Hurayrah said:

“O Messenger of Allah, tell me: during your silence between the opening declaration of Allah’s greatness and the recitation, what do you say?”

He replied: “I say: ‘O Allah, distance me from my sins as You have distanced the East from the West.’”

The hadith continues.

Abū Hurayrah thus described him as silent and asked him, “What do you say?” He replied that he spoke during his silence—that is, his silence in the sense of not speaking aloud or publicly.

Yet neither of these two familiar meanings of silence is compatible with the position of those who say that He possesses speech just as He possesses knowledge, but does not utter anything when addressing His servants; rather, He creates in them a perception by which they hear His eternal speech, whether that speech is said to be an abstract meaning or meaning and letters. This is the position of Ibn Kullāb, al-Ashʿarī, and those jurists, hadith scholars, and Sufis, among the Hanbalīs and others, who hold this view.

These people must therefore either reject attributing silence to Him—which is their best-known position—or use the term and explain it as His not creating in created beings a perception through which they hear the eternal speech. Yet the scriptural texts

“When Allah speaks revelation, the inhabitants of heaven hear something like a chain being dragged across smooth rock.”

There are also the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, after he led them in the dawn prayer at al-Hudaybiyyah:

“Do you know what your Lord said last night?”

Likewise, there is His speaking to Moses and calling to him, as established by the Quran and Sunnah. According to their position, anyone could hear the speech that Moses heard.

Among those of them who adopted philosophy, one finds al-Ghazālī, in Mishkāt al-anwār (The Niche of Lights), allowing something similar for people of spiritual purity and discipline: the inspirations that descend upon their hearts. This is akin to the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Among the nations before you there were people who were inspired.”

And the saying of Abū al-Dardā’ and ‘Ubādah ibn al-Sāmit:

“The believer’s dream is speech uttered by the Lord in his presence during his sleep.”

They thus make “revelation” and inspiration received while awake or asleep exactly equivalent to Moses hearing Allah’s speech, with no difference between them—except that Moses was the intended recipient of that address, whereas someone else hears what was addressed to another. Then, upon “closer examination,” they revert to pure philosophy, holding that there is no difference whatsoever between Moses and anyone else.

Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Hārith ibn Asad al-Muhāsibī reported both positions from Ahl al-Sunnah concerning will, hearing, and sight in his book Fahm al-Qur’ān (Understanding the Quran). He discussed His words, “Until We know those who strive,” and similar passages, explaining that Allah’s knowledge is eternal and that only the thing known comes into being. He went on to say:

“This is found even in us, despite our ignorance and the fact that our knowledge comes into being. We may know that every human being will die; then, whenever someone dies, we say, ‘We now know that he has died,’ without having been ignorant before his death that he would die. Yet a visual perception and a stirring of the heart may newly arise in us when we look upon him dead, because he is dead. But no newly occurring events arise within Allah.”

He went on to say:

“The same applies to His words, ‘You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills’; His words, ‘When We intend to destroy a town’; and His words, ‘His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, “Be,” and it is.’

“This does not mean that, with the onset of events, a will comes into being in Him, or that He begins to exercise a will He did not previously possess. That is the conduct of someone ignorant of outcomes, who wills something without knowing its consequences. Rather, He has always willed what He knows will be; He has not acquired a will that did not previously exist. Acts of willing arise only in proportion to what the one who wills knows. As for the One who has always known what will and will not occur, whether good or evil, He has willed what He knew, in accordance with what He knew. Nothing newly becomes apparent to Him, since no new knowledge of it arises within Him.”

Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Hārith said:

“Some who claim to follow the Sunnah, and some adherents of innovation, have interpreted this as referring to newly occurring events. Those who claimed to follow the Sunnah intended to affirm divine decree. They therefore explained ‘Allah’s will’ as an occurrence arising from His decree and antecedent will. Some adherents of innovation, however, claimed that will is a newly occurring act of creation, though it is not itself created; rather, through it Allah brought created beings into existence.”

He said:

“You have thus claimed that the act of creation is distinct from created beings, that this act is the will, and that it is not an attribute intrinsic to Allah Himself. Exalted is He above anything occurring without His willing it, and exalted is He above newly arising intentions and changes of will.”

He then explained that what newly occurs is the appointed time of the thing willed, not the will itself, as when people ask, “When do you want me to come?” Later he said:

“Likewise, His words, ‘Indeed, We are with you, listening,’ do not mean that hearing newly arises in Us, or that We exert Ourselves to hear what they say.”

He said:

“Some among Ahl al-Sunnah have held that a new act of listening arises within Allah’s essence. Such a person has relied on what he understands of created beings: knowledge through hearing newly arises in the person who hears what is said. For when a created being hears something, an awareness newly arises through which he understands the sound perceived by his ear.”

He said:

“Likewise, His words, ‘Work, for Allah will see your deeds, and so will His Messenger,’ do not mean that He acquires new sight or that a new act of looking arises within His essence. Rather, the thing comes into being, and He sees it in existence, just as He has always known it before it existed. He misses nothing, and nothing about it is hidden from Him.

“Similarly, some of them said that a new act of seeing occurs. Others said: ‘The only meaning of “will see”

translated_text:
and “Indeed, We are with you, listening” is that what is heard and seen is not hidden from My eye or My hearing: I perceive it through hearing and sight, not through newly occurring events within Allah.’”

Abū ‘Abd Allāh said:

“Whoever holds that a new act of listening arises in Allah when something audible comes into existence, and a new act of seeing when something visible comes into existence, has attributed to Allah something He has not said. His servants must simply accept what Allah has said: that He is All-Hearing, All-Seeing. We do not add anything He has not said. Its meaning is like His words, ‘Until We know’: until what is known comes into existence. Likewise, it means until what is seen and heard comes into existence. It is not hidden from Him: He knows it and hears it when it exists, just as He knew it before, without any new knowledge, sight, or hearing arising in Allah, nor anything arising within Allah’s essence. Exalted is He above newly occurring events within Himself.”

In his book Jumal al-Kalām fī Usūl al-Dīn (A Summary of Theological Discourse on the Foundations of Religion), Muhammad ibn al-Haysam al-Karrāmī set out the main points of the discussion concerning the Quran, explaining that they rest on five sections:

(First: The Quran is Allah’s speech. He reported that Jahm held that the Quran is not truly Allah’s speech, but rather speech Allah created, which is therefore attributed to Him, just as one says “Allah’s heaven and earth,” “Allah’s House,” and “Allah’s month.” As for the Mu‘tazilah, they stated without qualification that it is truly Allah’s speech, but then agreed with Jahm in substance by saying that it is speech He created separately from Himself.

He said:

“The Muslims generally hold that the Quran is truly Allah’s speech and that He spoke it.”

translated_text:
The second section is that the Quran is not beginningless. The Kullābiyyah and the followers of al-Ash‘arī claimed that Allah had always been speaking the Quran. The people of the Community, however, said that He spoke the Quran only when He addressed Gabriel with it; the same applies to the other scriptures.

(The third section: The Quran is uncreated. The Jahmiyyah, the Najjāriyyah, and the Mu‘tazilah claimed that it is created, whereas the people of the Community said that it is uncreated.

(The fourth section: It is not separate from Allah. The Jahmiyyah and their followers among the Mu‘tazilah said that the Quran is separate from Allah, as is all His other speech. They claimed that Allah created speech in the tree, which Moses heard, and created speech in the air, which Gabriel heard. According to them, speech cannot come from Allah and truly subsist in Him.

The people of the Community, however, said that the Quran is not separate from Allah; rather, it originates from Him and subsists in Him. In discussing will, the act of creation, that which is created, and other matters, he also made statements consistent with what he mentioned here concerning the attributes of action that subsist in Allah and are neither beginningless nor created.

Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

Praise be to Allah. We seek His help and forgiveness, and we seek refuge in Allah from the evil within ourselves and from our evil deeds. Whomever Allah guides, none can lead astray; and whomever He leads astray, none can guide. I bear witness that none is worthy of worship except Allah alone, without partner, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. May Allah bless him and his family and grant them abundant peace.

Section: “The Name and What It Names”

Is the name identical to what it names, or distinct from it? Or should it be described as neither identical to it nor distinct from it? Or does the name belong to what it names? Or must distinctions be made in this matter?

People have disagreed over this, and the controversy became widespread after the time of the imams—after Ahmad and others. The known position of the imams of the Sunnah, Ahmad and others, was to denounce the Jahmiyyah, who say: “Allah’s names are created.”

translated_text:
Thus they say: “The name is distinct from what it names; Allah’s names are distinct from Him; and whatever is distinct from Him is created.” These are the people whom the early generations condemned and sternly denounced, because Allah’s names are part of His speech, and Allah’s speech is uncreated. Rather, He Himself speaks it, and He names Himself with the names it contains.

The Jahmiyyah say: “His speech is created, and His names are created. He Himself has not uttered speech that subsists in His essence, nor has He named Himself with a name that He Himself has spoken.” They may instead say that He spoke it and named Himself with these names, meaning that He created them in something other than Himself—not that He Himself uttered them as speech subsisting in Him. Thus, discussion of His names is one aspect of discussion of His speech.

Those who agree with the early generations that His speech and His names are uncreated say that His speech and names are attributes of His essence. But does He speak by His will and power, and name Himself by His will and power? There are two positions on this. Denial is the position of Ibn Kullāb and those who agree with him. Affirmation is the position of the imams of the people of hadith and the Sunnah, as well as many groups of speculative theologians, such as the Hishāmiyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, and others, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

Thus, al-Shāfi'ī, al-Asma'ī and others are reported to have said: “If you hear a man say that the name is distinct from what it names, bear witness to his heresy.” Nor is any of the early generations known to have said that the name is identical with what it names. Rather, many who affiliated themselves with the Sunnah after the imams said this, and most of the people of the Sunnah rejected their assertion.

Some refrained from either affirming or denying anything concerning this question, since either unqualified formulation was an innovation. Al-Khallāl reported this from Ibrāhīm al-Harbī and others, as did Abū Ja'far al-Tabarī in the treatise he entitled Sarīh al-Sunnah (The Sunnah Clearly Stated). In it, he set out the well-known position of the people of the Sunnah concerning the Quran, seeing Allah, faith, divine decree, the Companions and other matters. He stated that none of the earlier scholars had spoken on “the question of utterance,” saying: “We have found no statement on it from any Companion who has passed away, nor from any Successor who followed them, except from one whose words provide healing and suffice, and whom we regard as holding the standing of the earliest imams: Abū 'Abd Allāh Ahmad ibn Hanbal.” He used to say: “The Lafziyyah are Jahmiyyah.” He also said: “Whoever says, ‘My utterance of the Quran is created,’ is a Jahmī; and whoever says, ‘It is uncreated,’ is an innovator.”

Al-Tabarī also stated that discussion of the name and what it names is among the foolish innovations on which no statement is known from any of the imams, and that it suffices a person to go no further than the words of the Most High:

“To Allah belong the most beautiful names.”

This amounts to saying that the name belongs to what it names. This formulation is preferred by most of those affiliated with the Sunnah among the followers of Imam Ahmad and others.

'Abd al-'Azīz, Abū al-Qāsim al-Tabarī, al-Lālakā'ī, Abū Muhammad al-Baghawī, the author of Sharh al-Sunnah (Commentary on the Sunnah), and others. This is also one of the two views held by the followers of Abū al-Hasan al-Ash'arī, adopted by Abū Bakr ibn Fūrak and others. The second view, which is the one widely attributed to Abū al-Hasan, is that names fall into three categories: sometimes the name is identical with what it names, as with “the Existent”; sometimes it is distinct from what it names, as with “the Creator”; and sometimes it is neither identical with nor distinct from what it names, as with “the All-Knowing” and “the All-Powerful.”

Those who said that the name is identical with what it names did not mean that the verbal expression composed of letters is the very person named by it, for no rational person would say this. Hence the objection: if the name were identical with what it names, anyone who said “fire” would burn his tongue. Some people imagine that this is what they meant and denounce them for it, but this misrepresents their position.

Rather, they say that the verbal expression is the act of naming, whereas the name is not the verbal expression but what is intended by it. When you say, “O Zayd! O 'Umar!” you do not intend to call out to the verbal expression; rather, you intend to call the person named by it. You have mentioned the name, and what is intended by that name is the person it names.

There is no doubt about this. When statements are made about things and their names are mentioned, as in:

“Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,”

“and the Seal of the Prophets,”

“And Allah spoke to Moses directly,”

the meaning is not that the verbal expression itself is the Messenger or the one to whom Allah spoke. Likewise, when one says, “Zayd has come,” “I bear witness concerning 'Amr,” “So-and-so is upright,” and similar statements, the names are mentioned, but what is intended by them is what they name. That is the purpose of the speech.
