translated_text:
Thus, since what is intended when the names of things are mentioned in connected speech is the things named, these scholars said: “The name is identical with what it names.” They regarded the verbal expression that people ordinarily call the name as the act of naming. As al-Baghawī said:

“The name is the thing named—its very self and essence. Allah Most High says:

‘We give you good news of a boy whose name will be John.’

He declared that his name was John, then addressed the name, saying:

‘O John!’

He also says:

‘You worship besides Him nothing but names you have named.’

He meant the actual objects of worship, for they worshipped the things named. He also says:

‘Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High,’

and:

‘Blessed is the name of your Lord.’”

He said: “The act of naming is also called a ‘name.’ Indeed, this word is used more often for the act of naming than for the thing named.”

Abū Bakr ibn Fūrak said:

“People have differed over the true nature of a ‘name.’ Linguists have discussed it, those concerned with the realities of things have offered explanations, and theologians have disagreed about it. Linguists say that a name is a sequence of letters signifying a single meaning. Some say that it is an expression denoting something spoken of, to which a statement or report is ascribed.”

He said:

“Those concerned with the realities of things have also differed over its meaning. Some say that the name of a thing is its essence and very self, while the act of naming is an expression referring to it and indicating it, and is therefore called a ‘name’ by extension. The Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah say that ‘names and attributes’ are expressions indicating the things named. This is close to what some linguists have said.

“The third view is that the name is neither identical with what it names nor distinct from it, as with knowledge and the world. Some say that the name of a thing is its attribute and description.

translated_text:
He said:

“The view we hold to be correct is that the name of a thing is its very self and essence, and that Allah’s name is Allah. When someone says, ‘In the name of Allah I act,’ the meaning is, ‘By Allah I act,’ for His name is He Himself.”

He said:

“Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām adopted this view, citing the words of Labīd:

‘For a year; then the name of peace be upon you both—
Whoever weeps a whole year is free of blame.’

“The meaning is, ‘Then peace be upon you both,’ for the name of peace is peace itself.”

He said:

“Our scholars supported this view with the words of Allah, Blessed and Exalted:

‘Blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honor.’

“This describes the One named, not words or speech. They also cited His words:

‘Glorify the name of your Lord.’

“For the One glorified is the One named, namely Allah. They also cited His words, glory be to Him:

‘We give you good news of a boy whose name will be John.’

“He then said:

‘O John! Hold firmly to the Scripture.’

“He thus addressed the name, which is the one named. They also argued that the jurists unanimously agree that swearing by Allah’s name is like swearing by Allah, in that either form constitutes a binding oath. If Allah’s name were other than Allah, the person would be swearing by other than Allah, and his oath would not be binding. Since the oath is binding and breaking it requires expiation, this indicates that His name is He Himself.

“This is also indicated by the fact that, when someone asks, ‘What is the name of the One you worship?’ we answer, ‘Allah.’ Then, if he asks:

‘And what do you worship?’ we answer, ‘Allah.’ Thus, we give the same answer concerning the name as we do concerning the One worshipped. This indicates that the name of the One worshipped is none other than the One worshipped Himself. They also cite His words:

‘You worship besides Him nothing but names which you and your fathers have named.’

“What they worshipped were the things named, not the utterances, which are accidents and are not worshipped.”

He said:

“If it is objected, ‘Is it not said that Allah is one God and has many names? How, then, can the one be many?’ the answer is: When the term ‘names’ is used, what is meant is what the name-givers have named. A thing may be called by the name of that which signifies it, just as an object of power may be called ‘power.’”

He said:

“Accordingly, ‘In the name of Allah’ means ‘By Allah.’ The preposition ‘by’ expresses seeking assistance and acknowledging one’s need. Its sense is: ‘From You I seek assistance, and of You I am in need.’ It has also been said that the implied wording is: ‘I begin,’ or ‘I start, in Your name, in what I say and do.’”

I say:

Had they confined themselves to saying that, when the names of things occur in speech, what is intended is the things named—as they explained concerning His words, ‘O John,’ and similar expressions—this would have been a clear meaning that no one who understood it would dispute. But they did not confine themselves to that. For this reason, most people, both Ahl al-Sunnah and others, rejected their position because of the false claims it contains. These include their claim that the word ism (‘name’), spelled alif–sīn–mīm, means the very essence and self of a thing; and that actual names, such as Zayd and ‘Amr, are acts of naming, not names of the things named. Both claims are false, contrary to what all people of every nation know and to what they say.

is the act of making something a name for something else. It is the verbal noun in sammaytuhu tasmiyatan (“I named it”), used when you give something a name. A “name” is an utterance that signifies the thing named. The word ism (“name”) is not itself the thing named, though the thing named may be intended by it, because it conveys a judgment concerning that thing and points to it.

Moreover, they went to these strained lengths in order to say that Allah’s name is uncreated, meaning that Allah is uncreated. Yet this is something that neither the Jahmiyyah nor the Mu‘tazilah dispute. For the former said that names were created only when these people said that they were acts of naming. Thus, they agreed with the Jahmiyyah and the Mu‘tazilah in meaning, and with Ahl al-Sunnah in wording. By that wording, however, they intended something no one before them had asserted: that the word ism, spelled “alif–sīn–mīm,” means, when used without qualification, the very essence of the thing named. Rather, this word means the utterances that serve as names for things, such as Zayd, ‘Amr, “learned,” and “ignorant.” The word “name” does not indicate that these names are themselves the thing named.

It is also well known that when a name occurs within connected speech, what is intended is the thing named. Hence, when someone asks, “What is this person’s name?” the answer is “Zayd.” The answer is given with the utterance. One does not answer the question “What is this person’s name?” by saying, “He is himself.” The examples they cited are, in fact, evidence against them.

As for His words:

“We give you glad tidings of a boy whose name will be John; We have never given this name to anyone before,”

followed by His words:

“O John,”

the name Yahyā (John) is this utterance, composed of the letters (yā’, hā’, and yā’). This is his name; his name is not his very self. To claim otherwise is sheer obstinacy.

Then, when He addressed him, saying:

“O John,”

the intention in calling out the name was to address the person named, not the utterance. But a speaker cannot address the person being called except by mentioning his name and calling it out; so he understands

then that the intention is to call the person named. This is one of the benefits of language. A person may also be summoned by a gesture: the movement is not the person himself, but points to him.

As for His words:

“Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of majesty and honor,”

there are two readings. Most reciters read “Possessor of majesty” as dhī al-jalāl. Thus, the Lord who is named is the Possessor of majesty and honor. Ibn ‘Āmir read “Possessor of majesty and honor” as dhū al-jalāl wa-l-ikrām. This is also how it appears in the Syrian Quran manuscript, whereas in the Quran manuscripts of the people of the Hijaz and Iraq it is written with yā’.

As for His words:

“And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Possessor of majesty and honor,”

all agree that it is written with wāw.

Ibn al-Anbārī and others said that tabāraka (“blessed is”) follows the pattern tafā‘ala and is derived from barakah (“blessing”). The meaning is that blessing is acquired and attained through mentioning His name. If the word “name” meant the one named, it would have sufficed to say, “Blessed is your Lord,” since, in their view, the name itself is the Lord Himself; the wording would thus be repetitive.

Some people have said that the word “name” here is merely supplementary, and that the intended meaning is “Blessed is your Lord,” rather than an assertion that His name is blessed. This is mistaken, for on this interpretation, when someone praying says, “Blessed is Your name,” it would mean, “Blessed are You,” while the Lord’s names themselves would contain no blessing. Yet it is well known that His names themselves are blessed, and their blessing comes from their signifying the One named.

For this reason, the Sharia distinguishes between that over which Allah’s name is mentioned and that over which His name is not mentioned, as in His words:

“So eat of that over which Allah’s name has been mentioned,”

and His words:

“And why should you not eat of that over which Allah’s name has been mentioned?”

and His words:

“And mention Allah’s name over it,”

“If other dogs mingle with your dog, do not eat, for you mentioned Allah’s name only over your dog, not over any other.”

As for His words, exalted is He:

“You worship nothing besides Him but names that you and your forefathers have given,”

the meaning is not, as they have claimed, “You worship the idols bearing those names,” for this is something they themselves acknowledge. Rather, the Lord, exalted is He, denied what they believed and affirmed its opposite. The meaning is that they called these idols gods and believed that they possessed divinity, although they possess no divinity whatsoever. Thus, when they worshipped them, believing them to be divine and calling them gods, they worshipped nothing but names they themselves had invented, for which Allah had sent down no authority. For Allah neither commanded that these things be worshipped nor made them gods, as He said:

“Ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you: Did We appoint any gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?”

Their worship, then, is directed toward the notion of divinity that they conceived within themselves and expressed with their tongues. This is something that exists in their minds and on their tongues but has no reality outside them. Thus, they worshipped nothing but these names, which they conceived in their minds and whose meanings they expressed with their tongues. They intended to worship the idol only because they regarded it as a god; yet its divinity exists within their own minds, not in external reality. In truth, therefore, they worshipped nothing but that false imagining to which they had given expression.

For this reason, He said in another verse:

“They have assigned partners to Allah. Say: ‘Name them! Or are you informing Him of something He does not know on earth, or merely speaking empty words?’”

He is saying: Give them the names they deserve:

{أَمْ تُنَبِّئُونَهُ بِمَا لَا يَعْلَمُ فِي الْأَرْضِ}
 وَمَا لَا يُعْلَمُ أَنَّهُ مَوْجُودٌ فَهُوَ بَاطِلٌ لَا حَقِيقَةَ لَهُ وَلَوْ كَانَ مَوْجُودًا لَعَلِمَهُ مَوْجُودًا 
{أَمْ بِظَاهِرٍ مِنَ الْقَوْلِ}
 أَمْ بِقَوْلِ ظَاهِرٍ بِاللِّسَانِ لَا حَقِيقَةَ لَهُ فِي الْقَلْبِ؛ بَلْ هُوَ كَذِبٌ وَبُهْتَانٌ.
 وَأَمَّا قَوْلُهُمْ:
 إنَّ الِاسْمَ يُرَادُ بِهِ 
" التَّسْمِيَةُ "
 وَهُوَ الْقَوْلُ: فَهَذَا الَّذِي جَعَلُوهُ هُمْ تَسْمِيَةً هُوَ الِاسْمُ عِنْدَ النَّاسِ جَمِيعِهِمْ وَالتَّسْمِيَةُ جَعْلُهُ اسْمًا وَالْإِخْبَارُ بِأَنَّهُ اسْمٌ وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ وَقَدْ سَلَّمُوا أَنَّ لَفْظَ الِاسْمِ أَكْثَرُ مَا يُرَادُ بِهِ ذَلِكَ وَادَّعَوْا أَنَّ لَفْظَ الِاسْمِ الَّذِي هُوَ 
" أَلِفٌ سِينٌ مِيمٌ "
: هُوَ فِي الْأَصْلِ ذَاتُ الشَّيْءِ وَلَكِنَّ التَّسْمِيَةَ سُمِّيَتْ اسْمًا لِدَلَالَتِهَا عَلَى ذَاتِ الشَّيْءِ: تَسْمِيَةً لِلدَّالِّ بِاسْمِ الْمَدْلُولِ وَمَثَّلُوهُ بِلَفْظِ الْقُدْرَةِ؛ وَلَيْسَ الْأَمْرُ كَذَلِكَ؛ بَلْ التَّسْمِيَةُ مَصْدَرُ سَمَّى يُسَمِّي تَسْمِيَةً وَالتَّسْمِيَةُ نُطْقٌ بِالِاسْمِ وَتَكَلُّمٌ بِهِ لَيْسَتْ هِيَ الِاسْمُ نَفْسُهُ وَأَسْمَاءُ الْأَشْيَاءِ هِيَ الْأَلْفَاظُ الدَّالَّةُ عَلَيْهَا لَيْسَتْ هِيَ أَعْيَانُ الْأَشْيَاءِ. وَتَسْمِيَةُ الْمَقْدُورِ قُدْرَةً هُوَ مِنْ بَابِ تَسْمِيَةِ الْمَفْعُولِ بِاسْمِ الْمَصْدَرِ وَهَذَا كَثِيرٌ شَائِعٌ فِي اللُّغَةِ كَقَوْلِهِمْ لِلْمَخْلُوقِ خَلْقٌ وَقَوْلِهِمْ دِرْهَمٌ ضَرْبُ الْأَمِيرِ أَيْ مَضْرُوبُ الْأَمِيرِ وَنَظَائِرُهُ كَثِيرَةٌ.
 وَابْنُ عَطِيَّةَ سَلَكَ مَسْلَكَ هَؤُلَاءِ وَقَالَ:
 الِاسْمُ الَّذِي هُوَ 
" أَلِفٌ وَسِينٌ وَمِيمٌ "
 يَأْتِي فِي مَوَاضِعَ مِنْ الْكَلَامِ الْفَصِيحِ يُرَادُ بِهِ الْمُسَمَّى وَيَأْتِي فِي مَوَاضِعَ
translated_text:
are they creators, providers, givers of life and causes of death, or are they created beings with no power to harm or benefit? Once they name them and describe them with the attributes they deserve, their error becomes clear.

He, exalted is He, said:

“Or are you informing Him of something He does not know on earth?”

Whatever is not known to Him to exist is false and has no reality. If it existed, He would know it to exist.

“Or merely speaking empty words?”

That is, words outwardly uttered by the tongue, with no reality in the heart; rather, they are lies and fabrications.

As for their statement that “name” means “naming,” namely, the spoken expression: what they call “naming” is precisely what everyone calls the name. Naming consists in assigning a name, declaring something to be a name, and the like. They have conceded that this is what the word “name” most often means. Yet they claim that the word ism (“name”), spelled “alif, sīn, mīm,” originally denotes the entity itself, and that naming is called a “name” because it signifies the entity itself—thus applying the name of what is signified to that which signifies it. They illustrated this with the word “power.”

But this is not so. Rather, tasmiya (“naming”) is the verbal noun in the sequence sammā, yusammī, tasmiyatan (“he named, he names, naming”). Naming is uttering and speaking a name; it is not the name itself. The names of things are the expressions that signify them, not the things themselves. Calling the object of power “power” is an instance of using a verbal noun to denote its object. This is common and widespread in the language, as when a created thing is called “creation,” or when people say, “a dirham of the ruler’s minting,” meaning one minted by the ruler. There are many similar examples.

Ibn ‘Atiyya followed their approach and said:

“The word ism (‘name’), spelled ‘alif, sīn, mīm,’ occurs in some passages of eloquent speech with the meaning of the thing named, and occurs in other passages

translated_text:
with the meaning of naming, as in the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘Allah has ninety-nine names,’ and elsewhere. Whenever it denotes the thing named, it is merely a supplementary element, effectively redundant, as though He had said in this verse, ‘Glorify your Lord, the Most High,’ meaning: declare Him free of all imperfection.”

He said:

“When the name is a particular name, such as Zayd or ‘Amr, it is used in speech as I have explained to you. You say, ‘Zayd is standing,’ intending the person named, and you say, ‘Zayd consists of three letters,’ intending the naming itself—in the sense of keeping your Lord’s name from being given to an idol or image, so that it is called ‘a god’ or ‘a lord.’”

I say:

No attestation is known for what they have stated, whether in eloquent speech or otherwise. Nor is the word ism (‘name’), spelled ‘alif, sīn, mīm,’ known to denote the thing named. Rather, it denotes the name, which they call ‘naming.’

As for his statement that when you say ‘Zayd is standing,’ Zayd denotes the person named: Zayd is not the word spelled ‘alif, sīn, mīm.’ Rather, Zayd is what the expression ‘Zayd’ names. Thus, ‘Zayd’ can denote either the person named or the expression itself. Likewise, ism, spelled ‘alif, sīn, mīm,’ can denote this expression itself or its meaning: an expression such as ‘Zayd,’ ‘Amr,’ or ‘Bakr.’ These are the names denoted by the word ism; the word ism does not denote the individuals themselves. I know of no sound attestation for this, let alone for its being the original meaning, as these people claim.

translated_text:
Allah Most High says:

“And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so invoke Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names.”

His most beautiful names include “the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful” and “the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful.” These expressions are His most beautiful names, and when used in supplication or statements, they refer to the One named. When He says:

“And put your trust in the Almighty, the Most Merciful,”

the One named is intended. It does not mean that one should put one’s trust in the names, which are expressions. This is how all other speech works, whether the speech of the Creator or that of created beings.

They argue that if someone asks, “What is the name of the One you worship?” and we answer, “Allah,” we give the same answer about the name as we do about the One worshipped; this therefore proves that the name of the One worshipped is the One worshipped Himself. This argument is invalid: it counts against them, not in their favour.

For if someone asks, “What is the name of the One you worship?” and we answer, “Allah,” what is meant is that His name is this expression—not that His name is His very Being, the One who created the heavens and the earth. The question was only about His name, not about Him Himself, so the answer was to mention His name.

But if someone asks, “What do you worship?” and we answer, “Allah,” then the One named is intended, not that the object of worship is the expression. Since the questions differ in the two cases, the intended meanings of the answers also differ. Although the answer in both cases is “Allah,” in one case this spoken expression is intended, while in the other the One named by this expression is intended.

Likewise, if someone asks, “What is so-and-so’s name?” and the answer is “Zayd” or “ʿUmar,” the expression is intended. But if someone asks, “Who is your ruler?” or “Whom

have you given in marriage?” and the answer is “Zayd” or “ʿAmr,” the person is intended. How, then, can what is intended in the two cases be regarded as the same?

Thus, when Allah Most High says:

“And to Allah belong the most beautiful names,”

the meaning is that He Himself possesses the most beautiful names. Among them is His name “Allah,” as He says:

“Say, ‘Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Compassionate. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.’”

The One who possesses the most beautiful names is the One named by them. Thus, in Imam Ahmad’s statements, he says that this name is among His most beautiful names; at other times, he says that the most beautiful names belong to Him—that is, to the One named, who is not one of the names. Accordingly, in His statement, “And to Allah belong the most beautiful names,” He did not mean that this name possesses the most beautiful names. Rather, He meant that the One named possesses the most beautiful names.

In the authentic hadith of Anas, it is reported:

“The inscription on the ring of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was ‘Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah’: ‘Muhammad’ on one line, ‘Messenger’ on one line, and ‘Allah’ on one line.”

What is intended is the written script in which these words were inscribed: the writing of “Muhammad” occupied one line, the writing of “Messenger” occupied one line, and the writing of “Allah” occupied one line.

Likewise, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah Most High says: ‘I am with My servant as long as he remembers Me and his lips move in remembrance of Me,’”

it is clear that what is meant is that his lips move as he mentions Allah’s name, which is an utterance. It does not mean that his lips move with Allah Himself, exalted is He.

As for their argument based on His saying:

“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High,”

and their claim that it means, “Glorify your Lord, the Most High,” and likewise His saying:

“Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour,”

and similar passages, there are two well-known views on this matter, both of which constitute evidence against them.

translated_text:
Some have said that “name” here is an expletive, and that the meaning is “Glorify your Lord” and “Blessed is your Lord.” If it is said to be an expletive, then it is redundant and carries no meaning. This invalidates their claim that the word “ism” (“name”), spelled “alif, sīn, mīm,” denotes the One named. For if it had an intended meaning, it would not be an expletive. Whoever says both that it is the One named and that it is an expletive—as Ibn ʿAtiyya did—has contradicted himself. Someone who calls it an expletive assigns it no meaning, just as some say concerning redundant particles used for emphasis, as in His sayings:

“It was by mercy from Allah that you were gentle with them,”

and:

“He said, ‘Before long they will surely be filled with regret,’”

and similar passages.

As for those who say that it is not an expletive, but that what is intended is glorifying the name itself, their interpretation plainly contradicts the claim in question.

The correct understanding is that it is not an expletive. Rather, Allah commanded that His name be glorified, just as He commanded that His name be mentioned. The purpose of glorifying and mentioning His name is to glorify and remember the One named. For the person who glorifies and remembers Him glorifies His name and mentions His name, saying, “Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.” He has thus uttered the words “my Lord, the Most High,” while what he intends is the One named by these words. Glorifying the name is therefore glorifying the One named.

Those who interpret this as glorifying the name say that it means that you must not give this name to anyone other than Allah or deviate concerning His names. This is indeed part of what is due to Allah’s name, but it follows from the intended meaning of the verse; it is not its primary purpose.

Several Quranic commentators have mentioned these three views, including al-Baghawī, who said: “His words, ‘Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High,’ mean: say, ‘Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.’ This was the view of a group

I say: On this subject there is the hadith of ʿUqba ibn ʿĀmir, who reported concerning the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: “When ‘So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great’ was revealed, he said, ‘Use this in your bowing.’ When ‘Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High’ was revealed, he said, ‘Use this in your prostration.’”

What is meant is that they should say while bowing, “Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great,” and while prostrating, “Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.” This accords with what is established in the Sahīh, where Hudhayfa reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “stood in prayer reciting al-Baqarah, al-Nisā’ and Āl ʿImrān, then bowed for approximately as long as he had stood, saying, ‘Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great.’ He prostrated for approximately as long as he had bowed, saying, ‘Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.’”

In the Sunan, Ibn Masʿūd reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “When a servant says three times while bowing, ‘Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great,’ his bowing is complete, and that is its minimum. When he says three times while prostrating, ‘Glory be to my Lord, the Most High,’ his prostration is complete, and that is its minimum.” The majority of scholars have adopted this.

Al-Baghawī said: “Others have said that it means: declare your Lord, the Most High, free of what those who deviate attribute to Him. They regarded ‘name’ as an expletive.” He continued: “Those who regard the name and the One named as one and the same cite this as evidence, since no one says, ‘Glory be to the name of Allah,’ or ‘Glory be to the name of our Lord.’ Rather, they say, ‘Glory be to Allah,’ and ‘Glory be to our Lord.’ Thus, ‘Glorify the name of your Lord’ means ‘Glorify your Lord.’”

has merely uttered the name “Allah” and the name “our Lord.” His glorification has thus been applied to the name, but he intends the One named. This shows that one utters the name of the One named while intending the One named. There is no doubt about this. It does not, however, show that the word ism (name), spelled “alif, sīn, mīm,” is intended to mean the One named. Rather, it shows that “Allah’s names,” such as “Allah,” “our Lord,” “my Lord, the Most High,” and the like, are intended to refer to the One named. Although they are not themselves the One named, they are used to refer to Him.

As for the name given to these names—ism, spelled “alif, sīn, mīm”—it neither is the One named, that is, the Essence, nor is it intended to refer to the One named, that is, the Essence. Rather, it refers to what it designates: the names themselves, such as Allah’s most beautiful names mentioned in His words:

“To Allah belong the most beautiful names.”

To them, then, belong these most beautiful names, which these people regarded as designations, maintaining that calling them “names” was an extended use of the term. They thereby contradicted the consensus of all peoples, Arabs and non-Arabs alike, as well as clear reason and authentic transmitted evidence.

Those who shared this premise and said, “Names are of three kinds: they may be identical with the One named, different from Him, or neither identical with Him nor different from Him”—and who regarded “the Creator,” “the Provider,” and similar names as different from the One named, while regarding “the All-Knowing,” “the All-Wise,” and similar names as belonging to the One named—erred in another respect. Even if we grant them that the word ism, spelled “alif, sīn, mīm,” means the One designated by the names, His name “the Creator” is the Lord, the Creator Himself, not the created things that are separate from Him. His name “the All-Knowing” is the All-Knowing Lord, whose attribute is knowledge. Knowledge, then, is not the One named; rather, the One named is the All-Knowing. On their own premise, therefore, they ought to have said: here, the name is the One named together with His attribute.

 إلَى الْحَوْلِ ثُمَّ اسْمُ السَّلَامِ عَلَيْكُمَا فَمُرَادُهُ ثُمَّ النُّطْقُ بِهَذَا الِاسْمِ وَذَكَرَهُ وَهُوَ التَّسْلِيمُ الْمَقْصُودُ؛ كَأَنَّهُ قَالَ ثُمَّ سَلَامٌ عَلَيْكُمْ لَيْسَ مُرَادُهُ أَنَّ السَّلَامَ يَحْصُلُ عَلَيْهِمَا بِدُونِ أَنْ يَنْطِقَ بِهِ وَيَذْكُرَ اسْمَهُ. فَإِنَّ نَفْسَ السَّلَامِ قَوْلٌ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَنْطِقْ بِهِ نَاطِقٌ وَيَذْكُرْهُ لَمْ يَحْصُلْ. وَقَدْ احْتَجَّ بَعْضُهُمْ بِقَوْلِ سِيبَوَيْهِ إنَّ الْفِعْلَ أَمْثِلَةٌ أُخِذَتْ مِنْ لَفْظِ أَحْدَاثِ الْأَسْمَاءِ وَبُنِيَ لِمَا مَضَى وَلَمَّا لَمْ يَكُنْ بَعْدُ وَهَذَا لَا حُجَّةَ فِيهِ؛ لِأَنَّ سِيبَوَيْهِ مَقْصُودُهُ بِذِكْرِ الِاسْمِ وَالْفِعْلِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ الْأَلْفَاظُ. وَهَذَا اصْطِلَاحُ النَّحْوِيِّينَ سَمَّوْا الْأَلْفَاظَ بِأَسْمَاءِ مَعَانِيهَا؛ فَسَمَّوْا قَامَ وَيَقُومُ وَقُمْ فِعْلًا؛ وَالْفِعْلُ هُوَ نَفْسُ الْحَرَكَةِ؛ فَسَمَّوْا اللَّفْظَ الدَّالَّ عَلَيْهَا بِاسْمِهَا.
 وَكَذَلِكَ إذَا قَالُوا:
 اسْمٌ مُعَرَّبٌ وَمَبْنِيٌّ فَمَقْصُودُهُمْ اللَّفْظُ لَيْسَ مَقْصُودُهُمْ الْمُسَمَّى وَإِذَا قَالُوا هَذَا الِاسْمُ فَاعِلٌ فَمُرَادُهُمْ أَنَّهُ فَاعِلٌ فِي اللَّفْظِ؛ أَيْ أُسْنِدَ إلَيْهِ الْفِعْلُ وَلَمْ يُرِدْ سِيبَوَيْهِ بِلَفْظِ الْأَسْمَاءِ الْمُسَمَّيَاتِ كَمَا زَعَمُوا؛ وَلَوْ أَرَادَ ذَلِكَ فَسَدَتْ صِنَاعَتُهُ.
translated_text:
and in the case of “the Creator,” the name is the One named together with His act. Moreover, their claim that the act of creation is identical with what is created, rather than an act subsisting in His Essence, is a weak position contrary to that of the majority of Muslims, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

It is thus clear that all that can be conceded to those who say, “The name is the One named,” is that when the names of things occur in speech, what is intended is the things named. No rational person disputes this. It does not mean that the word ism (name), spelled “alif, sīn, mīm,” refers to the individual.

As for their citation of Labīd’s words:

“For a year; then the name of peace be upon you both,”

he means then uttering and mentioning this name, which constitutes the intended greeting. It is as though he had said, “Then peace be upon you.” He does not mean that peace comes upon the two of them without anyone uttering it and mentioning its name. The greeting of peace is itself an utterance: unless someone utters and mentions it, it does not occur.

Some of them have cited Sībawayh’s statement: “Verbs are patterns derived from the wording of the events expressed by nouns, and are formed to refer to what has passed and what has not yet occurred.” This provides no evidence for their claim, because by “noun,” “verb,” and the like, Sībawayh means verbal expressions. This is the terminology of grammarians: they named expressions after the meanings they convey. Thus they called qāma (he stood), yaqūmu (he stands), and qum (stand!) fi‘l (verb, literally “act”), although the act is the movement itself. They therefore named the expression denoting it after it.

Likewise, when they speak of “an inflected noun” or “an indeclinable noun,” they mean the expression, not the thing named. When they say, “This noun is the subject,” they mean that it is the subject grammatically—that is, the verb is predicated of it. By the word “nouns,” Sībawayh did not mean the things named, as they claimed. Had he meant that, his grammatical system would have broken down.

{خَلَقَ الْإِنْسَانَ}
 
{عَلَّمَهُ الْبَيَانَ}
 وَقَدْ عَلَّمَ آدَمَ الْأَسْمَاءَ كُلَّهَا سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى.
translated_text:
Section

As for those who say, “The name is other than the thing named,” if they mean that names, which are utterances, are not themselves the things named, this too is something no rational person disputes. Those who hold the first position do not dispute this; rather, they refer to names in this sense as “designations.” Nor can they dispute that names mentioned in speech, as when one says, “O Adam! O Noah! O Abraham!” are intended only to address those who bear these names.

When someone says, “Allah created the heavens and the earth,” the meaning is that He created the things designated by these words. The speaker does not mean that He created the word “heaven” and the word “earth.” People understand from this only the intended meaning; it does not occur to anyone that the words themselves are intended. This is because it is firmly established in their minds that these words and names are used to convey meanings and designate the things named. When someone uses them in speech, this is what is intended. Yet that intention cannot be known unless the speaker utters the words and names that clarify and indicate it.

This is part of the gift of expression with which Allah has blessed the children of Adam, as He says:

“He created man;
He taught him eloquence.”

He—glorified and exalted is He—also taught Adam all the names.

translated_text:
But those Jahmiyyah and Muʿtazilah who stated without qualification that the name is other than the thing named intended to say that Allah’s names are other than Him, and that whatever is other than Him is created.

For this reason, the third group said: “We say neither that they are the thing named nor that they are other than the thing named.”

They may be answered as follows: Your statement that His names are other than Him is like your statement that His speech is other than Him, that His will is other than Him, and similar assertions. This is the position of the Jahmiyyah, who deny the divine attributes. You have already learned elsewhere of their specious arguments and their invalidity. They contradict themselves in several respects, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

For they say: “We affirm nothing beginningless other than Allah,” or “nothing beginningless that is not Allah.” They have gone so far as to declare those who affirm the attributes unbelievers, even when their position rests on interpretation. Thus Abū al-Hudhayl said:

“Anyone whose interpretation amounts to likening Him to His creation, attributing injustice to His actions, and denying what He has revealed is an unbeliever. Anyone who affirms something beginningless that is not called Allah is an unbeliever.”

His intention was to declare unbelievers those who affirm the divine attributes and divine decree, as well as those who say that Muslims will come out of the Fire and will not remain in it forever.

One response to these people is this: This argument rebounds upon you. You are more deserving of the charges of likening Allah to His creation, attributing injustice to Him, denying what He has revealed, and affirming something beginningless that is not called Allah. For you liken Him to inanimate objects—indeed, to nonexistent things, and even to things whose existence is impossible. You say that He nullifies great good deeds on account of a single sin, for which the sinner is made to remain in the Fire forever. And you deny what He has told us of His forgiveness and mercy

and His bringing those guilty of major sins out of the Fire through intercession and other means, and His declaration that whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.

You yourselves affirm something beginningless that is not called Allah, for you affirm an essence devoid of attributes. Yet it is known that whatever possesses neither life, knowledge, nor power is not Allah. Whoever affirms an essence devoid of attributes has therefore affirmed something beginningless that is not Allah. If someone says, “I say that He has always possessed life, knowledge, and power,” this is precisely the position of those who affirm the attributes. His having life is not the same as His having knowledge, and His having knowledge is not the same as His having power. Nor is any of this the same as His being an essence characterized by these attributes. These are meanings distinguished by the intellect; one is not identical to another.

If you say that they are beginningless, you have affirmed beginningless meanings. If you say that they are all one thing, you have made each attribute identical to the others, and the attribute identical to the One it describes. You have thus made His having life identical to His having knowledge, and made that identical to the essence itself. Clearly, this is a denial of the obvious. These meanings are the meanings of His Most Beautiful Names, and He—glorified be He—has always spoken whenever He willed.

He is therefore the One who named Himself with His Most Beautiful Names. As al-Bukhārī relates in his Sahīh, Ibn ʿAbbās was asked about His words:

“And Allah has always been Almighty, All-Wise,”

“Ever-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

He replied: “He named Himself thus, and He has always been so.” He thereby affirmed that the meanings of His Most Beautiful Names are beginningless and that He Himself is the One who named Himself with them.

a person may mention Allah and think of Him without being aware at that moment of all the meanings of His names. Indeed, it may not even occur to him then that He is Almighty and All-Wise. It is thus possible to know one without the other. If this is what is meant by “other,” it indicates only a distinction in the human mind, since a person may know one without the other. This does not negate their inseparability in reality: these meanings are mutually inseparable. The essence cannot exist without these meanings, nor can these meanings exist without the essence.

When one says, “Praise be to Allah,” or “In the name of Allah,” the name “Allah” encompasses His essence and His attributes; it does not denote an essence devoid of attributes, nor attributes devoid of an essence. The imams of the Sunnah—such as Ahmad and others—have explicitly stated that His attributes are included in what His names designate. Thus, one should not say that Allah’s knowledge and power are additional to Him. Some of those who affirm the attributes, however, have said that they are additional to the essence.

If this means that they are additional to the bare essence affirmed by those who deny the attributes, then it is correct. Those people fell short in what they affirmed, so this person affirmed more than they did, saying, “The Lord has attributes beyond what you have recognized.” But if he means that they are additional to the essence as it actually exists, this is a contradictory statement. In reality, there is no bare essence such that the attributes could be said to be additional to it. Rather, the essence cannot exist without the attributes by virtue of which it is an essence, nor can the attributes exist without the essence by virtue of which they are attributes. To imagine one existing without the other, and then the other being added to it, is therefore a false conception.

“To Allah belong the most beautiful names.”

And He says:

“Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Indeed, Allah has ninety-nine names.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have five names: I am Muhammad, Ahmad, al-Māhī, al-Hāshir, and al-‘Āqib.”

Both reports are recorded in the two Sahīh collections.

When they are asked, “Is the name the one named, or other than him?” they distinguish between the possible meanings, saying: “It is not the very one named, but it refers to the one named.” If it is said to be other than him in the sense that it must be separate from him, this is false. A created being may utter his own names without their being separate from him. How much more so with the Creator, whose names are part of His speech! His speech is not separate from Him.

The name itself may, however, be separate, as when a man gives someone else a name or utters that person’s name. This name itself does not subsist in the one named, but refers to him, for the purpose of a name is to make the one named known and identify him.

The word ism (“name”) is derived from sumuww, meaning elevation, as the Basran grammarians stated. The Kufan grammarians said that it is derived from sima, meaning a mark. This is correct in terms of “intermediate derivation,” in which two words share the same root letters but not their order: both contain the letters sīn, mīm, and wāw. The meaning is also sound, since sima and sīmā mean a mark. Hence one says wasamtuhu, asimuhu (“I marked him; I mark him”), as in His saying:

“We shall mark him on the snout.”

From this also comes tawassum (discerning signs), as in His saying:

“Indeed, in that are signs for those who discern.”

translated_text:
in its verbal forms, sammaytu (“I named”), not wasamtu (“I marked”); its plural is asmā’, not awsām; and its diminutive is sumayy, not wusaym. The one bearing the name is called musammā (“named”), not mawsūm (“marked”). This meaning is more specific.

“For elevation goes hand in hand with being manifest.” The higher a thing is, the more manifest it is, and each of these meanings implies the other. An example is the Prophet’s saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in an authentic hadith:

“You are the Manifest, and nothing is above You.”

He did not say, “Nothing is more manifest than You,” because being manifest here implies elevation and being above. Thus he said, “Nothing is above You.”

Another example is His saying:

“They could not scale it,”

meaning rise above it. Likewise, one says that the preacher “rose upon the pulpit” when he ascends it. A great mountain is called an ‘alam (landmark), because its height and prominence make it recognizable and enable other things to be located by it. Allah Most High says:

“And among His signs are the ships sailing through the sea like mountains.”

Similarly, a raised banner marking the location of the commander and the armies is called an ‘alam. So too is a distinctive marking on a garment, because it stands out. Likewise, a cock’s comb and lofty mountain heights are called a‘rāf, because their height makes them recognizable.

Thus, a name makes the one named manifest and raises his profile. Hence, concerning the person to be named, one says, “Name him,” meaning: make him manifest and raise him—that is, raise his mention through the name by which he is mentioned. Yet a person may be mentioned in terms of praise or in terms of blame. Allah Most High says:

“And We granted them a lofty reputation of honour.”

And He says:

“And We raised high your renown.”

And He says:

“And We left for him among later generations,”

“Peace be upon Noah among all peoples.”

Concerning blameworthy mention, He says:

“And We caused a curse to follow them in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised.”

Allah Most High also says:

“We recount to you some of the story of Moses and Pharaoh.”

Both, then, became widely known; but one is a leader in good and the other a leader in evil.

translated_text:
Some grammarians say:

“It is called an ism (name or noun) because it rises above the one named, or because it rises above its two fellow categories: the verb and the particle.”

But this is not what is meant by “name.” Rather, it raises the one named and makes him manifest. Hence one says, sammaytuhu (“I named him”), meaning, “I raised him and made him manifest.” Thus, it is the one named who is raised and made manifest, and this is accomplished through the name.

Its morphological patterns are fu‘l and fi‘l, and its plural is asmā’, like qinw and aqnā’ (“date cluster” and “date clusters”), or ‘udw and a‘dā’ (“limb” and “limbs”). The forms summ and simm are also used, with the final root consonant omitted. The form sammā is also used, as in the verse:

“And Allah gave you a blessed name.”

Whatever has no name is neither mentioned nor made manifest, nor does its mention gain prominence. Rather, it is like something hidden and unknown. Hence it is said that a name points to the one named and serves as a distinguishing mark for him, and similar expressions.

Thus, the “people of Islam and the Sunnah,” who mention Allah’s names, know Him, worship Him, love Him, remember Him, and make His remembrance manifest. The “heretics,” by contrast, deny His names, and their hearts turn away from knowing Him, worshipping Him, loving Him, and remembering Him, until they forget to remember Him:

“They forgot Allah, so He forgot them.”

“And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves.”

“Remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with fear, without raising your voice, in the mornings and evenings, and do not be among the heedless.”

A name encompasses both the utterance and the meaning conceived in the heart. It may refer to the utterance alone, or to the meaning alone, for it is part of speech. “Speech” denotes both the utterance and its meaning, and it may

refer to either one alone. Thus, whoever remembers Allah in his heart or with his tongue has remembered Him, but remembering Him with both is more complete. Allah Most High has commanded that His name be glorified and that He be glorified using His name, just as He has commanded that He be invoked by His most beautiful names. He is therefore invoked by His most beautiful names, and His name is glorified. Glorifying His name is glorifying Him, since what is intended by the name is the One named, just as invoking the name is invoking the One named.

Allah Most High says:

“Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.”

Allah Most High sometimes commands that He be remembered and sometimes that His name be remembered, just as He sometimes commands that He be glorified and sometimes that His name be glorified. He says:

“Remember Allah with much remembrance.”

“Remember your Lord within yourself.”

There are many such passages. He also says:

“Remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself wholly to Him.”

Likewise, He says:

“So eat of that over which Allah’s name has been mentioned.”

“Do not eat of that over which Allah’s name has not been mentioned.”

“So eat of what they catch for you, and mention Allah’s name over it.”

Here, however, one says, “In the name of Allah,” thus mentioning the very word “name,” spelled alif, sīn, mīm. By contrast, in response to His words, “Remember the name of your Lord,” one says, “Glory be to Allah,” “Praise be to Allah,” and “There is no god but Allah.” This, too, demonstrates the error of those who identify the name with the One named.

His words concerning slaughtered animals,

“So eat of that over which Allah’s name has been mentioned,”

are like His words,

“Recite in the name of your Lord who created,”

and His words,

“In the name of Allah are its course and its anchorage.”

Thus, His words, “Recite in the name of your Lord,” mean reciting “In the name of Allah” at the beginning of the surahs.

This matter has been discussed at length elsewhere, where it has been explained that this verse indicates that the reciter is commanded to recite “In the name of Allah,” and that this formula is not like the rest of the Quran; rather, it is ancillary to other passages. Here one says, “In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate,” as Solomon wrote, as established by the mass-transmitted Sunnah, and as unanimously agreed upon by the Muslims. Thus one pronounces the very word “name,” which is itself a name for something named; one does not say, “By Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.”

In the case of His words,

“Remember the name of your Lord,”

one says, “Glory be to Allah,” “Praise be to Allah,” “There is no god but Allah,” and similar expressions. Here, however, He says:

“Recite in the name of your Lord.”

He did not say, “Recite the name of your Lord.” His words, “Remember the name of your Lord,” require remembering Him with the tongue, whereas His words, “Remember your Lord,” may also encompass remembrance in the heart.

His words, “Recite in the name of your Lord,” are like a person saying, “In the name of Allah,” when eating or slaughtering, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever has not yet slaughtered should slaughter in the name of Allah.”

As for glorification, He says:

“And glorify Him morning and evening.”

He also says:

“Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High.”

And:

“So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great.”

Regarding invocation, He says:

“Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.”

His words, “Whichever you call upon,” imply a plurality of objects of invocation because of the word “whichever.” His words, “To Him belong the most beautiful names,” imply that the One invoked is one, possessing the most beautiful names. His words, “Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful”—He did not say, “Call in the name of Allah or in the name of the Most Merciful”—convey that it is the one Lord who is invoked by that name.

Thus, the name is sometimes treated as that which is invoked, and sometimes as that by which invocation is made, as in His words:

“To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them.”

The name is that by which invocation is made because the One invoked is the One named, who is invoked by His name. The name is treated as that which is invoked because what is intended by it is the One named, even though, in the wording, it is the name that is invoked and called out, as He says:

“Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful.”

That is, invoke this name or that name; when you invoke it, what you intend is the One named. Whichever of the two names you invoke, you intend the One named:

“To Him belong the most beautiful names.”

Whoever reflects upon these subtle meanings will come to understand something of the Quran’s wisdom and secrets. Blessed, then, is He who sent down the Criterion to His servant. It is indeed a blessed Book, a revelation from One who is All-Wise, Praiseworthy. Its wonders never cease, and scholars never have their fill of it. Whoever seeks guidance elsewhere, Allah will lead him astray; any tyrant who abandons it, Allah will crush him. It is Allah’s firm rope, the wise Reminder, and the straight path. It is a wondrous Quran that guides to right conduct. Allah sent it down as guidance, mercy, healing, clarification, insight, and a reminder.

All praise, then, belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds—abundant, pure, blessed praise, as our Lord loves and is pleased with, and as befits His noble Face—exalted is His majesty.

Here it ends. To Allah belong all praise and favour. May Allah bless Muhammad, his family, and his Companions, and grant them peace.

translated_text:
He was asked about someone who claimed that “Imam Ahmad” had been among the foremost deniers of the attributes—the attributes of Allah Most High—and that his followers within his school had merely supposed him to uphold the affirmation of the attributes, as opposed to their negation, because they were unaware of what had happened to him. For something remarkable had happened to him:

Some “heretics” knew of Ahmad’s asceticism, scrupulousness, and piety, and that people followed the views he adopted. They therefore compiled statements affirming the attributes and attributed them to Quran commentaries and hadith collections. They also attributed much of this material to the Companions, the imams, and others—even to Ahmad himself, putting words into his mouth. They placed it all in a locked chest and asked Imam Ahmad to accept the chest from them for safekeeping. They made out that they were setting out on a journey or something of the sort, and that they intended to return to collect what they had entrusted to him. They knew that he would not examine the contents of the chest.

It remained with him until Allah took his soul. His followers and those who had studied under him then entered, found the chest, and opened it. Inside, they found those “fabricated hadiths” and “commentaries and transmitted reports” supporting the affirmation of the attributes.

They said: “Had Imam Ahmad not believed what was in these books, he would not have placed them in this chest and guarded them so carefully.” They then read those books and circulated them among the writings and teachings of his that they made public

and were unaware of the intentions of those heretics who sought to corrupt this Islamic community, just as Paul achieved his aim of corrupting the Christian faith through the epistles he composed for them.

He answered:

Whoever relates that fabricated tale about Ahmad ibn Hanbal—claiming that chests containing books were entrusted to him, that he died without knowing their contents, and that his followers then took them and adopted the beliefs they contained—thereby displays his utter ignorance. For Muslims have not taken from Ahmad a single statement concerning Allah Most High’s attributes that originated with him. Rather, the hadiths that scholars transmit concerning Allah Most High’s attributes already existed among the Muslim community before Imam Ahmad was born. Scholars other than Imam Ahmad also transmitted them, so people have no need to rely on Ahmad’s transmission of them. They would still be well known and authentically established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, even if Ahmad had never been created.

It was only when the persecutions of the “Jahmiyyah” arose that Ahmad became renowned as the imam of the people of the Sunnah and as one who patiently endured the ordeal. They deny Allah Most High’s attributes and say that Allah will not be seen in the Hereafter; that the Quran is not Allah’s speech but a created thing among other created things; that He Most High is not above the heavens; and that Muhammad did not ascend to Allah. They led some rulers astray, and these rulers subjected people to tests through inducements and threats. Some people complied out of desire for reward, others out of fear, while others went into hiding and did not appear before them. Whoever refused to comply had his livelihood cut off and was removed from office. If he was a captive, they would not secure his release, nor would they accept his testimony. They might even kill or imprison him.

The “ordeal” is famous and well known. It took place during the rule of al-Ma’mūn, al-Mu‘tasim, and al-Wāthiq;

then al-Mutawakkil brought it to an end. Allah kept Imam Ahmad steadfast, so he did not agree with them in denying Allah Most High’s attributes. He debated them on scholarly grounds and refuted their arguments. They tortured him, but he patiently endured their torture, so Allah made him one of the leaders who guide by His command. As He Most High says:

“And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient and had certainty in Our signs.”

Whoever is granted patience and certainty, Allah makes him a leader in religion. His statements concerning the “Sunnah” were attributed to him only because he made it known and brought it to light, not because he originated or introduced it. Otherwise, the Sunnah is the Sunnah of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The truest speech is Allah’s speech, and the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad ibn ‘Abd Allāh. What Imam Ahmad said was also the position of the imams before him, such as Mālik, al-Thawrī, al-Awzā‘ī, Hammād ibn Zayd, and Hammād ibn Salamah; the position of the Successors before them; and the position of the Companions, who received it from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The hadiths concerning the “Sunnah” are well known in the two Sahīh collections and other Islamic works.

The affirmation of Allah Most High’s attributes has been transmitted through numerous independent channels from Ahmad and other imams of the Sunnah. In this, they follow what has been transmitted through numerous independent channels from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

As for the claim that Muslims base their creed concerning the fundamentals of religion on his statements or those of other scholars, only an ignorant person would say this. “Ahmad ibn Hanbal” forbade uncritical adherence to himself or other scholars in subsidiary legal matters. He said, “Do not follow men uncritically in your religion, for they cannot avoid making mistakes.” He also said, “Do not follow me uncritically, nor Mālik, nor al-Thawrī, nor al-Shāfi‘ī.” In this, he followed the example of others

Ahmad’s associates—such as Abū Dāwūd al-Sijistānī, Ibrāhīm al-Harbī, ‘Uthmān ibn Sa‘īd al-Dārimī, Abū Zur‘ah, Abū Hātim, al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Baqī ibn Makhlad, Abū Bakr al-Athram, his two sons Sālih and ‘Abd Allāh, ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān al-Dārimī, Muhammad ibn Muslim ibn Wārah, and others among the foremost scholars of religious knowledge and jurisprudence—would accept the statements of Ahmad or anyone else only with supporting evidence that he explained to them. They had received knowledge through direct transmission just as he had, and they shared many of his teachers. Those teachers whom they had not met, they learned from through their students, who were Ahmad’s peers. These matters are known to anyone familiar with the history of Islam and its scholars.

Shaykh al-Islām Abū al-‘Abbās Taqī al-Dīn ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah sanctify his soul and illuminate his grave—said:

Section: On Attributes Dependent on the Divine Will

These are the attributes of the Lord, Almighty and Majestic, which subsist in His Essence by His will and power: His speech, hearing, sight, will, love, pleasure, mercy, anger, and displeasure; His creating, beneficence, and justice; His rising above, coming, arrival, and descent; and other such attributes declared in the Noble Book and the Sunnah.

The Jahmiyyah, along with those of the Mu‘tazilah and others who agree with them, say that none of these attributes, nor any others, subsist in His Essence.

The Kullābiyyah, along with those of the Sālimiyyah and others who agree with them, say: “Attributes subsist in Him independently of His will and power. As for whatever occurs by His will and power, it can only be something created and separate from Him.”

translated_text:
As for the early generations and the imams of the Sunnah and hadith, they affirm that He possesses these attributes, as declared in the Book and the Sunnah. This is also the position of many—or most—speculative theologians and philosophers, whose statements we have quoted verbatim elsewhere.

Speech is one such example. The early generations and the imams of the Sunnah and hadith maintain that He speaks by His will and power, and that His speech is not created; rather, it is an attribute of His that subsists in His Essence.

Among those who have identified this as the position of the imams of the Sunnah are Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mandah, Abū ‘Abd Allāh ibn Hāmid, Abū Bakr ‘Abd al-‘Azīz, Abū Ismā‘īl al-Ansārī, and others. Likewise, Abū ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-Barr stated something similar concerning His rising above.

The imams of the Sunnah—such as ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Bukhārī, ‘Uthmān ibn Sa‘īd al-Dārimī, and countless other imams—and all other adherents of the Sunnah and hadith agree that He speaks by His will and that He has always spoken whenever He wills and however He wills. Harb ibn Ismā‘īl al-Kirmānī also reported this from Sa‘īd ibn Mansūr, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Ishāq ibn Ibrāhīm.

Allah has called the Noble Quran “discourse,” saying:

“Allah has sent down the best discourse.”

And He says:

“And who is more truthful than Allah in speech?”

And He says:

“No new reminder comes to them from their Lord…”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Indeed, Allah introduces into His commands whatever He wills.”

This is among the evidence al-Bukhārī cited in his Sahīh and elsewhere. Others besides al-Bukhārī also cited it as evidence, including Nu‘aym ibn Hammād and Hammād ibn Zayd.

translated_text:
It is well known that the early generations taught that the Noble Quran is Allah’s speech, uncreated: it originated from Him and to Him it returns.

As for the Jahmiyyah and the Mu‘tazilah, they say that He has no speech subsisting in His Essence; rather, His speech is separate from Him and created by Him. The Mu‘tazilah state without qualification that He speaks by His will, but what they mean is that He creates speech separate from Himself.

The Kullābiyyah and the Sālimiyyah say that He does not speak by His will and power; rather, His speech subsists in His Essence without involving His power or will, just like His life. They say that speech is an attribute of His Essence, not an attribute of action connected to His will and power. The former groups say that it is an attribute of action, but by “action” they mean the created result brought about by His will and power.

The early generations and the imams of the Sunnah, along with many speculative theologians—such as the Hishāmiyyah, the Karrāmiyyah, the followers of Abū Mu‘ādh al-Tūmanī and Zuhayr al-Yāmī, and other groups—say that speech is “an attribute of both His Essence and His action”: He speaks by His will and power, with speech that subsists in His Essence.

This is what is understood by the attribute of speech in any speaker. Whoever is described as speaking—whether angels, humans, jinn, or others—must have speech that subsists in themselves, and they speak by their own will and power. Speech is an attribute of perfection, not deficiency, and one who speaks by his own will is more perfect than one who does not speak by his own will. How, then, could created beings possess attributes of perfection that the Creator does not?

But the “Jahmiyyah and the Mu‘tazilah” base their position on “their premise” that no attribute subsists in the Lord, because, they claim, this would entail corporeality and an inadmissible resemblance to creation: an attribute is an accident, and an accident can subsist only in a body.

The “Kullābiyyah” say that He possesses attributes over which He has no power and which are not subject to His will. Whatever occurs by His will, however, is temporally originated, and temporal events do not subsist in the Lord—exalted is He. They refer to “attributes connected to His will” as the question of “the inherence of temporal events.” For if He spoke to Moses son of ‘Imrān by His will and power, and called to him by His power and will when Moses came to Him, that call and speech would be temporally originated.

They say: If the Lord possessed such an attribute, temporal events would subsist in Him. They further say: If temporal events subsisted in Him, He would never be free of them, and whatever is never free of temporal events is itself temporally originated.

They also argue: If His being receptive to that attribute is inseparable from His Essence, He must have been receptive to it from eternity. It would therefore follow that its existence from eternity is possible. Yet temporal events cannot exist from eternity, since that would entail temporal events with no beginning, which is impossible for “reasons” explained elsewhere.

They say: By this argument we have demonstrated that bodies came into existence, and through it we have established that the world came into existence. By it we have also established the existence of the Preventer and the truthfulness of His messengers. Instead, he argued from a composite consensus—an exceedingly weak proof—because he had nothing else with which to defend the Kullābiyyah’s position. This is widely known among scholars; even al-Hillī ibn al-Mutahhar stated in his books that there is no proof for denying “the inherence of temporal events.” Thus, anyone who disputes this is ignorant of both reason and revelation.

Likewise, earlier scholars such as Abū al-Maʿālī and his associates relied chiefly on the argument that the Karrāmiyyah had affirmed this position and contradicted themselves. They would expose the Karrāmiyyah’s contradictions, imagining that, by exposing the contradictions of their opponents, they had won the argument. They did not realize that the early generations and the leading scholars of the Sunnah and hadith—indeed, groups predating the Karrāmiyyah—paid no heed to the Karrāmiyyah or their like. Rather, they had spoken of this before the Karrāmiyyah even existed. Ibn Karrām came later, after Ahmad ibn Hanbal, in the time of Muslim ibn al-Hajjāj and his contemporaries. The leading scholars of the Sunnah and the speculative theologians had discussed these matters before them, and the early generations had always affirmed what this entails.

However, when the Jahmiyyah, who denied the divine attributes, emerged in the early second century AH, Muslim scholars explained their misguidance and errors. Then the folly of the Jahmiyyah came to the fore in the early third century AH, and the scholars—Imam Ahmad and others—were subjected to persecution. They therefore devoted themselves to refuting the Jahmiyyah and exposing their misguidance. Imam Ahmad even compiled the Quranic verses demonstrating the falsity of their position, and these are very numerous. Indeed, the verses indicating “attributes exercised by His will,” which they call “the inherence of temporal events,” are very numerous. An example is His statement, Exalted is He:

“We created you, then fashioned you, then said to the angels, ‘Prostrate before Adam,’ so they prostrated.”

This clearly shows that He commanded the angels to prostrate only after creating Adam; He did not command them in pre-eternity. Likewise, He says:

“Indeed, the likeness of Jesus in Allah’s sight is that of Adam: He created him from dust, then said to him, ‘Be,’ and he was.”

Thus, He said this to him only after creating him from dust, not in pre-eternity.

translated_text:
Section

The same applies to “will” and “love,” as in His words, Exalted is He:

“His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

And His words:

“Never say of anything, ‘I will do that tomorrow,’ unless Allah wills.”

“You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in safety.”

“When We will to destroy a town, We command its affluent inhabitants, but they defiantly disobey within it, so the decree becomes due against it.”

“When Allah wills harm for a people, none can avert it.”

“When We will, We shall replace them entirely with others like them.”

“If We so will, We shall surely take away what We have revealed to you.”

There are many similar passages in the glorious Quran. The particles that put the imperfect verb into the jussive or subjunctive make its reference exclusively future, such as in (“if”) and an (“to”). Likewise, idhā (“when”) is an adverb referring to future time. Thus, His words “when He wills,” “if Allah wills,” and similar expressions entail the occurrence of an act of willing in the future.

The same applies to love and pleasure. Allah, Exalted is He, says:

“Say: ‘If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you.’”

This indicates that when they follow him, Allah loves them. He puts the expression “will love you” into the jussive as the consequence of the imperative, which carries a conditional meaning. Thus, the meaning is: “If you follow me, Allah will love you.” It is well known that the consequence of a condition or command comes only after it, not before it. Allah’s love for them therefore comes only after their following the Messenger.

Among those who dispute this, some say: “There is no

love; rather, what is meant is a created reward.” Others say: “Rather, there is an eternal, beginningless love—either the will or something other than it.” The Quran supports the position of the early generations, the imams of the Sunnah, who oppose both views.

Likewise, His words:

“That is because they followed what angered Allah and disliked His pleasure.”

This indicates that their deeds angered Him and are therefore a cause of His wrath. His wrath against them comes after their deeds, not before them.

Likewise, His words:

“When they provoked Our anger, We exacted retribution from them.”

And likewise, His words:

“If you disbelieve, Allah has no need of you. He does not approve of disbelief for His servants; but if you are grateful, He approves it for you.”

He made His approval conditional upon their gratitude and put the verb into the jussive as its consequence. The consequence of a condition comes only after it.

Likewise, His words:

“Indeed, Allah loves those who repeatedly repent and loves those who purify themselves.”

“He loves the God-fearing.”

“He loves those who act justly.”

“He loves those who fight in His cause in ranks.”

These and similar passages indicate that love is on account of these deeds and is a recompense for them. Recompense comes only after the deed and the cause that brings it about.

Section

The same applies to “hearing,” “sight,” and “looking.” Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘Act, for Allah and His Messenger will see your deeds.’”

This concerns the hypocrites. Concerning those who repent, He says:

“Say, ‘Act, for Allah, His Messenger, and the believers will see your deeds.’”

His words, “Allah will see,” indicate that He sees those deeds after this noble verse was revealed. The opponent either denies seeing altogether or affirms an eternal, beginningless seeing.

Likewise, He says:

“Then We made you successors in the land after them, to see how you would act.”

The lām expressing purpose entails that what follows it occurs after the act undertaken for that purpose. Thus, His looking at how they act comes after His making them successors.

Likewise:

“Allah has certainly heard the words of the woman who disputes with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah. And Allah hears your conversation.”

He states that He hears their conversation while she is disputing and complaining to Allah. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When the imam says, ‘Allah hears whoever praises Him,’ say, ‘Our Lord, to You belongs all praise,’ and Allah will hear you.”

He thus made His hearing us a recompense and response to praise, so it comes after the praise. Here, hearing includes not only hearing the words but also accepting and answering them. This includes the words of Allah’s intimate friend:

“Indeed, my Lord is the Hearer of supplication.”

Likewise, He says:

“Allah has certainly heard the words of those who said, ‘Allah is poor, while we are rich.’”

And He said to Moses:

“Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and see.”

translated_text:
“Clear reason” also demonstrates this, for what does not exist can neither be seen nor heard, according to clear reason and the agreement of rational people. Some among the “Sālimiyyah,” however, have said that He hears and sees it as existing in His knowledge, not as existing apart from Him. They did not say that He hears and sees it as something distinct from the Lord.

Once He has created His servants and they have acted and spoken, either we say that He hears their words and sees their deeds, or that He neither sees nor hears them. Denying this amounts to denying these two attributes and rejecting the Quran. Both are attributes of perfection involving no deficiency: one who hears and sees is more perfect than one who neither hears nor sees. Created beings possess hearing and sight, and it is impossible for created beings to possess attributes of perfection that the Creator—glorified and exalted is He—does not possess. In several passages, Allah Most High has censured those who worship what neither hears nor sees. Moreover, He is living, and a living being that does not possess hearing and sight possesses their opposites: blindness and deafness. That is impossible for Him. A fuller discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

“The point here” is simply that, if He hears people’s words and sees their deeds after they have come into existence, then either it is said that this is a new occurrence, and that He did not hear or see them, so that after creating them He does not hear or see them. If something new has occurred, it must be either something existent or something nonexistent. If it is nonexistent, then nothing new has occurred. If it is existent, it must subsist either in Allah’s own essence or in the essence of another. “The second” entails that this other is the one who hears and sees. It therefore necessarily follows that this existing hearing and seeing subsist in Allah’s own essence. There is no way around this.

translated_text:
And the “Kullābiyyah” say throughout this discussion: What newly arises is a relation between the command and the person commanded, between the will and what is willed, and between hearing and sight and what is heard and seen. They are told: This relation must be either existent or nonexistent. If it is nonexistent, nothing new has arisen, for nonexistence is nothing. If it is existent, their position is invalidated.

Moreover, it is impossible for a “relation”—a relationship or relational attribution—to arise without something arising that necessitates it. A relationship or relational attribution arises only when something existent arises that entails it. A group, including Ibn ʿAqīl, call this relationship “states.” The various “groups” agree that “relationships,” “relational attributions,” and “relations” arise anew. Yet relationships cannot arise without something arising that necessitates them. A relationship or relational attribution can therefore only follow from an attribute with real existence, as with fatherhood, sonship, being above or below, and being to the right or left: these necessarily entail realities that actually exist.

The same applies to His being “Creator,” “Provider,” “Beneficent,” and “Just.” These are acts He performs by His will and power, since He creates by His will, provides by His will, acts justly by His will, and bestows goodness by His will. The position of the “vast majority of Muslims,” among both the early and later generations, is that the act of creation is distinct from the created thing: creation is the Creator’s act, while the created thing is what His act produces. This is why the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would seek refuge in the Lord’s acts and attributes, as in his words:

“I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your displeasure, in Your protection from Your punishment, and in You from You. I cannot adequately praise You; You are as You have praised Yourself.”

Thus he sought refuge in His act of granting protection, just as he sought refuge in His pleasure.

The imams of the Sunnah, such as Ahmad and others, have argued that “Allah’s speech is uncreated” on the grounds that the Prophet sought refuge in it, saying:

“Whoever stops at a place and says, ‘I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah from the evil of what He has created,’ will not be harmed by anything until he leaves that place.”

Likewise, His act of granting protection and His pleasure are uncreated, for he sought refuge in both. The well-being present in a servant’s body, however, is created, since it results from His granting protection.

Since creation is His act, while the created thing is what His act produces, and since He created all creatures by His will, this demonstrates that creation is an act that occurs by His will. It cannot subsist in anything other than Him. This therefore demonstrates that His acts subsist in His own essence, while occurring by His will and power. Al-Bukhārī reported the scholars’ consensus on the distinction between creation and the created thing. Sound reason plainly indicates this as well.

For both rational and scriptural evidence establish that everything other than Allah Most High is created and originated, coming into existence after not having existed, and that Allah alone possesses eternity and beginninglessness. He Most High says:

“He who created the heavens and the earth and all that is between them in six days.”

Thus, when He first created the heavens, either He performed an act constituting the creation of the heavens and the earth, or He performed no act, and created things came into existence without an act. It is evident that if the Creator were in exactly the same state before, during and after their creation, their creation could not be assigned to one time rather than another without a cause necessitating that selection.

Furthermore, that a created thing should come into existence without a newly occurring cause is impossible according to the most elementary dictates of reason. If it is said that will and power account for the selection, the reply is that the eternal will stands in the same relation to all times. Moreover, a will to single out one of two identical alternatives is inconceivable without a cause that necessitates

Otherwise, if the previously existing will and power alone were sufficient, it would necessarily have existed earlier, for complete will together with complete power necessarily entails the existence of the object of that power.

Those who maintain that creation is identical to the created thing—such as Abū al-Hasan and his followers, including Ibn ʿAqīl—have argued as follows: If creation were distinct from the created thing, it would have to be either eternal or originated. If it were eternal, the created thing would necessarily be eternal, since the two are correlatives. If it were originated, this would entail that originated events subsist in Him. That created thing would then require another act of creation, entailing an infinite regress.

The majority answered them, each group proceeding according to its own principles. One group said: Creation is eternal, even though the created thing is originated. Many adherents of the four schools hold this view, as do most Hanafīs. They said: You concede that will is eternal and beginningless, while what is willed is originated. We therefore say concerning creation what you say concerning will.

Another group said: Rather, the act of creation occurs within His essence and does not require another act of creation; instead, it occurs through His power. You yourselves say that the created thing comes into existence through His power after not having existed. If something separate from Him can come into existence through His power alone, then this applies all the more to what is inherent in Him. This is the answer given by many of the Karrāmiyyah, the Hishāmiyyah and others.

Actions are of two kinds: transitive and intransitive. Transitive actions include creating, giving, and the like. Intransitive actions include rising over the Throne, descending, coming, and approaching. Allah Most High says:

“It is He who created the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them in six days, then rose over the Throne.”

He thus mentions both kinds of action: transitive and intransitive. Both occur by His will and power, and both are attributes of His. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

The point here is that the Quran indicates this principle in more than a hundred places. As for authentic hadiths on this subject, they are too numerous to enumerate. For example, the two Sahīh collections contain the report from Zayd ibn Khālid al-Juhanī that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, led his Companions in the dawn prayer at al-Hudaybiyah after rain had fallen during the night. He then said:

“Do you know what your Lord said tonight? He said: ‘This morning, some of My servants believe in Me and others disbelieve. Whoever says, “We were given rain by Allah’s grace and mercy,” believes in Me and disbelieves in the stars. But whoever says, “We were given rain by such-and-such a star and such-and-such another,” disbelieves in Me and believes in the stars.’”

The authentic hadith collections also contain the hadith of intercession:

“Each of the Messengers, when people come to him, will say: ‘My Lord has today become angry with an anger

the like of which He has never had before and will never have again.’” This makes clear that the anger occurred on that day, not before it.

An authentic hadith states:

“When Allah speaks revelation, the inhabitants of the heavens hear something like a chain being dragged across smooth stone.”

The words, “When Allah speaks revelation, they hear,” indicate that He speaks it when they hear it, which rules out its being beginningless. Moreover, something resembling a chain being dragged across smooth stone occurs in succession, and whatever is preceded by something else cannot be beginningless.

Likewise, an authentic hadith states:

He thus tells us that when the servant says, “All praise is for Allah,” Allah says, “He has praised Me”; and when he says, “The Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful,” Allah says, “My servant has extolled Me”—and so on through the hadith.
