“Allah listens more attentively to a man with a beautiful voice reciting the Quran than the owner of a singing slave girl listens to her.”

Another authentic hadith states:

“Allah listens to nothing as He listens to a prophet with a beautiful voice reciting the Quran melodiously and aloud.”

The forms adhina, ya’dhanu, and udhunan signify listening—in the past tense, present tense, and verbal noun respectively—as in:

“And it listens to its Lord, as it must.”

He thus tells us that He listens to both. An authentic hadith also states:

“My servant continues to draw near to Me through voluntary acts of worship until I love him. When I love him, I become his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks.”

He thus tells us that the servant continues to draw near through voluntary acts of worship after fulfilling the obligatory duties.

In the two Sahīh collections, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, relates from his Lord, Most High:

“Allah said: ‘I am as My servant thinks of Me, and I am with him when he remembers Me. If he remembers Me within himself, I remember him within Myself; and if he remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than theirs.’”

The particle in (“if”) introduces a condition, and the consequence follows the condition. This makes clear that He remembers the servant if the servant remembers Him within himself; and if the servant remembers Him in a gathering, He remembers him in a gathering better than theirs. The opponent, however, says that He has always remembered him, without beginning or end. He then says that His remembrance of this servant, His remembrance of others, and everything else Allah says are all one single thing, admitting neither division nor plurality. Thus, what his position really amounts to is that Allah has never spoken, does not speak, and does not remember anyone.

The opposing “negators” are likewise divided. Some deny the attributes altogether; discussion with them therefore concerns the attributes in general, not specifically the “attributes pertaining to His will.” Others affirm the attributes but maintain that nothing subsists in His essence through His will and power. Such a person says that He does not speak by His will and choice, and that His being pleased or displeased, loving or hating, and choosing do not occur by His will and power. He also says that He does not perform an act—“namely, creation”—by which He creates the created thing. This is a point on which the negators themselves disagree. Some say that the “object of His power” can only be something distinct from Him, as the Jahmiyyah, Kullābiyyah, and Muʿtazilah maintain. As for “power over entities,” it is reported in the Sahīh that Abū Mas‘ūd said: “I was beating a slave of mine when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saw me and said, ‘Know, Abū Mas‘ūd, that Allah has greater power over you than you have over this slave.’” His words, “Allah has greater power over you than you have over this slave,” demonstrate that power pertains to entities separate from the agent—both “the Lord’s power” and “the servant’s power.”

Some, such as the Karrāmiyyah, say that both powers pertain to acts. Others, such as the Ash‘ariyyah, say that the Lord’s power pertains to what is separate from Him, whereas the servant’s power pertains only to an act occurring in the locus in which that power subsists. The “scriptural texts,” however, indicate that both powers pertain to what subsists in the agent and to what is separate from him. For Allah, Exalted is He, has stated that the servant has the ability to perform his acts, as in His words:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And His words:

“And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women, then let him marry from among the slave women whom you possess.”

This indicates that some of us have this ability while others do not. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Young men, whoever among you is able to marry should marry. Whoever is unable should fast, for it will curb his sexual desire.”

Both al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded it in their Sahīhs.

He also said:

“If you can act with contentment and certainty, then do so.”

And in the hadith recorded in the Sahīh, he said:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

He has also stated that Allah has power over His servant.

Those who say that “matters pertaining to His will” do not subsist in Him rely principally on the argument that, if temporally occurring events subsisted in Him, He would never be free of them, and whatever is never free of temporally occurring events must itself have come into existence. As for their statement, “Through this method we came to know that the world had a beginning, and thereby established the existence of the ‘Maker,’” they are told: Indeed, you have devised a method that accords with neither revelation nor reason. Those knowledgeable about the revealed religion acknowledge that you are innovators, introducing into Islam what does not belong to it. Those who speak with understanding know that reason contradicts your claims, and that what you have presented as proof of the Maker’s existence does not establish His existence; rather, it is an argument for denying the “Maker.” The existence of the “Maker” is a truth, and this truth necessarily invalidates your argument that whatever is never free of temporally occurring events must itself have come into existence.

As for “your method being an innovation,” followed neither by the prophets, nor their followers, nor the early generations of the Muslim community, this is because everyone acquainted with what the Messenger brought—even someone whose knowledge is only moderate and falls short of complete mastery—knows that, in calling people to know the Maker, His oneness, and the truthfulness of His messengers, the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not direct them to argue from the existence of accidents: that these accidents come into existence and are inseparable from bodies; that whatever is never free of temporally occurring events must itself have come into existence; and that this follows from the impossibility of a beginningless succession of events.

It is thus known with certainty that the Messenger neither spoke of “this method” nor called people to it. Nor did his Companions speak of it or use it to call people. This establishes something necessarily known from the Messenger’s religion, for the Messenger and those who believe in him hold that Allah can be known

Revelation thus establishes conclusively that this method is unnecessary, while its contradictions of the texts of the Quran and Sunnah establish its invalidity. Revelation therefore shows both that it is unnecessary and that it is invalid.

As for reason, everything said concerning this method has been discussed at length elsewhere, and it has been shown that leading figures among its adherents sometimes acknowledge its rational invalidity. Explanations of its invalidity can be found in the writings of Abū Hāmid, al-Rāzī, and others. When its invalidity became rationally apparent, the “philosophers” gained the upper hand over those who followed it. The philosophers imagined that, by discrediting it, they had discredited the proofs of revelation, supposing that revelation taught what this method entailed. They were even more ignorant of revelation and reason than those who followed it. Its followers thus neither defended Islam nor defeated its enemies; rather, they gave the philosophers an advantage over themselves and over Islam. All this has been discussed at length elsewhere.

The “point here” is simply to recognize that they have no rational proof for denying the “attributes dependent on His will,” which they call the inherence of temporally occurring events. Their most discerning scholars acknowledge this. As for revelation, it is undoubtedly filled with statements contradicting their denial. Reason likewise establishes the opposite in several ways, some of which we have indicated.

First: These people say that His freedom from imperfection is not known through reason, but only “by consensus”—which is what they rely upon to deny imperfection of Him. We therefore return to their appeal to consensus. It is well known that consensus cannot be invoked as proof on the very points under dispute. Their opponent says: “I have not agreed with you in denying this meaning, even though I agree with the general statement that Allah is free of imperfection. In my view, this meaning is not an imperfection and is not included in what I have conceded to you. Unless you establish its negation through reason or revelation, your appeal to my words, despite my not having intended that meaning, misrepresents me. You invoke consensus, yet those who affirm these attributes are among those whose agreement constitutes consensus, and they have not conceded this.”

Second: The absence of these things before they come into existence is an imperfection; rather, if they existed before they came into existence, that would be an imperfection. An example is Allah’s speaking to Moses, peace be upon him, and calling him. His calling him when He did was an attribute of perfection; had He called him before he arrived, that would have been an imperfection. Each of these is thus a perfection at the time of its occurrence, but not before it occurs. Indeed, its occurrence before the time at which wisdom requires it to occur would be an imperfection.

Fourth: This objection applies to everything the Lord has done and created. It may be said: If His creating this is an imperfection, then He has been characterized by imperfection; and if it is a perfection, then He previously lacked it. If you say, “In our view, the ‘attributes of action’ are neither imperfections nor perfections,” the response is: If you say that, your opponent can likewise say that these occurrences in time are neither imperfections nor perfections.

Fifth: It may be said: If sound reason is presented with a being capable of speaking by its own power and itself doing whatever it wills, and another being incapable of speaking by its will or acting itself in any way—being instead like an incapacitated person in whom no act can occur by his own choice—sound reason judges the former being to be more perfect. Thus, it is you who have attributed imperfection to the Lord. Perfection lies in His possessing these attributes, not in denying that He possesses them.

Sixth: It may be said: Concerning occurrences in time, none of which can be beginningless and which can only come into existence successively, suppose one asks: Which is more perfect—to have the power to bring them about successively, or to lack that power? Sound reason clearly recognizes that one who can bring them about successively is more perfect than one who cannot.

Yet you say that the Lord has no power over any of these things, while also saying that He has power over things separate from Him. It is well known that an agent’s power to perform an act inherent in himself is prior to his power over things separate from him. Thus, if you say

Thus, your position entails that He has no power over anything and cannot do anything, which in turn entails that He is not the Creator of anything. This is an inescapable consequence for those who deny His attributes.

For this reason, it has been said: The method they followed to establish that the world had a beginning and that a Maker exists contradicts both the world’s having a beginning and the existence of a Maker. These can only be soundly affirmed by refuting that method, not by upholding it. Thus, what they relied upon and made into foundations of religion and evidence for it is itself invalid according to both revelation and reason, and contradicts and opposes religion.

This is why “the early generations and the imams” criticized and condemned this discourse of theirs, saying: “Whoever seeks knowledge through speculative theology falls into heresy,” as Abū Yūsuf said—a saying also related from Mālik.

Al-Shāfiʿī said: “My judgment concerning the practitioners of speculative theology is that they should be beaten with palm branches and sandals and paraded among the tribes, while it is proclaimed: ‘This is the recompense of whoever abandons the Book and the Sunnah and turns to speculative theology.’”

Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: “The scholars of speculative theology are heretics. No one who has donned the cloak of speculative theology has prospered.”

The imams spoke truly concerning this, for these people base their approach on “vague statements” that pass as sound among those who do not understand their true nature. Once someone believes such discourse to be true, and it becomes clear that it contradicts the Book and the Sunnah, disease, hypocrisy, misgiving, and doubt remain in his heart. Indeed, he may go so far as to disparage what the Messenger brought, and this is heresy. “Like a mirage on a level plain which a thirsty person mistakes for water, until, when he reaches it, he finds nothing there, but finds Allah before him, who pays him his account in full. And Allah is swift in reckoning.”

This is compound ignorance. Since they were in doubt and bewilderment, they are amid layers of darkness, one above another: when one stretches out his hand, he can scarcely see it. Whoever Allah does not grant light has no light. How far these people are from the light of the Quran and faith!

Allah Most High says:

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His light is that of a niche containing a lamp; the lamp is within glass, and the glass is like a brilliant star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, whose oil would almost glow even without being touched by fire. Light upon light! Allah guides to His light whom He wills. Allah sets forth parables for people, and Allah knows all things.”

If it is said:

“It is clear that speech and action fall under ‘attributes exercised by choice,’ since they occur by the Lord’s will and power. But whether ‘will,’ ‘love,’ ‘pleasure,’ and ‘anger’ do so requires consideration. For ‘will’ is itself volition. When He, glorified is He, creates someone He loves, such as His intimate friend, He loves him; He loves the believers, and they love Him. Likewise, when people perform deeds, He sees those deeds. This necessarily follows and cannot be otherwise. How, then, can it be subject to choice?”

The reply is:

Whatever comes to be after not having been does so only by Allah’s will and power. Whatever He, glorified is He, wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be. Thus, whatever He wills must come to be, and it is subject to the Lord’s will and power. Whatever He does not will cannot come to be, although He has power over it, as He Most High says:

translated_text:
“Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance.”

“Had Allah willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another.”

“Had your Lord willed, they would not have done so.”

The fact that something must occur because it has already been decreed that it will inevitably come to be does not preclude its occurring by His will, power, and volition—even if His volition is inseparable from His essence, like His life and knowledge. For “His willing of future things” is preceded by “His willing of what is past”:

“His command, when He wills something, is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.”

He only willed “this second thing” after first willing that which entails His willing it. Thus, the later act of willing came about through the earlier act of willing.

People have differed greatly over “the question of Allah’s will, glorified and exalted is He,” adopting numerous positions. Some have denied it, and al-Rāzī favoured this view in his al-Matālib al-Āliya (The Lofty Pursuits). Yet, praise be to Allah, we have established it and exposed the falsity of the specious arguments against it. We have shown that what the Quran and Sunnah teach is the unalloyed truth, attested by clear rational arguments, and that “clear reason accords with authentic transmitted evidence.”

We had “first” explained that conclusive proofs cannot conflict: two conclusive proofs cannot contradict one another, whether both are rational, both are drawn from revelation, or one is rational and the other drawn from revelation. We then explained that they agree with, support, and reinforce one another. Reason establishes the soundness of revelation, and revelation makes clear the soundness of reason; whoever follows either is led to the other.

and that those who deserve punishment are those who neither listen nor reason. As Allah Most High says:

“Or do you think that most of them listen or reason? They are only like cattle—rather, they are further astray.”

He Most High also says:

“Whenever a group is cast into it, its keepers will ask them, ‘Did no warner come to you?’”

“They will say, ‘Yes, a warner did come to us, but we denied him and said, “Allah has revealed nothing; you are only in great error.”’”

“And they will say, ‘Had we listened or reasoned, we would not have been among the inhabitants of the Blaze.’”

And He says:

“Have they not travelled through the land, so that they may have hearts with which to reason or ears with which to hear? For it is not the eyes that are blind, but the hearts within the breasts.”

He Most High also says:

“Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart or gives ear with full attention.”

The Quran has thus made clear that whoever reasons or listens will be saved and blessed, and will believe in what the messengers brought. These matters have been discussed at length in several places. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
Section

Leading speculative thinkers, “such as Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Rāzī and Abū al-Hasan al-Āmidī,” and others presented the arguments of those who deny “the inherence of temporal events in Him” and demonstrated the invalidity of them all. They cited four arguments advanced by these deniers:

The first is the “well-known argument”: if temporal events subsisted in Him, He would always have either them or their opposites, and whatever is never free of temporal events must itself have a beginning. They challenged the first premise; as for the second, al-Rāzī and others explained its invalidity. This has been discussed at length elsewhere.

The second is that if He were receptive to them in beginningless eternity, this receptivity would be inseparable from His essence. Receptivity would entail the possibility of what is received, yet the existence of temporal events in beginningless eternity is impossible. They refuted this argument themselves by countering it with the parallel case of divine power: He has the power to bring temporal events into existence, and power entails the possibility of its object; yet “the existence of the object of His power”—namely, temporal events—in beginningless eternity is impossible.

“This argument” is invalid on several grounds. The first is that “the existence of temporal events” must be either impossible or possible. If it is possible, then receptivity to them and power over them can always be possible. In that case, the existence of their kind in beginningless eternity would not be impossible; rather, their kind could be both an object of power and something capable of being received;

In that case, they would not be possible in beginningless eternity—neither objects of power nor capable of being received. Yet their impossibility thereafter does not follow. Temporal events do exist, so their perpetual impossibility cannot be maintained. This exhaustive division demonstrates the invalidity of “this argument.”

The second ground is as follows: There is no doubt that the Lord, Exalted is He, possesses power. Either He has always possessed power—which is correct—or He acquired power after having lacked it. If it is said that He has always possessed power, the response is: If He has always possessed power, and the object of His power has always been possible, then the perpetual existence of possible things would be possible, and thus so would the perpetual occurrence of temporal events. In that case, His being receptive to them in beginningless eternity would not be impossible.

If it is said, “Rather, action was impossible and then became possible,” the response is: This combines two contradictories, for one who possesses power cannot have power over something impossible. How, then, could He possess power while the object of His power is impossible? Furthermore, even supposing this were possible, it could be said that in beginningless eternity He has power over whatever can occur in the endless future. The same applies to what can be received: it could be said that in beginningless eternity He is receptive to whatever can occur in the endless future.

The third ground: If He is said to be receptive to something in beginningless eternity, He is receptive only to that over which He has power and whose existence is possible. As for what is impossible and falls outside the scope of power, He is not receptive to it.

(Their third argument:

They said: If temporal events subsisted in Him, this would necessarily entail “His changing,” and change is impossible for Allah. They themselves—al-Rāzī and others—refuted “this argument” by saying:

What do you mean when you say, “If they subsisted in Him, He would change”? By change, do you mean their very subsistence in Him, or something else? If you mean the former, then the antecedent is identical to the consequent, and what entails is identical to what is entailed. This serves no purpose, for the statement would amount to saying: “If temporal events subsisted in Him, temporal events would subsist in Him.” Such a statement conveys nothing. If, however, by change you mean something else, that implication is disputed: we do not concede that, if they subsisted in Him, this would necessarily entail any “change” other than the inherence of temporal events. This is their answer.

To clarify: “The term ‘change’” is ambiguous. In ordinary language, change does not mean merely that temporal events subsist in a subject. People do not say that the sun, moon, and stars have changed when they move. Nor do they say that someone has changed when he speaks and walks, or when he circumambulates, prays, commands, forbids, or rides, if these are his customary activities. Rather, they say that something has changed when it passes from one condition to another. Thus, when the sun’s light visibly recedes, it is not said to have changed; but when it turns yellow, it is said to have changed.

Likewise, when someone falls ill, or his body changes through hunger or exhaustion, people say that he has changed. The same applies when his character and religious conduct change—for example, when he turns from wickedness to righteousness, or from righteousness to wickedness: people say that he has changed. Yet he did not describe his movements as a change. Likewise, people say, “So-and-so has changed toward so-and-so,” when he begins to hate him after having loved him. If his affection remains constant, his warm welcome and conversation with him are not described as a change. When someone follows his customary manner in speech and action, he is not said to have changed. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.”

It is evident that, when people continue their established practice of saying and doing what is good, they have not changed what is in themselves. But when they depart from that practice, replacing the intention to do good with the intention to do evil, and belief in truth with belief in falsehood, it is said that they have changed what is in themselves. An example is someone who loved Allah, His Messenger, and the Hereafter, but whose heart then changed so that he no longer loves Allah, His Messenger, and the Hereafter. Such a person has changed what is within himself.

If this is the “meaning of change,” then the Lord Most High has always been, and will always be, possessed of the attributes of perfection and characterized by majesty and honour. His perfection is inseparable from His essence. It is therefore impossible for Him to lose any of His attributes of perfection, or to become deficient after being perfect.

“This principle” underlies the statement of the early generations and Ahl al-Sunnah: He has always spoken whenever He wills, has always possessed power, and has always possessed the attributes of perfection. He will always remain so, and thus does not change. This is the meaning of the invocation, “O You who brings about change but does not change!” For He alters the attributes of created beings, stripping them, whenever He wills, of qualities they previously possessed, and granting them qualities of perfection they did not previously possess. If they say, “In pre-eternity, He had power over all that would ever be,” the reply is: This combines negation and affirmation. He was, then, capable in pre-eternity. Was speaking possible for Him, or was it impossible?

If you say, “It was possible for Him,” then you have admitted the possibility that He has always been acting and that He has power over an endless succession of events.

If you say, “Rather, it was impossible,” the reply is: No one endowed with power can have power over an act that remains impossible rather than possible. Power extends only to what is possible, not to what is impossible.

If you say, “It became possible for Him thereafter,” then you have said that it became possible for Him to act after it had been impossible for Him to act. This explicitly means that He became capable after having been incapable, and this explicitly entails change.

Thus, the claim of these negators—that those who affirm the attributes must maintain that He undergoes “change”—has been shown to be false. Rather, it is they whose position entails that He changes.

(The fourth argument:

They say: For temporal events to inhere in Him constitutes “setting.” Abraham, the intimate friend of Allah, said:

“I do not love those that set.”

And “that which sets” is that which moves and in which temporal events occur. Thus, Abraham denied love for anyone in whom temporal events occur; such a being, therefore, cannot be God.

If the disputant says, “By His having changed, I mean that He spoke by His will and power, that He loves obedience from us, rejoices in the repentance of the repentant, and comes on the Day of Resurrection,” the reply is: Even granting that you call this change, why do you say that it is impossible? This is precisely the point at issue. As al-Rāzī said: “The antecedent is the second.”

Indeed, authentic hadiths establish that Allah is described as having ghayrah (protective jealousy), a word derived from taghayyur (change). The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“No one has greater protective jealousy than Allah when His male or female servant commits illicit intercourse.”

He also said:

“No one loves praise more than Allah; for this reason He praised Himself. No one loves an excuse more than Allah; for this reason He sent the messengers and revealed the scriptures. No one has greater protective jealousy than Allah; for this reason He prohibited shameful deeds, both open and concealed.”

He also said:

“Are you amazed at Saʿd’s protective jealousy? I have greater protective jealousy than he does, and Allah has greater protective jealousy than I do.”

(The reply:

The account of Abraham, Allah’s intimate friend, is evidence against them, not in their favour. It is they who oppose Abraham, our Prophet, and the other prophets—may blessings and peace be upon them. For Allah Most High said:

“When the night covered him, he saw a star. He said, ‘This is my Lord.’ But when it set, he said, ‘I do not love those that set.’

“When he saw the moon rising, he said, ‘This is my Lord.’ But when it set, he said, ‘Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among those who go astray.’

“When he saw the sun rising, he said, ‘This is my Lord; this is greater.’ But when it set, he said, ‘O my people, I am free of whatever you associate with Allah.

“‘Indeed, I have turned my face towards the One who originated the heavens and the earth, in pure devotion, and I am not one of those who associate partners with Him.’”

Thus, Allah has informed us in His Book that, from the time the star, moon, and sun rose until they set, His intimate friend did not say, “I do not love those that rise, or those that move, or those that change state; nor do I love anyone in whom movements or temporal events occur.” Nor, when the star, sun, and moon set, did he say anything of what the negators say.

translated_text:
And “setting,” by the unanimous agreement of linguists and Quranic commentators, means disappearing and becoming concealed. Indeed, this is self-evident in the Arabic language in which the Quran was revealed, and scholars unanimously agree that this is the intended meaning.

Thus, Abraham did not say, “I do not love those that set,” until the star had set and disappeared from sight, so that it was no longer visible or witnessed. Only then did he say, “I do not love those that set.” This entails that its movement and change of place, with temporal events occurring in it—indeed, its being a body occupying space in which temporal events occur—were not, in Abraham’s view, grounds for withholding love from it.

If Abraham inferred from its “setting” that it was not the Lord of the worlds—as they claim—then it follows that the characteristics of the thing that sets—its movement and change of place, its being subject to temporal events, indeed its being a body occupying space—were not, for Abraham, evidence that it was not the Lord of the worlds. Accordingly, Abraham’s account must be evidence for the opposite of what they seek to establish, not for their particular conclusion. Such is the way of the people of innovation: scarcely do they advance an argument from revelation or reason without its proving, upon reflection, to be evidence against them rather than in their favour.

However, when Abraham, peace be upon him, said, “This is my Lord,” he did not mean that it was the Lord of the worlds. Nor did any of his people say that it was the Lord of the worlds—assuming that such a belief could be attributed to them. Rather, they were polytheists who acknowledged the Maker. They took the stars, the sun, and the moon as lords, invoking them besides Allah and building temples for them. Books have been composed on doctrines like theirs, such as The Hidden Secret: On Magic and Addressing the Stars, and other works.

For this reason, Abraham, Allah’s close friend, said:

“Have you considered what you have been worshipping—you and your forefathers? They are enemies to me, except the Lord of all worlds.”

Allah Most High also said:

“You have an excellent example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people, ‘We disavow you and whatever you worship besides Allah. We reject you, and enmity and hatred have arisen between us and you forever, until you believe in Allah alone.’”

For this reason, Abraham said at the conclusion of his speech:

“I disavow whatever you associate with Allah. I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth, devoted to Him alone, and I am not one of the polytheists.”

He made clear that he worshipped Allah alone. To Him he directed his face when his intention turned toward Him: his face followed his intention, turning wherever his heart turned. Thus his heart, his intention, and his face were all directed toward Allah Most High. This is why he said:

“And I am not one of the polytheists.”

He did not mention acknowledging the existence of the Maker, for this was already known among his people. They did not dispute with him over the existence of the Creator of the heavens and the earth. Rather, the dispute concerned worshipping something other than Allah and taking it as a lord. They worshipped the heavenly stars and made earthly idols to represent them.

This is “the second form of polytheism.” Polytheism among Noah’s people originated in the worship of righteous people—the occupants of graves. They then fashioned statues of them, so their polytheism involved earthly beings. Satan only leads people astray according to what is possible, and it was easier for him to begin by establishing the worship of righteous people alongside Allah.

Then Abraham’s people moved on to associating heavenly beings—the stars—with Allah. They made “idols” for them according to what they perceived their natures to be, preparing for each star food and a ring

and incense and valuables suited to it. This had become widespread in the time of Abraham, the leader of those devoted to Allah alone. For this reason, Allah’s close friend said:

“What do you worship? Is it falsehood—gods besides Allah—that you desire? What, then, do you think of the Lord of all worlds?”

He also said to them:

“Do you worship what you carve, when Allah created you and what you make?”

The story of Abraham’s dealings with his people is mentioned in several places in the Quran; it concerns only his forbidding them to associate partners with Allah. This contrasts with the story of Moses and Pharaoh, which clearly shows that Pharaoh openly denied and rejected the Creator.

Allah also relates how Abraham argued with the man who disputed with him concerning his Lord:

“Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord because Allah had granted him kingship? When Abraham said, ‘My Lord is the One who gives life and causes death,’ he replied, ‘I give life and cause death.’ Abraham said, ‘Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west.’”

It may be said that this man denied the Maker. Even so, the account does not explicitly establish this. A person may call others to worship him without explicitly denying the Creator as Pharaoh did. In any event, “the story of Abraham” is more readily an argument against them than an argument in their favour. This is clear—all praise belongs to Allah. Indeed, what Allah relates about Abraham indicates that he affirmed of Allah what they deny of Him. Abraham said:

“Indeed, my Lord hears supplication.”

What is meant is that He answers supplication, just as a person praying says, “Allah hears whoever praises Him.” He hears and answers a supplication only after it comes into existence, not before it exists. As Allah Most High said:

“Allah has indeed heard the words of the woman who disputes with you concerning her husband and complains to Allah. And Allah hears your conversation.”

translated_text:
Thus, she disputes and complains while Allah hears their conversation. This indicates that His hearing is like His seeing mentioned in His words:

“Say, ‘Do deeds, for Allah will see your deeds, as will His Messenger and the believers.’”

He also said:

“Then We made you successors in the land after them, so that We might see how you would act.”

This is a distinct instance of seeing and a distinct instance of looking. It has already been explained that, by the agreement of all rational people, what does not exist cannot be seen or heard as something separate from the one who sees and hears. Once words and deeds come into existence, He hears and sees them. “Seeing” and “hearing” are realities that exist and must have a subject characterized by them. If He is the One who sees and hears them, it is impossible for someone else to be characterized by this hearing and seeing, or for them to subsist in someone else. It follows necessarily that this hearing and seeing subsist in Him after the deeds and words have been created. This is an objection that cannot be evaded.

“This issue” and the positions taken on it across the various groups have been discussed at length elsewhere. Their own formulations have been quoted, making it certain that the one who denies this has no evidence, whether from revelation or reason, and that clear rational proofs accord with the position of the early generations and the people of hadith. The Quran and Sunnah indicate this, as do “the earlier scriptures”: the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms. The prophetic texts, the statements of the early generations and the leading scholars all agree on it, and clear rational arguments establish it.

Anyone who disagrees on this issue is like those who disagree on comparable matters without any evidence from revelation or reason. Rather, he resembles those who said:

“Had we only listened or reasoned, we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze.”

translated_text:
Allah Most High said:

“Have they not travelled through the land, so that they may have hearts with which to reason or ears with which to hear? For it is not the eyes that are blind, but the hearts within the breasts.”

Yet doubts arose among later generations concerning “this issue,” the “issue of visitation,” and other matters. Others and I used to follow “the way of our forefathers” in this regard, adopting the position of the people of innovation on “the two foundational matters.” When what the Messenger brought became clear to us, the choice was between following what Allah had revealed and following what we had found our forefathers practising. Our duty was therefore to follow the Messenger and not to be among those of whom it was said:

“When they are told, ‘Follow what Allah has revealed,’ they say, ‘Rather, we follow what we found our forefathers practising.’”

The Most High also said:

“He said, ‘Even if I bring you better guidance than what you found your forefathers following?’”

And the Most High said:

“We have enjoined upon man care for his parents. His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years. Be grateful to Me and to your parents; to Me is the final return. But if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them. Yet keep their company in this world with kindness, and follow the path of those who turn to Me.”

Our duty, then, is to follow the revealed Book, the Messenger who was sent, and the path of those who turn to Allah. We therefore followed the Book and the Sunnah, as did the Emigrants and the Helpers, rather than whatever contradicted them in the religion of our forefathers or anyone else. May Allah guide us and all our brothers to the straight path—the path of those whom Allah has blessed: the prophets, the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. What excellent companions they are!

Allah, glorified is He, sent down the Quran, guided His creation through it, and brought them through it out of darkness

into light. The Mother of the Quran is the Opening of the Book. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“Allah says: ‘I have divided the prayer into two halves between Myself and My servant: half is for Me and half is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for. When the servant says, “All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds,” Allah says, “My servant has praised Me.” When he says, “The Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful,” Allah says, “My servant has extolled Me.” When he says, “Master of the Day of Judgment,” Allah says, “My servant has glorified Me.” When he says, “You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help,” Allah says, “This is between Myself and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.” When he says, “Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed, not those who have incurred Your wrath, nor those who have gone astray,” He says, “These are for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.”’”

This “surah” thus contains praise for Allah—to Him belongs all praise in this world and the Hereafter—and supplication by the servant. It contains worship devoted to Allah alone and the servant’s seeking help. The Lord’s right, then, is that He be praised and that He alone be worshipped. These two things—“praising the Lord and affirming His oneness”—are the foundation upon which the whole religion rests.

The “question of volitional attributes” is part of praising Him fully. Whoever does not affirm these attributes cannot affirm at all that Allah is praiseworthy or that He is Lord of the worlds. Praise is the opposite of blame: praise means speaking of the praiseworthy qualities of the one praised while loving him, whereas blame means speaking of the faults of the one blamed while hating him. All blameworthy qualities are summed up in doing evil, just as all praiseworthy qualities are summed up in doing good. If He does good by His will and power, He deserves “praise.” Thus, one who has no act of his own will subsisting in him—indeed, who is not even capable of such an act—can be neither a creator nor Lord of the worlds.

translated_text:
As for His words:

“All praise is for Allah, who created the heavens and the earth,”

“All praise is for Allah, who sent down the Book to His servant,”

and similar statements—all of this would be impossible if He had no act of His own choosing subsisting in Him. For “reason” plainly establishes that, if He created the heavens and the earth, there must be an act by which He became their Creator. Otherwise, if matters remained unchanged, with no act occurring, the situation would remain as it was before He created. The created thing did not exist then; likewise, it must not exist if the future state remains just as the past state was, with no act proceeding from the Lord—namely, the creation of the heavens and the earth.

The Exalted has said:

“I did not make them witnesses to the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor to their own creation.”

It is well known that they have witnessed the created thing itself. This therefore shows that the “creation” they did not witness—His bringing these things into being and originating them—is distinct from the created thing that endures. He also said:

“He created the heavens and the earth in six days.”

Their creation thus took place in six days, while they exist after the act of willing. What was specific to the act of willing is therefore distinct from what exists after that act of willing.

The same applies to:

“The Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.”

For the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful is the One who shows mercy to His servants by His will and power. If His mercy were nothing but an eternal will, or some other eternal attribute, He could not be described as showing mercy to whom He wills and punishing whom He wills. Allah’s intimate friend said:

“Say: Travel through the earth and observe how He began creation. Then Allah will bring about the final creation

—indeed, Allah has power over all things.”

“He punishes whom He wills and shows mercy to whom He wills, and to Him you will be returned.”

Mercy is the opposite of punishment. Punishment is His act and occurs by His will; likewise, mercy occurs by His will, as He says:

“And shows mercy to whom He wills.”

But the eternal will inseparable from His essence—or another attribute of His essence—is not subject to His will; mercy, then, would not occur by His will.

If it is said that only created things distinct from Him come about by His will, it follows that mercy would not be an attribute of the Lord, but something He creates. Yet He is described only by what subsists in Him, not by created things. Thus, He would not be the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When Allah had completed creation, He wrote in a Book, which is kept with Him above the Throne: ‘My mercy prevails over My wrath.’” In another narration: “precedes My wrath.”

Whatever precedes something that comes after it can only do so by the Lord’s will and power. On the view of anyone who says that mercy is nothing but an eternal will or something similar, it would be impossible for Him to have wrath preceded by that mercy. For if wrath is interpreted as will, will does not precede itself. Likewise, if it is interpreted as an attribute that is itself eternal, one eternal attribute does not precede another. If it is interpreted in terms of created things, He would possess neither mercy nor wrath.

He has distinguished His wrath from His punishment in His words:

“His recompense is Hell, where he will remain forever. Allah is angry with him, has cursed him, and has prepared for him a tremendous punishment.”

And His words:

“And that He may punish the hypocrites, men and women, and the polytheists, men and women, who harbour evil thoughts about Allah. Upon them shall fall an evil turn of fortune. Allah is angry with them, has cursed them, and has prepared Hell for them—what an evil destination!”

In the hadith narrated by Imam Ahmad from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he used to say:

translated_text:
“I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah from His wrath and punishment, from the evil of His servants, and from the promptings of the devils and their presence with me.”

This is also indicated by His words:

“Your Lord knows you best. If He wills, He will have mercy on you, or if He wills, He will punish you.”

He thus makes mercy dependent on His will, just as He makes punishment dependent on it. Whatever attributes of the Lord depend on His will belong to the “volitional attributes.”

The same applies to His being Master of the Day of Recompense, when His servants will be requited for their deeds: good for good and evil for evil. The Day of Recompense—and what will make you realize what the Day of Recompense is?

“The Day when no soul will have any power to help another; all command that Day will belong to Allah.”

A “king” exercises authority through commands that are obeyed. Thus, only a living being whose commands are obeyed is called a “king.” The possessor of inanimate objects is not called their “king,” but their “owner.” The leader of the bees is called the “king of the bees” because he commands and is obeyed. An owner is one who can exercise control over what he owns.

Since a “king” is one who commands and forbids and is obeyed, if he commands and forbids by his own will, then his commanding and forbidding belong to the “volitional attributes.” This is what the Quran declares. Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, fulfil your contracts. Livestock have been made lawful for you, except what is recited to you, but hunting is not permitted while you are in a state of consecration for pilgrimage. Indeed, Allah decrees whatever He wills.”

If, however, he does not command and forbid by his own will—rather, his command is inseparable from him and exists without his will or power—then he would not be an owner either. Indeed, he would more aptly be described as owned. For Allah Most High created the human being and gave him attributes inseparable from him—such as colour, height, breadth, and modesty

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

Only those who distinguish between “prescribed visitation” and “innovated visitation” truly fulfil this. Prescribed visitation is worship of Allah, obedience to His Messenger, affirmation of Allah’s oneness, kindness to His servants, and a righteous deed for which the visitor is rewarded. “O Allah, forgive him, have mercy on him, grant him well-being, and pardon him. Grant him an honourable welcome, make his resting place spacious, and wash him with water, snow, and hail. The second, however, would be associating partners with Allah, causing harm, acting unjustly, transgressing against the deceased, and wronging himself.

These are some of the differences between “innovated visitation” and “prescribed visitation.” The point is that when the one who practises “prescribed visitation” says:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help,”

he is speaking truthfully, for he has worshipped none but Allah and sought help from none but Him. As for the one who practises “innovated visitation,” he has worshipped someone other than Allah and sought help from someone other than Him.

This is part of what demonstrates that “al-Fātihah,” the Mother of the Quran, contains an explanation of the two disputed issues: “the issue of volitional attributes” and “the issue of the distinction between prescribed visitation and innovated visitation.”

It is Allah Most High whom we ask to guide us and all our brothers to His straight path—the path of those upon whom He has bestowed His favour: the prophets, the steadfast affirmers of truth, the martyrs, and the righteous. What excellent companions they are!

This is further clarified by the Prophet’s statement (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“When the servant says, ‘All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds,’ Allah says, ‘My servant has praised Me.’ When he says, ‘The Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful,’ He says, ‘My servant has extolled Me.’ When he says, ‘Master of the Day of Judgment,’ Allah says, ‘My servant has glorified Me.’”

Thus, he mentioned praise, commendation, and glorification. After that, the servant says, “You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help,” continuing to the end of the surah. This occurs at the beginning of the recitation while standing in prayer. Then, in the final standing after bowing, he says:

“Our Lord, to You belongs all praise, filling the heavens and filling the earth,”

and continues until the words:

“You who are worthy of all commendation and glory! This is the most fitting thing a servant can say—and we are all Your servants. None can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold; nor can the fortune of anyone favoured by fortune avail him against You.”

The phrase “the most fitting thing a servant can say” is the predicate of an omitted subject; that is, “These words are the most fitting thing a servant can say.” It is therefore clear that praising and extolling Allah is the most fitting thing a servant can say. This includes affirming His oneness when the servant says, “To You belongs all praise”—meaning, to You alone, not to anyone else. At the end, he says, “None can withhold what You give, and none can give what You withhold.” This entails that He alone gives and withholds, so help is to be sought from Him alone, and requests are to be directed to Him alone.

Then he says, “Nor can the fortune of anyone favoured by fortune avail him against You.” This makes clear that even if a person is granted dominion, wealth, and leadership, none of this can save him from You. Only faith and piety can save him. This gives full expression to the words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

This remembrance therefore comes at the end of the standing, just as it was recited at the beginning. The words “the most fitting thing a servant can say” imply that praising Allah is the utterance most deserving of being spoken by the servant. Whatever utterance is most deserving is also the best and the most incumbent upon a person.

For this reason, Allah has made it obligatory for His servants to begin every prayer by saying:

“All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds.”

For this reason, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) will offer praise before interceding on the Day of Resurrection. Likewise, he instructed us to extol Allah in the tashahhud before making supplication. The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Every important undertaking that is not begun with ‘All praise is for Allah’ is incomplete. The first to be called to Paradise will be those who constantly praise Allah, praising Him in prosperity and adversity.”

He described the words “The Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful” as commendation, and the words “Master of the Day of Judgment” as glorification.

The words “All praise is for Allah” express praise without qualification. “Praise” is a generic noun, and a genus has both quantity and quality. Commendation expresses its quantity, while declaring His greatness and magnifying Him expresses its quality. “Glory” denotes vastness and loftiness; it thus magnifies the quality, degree, and continuous magnitude of praise. This is because these words describe Him as possessing sovereignty. Sovereignty entails power and the ability to do whatever He wills. “The Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful” describes Him as possessing mercy, which entails His bestowing goodness upon His servants through His will and power as well. Good comes about through power and a will that encompasses mercy.

When He has the power and the will to bestow goodness, every good comes about. Deficiency arises only from a lack of power or a lack of will to do good. Thus, “the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful, the Sovereign” possesses the utmost will to bestow goodness and the utmost power. Through this, the good of this world and the Hereafter is attained.

The words “Master of the Day of Judgment” are used even though He is also “the Sovereign of this world,” because on the Day of Judgment no one will claim to contest His sovereignty. It is the greatest day. This world, compared with the Hereafter, is only like what remains when one of you dips his finger into the sea: let him see what it brings back. “Judgment” is the outcome of the deeds of His servants. The wording may also indicate His sovereignty over this world by implication—and, according to some, through its general scope—so sovereignty belongs to Him

and to Him belongs all praise, as the Most High says:

“To Him belongs sovereignty, and to Him belongs all praise, and He has power over all things.”

This entails that He has the power to show mercy. His mercy and beneficence are attributes of His that come about by His will, and thus belong to the “attributes dependent on His will.” It is related in the Sahīh that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) used to teach his Companions to seek Allah’s guidance in all matters, just as he taught them a surah of the Quran. He would say:

“When one of you intends to undertake something, let him pray two units of prayer other than the obligatory prayer, then say: ‘O Allah, I seek Your guidance through Your knowledge, and I seek ability through Your power, and I ask You of Your immense bounty. For You have power, and I do not; You know, and I do not; and You are the Knower of all unseen things. O Allah, if You know that this matter—and he should name it—is good for me in my religion, my worldly life, my livelihood, and the outcome of my affairs, then decree it for me, make it easy for me, and then bless it for me. But if You know that this matter is bad for me in my religion, my livelihood, and the outcome of my affairs, then turn it away from me and turn me away from it, and decree good for me wherever it may be.’”

Thus, he asked Allah by His knowledge and His power, and asked of His bounty; His bounty comes about through His mercy. These attributes encompass all the attributes of perfection. Knowledge, however, is universal in its scope: it encompasses the Creator and the creation, the existent and the nonexistent. Power, by contrast, pertains only to what is created. Likewise, sovereignty is exercised only over created things.

Al-Fātihah thus encompasses perfection of will, expressed in mercy, and perfection of power, expressed in sovereignty over the Day of Judgment. This is fully realized only through the attributes dependent on His will, as explained above. And Allah, glorified and exalted is He, knows best.

I say:

This is because such a description rests upon the perfection of the quality from which the act proceeds, not upon the actual performance of the act. Accordingly, He is described in terms of everything He has the power to do, even if He does not do it.

I say:

Our fellow scholars have differed over Ahmad’s statement:

“Allah has always been Knowing, Speaking, and All-Forgiving.”

Is his statement that He has always been Speaking like his statement that He has always been All-Forgiving, or like his statement that He has always been Knowing? There are two views.

(The second approach:

The act is certain to proceed from Him in time to come, just as we are now certain, before the resurrection and the inheritance, that He is the Resurrector and the Inheritor. This is the approach of Abū Ishāq ibn Shāqilā and also of al-Qādī. This differs from the case of someone who may or may not perform the act. In some respects, it resembles describing the Prophet, before his prophethood, as the Seal of the Prophets, the foremost of Adam’s descendants, and the Seal of the Messengers; or describing Umar as the conqueror of the cities. Similarly, it was said, “The prophet of this community was born tonight,” and he said:

“Follow the two who come after me: Abū Bakr and Umar.”

A group of scholars of legal theory have stated that applying an attribute before the quality it signifies exists is figurative by agreement; applying it while that quality exists is literal; and applying it after that quality has existed and ceased to exist is disputed. However, the majority reject this claim of agreement, distinguishing between someone whose performance of the act is certain and someone whose performance of it is merely possible.

It may then be said:

His being, from eternity, the Creator of what is created throughout the endless future is comparable to His being, from eternity, Willing and Merciful. This makes clear the distinction between applying this designation to Him and applying an attribute to a created being in whom it will arise in the future.

On the first approach, being the Creator is analogous to having power; on this approach, being the Creator is analogous to being Merciful. This distinction leads back to the third line of reasoning: Allah, glorified be He, is, “in His essence,” the same before He acts as after He acts. His essence has not changed through His acts, nor has He acquired attributes of perfection through His acts as a created being does.

Al-Qādī also drew attention to this line of reasoning, saying:

“Furthermore, it is established that He is now the Creator. It is His essence that is the Creator, and His essence existed from eternity. If He had not been the Creator and then became the Creator, this would necessarily entail change and transformation in Him. Allah is exalted above that. Accordingly, this designation is analogous to the Merciful and the Forbearing.”

The fourth line of reasoning:

Creation is an attribute subsisting in His essence, not the created thing itself. Elsewhere, al-Qādī permitted saying, “He is eternal in His beneficence and bestowal of favors,” meaning that beneficence is an attribute subsisting in Him, distinct from the benefit bestowed. He prohibited saying, “O You whose creation is eternal,” because creation is the created thing. This is one of the two views held by our fellow scholars, and it is the view of the Karrāmiyyah and the Hanafīs. One group calls it takwīn (bringing into being).

Creation is the created thing, as the Ashʿarīs maintain.

“This is based on the issue discussed earlier: that He has been characterized from eternity by the attributes arising from acts.”

I say:

Whether an act of speech or will arises in His essence when created beings come into existence is disputed among our fellow scholars and others. This depends on their position concerning the “attributes of action,” such as rising over the Throne, descending, and the like. They nevertheless agree that He has always possessed His attributes, being eternally characterized by them, and that He has acquired no new attribute of perfection. But are the individual utterances and acts eternal, or does perfection consist in His having always been characterized by them in kind?

To summarize the discussion here: is He the Creator and the Generous because of the creatures and blessings He has brought into existence apart from Himself, or because of the attributes of creation and generosity subsisting in Him?

The second is the view of the Hanafīs, the Karrāmiyyah, many hadith scholars, and our fellow scholars according to one of their two views—indeed, the more correct of the two. This is what the statements of Ahmad and other scholars of the Sunnah indicate. According to this view, it is said that He has always been Generous, All-Forgiving, and Creator, just as it is said that He has always been the Speaker. There are two interpretations of this, just as there are two interpretations of “the Speaker”: is it to be classed with “the All-Knowing” or with “the All-Forgiving”?

The first view is that of the Ashʿarīs, based on the position that creation is the created thing itself. On this basis, our fellow scholars’ statement that He was the Creator from eternity means either that He possessed complete power—as one speaks of “a cutting sword”—or that the act would certainly occur subsequently, as when one says:

translated_text:
“This is the conqueror of the cities,” and “This is the prophet of this nation.” Understood in this sense, creation is a relational attribute.

If we regard creation as an attribute subsisting in Him, is it His will and speech, or a separate attribute? There are two views. The second is the view of the Hanafīs and most jurists and hadith scholars. Likewise, our fellow scholars differ concerning mercy, pleasure, and anger: are they identical with will, or distinct from it? There are two views, the sounder of which is that they are not identical with will. Whatever Allah wills comes to pass, yet He does not love corruption, nor is He pleased with disbelief for His servants.

As for our statement that He has been characterized from eternity by the attributes of action, such as creation, generosity, and forgiveness, this means that He is described in these terms beforehand. For a description is the speech by which something is stated about Him, and such speech admits of literal and figurative usage. Our fellow scholars regard it as literal here. As for His actually possessing these attributes—whether this entails a positive attribute distinct from power or a relational attribute—the preceding discussion applies.

translated_text:
The shaykh and imam, the learned and erudite scholar, the great scholar of the Muslim community and ocean of knowledge, Shaykh al-Islam Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him, be pleased with him, and admit him to Paradise—said:

All praise belongs to Allah. We praise Him, seek His help, and ask His forgiveness. We seek refuge in Allah from the evil within ourselves and from our evil deeds. Whomever Allah guides, none can lead astray; and whomever He leads astray, none can guide. I bear witness that none is worthy of worship except Allah alone, without partner, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. May Allah bless him and his family and grant him abundant peace.

Section

Concerning what al-Rāzī stated in al-Arba‘īn (The Forty) regarding “volitional attributes,” which they call “the inherence of temporal occurrences,” after establishing that most groups of rational thinkers hold this position, even though they deny it verbally.

He said:

“Know that attributes fall into three categories: real attributes devoid of relations, such as blackness and whiteness. The second consists of real attributes that necessarily entail relations, such as knowledge and power. The third consists of pure relations and pure relationships, such as a thing’s being prior to another

or alongside it, or to its right or left. For if you sit to someone’s right, and that person then gets up and sits on your other side, you were previously to his right but are now to his left. Here, no change has occurred in your essence or in any of your real attributes, but only in pure relations.

“Once you understand this, we say: There is no avoiding the occurrence of change in relations. As for change in real attributes, the Karrāmiyyah affirm it, while all the other groups deny it. Thus, the distinction between the position of the Karrāmiyyah and that of others in this matter becomes clear.”

He said: “Several considerations demonstrate the invalidity of the Karrāmiyyah’s position.

“First: Every attribute of Allah must be an attribute of perfection and a quality of majesty. If any of His attributes originated in time, His essence would have lacked that attribute of perfection and majesty before it originated. Whatever lacks an attribute of perfection is deficient. It would therefore follow that His essence was deficient before that attribute originated within it, and this is impossible. Thus, it is established that the origination of an attribute within Allah’s essence is impossible.”

I say:

One may respond: What you have stated does not establish the point at issue. This can be explained through several considerations.

First: The argument rests on premises, not one of which they have established through either rational or revealed evidence: that every attribute of Allah must be an attribute of perfection; that His essence would be deficient before possessing that attribute; and that such deficiency is impossible.

translated_text:
The substance of the argument is that, if something temporally originated were to subsist in Him, it would have been impossible for Him to have been without it beforehand. Yet no proof has been established for this.

(Second: You have presented no rational proof in your books that He must possess this perfection and be free of deficiency. Rather, you and your teachers, such as Abū al-Maʿālī and others, say that this is known not through reason, but through transmitted evidence. Since you acknowledge that you have not established this premise through reason, transmitted evidence must consist either of a scriptural text or of consensus. Yet you have cited no scriptural text as proof. Indeed, more than a hundred texts in the Quran constitute evidence against you, as do the mass-transmitted hadiths.

“And the claim of consensus”: if it is eternal, that which is received must be capable of existing from eternity. The proof of this is that a thing’s receptivity to something else is a relation between the recipient and what is received. A relation between two entities depends upon the actual existence of each, and the possibility of the relation depends upon the existence of both. Thus, since it has been possible from eternity for temporally originated things to subsist in the Creator, it necessarily follows that the existence of temporally originated things has been possible from eternity.

The response to you is this: The very same argument applies to His having power. For a thing’s having power over something else is a relation between the possessor of power and the object of that power. A relation between two entities depends upon the actual existence of each, and the possibility of the relation depends upon the existence of both. Thus, since

كَانَتْ صِحَّةُ اتِّصَافِ الْبَارِي بِالْقُدْرَةِ عَلَى الْغَيْرِ حَاصِلَةً فِي الْأَزَلِ:

translated_text:
it has been possible from eternity for the Creator to possess power over another, it necessarily follows that the existence of the object of His power has been possible from eternity. This corresponds exactly to what you have said. Accordingly, if you allow one of the two terms of the relation—namely, His having power—to exist from eternity while the object of His power cannot exist from eternity, then allow one of the two terms—namely, His being receptive—to exist from eternity while that which is received cannot exist from eternity. If, however, you do not allow this, but maintain that relations can exist only when both related terms actually exist, then either the object of His power must have been possible from eternity, or His having power from eternity must have been impossible.

In any event, your argument fails: whether you allow one of the related terms to exist while the other comes later, allow the object of His power to exist from eternity, or say that He did not possess power from eternity. Although he does not assert this last position, suppose someone were to commit himself to it and say that He comes to possess power after not possessing it, just as they say that He becomes receptive after not being receptive.

He would be told: If His having power is inseparable from His essence, then He must always have possessed power. The essence, which necessarily entails power, could not exist without power, its necessary concomitant. If power is not inseparable from the essence, then it is one of its contingent attributes. The essence would therefore be receptive to His having power, and would also be receptive to that receptivity. If receptivity to His having power is inseparable from the essence, the intended conclusion follows once again. If it is a contingent attribute, it requires a further receptivity. This necessarily leads either to an infinite regress or to an ultimate possession of power that is inseparable from the essence.

Others say that, rather, its effect may—or must—coexist with it in time. This is maintained by those philosophers who hold this view, and some speculative theologians have agreed with them regarding the efficient cause, saying that its effect coexists with it in time.

If someone says, “The existence of the one possessing power must precede the existence of the object of his power,” they reply: “If by precedence you mean separation by an interval, that is not conceded. The twelfth response is as follows:

The principal argument of those who deny this is that, if He were receptive to these events from eternity, this would entail their existence, or the possibility of their existence, from eternity. They established this in the “well-known method” by arguing that whatever is receptive to a thing cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite. The majority disputed this “premise,” as did al-Rāzī, al-Āmidī, and others.

They say that every body necessarily possesses one member of each genus of accidents, because whatever is receptive to a thing cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite. For this reason, some turned instead to the following argument: if He were receptive to these events, His receptivity to them would be inseparable from His Essence. This requires the following explanation: if He were receptive to temporally originated events, He would never be devoid of an originated event or its opposite.

As for their statement, “Whatever is receptive to a thing is not devoid of its opposite,” it may be argued, on this approach, that this applies exclusively to Him and not to anything else. Alternatively, it may be said that it applies universally as well.

Their own associates then say to them: What you have stated concerning Him is refuted by the receptivity of all other subjects to the attributes they receive. If their receptivity to what they receive is inseparable from their essence, they must always be receptive to it. If it is an accidental property of their essence, then they are receptive to that receptivity. This necessarily entails either an infinite regress or an ultimate receptivity that is inseparable from the essence. It would therefore follow that, for everything receptive to anything, its receptivity to it is inseparable from its essence. Yet this is not the case, for human beings and other existing things are receptive to attributes in one state but not in another.

(The fourteenth response:

It may be said: If whatever is receptive to something cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite, then whoever is capable of something cannot be devoid of both it and its opposite, since whoever possesses power is receptive to performing the act within his power. If receptivity to temporally originated events entails the possibility of their existence from eternity, then eternal power to bring about temporally originated events likewise entails the possibility of their existence from eternity. If it is possible to possess power while its object is impossible, it is also possible to be receptive while the object of that receptivity is impossible.

If it is said, “His receptivity to them is inseparable from His essence,” the reply is: “His power over them is inseparable from His essence.” Accordingly, if the perpetual occurrence of temporally originated events is possible, it is possible that He has always possessed power over them and been receptive to them. If their perpetual occurrence is not possible, then His receptivity to them and His power over them have become possible after not having been so. If this is admissible in one case, it is admissible in the other; if it is impossible in one, it is impossible in the other. Thus, the arguments advanced by the leading “philosophers” for the eternity of the world do not establish the eternity of anything in the world. Rather, they establish only the principles upheld by the imams of the Sunnah and hadith who devote themselves to what the Messenger brought. The ultimate result of rigorously examining the rational arguments of speculative theologians and philosophical thinkers is thus to agree with, support, and serve what the messengers brought.

Those speculative theologians who do not affirm this, but instead maintain that the perpetual occurrence of temporally originated events is impossible, have no basis for distinguishing between His receptivity to them and His power over them. Among these theologians, those who say that He speaks by His will and power, with speech subsisting in His essence, hold a position closer to reason and revelation than those who say that His speech is created, or that eternal speech subsists in Him without His being able to speak by His power or His will.

Any position closer to reason and revelation deserves preference over positions further removed from them. And Allah Most High knows best.

Section

Al-Rāzī said:

“The third argument”

The account of Allah’s close friend:

“I do not love those that set.”

Setting means change. This indicates that whatever undergoes change cannot be a god at all.

The response has several aspects:

First: We do not concede that setting means change. He has offered no proof for this, but merely asserted it.

Second: This contradicts the consensus of scholars of language and Quranic exegesis. Indeed, it contradicts what is necessarily known in religion, as well as the mass-transmitted record of linguistic usage and Quranic exegesis. For “setting” means disappearing from view. One says, afalat al-shamsu (the sun set), with the present-tense forms ta’fulu and ta’filu and the verbal noun ufūl, when it disappears from view.

No one has ever said that it means change, or that the sun is said to have set when its colour changes, or when it is moving through the sky. Nor is the wind said to have set when it blows, water when it flows, trees when they move, or human beings when they speak, walk, and perform their activities. Indeed, no one has ever said that a person who falls ill, or whose face turns yellow or red, is said to have set. This claim is thus among the gravest fabrications against Allah, against Allah’s close friend, and against

translated_text:
the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, against His Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), who conveys His message, against the entire community of Muhammad, against all those versed in the language, and against everyone who understands the meanings of the Quran.

Third: The account of Allah’s close friend, peace be upon him, is evidence against you. When he saw a star and it moved towards the horizon, it had indeed moved, yet he did not regard it as having set. When he saw the moon rising, he saw it in motion, yet he did not regard it as having set. When he saw the sun rising, he knew that it was moving, yet he did not regard it as having set. As it moved until it disappeared—and likewise the moon until it disappeared—he did not regard it as having set.

Fourth: Regarding his statement that setting means change: if by change he means transformation, then the sun, moon, and stars did not undergo transformation by disappearing from view. If he means motion, the celestial body is continually moving.

The words,

“But when it set,”

indicate that it sometimes sets and at other times does not. For lammā (“when”) is a temporal adverb that links the time of one action to that of the other. The meaning is that, when it set,

“he said, ‘I do not love those that set.’”

He said this only when it set.

The words,

“But when it set,”

indicate that setting occurs anew, whereas motion is inseparable from it. Setting, therefore, is not motion. The terms “change” and “motion” are ambiguous. If what is meant is motion or the occurrence of temporal events within a thing, that is not the linguistic meaning of change. Setting is not motion, nor is motion change. Rather, setting is narrower in scope than motion, and change is narrower in scope than motion. As for change and setting, each is broader in one respect and narrower in another. Thus, a thing may undergo change without

This holds even if change is narrower in scope than motion according to one of the two terminological usages. For “motion” may mean spatial motion, which does not necessarily entail change. It may also have a broader meaning, encompassing motion in quality and quantity, such as a plant’s motion through growth, or the motions of the human soul through love, contentment, anger, and remembrance. Such motion may be described as change, while in some contexts “change” may mean transformation.

In short, if an argument employing the term “change” is based on revelation, setting is not change. If it is a rational argument, and “change”—which is held to be impossible for the Lord—means the very matter under dispute, it cannot serve as evidence. If it means matters on which there is consensus, there is no dispute concerning them.

Still more unsound is the claim that setting means contingency, as Ibn Sīnā said: “Descending into the realm of contingency is, in a certain respect, a setting.” This would entail that everything other than Allah is setting and perpetually remains so, since everything other than Him is contingent and perpetually remains contingent. Setting would thus be an inseparable attribute of everything other than Allah, just as being contingent and dependent upon Allah is an inseparable attribute of it.

On this account, the sun, moon, and stars would always have been, and would forever remain, setting

According to these people who distort the words of Allah Most High and those of His intimate friend Abraham—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—away from their intended meanings, it was setting before it rose, from the moment it rose, and until it disappeared. And Allah knows best.
