translated_text:
Section

The arguments advanced by the philosophers and speculative theologians concerning “the temporal origination of the world” support only the position of the early Muslim generations and the imams. As for the “philosophers,” their argument establishes only that He has always acted, just as the argument of the “Ash'arīs” establishes only that He has always spoken. Both groups argue for the beginningless existence of the particular entity in question using evidence that does not entail this conclusion.

As for the “speculative theologians,” their principal argument is that whatever is never free of temporal events has a beginning, or that whatever does not precede temporal events has a beginning. Each of these propositions is correct when understood in a particular sense and points to the truth. Whatever does not precede bounded temporal events that have a beginning must itself have a beginning. This is evident to sound reason and agreed upon by rational people. Thus, anything known to have existed after an event that has a beginning, or alongside an event that has a beginning, necessarily also has a beginning. The same applies to whatever is never free of these temporal events.

Furthermore, whatever is never free of temporal events while depending upon them has a beginning. Whatever is never free of temporal events brought about within it by something else has a beginning. Indeed, whatever depends upon temporal events in any way has a beginning. Whatever has events brought about by something else subsisting in it has a beginning. Whatever depends upon something other than itself has a beginning. And whatever has temporal events subsisting in it has a beginning.

This refutes the position of the “philosophers” who maintain that the celestial sphere is beginningless, such as Aristotle and his followers. “Aristotle” says that it needs the First Cause in order to resemble it. Proclus, Ibn Sīnā, and others like them say that it is His effect—that is, necessitated by Him—and that the First is its efficient cause. Thus, they all say that it depends upon something other than itself, while temporal events subsist in it and it has never been free of them. Yet they say that it is beginningless. This position is false.

“Ibn Sīnā” says that it is contingent, admitting both existence and nonexistence, while temporal events subsist in it, yet that it is eternal and beginningless. This is false. Its dependence upon another precludes its being necessarily existent in itself, for whatever is necessarily existent in itself cannot depend upon another. If it is not necessarily existent in itself, then it is contingent, admitting both existence and nonexistence. In that case, it must have been brought into existence, for several reasons.

One reason is that whatever is contingent and admits both existence and nonexistence can only be something brought into existence. By contrast, that which is beginningless, whose nonexistence is impossible, does not admit both existence and nonexistence.

Another reason is that if, besides being dependent, it has temporal events brought about within it by another, this indicates that the other exercises control and domination over it: temporal events are brought about within it, and it cannot ward them off. Whatever stands in such subjection in relation to another neither exists through itself nor is self-sufficient; nor is it unassailable or independent in itself. Anything of this kind can only be something made and subject to a Lord, and must therefore have been brought into existence.

For this reason, the Companions would mention that the occurrence of temporal events in the world indicates that it is subject to a Lord, as we have discussed elsewhere. Whatever is subject to a Lord has been brought into existence. Everything other than Allah has temporal events brought about within it by another and is dependent upon another.

Every celestial sphere is moved by another, so its motion is brought about within it by another. The encompassing sphere sets them all in motion, yet its motion differs from theirs. Thus, a new relation arises within it without its choosing, while they are independent in their own motion and do not depend upon it for that. Hence, it cannot be their lord. The sun, the moon, and the stars are moved by another; all are subjected to His command.

Section

We have already mentioned two principles:

First: The scriptural and rational arguments they cite in support of their doctrines actually support the position of the early generations and what the Quran and Sunnah teach. They do not support the innovations through which they have contradicted the Quran and Sunnah.

Second: The arguments they cite establish the opposite of what they intend and demonstrate the falsity of their position. This is a distinct matter: an argument supporting a position they do not hold is one thing; its establishing the opposite of their position and demonstrating its falsity is another.

This occurs in the arguments of both the philosophers and the speculative theologians. Examples among the philosophers include their arguments for the beginninglessness of the world or some part of it. They have argued from the four kinds of causes: efficient, final, material, and formal. Their principal argument concerns the efficient cause: it is impossible for Him to become an agent after not having been one; therefore, He must always have been acting. This is the chief argument relied upon by their later thinkers, such as Ibn Sīnā and others like him. I believe it was transmitted from Proclus.

Aristotle and his followers, however, do not employ this argument, since, in their view, He is not an agent. Rather,

translated_text:
they argued from the necessary beginninglessness of time and motion—the argument from the formal cause—and from the necessary beginninglessness of matter. For everything that comes into being is preceded by the possibility of its existence, and this possibility must have a substrate. Thus, everything that comes into being is received by matter capable of receiving it. As for the “final cause,” it is of the same kind as the “efficient cause.”

The response to them is that these arguments support only the position of the early generations and the leading scholars, as explained above, and also demonstrate the falsity of their own position.

As for the beginninglessness of “agency”—meaning that He has always been acting—the response is: This expression is ambiguous. By an agent, you mean one whose effect coexists with him in time. If He is an agent in this sense, His effect must coexist with Him, and His action cannot come later. This is your principal argument. Yet an agent, according to rational people generally, your predecessors, and even yourselves outside this discussion, is one who does something and thereby brings it into being. Understood in this sense, the effect cannot coexist with Him. Rather, everything He brings about must come after Him. Nothing He brings about, therefore, shares His beginninglessness; everything other than Him comes into being.

People then take two approaches here.

“Some” say that everything He brings about must come after Him, and that He must remain inactive before subsequently acting. This is the position of the adherents of innovated speculative theology among the religious communities—the Jahmiyyah, the Mu'tazilah, and those who follow their path. This denial contradicts continuous agency and therefore contradicts what those arguments entail.

“The second” approach is to say that He has always been bringing one thing into being after another. Everything other than Him thus comes into being after not having existed, while He alone possesses beginninglessness and eternity. He is “the First,” beginningless and eternal, with nothing else sharing this with Him; and He has always been bringing one thing into being after another.

It may therefore be said to them:

The arguments you advance for the necessary beginninglessness of “agency” invalidate your own position just as they invalidate that of the adherents of innovated speculative theology. For if they established continuous agency in the sense you claim, it would follow that nothing could come into being in the world. According to you, an effect must coexist in time with its efficient cause, and everything other than the First is His effect. Everything other than Him would therefore coexist with Him, so nothing could come into being in the world. This contradicts observation and reason, is false by the agreement of all humanity, and runs contrary to sense perception and rational understanding.

Furthermore, if an effect must coexist in time with its cause, then whenever anything comes into being, an infinite number of other things must come into being simultaneously with it, none preceding another. This amounts to affirming the existence of an infinite number of causes, which is likewise false according to clear reason and the agreement of rational people. Nor is there any difference here between the impossibility of this concerning the cause itself and its impossibility concerning one of its conditions. Just as it is impossible for an infinite number of causes themselves to come into being at a single instant whenever anything comes into being, the same applies to the conditions that complete the cause, for these constitute one of its two components. An infinite number cannot therefore exist at a single instant in either component. This is agreed upon among people.

As for the dispute over “the existence of an infinite succession,” part of their argument has thus fallen away. Their argument does not yield what they claimed; rather, it entails “the other position”: that the agent has always been bringing one thing into being after another. In that case, every effect comes into being after not having existed. This is the very opposite of their position. This is unlike the argument advanced by the adherents of innovated speculative theology to establish that things came into being. For they said:

Consequently, those who claimed to answer them with “the overwhelming reply” fell into the contradiction mentioned earlier.

It has thus become clear that the very argument they advanced demonstrates the falsity of both their own position and that of the speculative theologians. It also establishes, by a sound and unassailable demonstration, that everything other than Allah came into being and that He alone is beginningless. Thus it has become clear—all praise belongs to Allah—that their principal argument for the beginninglessness of the world establishes only the opposite of their position: that everything other than Allah came into being. To Allah belong all praise and gratitude.

As for the “argument” they advanced to establish that motion and time have always existed, and that this kind could not have had a beginning—an argument relied upon by Aristotle and his followers—they may be told:

This does not establish the beginninglessness of any particular motion or its time, nor of any particular moving thing. It therefore does not establish what they seek to prove: the beginninglessness of the celestial sphere, its motion, and its time;

 مِنْ الْمَعْلُومِ بِصَرِيحِ الْعَقْلِ أَنَّ مَا لَمْ يَكُنْ فَاعِلًا فَلَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَحْدُثَ لَهُ سَبَبٌ يُوجِبُ كَوْنَهُ فَاعِلًا وَأَنَّهُ إذَا كَانَ حَالُ الْفَاعِلِ عَلَى الْحَالِ الَّتِي كَانَ عَلَيْهَا قَبْلَ الْفِعْلِ لَمْ يَفْعَلْ شَيْئًا وَلَمْ يَحْدُثْ عَنْهُ شَيْءٌ قِيلَ لَهُمْ: وَهَذَا الْمَعْلُومُ بِصَرِيحِ الْعَقْلِ مُوجَبُ أَنَّهَا لَا يَحْدُثُ عَنْهَا فِي الزَّمَانِ الثَّانِي شَيْءٌ لَمْ يَكُنْ فِي الزَّمَانِ الْأَوَّلِ إلَّا لِمَعْنَى حَدَثَ فِيهَا فَإِذَا لَمْ يَحْدُثْ فِيهَا شَيْءٌ لَمْ يَحْدُثْ عَنْهَا شَيْءٌ. فَإِذَا قِيلَ بِدَوَامِ الْحَوَادِثِ عَنْهَا مِنْ غَيْرِ أَنْ يَحْدُثَ فِيهَا شَيْءٌ كَانَ هَذَا قَوْلًا بِوُجُودِ الْمُمْتَنِعَاتِ دَائِمًا؛ فَإِنَّهُ مَا مِنْ حَادِثٍ يَحْدُثُ إلَّا قُلِبَتْ الذَّاتُ عِنْدَ حُدُوثِهِ لِمَا كَانَتْ قَبْلَ حُدُوثِهِ وَكَانَتْ قَبْلَ ذَلِكَ يَمْتَنِعُ عَنْهَا حُدُوثُهُ؛ فَالْآنَ كَذَلِكَ يَمْتَنِعُ عَنْهَا حُدُوثُهُ.
translated_text:
rather, it demonstrates the opposite of their position. For motion must have a mover, and all motions ultimately lead back to a first mover. They concede this. That first mover, from which the motion of everything else proceeds, must either be in motion or not be in motion. If it is not in motion, this entails motion proceeding from something that is not in motion, which contradicts sensory experience and reason.

For an effect must correspond to its cause. If the effect comes into being successively, its cause cannot remain in one unchanged state. As you yourselves have said, nothing can come into being from such a cause after not having existed. Indeed, continuous coming into being from such a cause is even more clearly impossible than a new occurrence proceeding from it, for the former entails more instances of the impossible than the latter.

For if it is said, “It is known by plain reason that, for anything that was not acting, a cause must arise that necessitates its acting; and that if an agent remains in the same state it was in before acting, it will do nothing and nothing will come into being from it,” the reply to them is:

This very truth, known by plain reason, entails that nothing can come into being from that cause at a later time which did not exist at an earlier time, unless some new factor has arisen in the cause itself. If nothing new arises in it, nothing new comes into being from it. Thus, to maintain that things continually come into being from it without anything new arising in it is to maintain that impossibilities continually occur. For whenever anything comes into being, the essence is turned, at the moment of its occurrence, into what it was before its occurrence. Previously, it was impossible for that thing to come into being from it; so now, likewise, it remains impossible for that thing to come into being from it.

translated_text:
Or it may be said:

It did not bring it into being before, so it does not do so now. Thus, whenever anything comes into being, the cause remains as it was before. Before that thing came into being, the cause was not bringing it into being; indeed, doing so was impossible. Likewise, at the time when it is supposed to come into being, its coming into being must be impossible.

Their most accomplished thinkers have acknowledged this as a necessary consequence, as Ibn Rushd, al-Rāzī and others have stated. They have acknowledged that something changing coming into being from something unchanging runs counter to the judgment of rational thinkers. Ibn Sīnā recognized this.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—was asked:

What do the esteemed scholars—may Allah be pleased with them all—say in response to the specious argument advanced by the Muʿtazilah in denying the divine attributes? They claim that “the Creator’s attributes are not additional to His essence,” arguing as follows:

Either His existence depends upon a particular attribute, such that supposing its nonexistence entails His nonexistence, or it does not. If it does, then His existence depends upon that attribute, and He becomes a composite of parts, whose existence is possible only through all those parts together. A composite, however, has a cause. If His existence does not depend upon that attribute, and supposing its nonexistence does not entail His nonexistence, then it is accidental, and an accident has a cause. Both are impossible with respect to Allah. The only remaining conclusion, therefore, is that the Creator’s attributes are not additional to His essence—which is what they seek to prove.

He replied—may Allah be pleased with him:

Praise be to Allah. The Quran and the Sunnah establish that Allah, glorified be He, possesses knowledge, power, mercy, will, might, and other attributes. For He, the Most High, says:

“They encompass nothing of His knowledge.”

And He says:

“But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He has sent it down with His knowledge.”

And He says:

“Indeed, Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of Power, the Firm.”

And He says:

“And might belongs to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers.”

And He says:

“Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge.”

translated_text:
And in the hadith of seeking Allah’s guidance, recorded in the Sahīh:

“O Allah, I seek Your guidance through Your knowledge, and I ask You to grant me ability through Your power, and I ask You of Your immense bounty.”

In the hadith of Shaddād ibn Aws, recorded in the Sunan, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“O Allah, by Your knowledge of the unseen and Your power over creation, keep me alive as long as life is better for me, and cause me to die when death is better for me.”

And in an authentic hadith:

“No, by Your might!”

Examples of this are numerous. It is also recorded in the Sahīh that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, questioned the man who recited “Say, ‘He is Allah, One’” in every unit of prayer while leading others. The man replied, “I love it because it is a description of the Most Merciful.” The Prophet said, “Tell him that Allah loves him.” Thus, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, approved his calling it a description of the Most Merciful. There are also numerous other reports to this effect.

These texts establish that words conveying information about Allah constitute a description of Him. Describing means making something manifest and clear to sight or hearing, as when jurists speak of a garment that reveals the skin or does not reveal it.

Allah Most High says:

“He will repay them for their descriptions.”

And He says:

“Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“A woman must not describe another woman to her husband as though he were looking at her.”

Here, ‘depicting’ means describing. Examples of this are numerous.

The word sifa (‘description’) is a verbal noun: one says wasaftu al-shay’a, asifuhu (‘I described something; I describe it’), with the verbal nouns wasf and sifa. Similarly, wa‘ada (‘he promised’) has the verbal nouns wa‘d and ‘ida (‘promising’), and wazana (‘he weighed’) has wazn and zina (‘weighing’).

They also apply a verbal noun to the object of the action. Thus, they call a created thing khalq (‘creation’), and say, ‘a dirham of the ruler’s minting.’ Accordingly, when the One being described is said to encompass all things in mercy and knowledge, the meaning attributed to Him through these words is called an attribute. Mercy, knowledge and power are therefore called attributes in this sense. This is the reality of the matter.

 وَقَدْ يُضَافُ إلَى الْأَعْلَامِ كَقَوْلِهِمْ ذُو عَمْرٍو وَذُو الْكُلَاعِ وَقَوْلِ عُمَرَ:
 الْغَنِيُّ بِلَالٌ وَذَوُوهُ. فَلَمَّا وَجَدُوا اللَّهَ قَالَ فِي الْقُرْآنِ 
{تَعْلَمُ مَا فِي نَفْسِي وَلَا أَعْلَمُ مَا فِي نَفْسِكَ}
 
{وَيُحَذِّرُكُمُ اللَّهُ نَفْسَهُ}
 وَ 
{كَتَبَ عَلَى نَفْسِهِ الرَّحْمَةَ}
 : وَصَفُوهَا،
 فَقَالُوا:
 نَفْسٌ ذَاتُ عِلْمٍ وَقُدْرَةٍ وَرَحْمَةٍ وَمَشِيئَةٍ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ ثُمَّ حَذَفُوا الْمَوْصُوفَ وَعَرَّفُوا الصِّفَةَ.
 فَقَالُوا:
 الذَّاتُ. وَهِيَ كَلِمَةٌ مُوَلَّدَةٌ؛
 لَيْسَتْ قَدِيمَةً وَقَدْ وُجِدَتْ فِي كَلَامِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَالصَّحَابَةِ لَكِنْ بِمَعْنَى آخَرَ مِثْلَ قَوْلِ خبيب الَّذِي فِي صَحِيحِ الْبُخَارِيِّ:
translated_text:
Many of the Mu‘tazilites and others like them maintain that wasf (‘description’) and sifa (‘attribute’) refer only to verbal statements, without any meanings subsisting in the eternal Essence. Many theologians who affirm the divine attributes distinguish between wasf and sifa, saying that wasf is the verbal statement, whereas sifa is the meaning subsisting in the one described. Discerning scholars, however, know that each of these two terms is sometimes applied to the statement and sometimes to the meaning. The Quran and Sunnah explicitly affirm the existence of such meanings as knowledge, power and others, as we have already explained.

As for the word dhāt (‘essence’), it is, in Arabic, the feminine form of dhū (‘possessor of’). This form is used in a genitive construction with common nouns as a means of describing something by them. Thus one says, ‘a person possessed of knowledge, wealth and honour,’ referring to his actual being; or ‘an entity or self possessed of knowledge, power, authority,’ and the like.

It may also be joined to proper names, as in Dhū ‘Amr and Dhū al-Kalā‘, and in ‘Umar’s statement: ‘The wealthy one is Bilāl, together with his kin.’

When they found that Allah said in the Quran:

‘You know what is within myself, and I do not know what is within Yourself,’

‘Allah warns you of Himself,’

and ‘He has prescribed mercy for Himself,’

they described this Self, saying: ‘A Self possessed of knowledge, power, mercy, will,’ and the like. They then omitted the noun being described and made the descriptive word definite, saying al-dhāt (‘the essence’). It is a later coinage, not an ancient term. It does occur in the speech of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the Companions, but with a different meaning, as in the words of Khubayb recorded in Sahīh al-Bukhārī:

" النَّفْسِ "

" 
{تَفَكَّرُوا فِي آلَاءِ اللَّهِ؛ وَلَا تَتَفَكَّرُوا فِي ذَاتِ اللَّهِ}
 "
 فَإِنْ كَانَ هَذَا اللَّفْظُ أَوْ نَظِيرُهُ ثَابِتًا عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَأَصْحَابِهِ: فَقَدْ وُجِدَ فِي كَلَامِهِمْ إطْلَاقُ اسْمِ 
" الذَّاتِ "
 عَلَى النَّفْسِ كَمَا يُطْلِقُهُ الْمُتَأَخِّرُونَ. وَإِذَا تَقَرَّرَ هَذَا الْأَصْلُ يَبْقَى 
" كَالْحَرَكَةِ "
 وَقَدْ اُخْتُلِفَ فِي بَقَائِهَا كَالطَّعْمِ وَاللَّوْنِ وَالرِّيحِ وَأَكْثَرُ الْعُقَلَاءِ عَلَى أَنَّهُ قَدْ يَبْقَى. وَهَؤُلَاءِ لَا يَصِحُّ عِنْدَهُمْ الِاسْتِدْلَالُ بِهَذِهِ الْأَعْرَاضِ عَلَى حُدُوثِ الْجِسْمِ؛
translated_text:
“And that is for Allah’s sake; and if He wills,
He will bless the limbs of a body torn apart.”

In the Sahīh, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is reported to have said:

“Abraham told only three lies, all of them for Allah’s sake.”

Abū Dharr said: “We are all fools for Allah’s sake.” Others have said: “We have suffered for Allah’s sake.” The meaning is on Allah’s side and in His cause—that is, for Allah’s sake and seeking His Face. The Self is not what is meant here. Similar expressions occur in the Quran:

“So fear Allah and set right relations among yourselves,”

and:

“He knows what is within the hearts.”

These refer, respectively, to the condition and circumstances pertaining to your mutual relations, and to His knowledge of the thoughts and the like that dwell within hearts. Thus, the word dhāt in the speech of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the Companions, and in pure Arabic usage, carries this meaning. The theologians and others subsequently applied it to the “Self” for the reason explained above: it possesses the attributes. Thus, when they say “the Essence,” they are saying “that which possesses the attributes.”

A report transmitted both with and without attribution to the Prophet states:

“Reflect on Allah’s blessings, but do not reflect on Allah’s Essence.”

If this wording, or something similar, is authentically established from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and his Companions, then their speech does contain the application of the word dhāt to the Self, as later scholars use it.

Once this principle is established, it remains “like motion.” Its persistence has been disputed, as has that of taste, colour and smell; most rational thinkers hold that it may persist. In their view, these accidents cannot validly be used to infer that the body came into existence;

original_text:

 فَإِنَّهُ إذَا سَاغَ لِقَائِلِ أَنْ لَا يُسَمِّيَ بَعْضَ مَا قَامَ بِنَفْسِهِ جَوْهَرًا:
 سَاغَ لَهُ أَيْضًا أَنْ لَا يُسَمِّيَ بَعْضَ مَا يَقُومُ بِغَيْرِهِ عَرَضًا؛ بَلْ نَفْيُ الْعَرَضِ عَنْ الْمَعَانِي الْبَاقِيَةِ أَقْرَبُ إلَى اللُّغَةِ فَإِنْ سَمَّى الْمُسَمِّي كُلَّ مَا قَامَ بِغَيْرِهِ عَرَضًا سَاغَ حِينَئِذٍ أَنْ يُسَمِّيَ كُلَّ مَا قَامَ بِنَفْسِهِ جَوْهَرًا.
translated_text:
so it is all the more clear that Allah’s attributes cannot validly be used to infer that the One possessing them came into existence. Moreover, “this argument” for the world’s having come into existence requires lengthy examination, for which this is not the place.

The same response may also be given to the philosophers. There is no doubt that He is the Originator of the world and the cause of its existence, and they ascribe to Him certain things concerning intellect and providence which they must affirm. Thus, the same reasoning applies to what the adherents of the Book and Sunnah affirm as applies to what all schools must affirm. His reality has been established through necessary knowledge and conclusive proofs, and they agree on this. It has also been established that He is self-subsisting and is not of the same kind as other self-subsisting things, whether spirits or bodies. Since they agree that He is self-subsisting and is not of the same kind as other bodies and spirits, likewise the attributes that belong to Him in His own right are not of the same kind as those belonging to other things.

If it is supposed that an originated accident inhering in a substance proves that the substance came into existence, this does not entail that everything subsisting in another is an accident unless it also entails that everything self-subsisting is a substance. For if someone may refrain from calling some self-subsisting things substances, he may likewise refrain from calling some things that subsist in another accidents. Indeed, declining to call enduring qualities accidents accords more closely with linguistic usage. If, however, someone calls everything that subsists in another an accident, he may then call everything self-subsisting a substance.

وَالطَّرِيقُ الثَّانِي:

" التَّرْكِيبِ "

" التَّرْكِيبَ "
 الَّذِي ذَكَرُوهُ مُوجِبًا لِلِافْتِقَارِ الْمَانِعِ مِنْ كَوْنِهِ وَاجِبًا بِنَفْسِهِ.
translated_text:
“In that case,” inferring from an accident or attribute having come into existence that its substance or bearer has likewise come into existence does not entail that every accident or attribute proves that its substance or bearer came into existence. If that followed, their claim that all substances and bodies came into existence would be invalid, since, on this supposition, the One without beginning would fall within this general category. Indeed, even the claim that any substance or body is contingent would be invalid.

The answer has thus become clear through two approaches.

The first has two aspects: counterargument and holding the opponents to the implications of their position; and demonstrating contradiction and invalidating their argument. These two aspects show that this specious argument is invalid according to the principles of all people on earth, and intrinsically invalid as well. For its truth entails its own negation, and anything whose truth entails its negation is intrinsically false.

The second approach consists in resolving the difficulty and clarifying the matter, as explained above.

As for the second specious argument—the argument concerning “composition,” which is shared by the philosophers and the Muʿtazilites, whereas the first is exclusively Muʿtazilite—the Muʿtazilites regard His most distinctive attribute as His being without beginning, and affirm that everything other than Him came into existence. The philosophers regard His most distinctive attribute as His necessarily existing in His own right, and hold that everything other than Him is contingent. They do not acknowledge coming into existence from nonexistence, and they maintain that the “composition” they describe entails a dependence that precludes His being necessarily existent in His own right.

The answer to this, too, has two approaches. The first comprises two methods: counterargument and demonstrating contradiction. The second consists in resolving the difficulty.

As for the first, they affirm that He is knowing and powerful, necessarily existent in His own right, and the producer of what is other than Him. It is self-evident that the concept of His being knowing differs from the concept of His producing other things. If His essence is composed of these meanings, the “composition” they allege necessarily follows; and if these meanings are accidental to His essence, the “dependence” they allege necessarily follows. In short, whatever they say concerning these matters is what the adherents of the Book and the Sunnah say concerning knowledge and power.

As for “demonstrating contradiction”: if the One necessarily existent in His own right is not distinguished from anything else by a positive attribute, then there is no necessarily existent being. If there is no necessarily existent being, no impossibility follows from composition. For they deny these meanings only because affirming them entails “composition,” which in turn entails the negation of necessary existence. Yet this is contradictory: denying these meanings itself entails denying necessary existence. How, then, can they deny them in order to affirm it?

The explanation is that the One necessarily existent in His own right is real, existent, knowing, powerful, and active; and a contingent being may also be existent, knowing, powerful, and active. What they share is not merely a word, but intelligible meanings known self-evidently.

If what they share entails what distinguishes them, then the necessarily existent has become contingent, and the contingent necessarily existent. If it does not entail it, then the necessarily existent has something by which He is distinguished from

He thus has an aspect of commonality and an aspect of distinction; and this, according to them, is an impossible “composition.” If this composition entails the nonexistence of the necessarily existent, then the existence of the One necessarily existent in His own right entails His nonexistence. This is contradictory. This “compelling demonstration” thus establishes that their argument is internally contradictory, just as it has been established that, on their own principles, it is countered by what they themselves affirm.

As for the answer that resolves the difficulty, we say:

“Composition,” as understood by human reason and in human language, is the composition of an existing thing from parts distinguishable from one another. This is the composition of a body from its parts, such as a human being’s composition from organs and humours, a garment’s composition from its parts, or a drink’s composition from its ingredients. It makes no difference whether one part is distinct from the other, as a hand is distinct from a foot, or diffused throughout it, as bile is diffused in blood and water in milk.

The “logicians,” however, speak of species as composed of genus and differentia, as a human being is composed of animality and rationality: that is, composed of what it shares with the other species and what distinguishes it from other species. They also divide attributes into the “essential,” from which essences are composed—namely, genus and differentia—and the “accidental,” namely, the common accident and the distinctive property. The essence composed of the shared and distinguishing elements is then the “species.”

We say: this “composition” is a mental construct with no existence outside the mind, just as the “essence of the species,” insofar as it is universal, has no existence outside the mind. Rather, the very

As we said concerning “the nonexistent,” it is a thing in the mind, not outside it, since it is an object of knowledge and will. A human being existing outside the mind does not contain distinct entities, some constituting animality, others rationality, others the capacity for laughter, and others sensory perception. Rather, the intellect apprehends in him a meaning whose counterpart is also found in another species, and therefore says that he possesses a shared meaning. It also apprehends a meaning peculiar to him, then combines the two meanings and says: “He is composed of them.” Yet when it apprehends these two meanings in him, it does not apprehend either as distinct and separate from the other. Likewise, when it apprehends existence, necessary existence, self-subsistence, and the sustaining of others, it does not apprehend any of these meanings as separate and distinct from the others.

An even clearer example is that the taste, colour, and smell inhering in a body are not distinguished from one another by occupying different locations; rather, the senses distinguish between these realities. This kind of “composition” is therefore unlike the composition of a body from its parts and humours: parts are not like accidents. We do not dispute calling this composite, for that is merely a verbal dispute. The point, however, is that this composition is not of the kind that human beings understand through their original innate disposition, such that the term “parts” may be applied to it.

Once this is understood, there are two approaches to resolving the difficulty, just as there were two approaches to refuting the argument.

The attributes of a thing are not its constituent parts or portions, distinct from one another or from the thing itself, such that it could properly be said to be composed of them or not composed of them. Affirming or denying composition presupposes a conception of it, and no such conception applies here.

The second answer is that, even supposing this were called composite, it would entail neither contingency nor origination. For what is known through reason and revelation is that it is impossible for the Lord, Most High, to depend upon His creation. Rather, He has no need of any of the worlds. It is known that He is Ever-Living and Self-Subsisting, that His holy Self subsists in itself and exists in its own right, and that He is One, the Self-Sufficient Master, needing nothing beyond Himself. His existence and self-sufficiency are not derived from another. Rather, He has always been and will always remain, in Himself, the True One, the Self-Sufficient Master, the Self-Subsisting Sustainer. Could it therefore be said that He depends upon Himself or needs Himself because His Self subsists only in Himself? What is said of His “attributes,” which are included in what is meant by His Self, is the same as what is said of His Self.

Thus, if it is said that His attributes are essential to Him, and that He needs them, this is equivalent to saying that He needs Himself, for His essential attributes are those without which His Self cannot be.

Likewise, if we say that His essence necessitates His existence, that He necessarily exists in Himself, or that He Himself entails the necessity of His existence, someone might object: “It follows that He is an effect, and an effect is dependent.” He would be answered: “The cause here is not something other than the effect. What is denied is His dependence upon another and His being the effect of anything besides Himself. As for His subsisting in Himself, that is true.”

Furthermore, as for these expressions that suggest an unsound meaning, whether they are used with the correct meaning in view or not used at all, neither course does any harm, provided the correct meaning is known and cannot be refuted. This profound point deserves careful attention, for it dispels illusory doubts that have led many people astray.

When we say that “essences” are brought into being, we mean essences existing in external reality, on the basis that the existence of each thing in external reality is identical to its essence. For an externally existing thing is not something other than its existence. It is this externally existing thing that depends upon another, whether it is simple or composite.

A composite existing in external reality does not depend upon an agent because it is composite, but because its reality is dependent and its very being is inescapably needy. It has no subsistence, existence, or actual being except from its Lord. For this same reason, a simple thing depends upon the Maker just as a composite does. As for the “essences” known to the intellect, whether simple or composite, they depend upon an agent only insofar as a servant’s knowledge must have a cause—not because a composite depends upon its parts.

It has thus become clear to you that a composite does not depend upon its parts, either in the mind or in external reality, except in the same sense that a simple thing depends upon itself. A part of a composite is therefore equivalent to the simple thing itself, and each depends upon something else in external reality.

From Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah:

Peace be upon you, and Allah’s mercy and blessings.

To proceed:

In addressing you, we praise Allah, besides whom there is no god. He is worthy of all praise and has power over all things. We ask Him to send blessings upon His chosen one from among His creation, the best of His creatures, the unlettered Prophet, “Muhammad,” and upon his family, and to grant him abundant peace.

I write to you—may Allah bestow His kindness upon you in this world and the Hereafter, raising you thereby to lofty ranks in goodness and well-being—amid blessings and mercy from Allah, and well-being encompassing us and all our brethren. Abundant praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds, as He deserves and as befits His noble Face and exalted majesty.

The three letters you sent have arrived. We ask Allah Most High, and hope from Him, that the illness and other worldly afflictions He has decreed will bring you to ranks that deeds have fallen short of attaining, but which were already recorded in the Mother of the Book as destined to be attained. We also ask that what Allah has chosen for His believing servants may prove to be what is best.

We know as a general principle that whatever Allah Most High decrees for a believer is good for him. Even when one intends and longs to do something that illness prevents, what is best—if Allah Most High wills—lies in what Allah has willed. May Allah Most High choose for you, in all your affairs, what will secure His good pleasure for you in goodness and well-being.

As for the affliction in your heart and religious life of which you complain, we ask Allah to take you into His gracious care without leaving you in the charge of any created being, and to set all your affairs right, beginning this rectification Himself and bringing it to completion. May He enable you truly to fulfil the words:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

There is no power nor strength except through Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.

Yet we hope that recognizing one’s shortcomings and seeing that one has fallen behind are among Allah’s favours to His believing servant: through this, the servant merits advancement, Allah perfects His favour upon him, and He spares him the trouble caused by his devil, who makes his evil deeds seem attractive to him, and by his own soul, which loves to be praised for what it has not done and to rejoice

 إنَّ اللَّهَ ذَكَرَ أَهْلَ الْجَنَّةِ فَذَكَرَهُمْ بِأَحْسَنِ أَعْمَالِهِمْ وَغَفَرَ لَهُمْ سَيِّئَهَا فَيَقُولُ الرَّجُلُ:
 أَيْنَ أَنَا مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ يَعْنِي: وَهُوَ مِنْهُمْ وَذَكَرَ أَهْلَ النَّارِ بِأَقْبَحِ أَعْمَالِهِمْ وَأَحْبَطَ حَسَنَهَا فَيَقُولُ الْقَائِلُ لَسْت مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ؟
 يَعْنِي:
 وَهُوَ مِنْهُمْ. هَذَا الْكَلَامُ أَوْ قَرِيبًا مِنْهُ.
فَلْيَبْرُدْ الْقَلْبُ مِنْ وَهَجِ حَرَارَةِ هَذِهِ الشَّهَادَةِ إنَّهَا سَبِيلٌ مَهِيعٌ لِعِبَادِ اللَّهِ الَّذِينَ أَطْبَقَ شُهَدَاءُ اللَّهِ فِي أَرْضِهِ أَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا مِنْ اللَّهِ بِالْمَكَانَةِ الْعَالِيَةِ مَعَ أَنَّ الِازْدِيَادَ مِنْ مِثْلِ هَذِهِ الشَّهَادَةِ هُوَ النَّافِعُ فِي الْأَمْرِ الْغَالِبِ مَا لَمْ يُفْضِ إلَى تَسَخُّطٍ لِلْمَقْدُورِ أَوْ يَأْسٍ مِنْ رَوْحِ اللَّهِ؛ أَوْ فُتُورٍ عَنْ الرَّجَاءِ؛ وَاَللَّهُ تَعَالَى يَتَوَلَّاكُمْ بِوَلَايَةٍ مِنْهُ وَلَا يَكِلُكُمْ إلَى أَحَدٍ غَيْرِهِ.
translated_text:
in what it has done.

He, glorified be He, has said:

“Indeed, those who stand in awe of their Lord, and those who believe in the signs of their Lord”—up to His words—“because they will return to their Lord.”

It is reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“It is the man who fasts, prays, and gives charity, yet fears that it will not be accepted from him.”

A report—I believe it is from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb or Ibn Masʿūd—states: “Whoever says that he is a believer is a disbeliever, and whoever says that he is destined for Paradise is destined for the Fire.”

He also said: “By Him besides whom there is no god, no one has ever been secure against being stripped of his faith at death.”

Abū al-ʿĀliya said: “I met thirty of the Companions of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, all of whom feared hypocrisy for themselves.”

Abū Bakr al-Siddīq—may Allah be pleased with him—said: “Allah has mentioned the people of Paradise, describing their finest deeds and forgiving their evil deeds. A man therefore says, ‘How could I compare with these people?’—although he is one of them. And He has mentioned the people of the Fire, describing their foulest deeds and rendering their good deeds worthless. A person therefore says, ‘Surely I am not one of these?’—although he is one of them.” These were his words, or something close to them.

Let your heart, then, find relief from the scorching heat of this awareness. It is a well-trodden path followed by servants of Allah whom His witnesses on earth unanimously acknowledged to have held a lofty station with Him. Indeed, a greater measure of this awareness is generally beneficial, so long as it does not lead to resentment of what has been decreed, despair of Allah’s relief, or a weakening of hope. May Allah Most High take you into His care and not leave you in the charge of anyone besides Him.

original_text:
وَأَمَّا مَا ذَكَرْت مِنْ طَلَبِ الْأَسْبَابِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ الَّتِي لَا بُدَّ فِيهَا مِنْ صَرْفِ الْكَلَامِ مِنْ حَقِيقَتِهِ إلَى مَجَازِهِ فَأَنَا أَذْكُرُ مُلَخَّصَ الْكَلَامِ الَّذِي جَرَى بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ بَعْضِ النَّاسِ فِي ذَلِكَ وَهُوَ مَا حَكَيْته لَك وَطَلَبْته وَكَانَ إنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ لَهُ وَلِغَيْرِهِ بِهِ مَنْفَعَةٌ عَلَى مَا فِي الْحِكَايَةِ مِنْ زِيَادَةٍ وَنَقْصٍ وَتَغْيِيرٍ.

 أَتُحِبُّ لِأَهْلِ الْحَدِيثِ أَنْ يَتَنَاظَرُوا فِي هَذَا؟

 أَنَّ أُمَّهَاتِ الْمَسَائِلِ الَّتِي خَالَفَ فِيهَا مُتَأَخِّرُو الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ - مِمَّنْ يَنْتَحِلُ مَذْهَبَ الْأَشْعَرِيِّ - لِأَهْلِ الْحَدِيثِ 
" ثَلَاثُ مَسَائِلَ "
translated_text:
As for your request concerning the four grounds that necessitate interpreting speech figuratively rather than literally, I shall summarize the discussion I had with someone on this subject—the discussion I recounted to you and whose account you requested. Allah willing, it benefited him and others, notwithstanding the additions, omissions, and alterations in this account.

Someone said to me:

“If we wish to follow the path of safety and silence—the way by which we remain safe—we say what al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: ‘I believe in Allah and in what has come from Allah, according to Allah’s intent; and I believe in Allah’s Messenger and in what has come from Allah’s Messenger, according to the intent of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’ But if we follow the path of inquiry and careful investigation, then the truth lies with those speculative theologians who interpret the verses and hadiths concerning the divine attributes nonliterally.”

I replied:

“What al-Shāfiʿī said is true, and every Muslim must believe it. Whoever believes it and makes no statement contradicting it follows the path of safety in this world and the Hereafter. But when a person investigates and examines the matter closely, he finds that all the nonliteral interpretations through which the speculative theologians oppose the people of hadith are false, and becomes certain that the truth lies with the people of hadith, both outwardly and inwardly.”

He was taken aback by this and said:

“Would you like the people of hadith to debate this?”

We therefore arranged a day to meet. Among the matters we discussed was that the principal issues on which the later speculative theologians who profess to follow al-Ashʿarī differed with the people of hadith were three:

 لِأَنَّ الظَّاهِرَ قَدْ صَارَ مُشْتَرِكًا بَيْنَ شَيْئَيْنِ:
translated_text:
describing Allah as being high above the Throne;
the question of the Quran;
and the question of interpreting the divine attributes nonliterally.

I said to him:

“Let us begin with the question of interpreting the divine attributes nonliterally, for this is the fundamental issue, and the remaining questions depend upon it.”

I also said to him:

“The position of the people of hadith—the early generations, comprising the first three generations, and those of later generations who followed their path—is that these hadiths are to be accepted as they have come, believed in, and affirmed as true. They must be safeguarded against nonliteral interpretation that leads to negating the attributes, and against specifying their manner in a way that leads to likening Allah to His creation.

“More than one scholar who has reported the consensus of the early generations—including al-Khattābī—has stated their position in general terms: these hadiths are understood according to their apparent sense, without specifying how the attributes are or likening them to those of creation. This is because what is said concerning the attributes follows from what is said concerning the divine essence, adhering to the same pattern and principle. Thus, just as affirming the divine essence means affirming its existence, not specifying how it is, so too affirming the attributes means affirming their existence, not specifying how they are. We therefore say that He has a hand and hearing, but we do not say that hand means power or that hearing means knowledge.”

I then said to him:

“Some people say, ‘The position of the early generations is that the apparent sense is not intended,’ and say, ‘We agree that the apparent sense is not intended.’ This expression is erroneous—either in both wording and meaning, or in wording but not in meaning—because ‘the apparent sense’ has come to be used for two different things:

أَحَدُهُمَا أَنْ يُقَالَ:
 إنَّ الْيَدَ جَارِحَةٌ مِثْلُ جَوَارِحِ الْعِبَادِ وَظَاهِرُ الْغَضَبِ غَلَيَانُ الْقَلْبِ لِطَلَبِ الِانْتِقَامِ وَظَاهِرُ كَوْنِهِ فِي السَّمَاءِ أَنْ يَكُونَ مِثْلَ الْمَاءِ فِي الظَّرْفِ فَلَا شَكَّ أَنَّ مَنْ قَالَ: إنَّ هَذِهِ الْمَعَانِيَ وَشِبْهَهَا مِنْ صِفَاتِ الْمَخْلُوقِينَ وَنُعُوتِ الْمُحَدِّثِينَ غَيْرُ مُرَادٍ مِنْ الْآيَاتِ وَالْأَحَادِيثِ فَقَدْ صَدَقَ وَأَحْسَنَ؛ إذْ لَا يَخْتَلِفُ أَهْلُ السُّنَّةِ أَنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ لَا فِي ذَاتِهِ وَلَا فِي صِفَاتِهِ وَلَا فِي أَفْعَالِهِ؛ بَلْ أَكْثَرُ أَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ مِنْ أَصْحَابِنَا وَغَيْرِهِمْ يُكَفِّرُونَ الْمُشَبِّهَةَ وَالْمُجَسِّمَةَ. لَكِنَّ هَذَا الْقَائِلَ أَخْطَأَ حَيْثُ ظَنَّ أَنَّ هَذَا الْمَعْنَى هُوَ الظَّاهِرُ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْآيَاتِ وَالْأَحَادِيثِ؛ وَحَيْثُ حُكِيَ عَنْ السَّلَفِ مَا لَمْ يَقُولُوهُ؛ فَإِنَّ 
" ظَاهِرَ الْكَلَامِ "
 هُوَ مَا يَسْبِقُ إلَى الْعَقْلِ السَّلِيمِ مِنْهُ لِمَنْ يَفْهَمُ بِتِلْكَ اللُّغَةِ ثُمَّ قَدْ يَكُونُ ظُهُورُهُ بِمُجَرَّدِ الْوَضْعِ وَقَدْ يَكُونُ بِسِيَاقِ الْكَلَامِ؛ وَلَيْسَتْ 
" هَذِهِ الْمَعَانِي "
 الْمُحْدَثَةَ الْمُسْتَحِيلَةَ عَلَى اللَّهِ تَعَالَى هِيَ السَّابِقَةَ إلَى عَقْلِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ بَلْ الْيَدُ عِنْدَهُمْ كَالْعِلْمِ وَالْقُدْرَةِ وَالذَّاتِ فَكَمَا كَانَ عِلْمُنَا وَقُدْرَتُنَا وَحَيَاتُنَا وَكَلَامُنَا وَنَحْوُهَا مِنْ الصِّفَاتِ أَعْرَاضًا تَدُلُّ عَلَى حُدُوثَنَا يَمْتَنِعُ أَنْ يُوصَفَ اللَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ بِمِثْلِهَا؛ فَكَذَلِكَ أَيْدِينَا وَوُجُوهُنَا وَنَحْوُهَا أَجْسَامًا كَذَلِكَ مُحْدَثَةً يَمْتَنِعُ أَنْ يُوصَفَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى بِمِثْلِهَا.
 ثُمَّ لَمْ يَقُلْ أَحَدٌ مِنْ أَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ:
 إذَا قُلْنَا إنَّ لِلَّهِ عِلْمًا وَقُدْرَةً وَسَمْعًا وَبَصَرًا إنَّ ظَاهِرَهُ غَيْرُ مُرَادٍ ثُمَّ يُفَسِّرُ بِصِفَاتِنَا.
 فَكَذَلِكَ لَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ يُقَالَ:
 إنَّ ظَاهِرَ الْيَدِ وَالْوَجْهِ غَيْرُ مُرَادٍ؛ إذْ لَا فَرْقَ بَيْنَ مَا هُوَ مِنْ صِفَاتِنَا جِسْمٍ أَوْ عَرَضٍ لِلْجِسْمِ.
translated_text:
the first is to say that the hand is a limb like the limbs of created beings; that the apparent sense of anger is the heart’s boiling in pursuit of vengeance; and that the apparent sense of His being in heaven is that He is like water in a vessel. Undoubtedly, anyone who says that these meanings and similar attributes of created beings and qualities of things brought into existence are not intended in the Quranic verses and hadiths has spoken truthfully and rightly. For Ahl al-Sunnah do not disagree that nothing resembles Allah Most High, whether in His essence, His attributes, or His actions. Indeed, most of Ahl al-Sunnah, both among the scholars of our school and others, declare those who liken Allah to His creation and those who ascribe a body to Him to be disbelievers.

However, this person has erred in supposing that this is the apparent sense of these verses and hadiths, and in attributing to the early generations something they never said. For ‘the apparent sense of speech’ is what first comes to a sound mind when someone understands the language in question. This sense may be apparent from the established meanings of the words alone, or from the context. Yet ‘these meanings’—created characteristics that cannot possibly apply to Allah Most High—are not what first comes to the minds of believers. Rather, they regard the hand as they regard knowledge, power, and the divine essence. Our knowledge, power, life, speech, and similar attributes are accidents indicating that we came into existence, and Allah—glorified be He—cannot possibly be described as having their like. Likewise, our hands, faces, and similar things are bodies that have also been brought into existence, and Allah Most High cannot possibly be described as having their like.

Yet no one among Ahl al-Sunnah has said that, when we affirm that Allah has knowledge, power, hearing, and sight, ‘the apparent sense is not intended,’ and then explained that apparent sense in terms of our own attributes. Likewise, it is impermissible to say that the apparent sense of the hand and face is not intended, for there is no difference between those of our attributes that are bodies and those that are accidents inhering in bodies.

translated_text:
Whoever says that the apparent sense of any of His names or attributes is not intended has erred. For with every name by which Allah Most High is called, the apparent sense applicable to a created being is not intended of Him. Thus, this person’s statement would imply that all His names and attributes convey meanings contrary to their apparent sense. The unsoundness of this is evident.

(The second meaning is that these attributes are indeed the attributes of Allah—glorified and exalted be He—in a manner befitting His majesty. They relate to His holy essence as the attributes of anything relate to its essence. Thus, knowledge is understood to be an attribute intrinsic to the one who possesses it, with its own distinctive characteristics; the same applies to the face.

It must not be said that He has no need of these attributes, for they necessarily belong to His essence. “God,” the One worshipped—glorified be He—is the One to whom all these attributes rightfully belong. Our purpose here is not to discuss matters with those who deny the attributes altogether, but with those who affirm some of them.

Likewise, regarding “His action,” we know that creation means bringing things into existence from nothing, although we do not specify the manner of that act. Nor does it resemble our actions, for we act only out of a need to act, whereas Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy.

Similarly, the “essence” is known in general terms, although it does not resemble created essences. None but He knows what He is, and its modality cannot be grasped. This, then, is the apparent meaning conveyed when these attributes are used without qualification, and this is how they must be understood.

translated_text:
Thus, the believer knows the implications and effects of these attributes, which is what he is meant to know. He knows that Allah has power over all things; that Allah encompasses all things in knowledge; that the entire earth will be in His grasp on the Day of Resurrection and the heavens will be rolled up in His right hand; and that the believers will gaze upon the face of their Creator in Paradise, experiencing a delight beside which all other pleasures pale—and other such matters. Likewise, he knows that he has a Lord, a Creator, and One whom he worships, without knowing the full reality of any of this.

Indeed, this is the utmost extent of created beings’ knowledge: they know things in certain respects but do not encompass their full reality. Their knowledge of themselves is of this kind.

I said to him, “Is it permissible, then, to say that ‘the apparent meaning is not intended,’ when understood in this sense?”

He replied, “That is not possible.”

I said to him, “If someone says that the apparent meaning is not intended, meaning that the attributes of created beings are not intended, we say to him: ‘You are correct in your meaning but mistaken in your wording. Your wording suggests religious innovation and gives the Jahmiyyah a means of achieving their aim. You could instead have said: These attributes are to be left as they have come, according to their apparent sense, while knowing that Allah Most High’s attributes are not like those of created beings, and that He is exalted and holy, free of anything that would imply that He has a beginning or is deficient.’

“But whoever says that ‘the apparent meaning is not intended’ according to the second interpretation—which is what the Jahmiyyah and their followers among the Muʿtazilah, some Ashʿarīs, and others intend—has erred. Now, the closest of these ‘Jahmiyyah,’ the Ashʿarīs, say that He has seven attributes: life

, knowledge, power, will, speech, hearing, and sight. They deny all other attributes. Some add only ‘the hand’ to these; others suspend judgment on denying the remaining attributes, while their extremists categorically deny them.

As for the ‘Muʿtazilah’, they deny the attributes altogether while affirming the corresponding predicates. For most of them, these amount to His being All-Knowing and All-Powerful. As for His having will and speech, they regard these as attributes that arise in time, express relations, or consist in negations. They are the closest of all people to the ‘Sabian philosophers’ among the Romans and those Arabs and Persians who followed their path, who claimed that all attributes amount to a negation, a relation, or a combination of negation and relation. All these people are misguided and reject the messengers. Whoever Allah has granted knowledge of what the messengers brought and penetrating insight, and who understands the true basis of these people’s views, knows with certainty that they deviate from the truth concerning His names and signs, and that they have rejected the messengers, the Scripture, and that with which His messengers were sent.

Hence they used to say: ‘Religious innovations spring from unbelief and lead back to it.’ They would also say: ‘The Muʿtazilah are the effeminate counterparts of the philosophers, and the Ashʿarīs are the effeminate counterparts of the Muʿtazilah.’

Yahyā ibn ʿAmmār used to say: ‘The Muʿtazilah are the male Jahmiyyah, and the Ashʿarīs are the female Jahmiyyah.’ They meant those Ashʿarīs who deny the attributes known through revelation. As for any of them who adheres to the book al-Ibānah, which al-Ashʿarī composed toward the end of his life, and has not openly expressed a position contradicting it, such a person is counted among Ahl al-Sunnah. Nevertheless, identifying oneself by affiliation with al-Ashʿarī is itself a religious innovation

I said to him:

When Allah describes Himself with an attribute, or His Messenger describes Him with it, or the believers—whose guidance and understanding the Muslims unanimously acknowledge—describe Him with it, diverting it from its apparent meaning, which befits the majesty of Allah, glorified be He, and from the literal meaning understood from it, to a hidden meaning contrary to its apparent meaning and a figurative sense incompatible with its literal meaning, requires four things:

First: The expression must admit of that figurative usage. The Quran, the Sunnah, and the speech of the early generations are in the Arabic language, and nothing in them may be understood in a manner contrary to Arabic usage or to the usage of all languages. That figurative sense must therefore be one that the expression can convey. Otherwise, anyone advancing falsehood could interpret any expression as whatever meaning occurred to him, even if it had no basis in the language.

Second: He must have evidence requiring the expression to be diverted from its literal meaning to its figurative meaning. Otherwise, when an expression is used literally in one sense and figuratively in another, all rational people agree that it may not be understood figuratively without evidence requiring that departure. If he claims that departing from its literal meaning is necessary, he must provide decisive evidence, whether rational or scriptural, requiring that departure. If he claims that departing from its literal meaning is the more likely interpretation, he must provide evidence favoring the figurative reading.

Third: The evidence requiring that departure must be free of countervailing evidence. Otherwise, if Quranic evidence or evidence grounded in faith establishes that the literal meaning is intended, it is impermissible

(Fourth:
When the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, says something while intending a meaning contrary to its apparent and literal meaning, he must explain to the Muslim community that he does not intend its literal meaning but a figurative one, whether or not he specifies that figurative meaning. This is especially so in discourse concerning knowledge, where what is required of them is belief and knowledge rather than bodily action. For Allah, glorified and exalted be He, made the Quran a light, guidance, clarification for humanity, and a healing for what is in their hearts. He sent the messengers to explain to people what had been revealed to them, to judge between them concerning their disagreements, and so that people would have no argument against Allah after the messengers.

Moreover, this “Messenger,” an unlettered Arab, was sent with the most eloquent of languages and the clearest speech and expression. Those of his community who learned from him possessed the deepest knowledge, were the most sincere in their concern for the community, and explained the Sunnah most clearly. Thus, neither he nor they could use words while intending something contrary to their apparent meaning without providing evidence that precludes understanding them according to that apparent meaning.

This evidence may be readily apparent rational evidence, as in His saying:

“She has been given of all things.”

Everyone knows through reason that this means she was given the kinds of things that someone like her would be given. Likewise, in the words:

“Creator of all things,”

the listener knows that the Creator is not included in this general statement. Or it may be clear scriptural evidence, such as the indications in the Quran and Sunnah that divert certain expressions from their apparent meanings.

It is not permissible for him to refer them to obscure evidence that only a few individuals can deduce, whether scriptural or rational. For if he uses words that convey a particular meaning and repeats them a number of times

—many times over—and addresses all people with them, including the intelligent and the dull-witted, those versed in religion and those who are not, requiring them to ponder that discourse, understand it, reflect upon it, and believe what it entails, but then requires them not to believe anything of its apparent meaning because some obscure evidence, discernible only to a few individuals, indicates that its apparent meaning was not intended, this would constitute deception and obfuscation. It would be the opposite of clarification and the very contrary of guidance, resembling riddles and puzzles more than guidance and explanation. How much more so if that discourse indicates its apparent meaning far more strongly than the obscure evidence indicates that this meaning was not intended? And what if that obscure evidence is merely a specious argument with no basis in reality?

The man conceded these points to me.

I said:

Let us discuss one of the attributes and make our discussion of it a model to follow, taking the attribute of the “Hand” as our example. Allah Most High says:

“The Jews say, ‘Allah’s Hand is shackled.’ May their hands be shackled, and may they be cursed for what they have said! Rather, both His Hands are outstretched; He spends however He wills.”

And He, Most High, said to Iblīs:

“What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two Hands?”

And He, Most High, says:

“They have not accorded Allah His true worth. On the Day of Resurrection, the earth in its entirety will be in His grasp, and the heavens will be rolled up in His Right Hand.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Blessed is He in whose Hand is dominion.”

And He says:

“In Your Hand is all good. Indeed, You have power over all things.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Do they not see that We have created livestock for them from what Our Hands have made, and that they own them?”

translated_text:
And references to the “Hand” are established in the Sunnah through mass-transmitted reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

What is understood from this discourse is that Allah Most High has two Hands, peculiar to Him and belonging to His Essence, in a manner befitting His majesty; that He, glorified be He, created Adam with His Hand, unlike the angels and Iblīs; that He, glorified be He, grasps the earth and rolls up the heavens with His Right Hand; and that “both His Hands are outstretched.” Their being outstretched means abundant generosity and bountiful giving, since giving and generosity usually involve opening and extending the hand, whereas withholding involves drawing the hand up to the neck. Such expressions have thus become literal in customary usage: when one says, “He is open-handed,” an actual hand is understood, while the apparent sense conveys generosity and miserliness. As Allah Most High says:

“Do not keep your hand shackled to your neck, nor extend it to its utmost extent.”

People also say, “So-and-so is tight-fingered,” and “He is open-fingered.”

I said to him:

If someone claims that He does not have a hand of the same kind as the hands of created beings, and that His Hand is not a bodily organ, this is true. But if he claims that He has no Hand beyond the seven attributes, he is asserting falsehood. He must therefore go through those four stages of argument.

As for the “first,” he says that “hand” can mean a favor or a gift, naming something after its cause, just as rain and vegetation are called “sky.” Examples include their saying, “So-and-so has done him many favors,” and the words of Abū Tālib when he could not find the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“O Lord, return my rider Muhammad to me …
[Return him, my Lord] and bestow a favor upon me.”

and the words of ‘Urwah ibn Mas‘ūd to Abū Bakr on the day of al-Hudaybiyah:

“Were it not for a favor you did me, which I have not yet repaid, I would have answered you.”

“Hand” may also mean power, naming a thing after what causes it, since power moves the hand. People say, “So-and-so has a hand in such-and-such.” Another example is what “Ziyād” said to Mu‘āwiyah: “I have held Iraq with one of my hands, while my other hand remains free.” He meant that controlling Iraq’s affairs took half his power.

Another example is His saying:

“In whose hand is the marriage tie.”

Marriage is contracted through spoken words; the meaning is simply that he has authority over it.

They may also attribute an action to the hand to attribute it to the person himself. Since most actions are performed with the hand, mentioning the hand came to indicate that someone performed an action himself. Allah Most High says:

“Allah has certainly heard the words of those who said, ‘Allah is poor, while we are rich’”

—down to His words—

“That is for what your hands have sent forth.”

That is, what you yourselves have sent forth, for some of what they sent forth consisted of words they spoke. Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“If only you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve, striking their faces and their backs”

—down to His words—

“That is for what your hands have sent forth.”

The Arabs say, “Your own hands tied it, and your own mouth inflated it,” rebuking anyone who brings trouble upon himself, because this was first said to someone who had acted with his own hands and mouth.

“Rather, both His Hands are outstretched,”

and His saying:

“What I created with My two Hands,”

translated_text:
, drawing on all these usages. They said: What is meant is His blessing—that is, the blessing of this world and the blessing of the Hereafter. They also said: “By His power.” They further said: The expression is an indirect reference to generosity itself, without there actually being a hand; rather, this expression has become a literal designation for giving and generosity.

His words:

“What I created with My two Hands”

mean: “I Myself created it,” even if there is no actual hand.

I said to him: “Are these, then, their interpretations?”

He replied: “Yes.”

I said to him: Let us, then, examine what we have already set out:

(The first point: The expression “two hands,” in the dual form, has not been used to mean either blessing or power. For the Arabs use the singular to mean the plural, as in His saying:

“Indeed, man is in loss.”

They also use the plural to mean the singular, as in His saying:

“Those to whom the people said, ‘Indeed, the people’”

and the plural to mean two, as in His saying:

“The hearts of you both have inclined.”

But using the singular to mean two, or the dual to mean one, has no basis. These expressions denote number and are explicit in their meanings; they cannot be used figuratively. One cannot say, “I have a man,” meaning two men, or “I have two men,” meaning the class as a whole. A singular noun can denote a class, and a class encompasses an indefinite range of individuals. Likewise, a plural noun carries the sense of a class, and a class is instantiated by even a single individual.

Thus, His words:

“What I created with My two Hands”

cannot mean power, because power is a single attribute, and the dual cannot be used to express the singular. Nor can they mean blessing, because Allah’s blessings are beyond counting, and blessings beyond counting cannot be expressed using the dual form.

translated_text:
Nor can it mean “what I Myself created,” for when they intend this meaning, they ascribe the action to the hand, thereby associating the hand with the action, as in His words:

“For what your two hands have sent forth,”

and:

“For what your hands have sent forth.”

This also includes His words:

“Livestock, among the things Our Hands have made.”

But when He ascribes the action to the agent and connects the verb to the hand through the preposition bi (“with”), as in His words:

“What I created with My two Hands,”

this explicitly states that He performed the action with His two Hands. Thus, one cannot say to someone who has spoken or walked, “You did this with your two hands,” although one may say, “Your two hands did this.” Simply saying “You did it” suffices to attribute the action to its agent. If an actual action performed with the hand were not intended, the additional wording would be entirely superfluous and serve no purpose.

In the speech of Arabs or non-Arabs, you will not find—if Allah Most High wills—an eloquent speaker saying, “I did this with my two hands,” or “So-and-so did this with his two hands,” unless he actually did it with his two hands. It cannot mean that he has no hand, or that he has a hand but the action was performed without it. This established distinction makes clear where expressions are figurative and where they are literal. It also makes clear that, on purely linguistic grounds, these verses admit no figurative interpretation whatsoever.

He said to me: “But they have used the dual in place of the singular in His words, ‘Cast him into Hell, you two,’ although the address is only to one.”

I said to him: This is not conceded. Rather, concerning His words, “Cast, you two,” it has been said that the agent takes the dual form because the action is repeated twice, the meaning being: “Cast! Cast!” It has also been said that the address is to the driver and the witness. Whoever says that it addresses one person says that a person has two companions with him: one on his right and the other on his left

There is no doubt about this. But why could He not have a “Hand” befitting His Essence, to which attributes of perfection belong just as they belong to His Essence?

He said: “Neither reason nor revelation establishes that this is impossible.”

I said: Since this is possible, and it is the word’s literal meaning, why should the word be diverted from that meaning to a figurative one? Whatever evidence the opponent adduces to show that He cannot be described by what the term denotes—provided that the evidence is sound—we concede that the meaning proper to a created being is excluded in His case. The word’s literal and apparent meaning, however, is a “Hand” befitting the Creator, just as knowledge and power befit Him—indeed, just as essence and existence do.

Adam to Him on the grounds that He created him with His two Hands necessarily means that He truly did create him with His two Hands, whereas He created these others by His command, “Be,” and they come into being, as the transmitted reports state.

Another point is that when the Arabs say, “In his hand is dominion,” or, “Your two hands made it,” two things are involved:

(First) Affirming the hand.

(Second) Attributing dominion or action to it.

The second frequently involves figurative usage. As for the first, however, they use such expressions only of a kind of being that truly has a “hand.” They do not speak of the “hand” of desire or the “hand” of water. Suppose, then, that His words, “In His Hand is dominion,” are understood to mean “by His power.” Even so, such figurative language is used only of one who truly has a hand.

The difference between His words, exalted is He, “what I created with My two Hands,” and His words, “what Our Hands have made,” is twofold:

(First): In the former, He attributes the act to Himself and explains that He created him with His two Hands; in the latter, He attributes the act to the hands.

(Second): In Arabic usage, a plural form may stand in place of the dual when there is no risk of confusion, as in His words, exalted is He:

“As for the man and woman who steal, cut off their hands”—that is, their two hands.

And His words:

“For your hearts have indeed deviated”—that is, your two hearts.

The same applies to His words, “what Our Hands have made.”

Allah, on pulpits of light, to the right of the Most Merciful—and both His Hands are right Hands—those who act justly in their judgments, with their families, and in whatever is entrusted to their care.” Narrated by Muslim.

And his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah’s Right Hand is full; no expenditure diminishes it, ever pouring forth by night and day. Have you considered how much He has spent since He created the heavens and the earth? It has not diminished what is in His Right Hand. The balance is in His other Hand; He raises and lowers it until the Day of Resurrection.”

Narrated by Muslim in his Sahih, and by al-Bukhārī, I believe.

Also in the Sahih, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“On the Day of Resurrection, the earth will be a single loaf of bread. The Compeller will turn it over in His Hand, just as one of you turns over his loaf in his hand while travelling.”

Also in the Sahih, Ibn ʿUmar, recounting the words of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The Lord, mighty and majestic, takes His heavens and His earth in His two Hands”—and he began clenching and opening his hands—“and says, ‘I am the Most Merciful.’ I looked at the pulpit moving beneath him, until I wondered, ‘Will it fall with the Messenger of Allah upon it?’”

In another version, he recited this verse from the pulpit:

“They have not appraised Allah with His true appraisal. The earth in its entirety will be in His grasp on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded in His Right Hand.”

He said: “He says, ‘I am Allah; I am the Compeller,’” and he went on to relate the report.

Also in the Sahih, Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘Allah will grasp the earth and fold up the heaven in His Right Hand, then say: “I am the King! Where are the kings of the earth?”’”

There is also the corresponding report of the rabbi.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section:

The objector said concerning the Most Beautiful Names:

“‘The Light, the Guide’: ‘the Light’ must certainly be interpreted figuratively, for light is a quality that inheres in what is corporeal, and it is the opposite of darkness. The True One—glory be to Him—is far above having an opposite. Were He light, it would not be permissible to attribute it to Himself in His words:

‘The likeness of His light’

for this would amount to attributing a thing to itself, which is impermissible.

“Regarding His words:

‘Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth,’

the Quran commentators said that this means the Guide of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth. This interpretation, however, is weak, because mentioning ‘the Guide’ after it would then be repetitive. It has also been said that He illuminates the heavens with the stars, or with clear proofs and compelling arguments. Light is a subtle, transparent body, so it cannot be predicated of Allah.

“Figurative interpretation is reported from Ibn ‘Abbās, Anas and Sālim. This refutes his claim that figurative interpretation negates the apparent meaning and has not been transmitted from the early generations. Were He truly light—as those who liken Allah to His creation maintain—there would necessarily be perpetual illumination, night and day.

translated_text:
And His words:

‘Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of good tidings and a warner,
and as one who invites to Allah, by His permission, and as an illuminating lamp.’

It is well known that he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was not a lamp in the familiar sense. Rather, he was called a lamp because of the guidance he brought; the clarity of his proofs was like an illuminating lamp. It is also reported from Ibn ‘Abbās, in another narration, and from Abū al-‘Āliyah and al-Hasan that this means the Illuminator of ‘the heavens and the earth’: their sun, moon and stars.

Among the sayings of those who know Allah is this: ‘The Light’ is He who illuminates the hearts of the sincere with belief in His oneness and illuminates the inmost hearts of those who love Him with His support. It has also been said: He is the One who gives life to the hearts of those who know Him through the light of knowing Him, and to the souls of His worshippers through the light of worshipping Him.”

(The answer): This statement and others like it do not constitute an objection to our position. Rather, it marks the beginning of their diminished respect for him, owing to what he supposes our position entails, or what he supposes we say in the manner he has described.

Allah Most High has said:

“Avoid much suspicion; indeed, some suspicion is sinful.”

And the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the falsest of speech.”

When a statement attributes to others views that are false according to reason and revelation, and then refutes those views, this constitutes falsehood and injustice. We seek refuge in Allah from that. Yet, despite its injustice towards us, if only it were sound and coherent discourse! We would then waive our claim against him, and people could benefit from the knowledge it contained. But it contains distortion of Allah’s Book, deviation concerning His verses and Names, and falsehood, injustice and transgression that infringe upon Allah’s rights. Even if we waive our own claim, Allah’s right rests with Him, not with anyone else.

translated_text:
And we shall set forth what is appropriate here in fulfilment of Allah’s rights and in defence of His Book and His religion. For the statements he has cited contain contradictions and flaws that I doubt he can keep track of, in several respects.

First: At the beginning, he said, “Light is a quality inhering in corporeality.” Then, at the end, he said, “A subtle, transparent body.” Thus, at the beginning he described it as an accident and an attribute, but at the end as a body—a self-subsisting substance.

Second: He reported that the Quran commentators interpreted this as meaning “the Guide,” and questioned that interpretation. Yet, at the end, he mentioned that among the sayings of those who know Allah is that “the Light” is He who illuminates the hearts of the sincere with belief in His oneness, illuminates the inmost hearts of those who love Him with His support, and gives life to the hearts of those who know Him through the light of knowing Him. This is precisely the meaning of “the Guide,” which he initially questioned. Thus, he first questions it, then presents it as a saying of “those who know Allah”—an expression that holds powerful sway over hearts. In fact, it is merely a saying of certain shaykhs who engage in a kind of exhortation that lacks rigorous examination.

Shaykh Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān included in Haqā’iq al-tafsīr various allusions: some are sound and beneficial statements; some are fabrications falsely attributed to their purported speakers, such as those transmitted from Ja‘far and others; and some are invalid, rejected reports.

The “allusions of the Sufi shaykhs” fall into two categories. One consists of allusions pertaining to spiritual states—those they make with their hearts. This is what distinguishes them, but this is not the place to discuss it. The other consists of allusions connected with words, such as those they derive from the Quran
