translated_text:
and the like. Such allusions involve drawing parallels and reasoning by analogy: relating cases not explicitly addressed in a text to those that are, much as jurists do when drawing parallels and reasoning by analogy in legal rulings. Here, however, this is employed in encouragement and warning, the merits of deeds, the ranks of men, and similar matters. If an “analogical allusion” constitutes a valid analogy, it is good and acceptable. If it resembles a weak analogy, it receives the same judgment. But if it distorts words by taking them out of their proper contexts and interprets them contrary to their true meaning, it belongs to the same category as the discourse of the Qarmatians, the Bātiniyyah, and the Jahmiyyah. Reflect carefully on this, for I have explained it in “The Principle of Allusions.”

(The third aspect)

Another contradiction is that he said this interpretation was transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbās, Anas, and Sālim, yet he mentioned only three interpretations.

(The first)

He is the Guide of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth. Yet he deemed this interpretation weak. If this weak interpretation is what was transmitted, then what a fruitless endeavour! For in everything he has said up to this point, he has transmitted nothing from the early generations except this interpretation, which he himself has deemed weak and discredited.

If, however, what was transmitted from these three is that He illuminates the heavens with the heavenly bodies, then he has contradicted himself in another respect. He subsequently mentioned that another report from Ibn ‘Abbās, as well as reports from Abū al-‘Āliyah and al-Hasan, states that He illuminates them with the sun, moon, and stars. This entails that what was initially transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbās and the other two must differ from what was transmitted from him in another report and from those not mentioned alongside him in the first.

And if the meaning is that He illuminated it with compelling arguments and proofs, then he has contradicted himself, for this is precisely the meaning of “the Guide”: His establishing proofs and arguments is part of His guidance. Yet he has deemed this interpretation weak. I do not know which is more astonishing: his presenting two interpretations, one of which falls within the meaning of the other, or his deeming the questioner’s interpretation weak, which entails deeming both interpretations weak—without realizing that he has rejected both. One must therefore understand the meanings of the interpretations one transmits and recognize that what one dismisses as weak must not be the very thing one has extolled.

(The fourth aspect)

It has become clear that he has transmitted from Ibn ‘Abbās, Anas, and Sālim only the interpretation he deemed weak, or something included within it. If their interpretation was “the Guide,” he explicitly declared it weak. If it was “the One who establishes proofs,” this falls within the meaning of “the Guide.” If it was “the One who illuminates through the heavenly bodies,” he presented that as a separate interpretation. If it was what he related from certain people of spiritual insight, that too falls within the meaning of “the Guide.” Since he has acknowledged the weakness of what he related from Ibn ‘Abbās, Anas, and Sālim, it provides no argument against us. Thus, regarding what he has related from “the early generations,” either he is reporting falsely or he is making a false allegation in declaring it weak. In either case, it provides no argument against us.

(The fifth aspect)

He has shown disrespect towards the early generations by attributing to them an interpretation he deems weak. He has presented them to people as having engaged in figurative interpretation, seeking thereby to establish an argument for figurative interpretation in general, even though he has acknowledged the weakness of this particular interpretation. Whoever advances an argument that he himself has declared weak, without realizing that he has done so, has shot himself with his own arrow. Whoever shoots the arrow of transgression will be struck down by it:

“Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.”

As for “demonstrating the unsoundness of the argument,” we say: Regarding his statement, “It must certainly be interpreted figuratively,” we concede neither that it must be interpreted figuratively nor that, even if this were obligatory, its obligation would be certain. Rather, the vast majority of Muslims do not interpret this name figuratively. This is the position of those who follow the early generations and of the majority of those who affirm the divine attributes among the theologians, jurists, Sufis, and others. It is also the position of Abū Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb, who mentioned it in al-Sifāt (The Attributes) and refuted the Jahmiyyah’s figurative interpretation of “the name Light.” He is the master of the Ash‘arī theologians who affirm the divine attributes—their earliest master. Abū Bakr ibn Fūrak reported this from him in his book Maqālāt Ibn Kullāb (The Doctrines of Ibn Kullāb), as did al-Ash‘arī. Neither attributed its figurative interpretation to anyone other than the Jahmiyyah, who are condemned by common agreement. This is also the position of Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī, which he mentioned in al-Mūjaz (The Epitome).

As for his statement that this occurs among the Most Beautiful Names, the hadith in which it is mentioned is the report of al-Tirmidhī. He narrated the Most Beautiful Names in his Jāmi‘ through al-Walīd ibn Muslim, from Shu‘ayb, from Abū al-Zinād, from al-A‘raj, from Abū Hurayrah. Ibn Mājah also narrated them in his Sunan through Mukhallad ibn Ziyād al-Qatawānī, from Hishām ibn Hassān, from Muhammad ibn Sīrīn, from Abū Hurayrah. Those versed in hadith have agreed that these two narrations are not the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Rather, each consists of the words of some of the early generations. Al-Walīd related these names from some of his Syrian teachers, as is explicitly explained in some transmission routes of his hadith.

For this reason, the particular names in the two versions transmitted from him differ: one narration includes names in place of those mentioned in the other. Those who compiled them would sometimes mention one name and sometimes another. They and others believed either that the Most Beautiful Names whose enumeration leads to Paradise were not a fixed set—rather, whoever enumerates ninety-nine of Allah’s names will enter Paradise—or that, even if they were a fixed set, two names with the same meaning could substitute for one another, such as al-Ahad (the One and Only) and al-Wāhid (the One).

Thus, the narration of Hishām ibn ‘Ammār from al-Walīd ibn Muslim, from him, as transmitted by ‘Uthmān ibn Sa‘īd, has “al-Ahad” in place of “al-Wāhid,” and “al-Mu‘tī (the Giver)” in place of “al-Mughnī (the Enricher),” the latter two being close in meaning. Al-Walīd lists these names after narrating the hadith from Khulayd ibn Da‘laj, from Qatādah, from Ibn Sīrīn, from Abū Hurayrah.

Hishām then said: “Al-Walīd also narrated to us, saying that Sa‘īd ibn ‘Abd al-‘Azīz had narrated the same to him. He said, ‘All of them are in the Quran: “He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity” …’” The list follows the one given by al-Tirmidhī, but al-Tirmidhī narrated it through Safwān ibn Sālih, from al-Walīd, from Shu‘ayb. Ibn Abī ‘Āsim also narrated it, and his list differs from al-Tirmidhī’s in some places.

All this makes clear that these names are material appended to and interpolated into the hadith from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in some transmission routes; they are not his words. For this reason, “others” compiled a different list, deriving the names from the Quran. Among them were Sufyān ibn ‘Uyaynah, Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others, as I mentioned in my discussion of this subject long ago. All this implies that, in their view, these names admit of substitution;

for the overwhelming majority of Muslims hold that Allah’s names are more than ninety-nine.

They—including al-Khattābī—said: In his statement,

“Allah has ninety-nine names; whoever enumerates them,”

the numerical restriction applies to the names described as being these particular names. Thus, the clause,

“Whoever enumerates them will enter Paradise,”

qualifies the ninety-nine. It is not an independent sentence, but occupies the accusative position grammatically. It may, however, be understood as an independent sentence without changing the meaning. The sense is: Allah has names numbering this many; whoever enumerates them will enter Paradise. This is like someone saying, “I have a hundred slaves whom I have set aside for emancipation, and a thousand dirhams which I have set aside for Hajj.” The numerical restriction applies to what bears this qualification, not to the total number possessed. For he did not say, “Allah’s names are ninety-nine.”

He said: This is supported by his words in the hadith narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad:

“O Allah, I ask You by every name belonging to You with which You have named Yourself, or which You have revealed in Your Book, or taught to any of Your creation, or kept exclusively with Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen.”

This indicates that Allah has more than ninety-nine names, which some believers enumerate.

Furthermore, the numerical specification in his statement,

“Allah has ninety-nine,”

is comparable to the Exalted’s words,

“Nineteen.”

When they considered them few, He said:

“And none knows the soldiers of your Lord except Him.”

It is all the more fitting, then, that none but He should know His names. Even if the former statement had been made on its own, it would imply the exclusion of any additional names only through the restrictive implication of a specified number. This is weaker than the restrictive implication of a qualifying attribute, and the disagreement over it is well known. that the ruling applies exclusively to it. For departing from the requirement of general inclusion in favor of singling something out—unless this is intended to restrict the ruling to it—would mean disregarding the grounds for general inclusion without any countervailing consideration, which is impossible.

Thus, in his statement,

“Allah has ninety-nine,”

giving this number may serve purposes other than restricting the total to it. (Among these) is his mention that enumerating them leads to Paradise. Had he stated the first sentence independently and followed it with the second as a separate sentence, that would have been perfectly sound. How much more so when speech is presumed to be connected rather than disconnected, making the conditional sentence a qualifying clause rather than an independent sentence. This is the preferable grammatical interpretation in Arabic, alongside the evidence already mentioned.

For this reason, he said:

“He is One and loves what is odd-numbered.”

His love for this indicates that it relates to enumeration: that is, He loves for this number of His names to be enumerated. If Allah’s names exceed ninety-nine, it is possible that enumerating any ninety-nine names leads to Paradise, without restriction to a particular set. This provides a basis for their view, although many people understand these to be specific names.

Among the latter, some say that there are only ninety-nine names in all. This is the view of Ibn Hazm and a group of others. Most of them, however, say: Even if Allah has more names, those for whose enumeration Paradise has been promised are a specific set.

In any event, identifying these names individually is not part of the Prophet’s own words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, as those knowledgeable about his hadith agree. Rather, various lists have been transmitted from the early generations, including the one mentioned by al-Tirmidhī and others besides it.

The hadith continues. In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Dharr said:

“I asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘Have you seen your Lord?’ He replied, ‘Light—how could I see Him?’ Or he said, ‘I saw light.’”

Thus, what occurs in the Quran and authentic hadith is “Light” in a construct phrase, as in His words:

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth,”

or “the Light of the heavens and the earth” and all who are in them.

As for his statement, “Since light is an inhering quality,” we say: Created light is perceptible to the senses and needs no explanation of its nature. It is, however, of two kinds: concrete entities and accidents.

“Concrete entities” include the very body of fire wherever it may be—the light of a lamp, of the lamp enclosed in glass, and the like. This is the light Allah used in His parable. Another example is the moon, for Allah called it a light, saying:

“He made the sun a radiance and the moon a light.”

There is no doubt that fire is a subtle, transparent body.

“Accidents” include the rays of the sun, moon, and fire that fall upon polished bodies and other surfaces. When a lamp is in a room, it illuminates the room’s various sides. That light and those rays falling upon the walls, ceiling, and floor constitute an accident: a quality inhering in a body.

It may be said that the attribute inhering in fire, the moon, and the like is not light, in which case the term would apply at one time to the substance and at another to an attribute. Hence daylight is called light, as He says

Allah has thereby opposed Allah in His command.” Narrated by Abū Dāwūd. Calling someone who opposes His command and judgment an “opposite” is like calling him an “enemy.” In this sense, Allah has many enemies and opponents. According to the first interpretation, however, there is undoubtedly nothing in reality that stands in opposition to Allah. Rather, such opposition occurs in the minds of the unbelievers: falsehood is the opposite of truth, and lying is the opposite of truthfulness. Thus, any belief about Allah that attributes to Him something from which He is exalted is contrary to sound faith in Him.

As for his statement:

“Light is the opposite of darkness, and the Truth is far too exalted to have an opposite,”

he is told:

The living is the opposite of the dead, and the knowledgeable is the opposite of the ignorant. One who hears, sees, and speaks is the opposite of one who is deaf, blind, and mute. Likewise, all the other names by which Allah is named have opposites, but He is exalted above being called by those opposites. Far exalted is Allah above being dead, powerless, needy, or anything of that kind.

As for the existence of a creature of His characterized by the opposite of one of His attributes—such as someone who is dead, ignorant, needy, or unjust—there are many such creatures. Indeed, most of His names have opposites found among existing beings. Such beings are not called “opposites of Allah”; rather, they are said to possess attributes opposite to Allah’s attributes. For incompatibility between attributes applies only within one and the same subject, not across two different subjects. Thus, for one characterized by death, life is incompatible with that state; and for one characterized by life, death is incompatible with that state.

translated_text:
And Allah, exalted is He, cannot be darkness or be characterized by darkness, just as He cannot be dead or be characterized by death. This objector has used the word “opposite” equivocally, without distinguishing between an opposite whose existence would be incompatible with the existence of the Truth, His attributes, and His actions; something among His creatures characterized by the opposite of His attributes; and something that opposes His commands and prohibitions. The first kind of opposite is impossible, whereas the other two occur frequently. Neither, however, is called an “opposite of Allah,” for possessing an attribute opposite to His attributes does not mean standing in opposition to Him.

Those who said, “Light is the opposite of darkness,” meant that the two cannot coexist in one and the same entity. They did not say that one thing cannot be characterized as light while another is characterized as darkness. Let anyone possessed of reason reflect on this denial of Allah’s attributes and this confusion.

As for his statement:

“If He were light, it would not be permissible to ascribe light to Himself in His words, ‘The likeness of His light,’”

there are two ways to answer this.

(First) We say: The texts of Allah’s Book and the Sunnah of His Messenger have named Allah the Light of the heavens and the earth. They have stated that Allah is light, and have also stated that He veils Himself with light. These, then, are three lights mentioned in the texts. The first has already been discussed.

(As for the second), it occurs in His words:

“And the earth will shine with the light of its Lord,”

and in His words:

“The likeness of His light,”

and in the report narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh from ‘Abdullāh ibn ‘Amr, who related a statement by

the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah created His creation in darkness and cast upon them some of His light. Whoever was reached by that light was guided, and whoever it missed went astray.”

Another instance is his supplication at Tā’if, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“I seek refuge in the light of Your Face, by which the darkness is illuminated and the affairs of this world and the Hereafter are set right, lest Your displeasure descend upon me or Your wrath befall me.”

This was narrated by al-Tabarānī and others.

Another instance is the statement of Ibn Mas‘ūd:

“With your Lord there is neither night nor day. The light of the heavens comes from the light of His Face.”

Another instance is his statement in the report narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh from Abū Mūsā, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stood among us and delivered four statements, saying: ‘Allah does not sleep, nor is it befitting for Him to sleep. He lowers the balance. The deeds of the night are raised to Him before the deeds of the day, and the deeds of the day before the deeds of the night. His veil is light—or fire. Were He to remove it, the radiance of His Face would burn all of His creation that His sight reaches.’”

This hadith mentions His veil. The narrator’s uncertainty between the words “fire” and “light” does not affect this, for pure fire of this kind, through which He spoke to Moses, may be called both fire and light. Likewise, Allah called the flame of a lamp light. This differs from dark fire, such as the fire of Hell, which is not called light.

There are thus three categories:

“Illumination without burning”: pure light, such as that of the moon.

“Burning without illumination”: dark fire.

(The second approach)

It may be said: This objection applies to you as well; it is not confined to those who call Him by the name He has given Himself and explained. Whether you say “Guide,” “Illuminator,” or something else, the one named “Light” is the Lord Himself, not the light ascribed to Him.

When you say, “He is the Guide, so His light is guidance,” you make one of the two lights a self-subsisting entity and the other an attribute. Those who call Him Light say the same. Since the objection applies to both positions and their proponents, singling out one of them as contradicting his own position is injustice and obstinacy in argument, or ignorance and deviation from the truth.

As for the views he has mentioned, there is no doubt that people have expressed more views on this matter than he has cited. The true and false reports, and the correct and mistaken opinions, circulating among the Muslim community are beyond anyone’s reckoning but Allah’s. Discussions of “the interpretation of Allah’s names, attributes, and speech” contain such quantities of sound and worthless material that none but the Lord of all worlds can reckon them. What matters, however, is truth, knowledge, and religion.

Long ago, in one of my writings addressed to a distinguished person, I wrote:

Knowledge is what is established by evidence, and beneficial knowledge is what the Messenger brought. What matters, then, is that we speak on the basis of knowledge: authenticated transmission and rigorous investigation. Anything else—even if some people embellish such things—is merely painted earthenware; otherwise, it is sheer falsehood, like what he has mentioned concerning this verse and others. translated_text:
commentary consisting of reports falsely attributed to the early generations and pronouncements about Allah and His Messenger based on mere opinion—indeed, on nothing more than a specious analogical or literary argument.

He has not named the commentators whose views he cites. Even so, he has challenged their position on false grounds. These commentators interpreted “Light” in the verse as “the Guide”; they were not interpreting “Light” among Allah’s Most Beautiful Names or in the hadith transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. His grounds for challenging their position are therefore invalid. We have mentioned this only to expose his inconsistency and show that none of the arguments he advances against us could persuade anyone of sound understanding, for inconsistency is the first stage of unsoundness. This interpretation has indeed been advanced by a group of commentators.

As for its being authentically attributable to Ibn ʿAbbās or anyone else, we have not established that.

It is well known that the “books of Quranic commentary” contain many fabricated reports attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, transmitted through al-Kalbī from Abū Sālih and through others. Reports must therefore be authenticated before they can serve as proof. One should consult the “books of Quranic commentary” in which transmitted reports are carefully scrutinized, such as the commentary of Muhammad ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī, who transmits the statements of the early generations with their chains of transmission—and set aside the commentaries of Muqātil and al-Kalbī. Earlier works include the commentaries of Baqī ibn Makhlad al-Andalusī, ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn Ibrāhīm Duhaym al-Shāmī, ʿAbd ibn Humayd al-Kashshī, and others, if one does not go further back to the commentaries of Imam Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and other imams. These are the most knowledgeable people on earth concerning authentic Quranic interpretations transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and reports from the Companions and Successors, just as they are the most knowledgeable concerning the Prophet’s hadith, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and reports from the Companions and Successors on foundational principles, subsidiary matters, and other branches of knowledge.

translated_text:
But if he establishes a principle on mere personal opinion and makes it a general rule, this will gain acceptance only among those ignorant of the evidence and unversed in the issues. It is through such transmitted reports—whose truth is not distinguished from falsehood—and such rational arguments—whose correctness is not distinguished from error—that those among the people of the East who went astray did so in foundational principles, subsidiary matters, jurisprudence, and Sufism.

How fitting that this should arise in connection with the verse of Light, in which Allah Most High says:

“And he to whom Allah has not granted light—for him there is no light.”

We ask Allah to grant us light.

We then say: Some commentators have explained His words,

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth,”

as meaning the Guide of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth. This interpretation neither undermines our position nor contradicts what we have said. They offered it when explaining the verse in which “Light” occurs in a possessive construction; they did not offer it as an explanation of “Light” without qualification, as you claim it occurs in the hadith. How can the two be equated?

Moreover, the statement of some of the early generations that He is the Guide of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth does not preclude His being Light in Himself. In their explanations, the early generations commonly mention some of the attributes of what a name denotes, or some of its types. This does not negate the other attributes of the entity so named—indeed, the two attributes may be inseparable—but the remaining types are not included in the particular type mentioned.

We have established this more than once in the preceding principles. Whoever reflects upon it will realize that most statements of the early generations concerning Quranic interpretation agree rather than conflict. An example is their explanation of

“the straight path”:

some say that it is Islam; another says that it is the Quran; and another, that it is the Sunnah

translated_text:
and the community; another says that it is the path of servitude to Allah. These are all inseparable descriptions of it, not divergent ones. Calling it by these names is like referring to the Quran and the Messenger by their various names—indeed, it is comparable to Allah’s Most Beautiful Names.

An example of the “second” is His saying, Most High:

“Among them are those who wrong themselves, those who are moderate, and those who are foremost in good deeds.”

A particular category among them may thus be mentioned, although the term “servant” encompasses them all. The one who wrongs himself neglects some obligations; the moderate one fulfills them; and the one foremost in good deeds draws near to Allah through voluntary acts after fulfilling the obligatory ones.

People engage in this according to their respective approaches to explanation and translation, illustrating the particular kind and the general category to make the meaning easier for the listener to grasp. It is like a non-Arab asking, “What is bread?” and being told, “This,” while someone points to a loaf. What is intended is the general category, not that particular loaf. Much of the early generations’ Quranic interpretation is of this kind: it is a form of teaching.

Thus, explaining

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth”

as meaning the Guide of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth is correct. One meaning of His being the Light of the heavens and the earth is that He guides their inhabitants. But it is not known that they excluded every other meaning. As for the claim that this was their intent, it is established that Ibn Masʿūd said:

“With your Lord there is neither night nor day; the light of the heavens comes from the light of His Face.”

The reports already cited from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—concerning the light of His Face, together with the narration mentioning “light,” are sufficient. This therefore establishes a meaning other than guidance.

Allah has also declared in His Book that the earth will shine with the light of its Lord. If it shines with His light, how could He not be light? This light cannot be attributed to Him merely on the grounds of creation, ownership, and special selection—as in His words, “Allah’s she-camel,” and similar expressions—for several reasons.

First: Light is never attributed to Allah when it is an attribute of independently existing entities. The lamps in this world are not called “Allah’s light,” nor are the sun and moon. Rather, one says, as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said:

“With your Lord there is neither night nor day; the light of the heavens comes from the light of His Face.”

In the supplication transmitted from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—it says:

“I seek refuge in the light of Your Face, by which the darkness is illuminated and the affairs of this world and the Hereafter are set right.”

Second: Created lights, such as the sun and moon, illuminate the earth in this world, and there is no light that is not among Allah’s creations. Likewise, saying that He is the Illuminator of the heavens and the earth does not contradict His being light. Every illuminator is light, so the two descriptions are inseparable.

Moreover, Allah Most High likened His light in the believers’ hearts to the light in a lamp: it is light in itself and illuminates other things. If His light in people’s hearts is both light and illuminating, then He Himself is all the more entitled to these descriptions. It is known that everything that is light also illuminates.

Moreover, He said:

“The likeness of His light is that of a niche containing a lamp.”

He thus gave a likeness of His light present in the believers’ hearts. This establishes that the light in the believers’ hearts—the light of faith and knowledge—is intended by the verse. He did not apply this likeness to the physical light of the stars. This also answers what he cited from Ibn ʿAbbās in another narration, and from Abu al-ʿĀliya and al-Hasan—though proof of the transmission’s authenticity must first be demanded, and the report from Ibn ʿAbbās is probably weak. For they included this among the meanings of light. But to claim that they understood His words,

“Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth,”

to mean nothing other than illumination by the sun, moon, and stars is certainly false. The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“You are the Light of the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them.”

It is known that the blind have no share in that illumination, nor does anyone screened from it by a barrier. The dead have no share in it, nor do the inhabitants of Paradise, for Paradise has neither sun nor moon. Indeed, it has been related that the inhabitants of Paradise distinguish night from day by lights appearing from the Throne, just as the sun appears to the people of this world. Those lights are therefore distinct from the sun and moon.

As for his statement, “It has been said: through proofs and arguments,” this is part of the meaning of “the Guide.” We have already discussed his statement: “This invalidates his assertion that interpretation involves setting aside the apparent meaning and has not been transmitted from

the early generations.” These words have been falsely attributed to me. Their author’s inconsistency has already been established, as has the fact that he cited nothing from the early generations except reports whose weakness he himself acknowledged.

What I now state and write—although I did not write it in my earlier responses, but have often stated it in gatherings—is that no disagreement has been transmitted from the Companions concerning the interpretation of any of the Quranic verses about Allah’s attributes. I have examined the Quranic commentaries transmitted from the Companions and the hadiths they narrated, consulting as many large and small works as Allah Most High has willed—more than a hundred commentaries. To this very moment, I have not found a report from any Companion interpreting any verse or hadith concerning the attributes contrary to its commonly understood meaning. Rather, their statements affirming and establishing these meanings, and explaining that these are attributes of Allah, contradict the claims of those who reinterpret them in ways that Allah alone can enumerate. Likewise, those who transmit and recount their statements relate a great deal of this.

To complete this point: I have found no disagreement among them except concerning passages such as His words, Most High:

“On the Day when a shin is laid bare.”

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās and a group of others that what is meant is hardship—that Allah will lay bare the hardship of the Hereafter. It is related from Abū Saʿīd and another group that they counted this among the attributes, on account of the hadith narrated by Abū Saʿīd in the two Sahih collections.

There is no doubt that the apparent meaning of the Quran does not indicate that this is one of the attributes, for He said:

“On the Day when a shin is laid bare.”

Such an interpretation is not a departure from the apparent meaning. Rather, that consists in diverting a verse from what it indicates, conveys, and is ordinarily understood to mean. Yet many of these people assign an expression a meaning it does not convey, then seek to divert it from that meaning and call this interpretation. This is mistaken on two counts, as we have explained more than once.

As for his statement:

“If He were truly light—as those who liken Him to creation falsely claim—there would necessarily be illumination continuously, night and day.”

We accept the implication of this statement of his. Those who liken Allah to creation say that He is light like the sun, whereas Allah Most High says:

“There is nothing like Him.”

He is not like any light, just as His essence is not like any other essence. Yet what the objector has mentioned is an argument against him, for He may be light that He veils from His creation, as stated in the hadith:

“His veil is light—or fire. Were He to remove it, the splendour of His Face would burn everything in His creation that His sight reaches.”

There is, however, an error in the attribution here: assigning this view to those who liken Allah to creation. It is also among the views of the Jahmiyyah, who deny the divine attributes, such as al-Marīsī. He used to say that He is light, although he was a leading figure among the Jahmiyyah. If, however, by those who liken Allah to creation he means those who affirm that Allah is truly light, then everyone who affirms the attributes is, in his view, guilty of likening Him to creation. This is “the language of the pure Jahmiyyah”: they describe everyone who affirms the attributes as someone who likens Allah to creation.

We have already mentioned that Ibn Kullāb, al-Ashʿarī, and others stated that denying that He is light in

Himself is the view of the Jahmiyyah and the Muʿtazilah, and that both affirmed that He is light. They and their leading followers established this position—how much more so the scholars of hadith and the imams of the Sunnah! Foremost among these believers in Allah and His names and attributes is the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, answered this very question raised by the objector when he said:

“His veil is light. Were He to remove it, the splendour of His Face would burn everything in His creation that His sight reaches.”

He thus explained that He is screened from created beings by His veil of light, so that the splendour of His Face does not reach them. Were He to remove that veil, the splendour of His Face would burn everything in His creation that His sight reaches. This veil, which prevents that splendour from burning them, clarifies the issue raised here.

As for what he cited from Ibn ʿAbbās in the other narration, it refers to certain forms of perceptible light. What he cited from the words of those who know Allah concerns some aspects of His guidance of His servants. These are simply particular examples, presented according to the needs of those being addressed. As we have mentioned, it was the practice of the early generations to explain such matters by mentioning particular instances as illustrations suited to their audience’s needs, not as exhaustive or restrictive definitions.

It has thus become clear that all the statements he cited come back to two meanings of His being the Light of the heavens and the earth. None of this indicates that He is not light in Himself.

and his saying:

“Indeed, I feel the breath of the Most Merciful from the direction of Yemen,”

and the words:

“Then He rose over the Throne,”

and:

“Allah’s hand is above their hands,”

and:

“And be patient with your Lord’s judgement, for you are under Our eyes.”

He replied—may Allah have mercy on him:

As for the first hadith, it has been narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through a chain of transmission that is not established as authentic. The well-known report is instead from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said:

“The Black Stone is Allah’s right hand on earth. Whoever clasps it and kisses it, it is as though he has shaken hands with Allah and kissed His right hand.”

Anyone who reflects on the transmitted wording will see that it presents no difficulty except to someone who has not reflected on it. For he said, “Allah’s right hand on earth,” qualifying it with the words “on earth.” He did not say simply, “Allah’s right hand,” without qualification. A qualified expression does not carry the same force as an unqualified one.

He then said:

“Whoever clasps it and kisses it, it is as though he has shaken hands with Allah and kissed His right hand.”

translated_text:
has been likened to someone who shakes hands with Allah. Thus, both the beginning and the end of the hadith make clear that the Stone is not one of Allah’s attributes, as everyone of sound reason knows. Rather, it explains that just as Allah Most High has appointed for people a House around which they perform circumambulation, He has appointed for them something to touch, so that this serves the same purpose as kissing the hands of persons of high rank. By customary practice, this brings the person kissing the hand closer and confers honour upon him. Allah and His Messenger do not speak in a way that misleads people; rather, people must be shown clearly what they should guard against. The hadith thus makes clear what rules out likening Allah to His creation.

As for the second hadith, the words “from Yemen” clarify its intended meaning. Yemen has no special connection with Allah’s attributes that would warrant such a supposition. Rather, from there came those whom He loves and who love Him, concerning whom He said:

“Whoever among you turns away from his religion, Allah will bring forth a people whom He loves and who love Him.”

It has been narrated that when this verse was revealed, he was asked who these people were, and he said that they were the people of Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī. Authentic hadiths have also been transmitted, such as his saying:

“The people of Yemen have come to you; their hearts are more tender and more gentle. Faith is Yemeni, and wisdom is Yemeni.”

These were the people who fought the apostates and conquered the cities. Through them, the Most Merciful relieved the believers of their distress. Anyone who confines this to Uways has strayed far from the intended meaning.

“Rising over the Throne is known; its manner is unknown. Belief in it is obligatory, and asking about its manner is an innovation. I consider you nothing but an innovator.” He then ordered that the man be removed, and he was taken out.

The statements of all the leading imams of religion—such as Ibn al-Mājishūn, al-Awzā‘ī, al-Layth ibn Sa‘d, Hammād ibn Zayd, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others—convey the same meaning as Mālik’s statement: we do not possess knowledge of the manner of the divine attributes. Knowing the manner of an attribute depends on knowing the manner of the one who possesses it. If the manner of the One possessing the attribute is unknown, the manner of His attribute cannot be known.

When the believer is kept clear of the path of distortion and denial of the divine attributes, and the path of likening Allah to His creation, he follows the straight path. For the Book, the Sunnah and consensus establish what is also known through reason: that Allah Most High—

“There is nothing like unto Him”

—has no likeness in His essence, His attributes or His actions. It is therefore impermissible to describe Him with anything peculiar to created beings, for He possesses the utmost perfection and is free from every deficiency. He, glorified be He, has no need of anything besides Himself, whereas everything besides Him stands in need of Him. Whoever claims that the Quran indicates such creaturely characteristics has made a false claim about the Quran. Nothing in the words of Allah, glorified be He, entails describing Him in this way.

Rather, a person may be led astray by his own faulty understanding, reading into the words of Allah and His Messenger meanings from which Allah, glorified be He, must be declared free. Yet the way one who upholds falsehood treats the words of Allah and His Messenger is as it has been said:

Many a critic finds fault with sound words,
Yet the fault lies in his own unsound understanding.

Scholars must make clear that Allah Most High’s attributes are free of the deficiencies that the ignorant imagine in them, and that the words of Allah and His Messenger do not imply any such deficiency. They must also explain that the Quran is clarification, guidance and healing. If anyone nevertheless goes astray through it, that is due to his own negligence. As the Most High says:

“And We send down of the Quran that which is healing and mercy for the believers, but it increases the wrongdoers only in loss.”

And He says:

“Say, ‘For those who believe, it is guidance and healing.’ But those who do not believe have deafness in their ears, and it is blindness for them.”

The shaykh, imam and eminent scholar, Shaykh al-Islām Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-'Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. I bear witness that none is worthy of worship except Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. May Allah bless him and his family and grant him abundant peace.

The hadith concerning “the believers’ seeing their Lord in Paradise on a day corresponding to Friday in this world” was narrated by Abū al-Hasan al-Dāraqutnī in his book on the vision of Allah. We know of no one who has compiled more on this subject than is found in the works of Abū Bakr al-Ājurrī and the hadith master Abū Nu'aym al-Asbahānī. Al-Dāraqutnī narrated it from Anas as traced back to the Prophet, and from Ibn Mas'ūd as a report stopping at him. Ibn Mājah also narrated it from Ibn Mas'ūd as traced back to the Prophet.

As for the hadith of Anas, al-Dāraqutnī narrated it through five or six chains of transmission, most of which state:

“The vision will take place at a time corresponding to Friday prayer in this world.”

Some versions explicitly state:

“Women will see Him on the festivals.”

Abū Hurayrah. Al-Tirmidhī said:

“This is a hadith that we know only through this chain.”

Suwayd ibn ‘Amr narrated something of this from al-Awzā‘ī. They said: Suwayd ibn ‘Abd al-‘Azīz also narrated it from al-Awzā‘ī. He said: He said: “A hadith from Sa‘īd.” Its meaning has also been narrated from Ka‘b al-Ahbār as his own statement, including the substance of the additional wording.

The basic hadith concerning the “marketplace of Paradise” was narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh, but he did not mention seeing Allah in it. Most of these hadiths, when their chains are considered individually, are open to criticism, whether mild or severe. Yet their number and the many routes through which they are transmitted make it highly probable that they are genuine; indeed, this may establish their authenticity with certainty. Moreover, statements agreeing with this have been transmitted from the “Companions” and the “Successors.” Such matters cannot be asserted on the basis of personal opinion; they can only be stated on the basis of received revelation.

Al-Dāraqutnī narrated through an authentic chain from Ibn al-Mubārak: Al-Mas‘ūdī informed us, from al-Minhāl ibn ‘Amr, from Abū ‘Ubaydah, from ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, who said:

“Hasten to Friday prayer, for Allah will appear before the people of Paradise every Friday on a mound of camphor. Their nearness to Him will correspond to their haste in attending Friday prayer in this world.”

He also narrated through an authentic chain to Shabābah ibn Sawwār, from ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Mas‘ūdī, from al-Minhāl ibn ‘Amr, from Abū ‘Ubaydah ibn ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, from ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, who said:

He said: No one used to precede ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd to Friday prayer. One day, however, he arrived to find that two men had preceded him. He said: “Two men, and I am the third! Indeed, Allah blesses the third.”

Ibn Battah also narrated it through this route with an authentic chain, adding:

“Then they return to their families and tell them of the honor He has newly bestowed upon them—something they had never seen before.”

This is a sound chain of transmission, deemed sound by al-Tirmidhī and others. It is said that Abū ‘Ubaydah did not hear directly from his father. Nevertheless, he knew his father’s circumstances well and received the reports concerning him from his father’s leading companions. This was a recurring practice of ‘Abd Allāh—may Allah be pleased with him—and would therefore have been well known among his companions, with many recounting it. None of ‘Abd Allāh’s companions was suspected of falsely attributing reports to him, such that one might fear that such a person was the intermediary. For this reason, people have relied on his son’s narrations from him as evidence, even though it is said that he did not hear directly from his father.

This has also been narrated from Ibn Mas‘ūd through another route. Ibn Battah narrated it in al-Ibānah with an authentic chain from al-Walīd ibn Muslim, from Thawr ibn Yazīd, from ‘Amr ibn Qays, reaching ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, who said:

“Allah will appear before the people of His Paradise every Friday on a mound of white camphor. Their nearness to Him will correspond to their haste in attending Friday prayer. He will then grant them life and honor such as they had never seen before.”

Faraj ibn Fadālah, from ‘Alī ibn Abī Talhah, from Ibn Mas‘ūd, who used to say:

“Set out early for Friday prayers in this world, for Allah appears before the people of Paradise every Friday on a mound of white camphor. Their nearness to Him will correspond to how early they set out for Friday prayer in this world.”

What Ibn Mas‘ūd reported is something known only to a prophet or someone who received it from a prophet. This establishes that Ibn Mas‘ūd received it from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. He cannot have received it from the People of the Book, for several reasons:

(First): The Companions were forbidden to affirm the truth of what the People of the Book told them. It is therefore inconceivable that Ibn Mas‘ūd—may Allah be pleased with him—would relate something reported by the Jews as religious instruction and base a ruling upon it.

(Second): Ibn Mas‘ūd—may Allah be pleased with him—in particular was among the Companions most vehement in censuring those who took reports from the People of the Book. May Allah be pleased with them all.

(Third): Friday prayer was prescribed only for us, and attending it early is prescribed only in our revealed law. It is therefore unlikely that such a report was received from earlier prophets. It is also unlikely that a Jew would relate such a virtue of this community, when they are described as concealing knowledge, withholding it, and envying this community.

Ibn Mājah also narrated it in his Sunan through another route, tracing it back to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, from ‘Alqamah, who said:

“I went with ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd to Friday prayer, and he found that three men had arrived before him. He said: ‘The fourth of four! Yet the fourth of four is not far behind. I heard the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him,

translated_text:
say: “People will be seated near Allah on Friday according to the order in which they went to Friday prayer: first, second, and third.”’ Then he said: ‘The fourth of four! Yet the fourth of four is not far behind.’”

This hadith is among those the scholars have cited as evidence that going early to Friday prayer is recommended. They have also included this meaning among the interpretations of His words:

“And the foremost will be the foremost.”

Some of them said: “Those who are foremost in attending Friday prayers in this world will be foremost on the Day of Increase in the Hereafter”—or words to that effect, for I do not presently recall the exact wording. This is supported by the Prophet’s statement, peace and blessings be upon him, recorded in the two Sahīh collections:

“We are the last, but will be the foremost on the Day of Resurrection, although they were given the Scripture before us and we were given it after them. This was their day, concerning which they differed, but Allah guided us to it. Thus, the people follow us in this regard: the Jews tomorrow and the Christians the day after tomorrow.”

Our precedence over them in the Hereafter is thus attributed to our having been given the Scripture after them, then being guided to the truth concerning which they differed, until we came to precede them in worship. Just as we preceded them in worship in this world, we shall precede them in receiving His honour in the Hereafter.

As for the hadith of Anas—the best-known of the hadiths concerning what will take place on Friday in the Hereafter, including visiting Allah, seeing Him, and going to the market of Paradise—the most authentic report from him is what Muslim narrated in his Sahīh, from Hammād ibn Salamah, from Thābit, from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“In Paradise there is a market which they will visit every Friday. A north wind will blow, sweeping over their faces and clothes, and they will increase in beauty and loveliness. Their families will say to them: ‘By Allah, you have increased in beauty and loveliness since we parted!’ They will reply: ‘And you, by Allah, have increased in beauty and loveliness since we parted!’”

translated_text:
This report states only that they visit the market, where they increase in beauty and loveliness, and that their families likewise increase in beauty and loveliness during their absence, even though they have not visited the market of Paradise.

If additional details found in some hadiths but not others are unacceptable, and are instead treated as a kind of contradiction, then no hadith concerning seeing Allah on Friday should be accepted in this discussion. None of those reports can match this hadith of Anas, for it alone, among all these reports, was included by the compilers of the Sahīh collections. Indeed, one might argue: if seeing Allah were exclusive, and the increase in the faces’ beauty and loveliness resulted from it, he would have mentioned that in this hadith. One might even argue that its apparent meaning is that their increased beauty and loveliness resulted only from the wind blowing over their faces and clothes.

If, however, the proper position is to say that the additional details in those hadiths do not contradict this report—even though this one is more authentic—because preference is given to one report over another only when they conflict, whereas, if one hadith relates something and another provides an additional detail that does not contradict it, that detail has the standing of an independent report, then this is indeed correct.

This is not the issue over which jurists differed when asking whether an addition to a scriptural text constitutes abrogation. That question concerns only legal rulings: commands, prohibitions, permissions, and their related matters. For example, Allah Most High says:

“As for the woman and the man guilty of unlawful sexual intercourse, flog each of them with a hundred lashes.”

And the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“For the unmarried with the unmarried: one hundred lashes and a year’s banishment.”

He also said to another man:

“Your son is liable to one hundred lashes and a year’s banishment.”

Here the scholars differed over whether this addition abrogates His words:

“As for the woman and the man guilty of unlawful sexual intercourse, flog each of them.”

The majority, however, hold that it does not constitute abrogation. This is the correct view, as established in the appropriate discussion.

translated_text:
As for one report containing additional details beyond another in “purely factual reports,” Muslims have not differed over the fact that this does not constitute abrogation, and that an addition is not rejected if it does not contradict the original report. If a man were to say, “I saw a man,” and then say, “I saw an intelligent man,” or “a learned man,” the two statements would not contradict one another. Thus unrestricted and qualified wording, and wording with or without additions, are treated differently in “prescriptive matters” and in “factual matters.”

That being so, it may be said: Other hadiths relate that the “market” comes after “seeing Allah, glorified be He,” just as people customarily disperse throughout the land and seek Allah’s bounty in this world after visiting Allah and turning to Him on Friday. This hadith’s mention of “their faces increasing in beauty and loveliness” does not imply that this results solely from the wind, for their wives have also increased in beauty and loveliness without sharing in that wind. Rather, the wind may have brought them a further increase beyond what they had already attained. It is also possible that this hadith gives an abbreviated account of what the other hadiths relate: that the cause of the increase is “seeing Allah Most High,” together with what accompanies it.

On this understanding, it is possible that “their believing wives” have seen Allah in their homes in Paradise, and that this “seeing” brought them increased beauty and loveliness—if seeing Him is the cause, as other hadiths explicitly explain. This is just as, in their earthly lives, the men would go to the mosques and turn to Allah there, while the women would turn to Allah in their homes through the noon prayer. The men increase in light in this world through this prayer, and the women likewise increase in light through their prayer, each according to their own measure. translated_text:
sees Him privately, at one and the same time, as related in several hadiths. Indeed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that each person can see one of His creations—the moon—privately whenever he wishes. With this clarified, we say:

Of “the hadiths containing details additional to this hadith,” some mention seeing Allah on Friday without relating its degree to Friday prayer in this world, as in Abū Hurayrah’s hadith about the market in Paradise. Others state that, on Friday in the Hereafter, people will sit near Allah in positions corresponding to when they set out for Friday prayer in this world, without mentioning seeing Him—as in the previously cited hadith of Ibn Masʿūd traced back to the Prophet. Still others mention both matters, and these constitute the majority of the hadiths.

The hadiths that mention “seeing Allah alone,” without relating its degree to Friday prayer, are not inferior to those that include this detail, either in number or in the strength of their chains of transmission. Rather, those that include this detail are more numerous, and some have stronger chains of transmission than those other reports. Even if those other reports were more numerous, and this additional detail were transmitted through only one chain comparable to theirs, its acceptance or rejection would be governed by the same ruling as the report to which it adds, since there is no contradiction.

Even supposing that some of these reports, but not others, became well known among “some of the general public” who hear hadiths from storytellers or critics, or among some who read hadiths without taking care to distinguish between them, this would carry no weight whatsoever. most of them—yet discerning hadith authorities regard them as having no basis; indeed, they may declare with certainty that they are fabricated. Conversely, how many things are well known among “those versed in hadith”—indeed, transmitted among them through numerous independent chains—yet most ordinary people, and even many scholars who have not devoted attention to hadith, have never heard them, or have heard them only at a distant remove. They either deny them or doubt them. Moreover, they have not mastered them as a scholar masters his discipline, as a grammarian masters grammar or a physician medicine. Even if they have retained something of them, it is merely a word here and a word there, which neither nourishes nor satisfies hunger. Such knowledge cannot be relied upon, nor can Allah’s religion be soundly maintained through it, nor does it discharge the community’s obligation to preserve the knowledge conveyed by prophethood and understand it. Imām Ahmad said: “Knowledge of hadith and understanding it are dearer to me than memorizing it.”

I shall now mention corroborating reports for what I have stated.

Al-Dāraqutnī narrated in his Book of the Vision of Allah—among the first reports he included in the section on Anas—through the following chain: Ahmad narrated to us; Sulaymān narrated to us; Muhammad ibn ʿUthmān ibn Muhammad narrated to us; Marwān ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us; Nāfiʿ Abū al-Hasan, the client of Banū Hishām, narrated to us; ʿAtāʾ ibn Abī Maymūnah narrated to us, from Anas ibn Mālik, who said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘On the Day of Resurrection, the believers will see their Lord, Mighty and Majestic. Those among them who have seen Him most recently will be those who see Him every Friday. Believing women will see Him on the Day of Eid al-Fitr and the Day of Sacrifice.’”

Al-Dāraqutnī also narrated, through a group of trustworthy transmitters, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawh al-Madāʾinī:

Sallām ibn Sulaymān narrated to us: Warqā’, Isrā’īl, Shu‘bah, and Jarīr ibn ‘Abd al-Hamīd—all of them—said: Layth narrated to us, from ‘Uthmān ibn Humayd, from Anas ibn Mālik, who said: I heard the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say:

“Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to me carrying in his palm something like a white mirror, with something like a black speck on it. I asked, ‘What is this in your hand, Gabriel?’ He replied, ‘This is Friday.’

“I asked, ‘What is Friday?’ He replied, ‘There is good in it for you.’ I asked, ‘What will there be for us in it?’ He replied, ‘It will be a festival for you and your people after you, and the Jews and Christians will follow you.’ I asked, ‘What do we have in it?’ He replied, ‘There is an hour in it during which, whenever Allah’s servant asks Him for something allotted to him, He gives it to him; and if it is not allotted to him, He stores up for him something greater in his Hereafter.’

“I asked, ‘What is this speck on it?’ He replied, ‘It is the Hour. We call it the Day of Increase.’ I asked, ‘What is that, Gabriel?’ He replied, ‘Your Lord has prepared a valley in Paradise containing dunes of white musk. When Friday comes, He, Mighty and Majestic, descends from ‘Illiyyīn upon His seat. The seat is surrounded by seats of light, and the prophets come and sit on those seats. The seat is also surrounded by pulpits of light and gold, adorned with jewels. Then the foremost in truthfulness and the martyrs come and sit on those pulpits. Then the inhabitants of the chambers descend from their chambers and sit on those dunes.

“‘Then He, Mighty and Majestic, reveals Himself to them and says, “I am the One who has fulfilled My promise to you and perfected My favour upon you. This is the place where I honour you, so ask Me.” They ask Him until they have exhausted their wishes. He then opens to them what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever imagined. This lasts as long as it takes you to disperse after the Friday prayer. These are of white pearl, green emerald, and red ruby, with chambers and doors of the same material, rivers flowing through them, spouses and servants within them, and fruit hanging low. Nothing do they long for more than Friday, when they may gaze still more upon their Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and receive still greater honour from Him.’”

Ibn Battah also narrated this hadith in similar wording from al-Qāfilānī: Muhammad ibn Ishāq al-Sāghānī narrated to us: ‘Abd Allāh ibn Muhammad ibn Abī Shaybah narrated to us: ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from Layth, from ‘Uthmān, from Anas. His version includes:

“Then their Lord, Exalted is He, reveals Himself to them and says, ‘Ask Me, and I shall give you.’ They ask Him for His pleasure. He says, ‘My pleasure has brought you into My abode and granted you My honour, so ask Me, and I shall give you.’ They ask Him for His pleasure, and He calls them to witness that He is pleased with them. He said: Then He opens to them what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever imagined. He said: This lasts as long as it takes you to disperse after the Friday prayer. Then He ascends, and the prophets, the foremost in truthfulness, and the martyrs ascend with Him, while the inhabitants of the chambers return to their chambers.”

He then related the remainder.

This chain establishes that this hadith was indeed transmitted from Layth ibn Abī Sulaym, thereby removing the objection concerning Sallām ibn Sulaym, since all the narrators preceding Layth in this second chain are leading authorities. As for the first chain, it seems to leave some misgiving, because Sallām narrated it from a group of well-known transmitters, and ‘Abd Allāh ibn Rawh al-Madā’inī narrated it from him. Assessments of this Sallām have differed. Ibn Ma‘īn once said, “There is nothing wrong with him.” Abū Hātim said, “He is truthful, and his hadith are acceptable.”

On another occasion, Ibn Ma‘īn was asked about him: “Is he trustworthy?” He replied, “No.” Al-‘Uqaylī said, “His narrations are not corroborated by other transmitters.”

Since the hadith has been transmitted through that sound chain, the grounds for blaming him fall away.

Al-Dāraqutnī also narrated it through this chain by a third route, from al-Hasan ibn ‘Arafah: ‘Ammār ibn Muhammad, the nephew of Sufyān al-Thawrī, narrated to us, from Layth ibn Abī Sulaym, from ‘Uthmān, from Anas ibn Mālik, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Gabriel came to me, holding in his palm something like a white mirror, with something like a black spot in it.”

He related the hadith in wording similar to what preceded, but did not mention: “That lasts as long as it takes you to disperse after the Friday prayer.” This strengthens the conclusion that the hadith has a basis in transmission from Layth. The omission of the additional wording does not undermine it, for neither the additions nor the omissions of ‘Ammār ibn Muhammad ibn Abī Ukht Sufyān may be relied upon as proof. We have mentioned his narration only as corroboration.

This hadith states that it is the righteous who return to their families. As for the prophets, the foremost in truthfulness, and the martyrs, they do not return at that time. It contains nothing either affirming or denying that women see Allah.

Abū al-‘Abbās Muhammad ibn Ishāq al-Sarrāj also narrated it: ‘Alī ibn Ashyab narrated to us: Abū Badr narrated to us: Ziyād ibn Khaythamah narrated to us, from ‘Uthmān ibn Muslim, from Anas ibn Mālik, who said:

translated_text:
Allah grants it to him, stores up its equivalent for him on the Day of Resurrection, or averts an equivalent evil from him. Friday is the best of days in Allah’s sight, and the people of Paradise call it the Day of Increase.”

I asked, “O Gabriel, what is the Day of Increase?”

He said, “In Paradise there is a spacious valley whose soil is white musk. Allah descends to it every Friday, and His seat is set in place. Then pulpits of light are brought and placed behind it, and the angels gather around it. Seats of gold are then brought and set in place. The prophets, the foremost in truthfulness, the martyrs, and the believers who dwell in the chambers then come and sit down. Allah smiles at them and says, ‘Ask.’ They say, ‘We ask for Your good pleasure.’ He says, ‘I am pleased with you, so ask.’ They ask for what they desire, and He grants them what they request many times over. He also grants them what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever imagined.

“Then He says, ‘Have I not fulfilled My promise to you and perfected My favor upon you? This is the abode of My honor.’ Then they return to their chambers, coming back every Friday.”

I asked, “O Gabriel, what are their chambers made of?”

He said, “Of a white pearl, a red ruby, and a green chrysolite, with their doors fashioned from the same material. Their spouses are within them, and their rivers flow continually.”’”

Abū Ya‘lā al-Mawsilī narrated a similar report in his (Musnad), from Shaybān ibn Farrūkh, from al-Sa‘q ibn Hazn, from ‘Alī ibn al-Hakam al-Bunānī, from Anas. I did not have its wording at hand.

Al-Dāraqutnī also narrated it through ‘Abd Allāh ibn al-Hamīm al-Rāzī: And ‘Amr ibn Qays narrated to us, from Abū Shabībah, from ‘Āsim, from ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Umayr Abū al-Yaqzān, from Anas. He also narrated it through Ishāq ibn Sulaymān al-Rāzī: ‘Anbasah ibn Sa‘īd narrated to us, from ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Umayr, from Anas ibn Mālik, in wording similar to the preceding account, without mentioning the additional wording.

It contains wording that reconciles the hadith of Anas in Sahīh Muslim with the other hadiths, including: “It remains so until the time corresponding to their dispersal after the Friday prayer.”

It was also transmitted through another chain, narrated by Abū ‘Umar Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Wāhid al-Zāhid, known as Ghulām Tha‘lab: Muhammad ibn Ja‘far ibn Abī al-Dumayk al-Marwazī narrated to us; Salamah ibn Shabīb narrated to us; Yahyā ibn ‘Abd Allāh al-Harrānī narrated to us; Dirār ibn ‘Amr narrated to us, from Yazīd al-Raqāshī, from Anas ibn Mālik. He related the hadith at greater length than the preceding versions. I did not have its wording at hand, but I think it contains the aforementioned addition. This chain of transmission is weak because of Yazīd al-Raqāshī and Dirār ibn ‘Amr, but it is considered alongside the preceding reports.

there according to the merit of their deeds. Then, at a time corresponding to Friday in this world, they are granted permission to visit their Lord. Those of the lowest rank—though none among them is lowly—sit upon dunes of musk and camphor. They do not consider those seated on chairs to have better seats than theirs.”

Abū Hurayrah said: “I asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, will we see our Lord, Mighty and Majestic?’

“He replied, ‘Yes. Do you have any doubt about seeing the sun, or the moon on the night when it is full?’

“We said, ‘No.’

“He said, ‘Likewise, you will have no doubt about seeing your Lord, Blessed and Exalted. No one in that gathering—meaning, no man—will be left without Allah addressing him directly. “‘The man will say, “My Lord, did You not forgive me?”

“‘He will reply, “Indeed. It is through the vastness of My forgiveness that you have attained this station.”

“‘While they are thus gathered, a cloud will cover them from above and rain down upon them perfume whose fragrance they have never encountered before. Our Lord will say, “Rise and go to the honours I have prepared for you, and take whatever you desire.”

“‘We will then come to a marketplace surrounded by angels, containing things the like of which eyes have never seen, ears have never heard, and hearts have never imagined. Then we will return to our dwellings, and our wives will come out to meet us

Al-Tirmidhī said: “This is a singular hadith; we know it only through this route. Suwayd ibn ʿAmr also narrated part of it from al-Awzāʿī.”

I say: Ibn Battah narrated this hadith in (al-Ibānah) through authentic chains of transmission from Abū al-Mughīrah ʿAbd al-Quddūs ibn al-Hajjāj, from al-Awzāʿī; and from Muhammad ibn Kathīr, from al-Awzāʿī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sālih, who said: “Al-Hiql related to me, from al-Awzāʿī, who said: ‘I was informed that Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib met Abū Hurayrah and said: “I ask Allah to bring us together in the marketplace of Paradise.”’” He then related the hadith as cited above.

This shows that the hadith is reliably preserved from al-Awzāʿī. In those narrations, however, he named the person who related it to him, whereas in the remaining, latter narrations he did not name him. Allah knows best.

The implication of this hadith is that their wives were not with them at the Friday gathering in the Hereafter or in its marketplace. However, it does not rule out their having seen Allah in their dwellings. The men attributed their increased beauty and splendour to sitting with the Compeller, and the women shared in this increase in beauty and splendour, as previously mentioned in the most authentic hadiths.

translated_text:
Section

What prompted me to write this was that, some time ago, a jurist asked me on behalf of the women of his household: “Will believing women see Allah in the Hereafter?”

I answered with what came to mind at the time: that the apparent meaning of the evidence is that they will see Him. I mentioned that Abū Bakr had narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that they would see Him on the Eids; that the hadiths concerning seeing Allah encompass all believers, men and women alike, as do the scholars’ statements; and that the reasoning underlying the matter supports this, according to my examination of the evidence. I also mentioned other points that do not come to mind at present.

It had occurred to me, concerning the report from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the reason for this was that the regular, communal occasions of “seeing Allah” in the Hereafter correspond to the regular congregational prayers. Since men have been prescribed to gather every Friday in this world to remember Allah, converse intimately with Him, behold Him with their hearts, and delight in meeting Him in prayer, He has appointed for them a gathering every Friday in the Hereafter to converse intimately with Him, behold Him directly, and enjoy meeting Him.

Likewise, since the established Sunnah directs women to go out for Eid—even young maidens and menstruating women—and believing women generally used to go out for Eid during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, their Eid of seeing Allah in the Hereafter was made to correspond to their Eid in this world.

translated_text:
What further supported this understanding for me was the report recorded in the two Sahīh collections from Jarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī, who said:

“We were sitting with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when he looked at the moon on the night of the full moon and said: ‘You will see your Lord just as you see this moon, with none of you deprived of seeing Him. So, if you can avoid being prevented from offering a prayer before sunrise and a prayer before sunset, then do so.’ Then he recited: ‘And glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting.’”

This is among the most authentic hadiths on earth, received with acceptance and unanimously acknowledged by hadith scholars and all other adherents of the Sunnah.

I observed that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, informed the believers that they would see their Lord, then followed this with his words:

“So, if you can avoid being prevented from offering a prayer before sunrise and a prayer before sunset, then do so.”

It is well known that when a ruling follows an attribute, or an attribute follows a ruling, linked by the particle fa (“so”), this indicates that the attribute is the cause of the ruling. This is especially so because mere temporal succession is impossible here: seeing Allah is mentioned in the hadith before the exhortation to observe the two prayers, yet that vision occurs in the Hereafter, whereas the exhortation occurs before it, in this world.

By “immediate succession,” grammarians do not mean that the wording of the second item comes after the first, for this occurs with or without fa, and with all the other conjunctions. Rather, they mean that what is expressed second occurs immediately after what is expressed first. Thus, when you say, “Zayd stood up, then ʿAmr,” this conveys that ʿAmr’s actual standing occurred immediately after Zayd’s—not merely that the speaker uttered the second expression immediately after the first. the ruling both logically and in actual existence, as in His words:

‘As for the male and female thief, cut off their hands.’”

“At other times,” its outcome precedes the ruling in knowledge and intention, but follows it in actual existence. For example, you might say, “The ruler will attend tomorrow.” If he does attend, his attendance will have been conceived and intended before the command to attend with him, even though it takes place after that command. This is called the final cause; jurists call it the wisdom underlying the ruling. It causes the intention to enact its ruling, while its ruling causes its actual realization.

Sometimes a “causal explanation” is expressed in terms of the actual beneficial outcome itself, making it appear that the cause follows its effect. In reality, however, the cause is seeking and desiring that outcome. Seeking and desiring well-being precede seeking the measures taken to achieve it, whereas those measures precede well-being itself in actual existence. There are many similar examples, as in the statements:

“When you recite the Quran, seek refuge.”

“When you rise for prayer, wash.”

Likewise, one says, “When you perform Hajj, take provisions.”

Thus, the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “You will see your Lord; so if you can avoid being prevented from observing two prayers,” continuing to “then do so,” imply that steadfastly observing them here is for the sake of seeking this vision, and that steadfast observance is a cause of this vision. This does not preclude such observance from bringing another reward for whose sake it is commanded, or from being a cause of that reward; nor does it preclude the vision from having another cause. For a single ruling may have several causes, and a single cause may give rise to several rulings.

The same applies to most hadiths promising reward, such as his words:

“Whoever prays two units of prayer without conversing during them with

himself will have his past sins forgiven. Whoever performs Hajj to this House, neither engaging in obscenity nor committing sin, will return free of sins as on the day his mother bore him.” And his words:

“A woman must not be married to a man who is already married to her paternal or maternal aunt, for if you do that, you will sever your ties of kinship.”

These and similar statements imply that offering those two units of prayer is a cause of forgiveness, as is an accepted Hajj, even though forgiveness has other causes.

This meaning is further supported by Allah’s words:

“Do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face.”

This supplication has been interpreted as referring to the Fajr and ‘Asr prayers. Since Allah has stated that they seek His Face through these two prayers, and has stated in this hadith that they will look upon Him, the exhortation to observe these prayers accords with this: whoever seeks His Face will look upon His Face—blessed and exalted is He.

When this is considered alongside the earlier point that Friday prayer is a cause of seeing Him at its corresponding time, as is the Eid prayer, it is fitting that these two prayers—the finest prayers, whose times are the finest times—should likewise be such a cause. Thus, it is fitting that prayer, which is the finest of deeds, and particularly the finest prayers offered at the finest times, should be a cause of the finest rewards at the finest times.

This is especially so given the hadith of Ibn ‘Umar narrated by al-Tirmidhī through Isrā’īl, from Thuwayr ibn Abī Fākhitah, who said: I heard Ibn ‘Umar say:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘The lowest-ranking inhabitant of Paradise is one who can see his gardens, spouses, delights, servants, and couches over a distance of a thousand years’ journey. The most honoured of them before Allah is one who looks upon His Face morning and evening.’ Then the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited: ‘Faces that Day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.’”

“Weak.” But Ibn Ma‘īn says this of more than one trustworthy narrator. As for Ibn Hibbān’s remarks, they introduce an innovation into the criticism of narrators.

The preceding hadith of Ibn ‘Umar promises the highest-ranking among them the vision “morning and evening.” The Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, made the morning and evening prayers a means of “seeing Allah,” and the Friday prayer a means of “seeing Allah” at its corresponding time. Together with the connection between prayer and the vision, these considerations strongly suggest that these two prayers are a means of seeing Allah at their corresponding times in the Hereafter. Allah knows best the reality of the matter.

This was what had occurred to me. Since women share with men in performing the deed that brings about the reward, they share with them in its reward. Where there was no shared participation in the Friday prayer, there was likewise no shared participation in looking upon Allah in the Hereafter; where there was shared participation in the Eid prayer, there was shared participation in its reward.

Then, a long time later, this “question” came up in discussion. I had forgotten what I had mentioned initially—not merely part of it—and the discussion prompted me to mention what I had said at first. I was told: “The hadith indicates that these two prayers constitute part of the cause of seeing Allah, not the whole cause. The evidence is that someone who performs them but does not perform the noon and afternoon prayers does not deserve the vision.”

I was also told: “The hadith indicates that the two prayers are a cause in general, so these two prayers could be a means of seeing Allah on Friday. Indeed, has it not been said that the highest-ranking person in Paradise is one who sees Him twice? How, then, can those who consistently observe these two prayers be the highest-ranking among them?”

I replied: The apparent meaning of the hadith indicates that these two prayers are the cause of this
