As for the Jahmiyyah, including the Muʿtazilah and others, meeting Allah is impossible according to their principles, since they hold that Allah cannot be seen either in this world or in the Hereafter. In this they contradict both the mass-transmitted reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the consensus of the Companions and the leading scholars of Islam that the believers will see their Lord in the Hereafter. They have advanced numerous rational and scriptural arguments whose invalidity we have explained at length, and we have set out the evidence from reason and revelation establishing the possibility of seeing Him.

This “issue” is one of the fundamentals concerning which the early generations and leading scholars sternly condemned those who disagreed, and on which they wrote well-known works.

Second: in their view, it is inconceivable that a servant should strive towards Him, be presented before Him, stand before Him, love Him, find Him, point to Him, return to Him, or turn back to Him. For these expressions imply that the servant’s condition in relation to Him in the Hereafter—with a distinction between the two—entails drawing closer to Him and coming near Him, and that the servant’s condition in relation to Him differs from his condition in this world. All of this is impossible in their view, for they do not acknowledge that the Creator is separate from creation—as the early generations and leading scholars unanimously affirmed, explicitly stating that He is separate from creation: He is not within created things, nor are created things within Him.

Rather, at times they maintain that His very essence dwells in every place; at times they identify His existence with the very existence of created things; and at times they describe Him in purely negative terms, such as being neither separate from the world nor dwelling within it. Either they describe Him in terms that entail His nonexistence and negate His reality, thus denying Him even while acknowledging Him. Their statements therefore combine acknowledgment with denial, and negation with affirmation. Some of them explicitly affirm that two contradictories can both be true, claiming that this is the pinnacle of true understanding and spiritual knowledge.

Or they describe Him in terms that entail His being identical with created things, a part of them, or an attribute of them. This likewise entails their affirming the Creator’s nonexistence and denying the Maker, although they acknowledge the existence of something other than Him, even while identifying Him with it. They then find among created things something distinct with respect to the lordship of the created being, and so affirm that two contradictories can both be true—as explained above.

They may also advocate idol worship, maintaining that idol worshippers are in the right, that worshippers of the calf are in the right, and that nothing other than Allah has ever been worshipped, since, in their view, there is no other: existence is one. They maintain that calling people to Him is impossible and that it is possible to draw near to Him and reach Him. They say: “He was not absent at the outset, such that one should be called to the final goal. Rather, He is identical with the one being called; how, then, can He call to Himself?”

The early generations and the leading scholars made very many statements condemning the Jahmiyyah and declaring them disbelievers. These people, together with those who agree with some of their claims that deny the reality of meeting Him, interpret “meeting” as encountering their Lord’s recompense. “They say, ‘When will this promise come to pass, if you are truthful?’”

The invalidity of interpreting the intended meaning as “meeting the recompense” rather than meeting Allah is necessarily evident upon reflection on the Book and the Sunnah. Its invalidity becomes apparent in several ways:

First: It contradicts the explanations transmitted from the Companions and the Successors.

Second: The omission of the genitive complement is accompanied by contextual indicators. The statement must therefore contain an indication that makes this clear, as has been explained concerning His words:

“Ask the town in which we were.”

If someone said, without qualification, “I saw Zayd” or “I met him,” while intending that he had met Zayd’s father or servant, this would indisputably be inadmissible in Arabic. Meeting Allah is mentioned in numerous places in the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger without qualification, and without any accompanying indication that meeting Allah means encountering some created thing of His, whether recompense or something else.

Third: If an expression occurs repeatedly in the Book, used time and again in the same way, yet what is intended differs from what it conveys and entails when used without qualification, and this is not explained, that would constitute concealment and obfuscation. Allah’s speech must be held above this. He has declared it to be a healing for what is in people’s hearts, guidance and mercy for the believers, and a clear exposition for mankind. O Allah, to You I have submitted, in You I have believed, upon You I have relied, to You I have turned, to You I have referred my disputes for judgment, and through You I have argued my case. O Allah, forgive me my past and future sins, what I have concealed and what I have done openly, and what You know better than I. You are my God; there is no god but You.”

In another wording:

“I seek refuge in You from Your leading me astray. You are the Ever-Living who never dies, whereas jinn and humans die.”

The hadith thus distinguishes between meeting Him and Paradise and Hell. Paradise and Hell encompass the recompense of the obedient and the disobedient. It is therefore clear that meeting Him does not mean encountering Paradise and Hell.

Fifth: The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained in several hadiths what it means for a servant to meet his Lord. For example, al-Bukhārī and Muslim report from ʿAdī ibn Hātim that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There is not one of you but Allah will speak to him, with neither a doorkeeper nor an interpreter between him and Allah. He will look to his right and see only what he has sent ahead, and he will look to his left and see only what he has sent ahead. The Fire will confront him. Whoever can protect himself from the Fire, even with half a date, should do so. If he cannot, then with a kind word.”

There are other similar hadiths.

Sixth: If “meeting Allah” meant encountering some created things—whether as recompense or otherwise—then this would occur both in this world and in the Hereafter, and the servant would constantly be meeting his Lord. Since Muslims know as a necessary truth of Islam that meeting Allah occurs only after death, it is clear that interpreting this “meeting” as encountering some created things is false. No Muslim has ever said that encountering these things in this world constitutes meeting Allah. If someone were to say that meeting Allah means a particular recompense—Paradise, for example, or Hell—he would be told: Nothing in this expression specifies such an encounter, nor is there any evidence for it. This interpretation is no more justified than saying that meeting Allah Most High means meeting some of His angels or some devils, or making similar arbitrary claims involving things found in both this world and the Hereafter. The wording gives no more grounds for specifying one of these than another. Thus, that interpretation is invalid.

Seventh: “Meeting Allah” has never been used to mean meeting anyone other than Him, either literally or figuratively. Nor has “meeting Zayd” ever been used to mean meeting someone else. Wherever such an expression occurs, it means meeting the one named, for the wording neither suggests nor indicates anyone else.

Eighth: His words:

“He is the One who sends blessings upon you, as do His angels, to bring you out of darkness into light. And He is ever Merciful to the believers.”

“Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be ‘Peace!’ And He has prepared for them a generous reward.”

If this “meeting” meant encountering His recompense, it would mean encountering the generous reward prepared for them. Having stated that they would encounter it, it would then be inappropriate to state that He had prepared it, since the purpose of preparing it is that they should receive it. How, then, could He mention the means after the intended end had been attained? This is an argument involving inarticulacy of a kind from which even an ordinary person’s speech is held free, let alone the speech of the Lord of the worlds. Moreover, the meeting is coupled with a greeting, which occurs only in a meeting in the familiar sense, not merely in receiving some created delight.

Ninth: In the authentic hadith, the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him; and whoever dislikes meeting Allah, Allah dislikes meeting him.”

Here he stated that Allah loves to meet one servant and dislikes meeting another. This cannot be interpreted as referring to recompense, because Allah does not dislike anyone’s recompense, nor is recompense something Allah meets. Moreover, if He may meet some created thing, such as recompense or anything else, then the servant may meet Him. The objection raised against His meeting the servant applies equally to His meeting all other created things. This, then, amounts to nullifying the text.

Alternatively, if it is said, “Rather, He does meet some of them,” then the Jahmī’s position becomes self-contradictory and collapses. The proofs that this position is false are almost innumerable. The present discussion of this request for a fatwa leaves no room to mention many of them, let alone most.

Section

As for the questioner’s words, “How is it conceivable for us to love what we neither know nor have any awareness of?” and the rest of his question, the answer is: this is another major question—the question of the believer’s love for his Lord.

The Quran and Sunnah expressly affirm this, as in His words:

“Among mankind are those who take others besides Allah as equals, loving them as they love Allah. But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

And His words:

“Say: If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins.”

And His words:

“Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your kindred, the wealth you have acquired, the trade whose decline you fear, and the homes you cherish are dearer to you than Allah, His Messenger, and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings about His command.”

And His words, exalted is He:

“Allah will bring forth a people whom He loves and who love Him”—to the end of the verse.

It is also authentically reported that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Whoever possesses three qualities will taste the sweetness of faith: that Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than all else; that he loves a person solely for Allah’s sake; and that he hates returning to disbelief as much as he hates being cast into the Fire.”

There are many other texts like these. The early generations of the Muslim community, its imams, and its shaykhs understood this love in its true sense. The first to deny its reality was the leading figure of the Jahmiyyah, al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham, who was consequently killed by

Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī in Wāsit on the Day of Sacrifice. He said:

“O people, offer your sacrifices—may Allah accept them—for I am sacrificing al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham. He claimed that Allah did not take Abraham as a close friend and did not truly speak to Moses. Exalted is Allah, far above what al-Jaʿd says!”

Then he stepped down and slaughtered him.

These people denied the reality of “close friendship” because close friendship is akin to love. They also denied the reality of “speaking,” interpreting it as something Allah creates in certain physical bodies, or as a kind of inspiration. Some groups among them even claimed that one of us might be spoken to just as Moses, peace be upon him, was spoken to—indeed, that he might hear the very same thing Moses heard. Yet Allah Most High has made clear that Moses was distinguished by this from the other prophets, let alone the rest of the believers and Allah’s allies. As He, Most High, says:

“Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes”—up to His words: “And Allah spoke to Moses directly.”

He thus distinguished between revelation and speaking, just as He distinguished between revelation and speaking from behind a veil in His words:

“It is not for any human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation or from behind a veil.”

He likewise made this distinction clear in His words:

“Those messengers—We favored some of them over others. Among them were those to whom Allah spoke, and He raised some of them in rank.”

If they reflected on their own words, they would realize that it is impossible to love worshipping Him or to love His allies unless He Himself is loved. If they suppose that He is not loved for His own sake, then loving the deeds through which food and drink are obtained is, in reality, merely loving food, drink, and sexual intercourse. This would be no different from loving other objects of desire. Thus, love for Allah and His Messenger would, in reality, amount only to loving food and drink, if—as these people maintain—Allah is not loved for His own sake.

This “issue” is the foundation of worshipping Allah, just as the “first issue” is the foundation of affirming Allah. That entails giving up one’s life and wealth, as the Most High says:

“Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for Paradise”—to the end of the verse.

For this reason, He describes those who love Him and whom He loves as:

“Humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers, striving in the cause of Allah and fearing no critic’s blame.”

Indeed, the root of “friendship” is love, and the root of “enmity” is hatred. Denying love and hatred entails denying Allah’s friendship and enmity—as when some jurists rejected the words, “Whoever You take as an enemy will never attain honor.” And He says:

“Do not take My enemies and your enemies as allies.”

This is an extensive subject. My writings on these two foundations run to numerous volumes, and the statements of earlier and later people of knowledge and faith on this subject are available.

translated_text:

Indeed, there is no one in existence whom we love or hate and whom we know as Allah knows them. Knowledge may also be attained through inference and reflection. Undoubtedly, believers know their Lord in this world, though they differ in their degrees of knowledge, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, knows Allah better than any of us. Yet he said:

“I cannot adequately praise You; You are as You have praised Yourself.”

This relates to understanding how knowledge increases and decreases, which is connected with the question of faith increasing and decreasing—a major question.

The position upheld by the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars is that faith itself, which resides in the heart, admits of degrees, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Bring out of the Fire whoever has an atom’s weight of faith in his heart.”

As for the increase and decrease of righteous deeds performed by the limbs, this is agreed upon, although there is disagreement over whether such deeds are included in faith as such. Some of this disagreement is merely verbal. Nevertheless, the position of the leading scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah and hadith—which is also the school of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and others—is that faith consists of words and deeds, and increases and decreases.

The leading Muslim scholars of the four schools and others, together with all the Companions and those who followed them in righteousness, agree that a believer does not become a disbeliever merely by committing a sin, as the Khawārij maintain, nor is he stripped of all faith, as the Muʿtazilah maintain.

Some people, however, have said that everyone’s faith is equal, so that the faith of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar does not differ in degree from the faith of the openly sinful. They base this on the premise that faith is assent in the heart and on the tongue, or in the heart alone, and that such assent does not admit of degrees.

The early generations and the leading scholars generally, however, hold that people’s faith is not equal but varies in degree, and that the faith of the earliest forerunners is more complete than that of those guilty of major sins.

The disagreement rests on two fundamental questions. The first is whether deeds are included in faith as such. Deeds unquestionably vary in degree, so those who include them in faith as such affirm that faith varies in degree.

Those who do not include deeds in faith as such must address the second question: does the faith within the heart vary in degree? Those who deny such variation have supposed that the heart contains nothing that unquestionably admits of degrees—such as love of Allah, fear of Him, hope in Him, reliance upon Him, and similar things that they may exclude from mere assent. Yet assent itself also varies in degree in several respects.

One is that assent to what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought may be general or detailed; the details fall within the general. The assent of someone who knows the Quran and its meanings, and the hadith and its meanings, and affirms all this in detail is not like that of someone who affirms that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, but does not know or understand most of what he brought.

Another is that firmly established assent, consciously held in mind, is more complete than knowledge whose attainment is sought while one is heedless of it.

Another is that assent itself varies in its very nature. Section

As for the questioner’s statement:

“An objection may be raised to this question: if his love of meeting Allah arises from the bliss he has seen, then his love is for the bliss he will enjoy, rather than for meeting Allah for its own sake.”

He may be answered as follows:

That is not so. Rather, meeting Allah is of two kinds: “a welcome meeting” and “an unwelcome meeting.” Sulaymān ibn ‘Abd al-Malik asked Abū Hāzim Salamah ibn Dīnār al-A‘raj, “What is it like to come before Allah Most High?”

He replied, “The doer of good is like someone returning to his master after an absence, whereas the evildoer is like a runaway slave brought before his master.”

Since there are two kinds of meeting—and when speaking of them, one can distinguish between them only by describing the qualities of each—the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, described the “welcome meeting” in terms of the good tidings that precede it and the honour that accompanies it, and the “unwelcome meeting” in terms of the tidings of evil that precede it and the humiliation that accompanies it.

The believer thus declares that his meeting with Allah will be welcome, while the unbeliever is informed that his meeting with Allah will be unwelcome. The believer therefore loves to meet Allah, while the unbeliever hates to meet Allah. Allah, in turn, loves to meet the former and hates to meet the latter: “a fitting recompense.” For the recompense is of the same nature as the deed, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “Those who show mercy

will be shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Show mercy and you will be shown mercy. Show mercy to those on earth, and the One in heaven will show you mercy.” He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“Whoever relieves a believer of one of the hardships of this world, Allah will relieve him of one of the hardships of the Day of Resurrection. Whoever makes things easier for someone in financial difficulty, Allah will make things easier for him in this world and the Hereafter. Whoever conceals a Muslim’s faults, Allah will conceal his faults in this world and the Hereafter. Allah helps His servant as long as His servant helps his brother.”

In an authentic hadith conveying Allah’s words:

“Whoever remembers Me within himself, I remember him within Myself. Whoever remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a better gathering. Whoever draws near to Me by a handspan, I draw near to him by an arm’s length. Whoever draws near to Me by an arm’s length, I draw near to him by the length of two outstretched arms. Whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him at a run.”

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“Whoever has two tongues in this world will have two tongues of fire on the Day of Resurrection.”

He also said:

“Whoever listens to people’s conversation when they dislike his doing so will have molten lead poured into his ears on the Day of Resurrection.”

He also said:

“A man may persist in begging until he comes on the Day of Resurrection without a shred of flesh on his face.”

Allah Most High said:

“Let them pardon and overlook. Would you not love for Allah to forgive you?”

Allah Most High also said:

“Whether you reveal a good deed or conceal it, or pardon a wrong, Allah is ever Pardoning, All-Powerful.”

There are many such passages in the Quran and Sunnah, showing that recompense is of the same nature as the deed.

In the authentic hadith narrated by al-Bukhārī in his Sahīh from Abū Hurayrah, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah says: ‘Whoever shows enmity to an ally of Mine has openly declared war against Me. My servant draws near to Me through nothing comparable to fulfilling what I have made obligatory upon him, and My servant continues

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām said in his “Letter to the People of Bahrain,” concerning their disagreement over the Friday prayer:

What prompted this was that your delegation told us of divisions and disagreements among you, even reporting that matters had come close to fighting. They mentioned that the cause was disagreement over “whether the unbelievers will see their Lord.” We had not imagined that this issue would bring matters to such a point, for the matter is a minor one.

What is essential, and what every Muslim must believe, is that the believers will see their Lord in the Hereafter, on the plain of Resurrection and after entering Paradise. This is established by the hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, which the scholars of hadith recognize as mass-transmitted. For he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, informed us:

“We shall see our Lord as we see the moon on the night when it is full and the sun at midday, without suffering any hardship in seeing Him.”

Seeing Him, glorified be He, is the highest degree of bliss in Paradise and the ultimate aspiration of those who worshipped Allah with sincere devotion to Him alone. Yet their vision of Him will vary in degree according to their closeness to Allah and their knowledge of Him.

The view held by the majority of the early generations is that whoever denies that Allah will be seen in the Hereafter is an unbeliever. If knowledge of this has not reached him, he is to be instructed, just as someone whom the laws of Islam have not reached is instructed. If he persists in denial after this knowledge has reached him, he is an unbeliever.

The hadiths and reports concerning this are numerous and well known. Scholars have devoted books to them, such as al-Dāraqutnī’s Book of the Vision of Allah and the works of Abū Nu‘aym and al-Ājurrī. They have also been cited by authors of works on the Sunnah, such as Ibn Battah, al-Lālakā’ī, and Ibn Shāhīn, and, before them, ‘Abd Allāh ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Hanbal ibn Ishāq, al-Khallāl, al-Tabarānī, and others. They have also been collected by the compilers of the Sahīh, Musnad, and Sunan collections, as well as others.

As for the question of whether the unbelievers will see Allah, widespread discussion and disagreement over it first arose—as far as we have learned—after three hundred years had passed since the Hijrah. Some scholars refrained from discussing it, while others addressed it and differed, holding three positions. Yet I know of no instance in which those who disagreed over it cursed or shunned one another on its account, for all three groups included people of virtue who adhered to the Sunnah.

Discussion of this question closely resembles discussion of whether the unbelievers will be called to account. By agreement, no one is declared an unbeliever over this question. The correct view is also that no one should be subjected to intolerance or shunned on its account. Abū al-Hasan ibn Bashshār is reported to have said: “One should not pray behind anyone who says that they will be called to account.”

translated_text:
the followers of Imām Ahmad, although most of them say that they will not be called to account. Other scholars and speculative theologians have also differed over this matter.

“Reckoning” may mean encompassing all their deeds in knowledge, recording them in scrolls, presenting them to the unbelievers, rebuking them for what they have done, and increasing or decreasing their punishment according to the greater or lesser degree of their unbelief. This kind of reckoning is established by agreement.

“Reckoning” may also mean weighing good deeds against evil deeds to determine which outweighs the other. The unbeliever has no good deeds to be weighed against his evil deeds, since all his deeds have been rendered void. His deeds are weighed only to show how light his scales are, not to establish that his good deeds outweigh his evil deeds.

“Reckoning” may also refer to the question of whether Allah Himself speaks to them. The Quran and hadith indicate that Allah speaks to them with rebuke, censure, and humiliation, not with words of nearness, honour, and mercy, although some scholars have denied altogether that He speaks to them.

The three positions concerning the unbelievers’ seeing Allah are:

First: The unbelievers will not see their Lord under any circumstances, whether they openly display their unbelief or conceal it. This is the position of most later scholars, and the general wording of the earlier scholars supports it. It is also the position of the majority of the followers of Imām Ahmad and others.

Second: He will be seen by those who outwardly profess monotheism among the believers and hypocrites of this nation, as well as those remaining from among the People of the Book. This will take place on the plain of the Resurrection; then He will veil Himself from the hypocrites

translated_text:
Tha‘lab say, concerning His words—

“And He is ever Merciful to the believers”;

“Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be, ‘Peace’”—

that the scholars of Arabic unanimously agree that meeting here can only mean seeing directly with one’s own eyes.’”

As for the first group, some of them maintained that the Quranic evidence that the believers will see their Lord is not His saying:

“Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be, ‘Peace.’”

Rather, the evidence lies in other verses, such as His words:

“Faces that Day will be radiant, looking at their Lord”;

“For those who do good is the best reward—and more”;

“Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss, on couches, looking on”;

and “They will have whatever they wish therein, and with Us is more”;

and other such verses.

Among the strongest evidence cited by those who affirm this vision is the report recorded by Muslim in his Sahīh, from Suhayl ibn Abī Sālih, from his father, from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said:

“People asked Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘O Messenger of Allah, will we see our Lord on the Day of Resurrection?’

He replied, ‘Do you have any difficulty seeing the sun at noon when no clouds obscure it?’

They said, ‘No, O Messenger of Allah.’

He said, ‘Do you have any difficulty seeing the moon on the night of the full moon when no clouds obscure it?’

They said, ‘No, O Messenger of Allah.’

He said, ‘By Him in whose Hand is my soul, you will have no more difficulty seeing your Lord than you have seeing either of them.’

He continued, ‘Then He will meet the servant and say, “O so-and-so, did I not honour you? Did I not make you a leader? Did I not give you a wife? Did I not subject horses and camels to you, and leave you to rule and take a quarter of the spoils?”

The servant will say, “Yes, my Lord.”

He will say, “Did you think that you would meet Me?”

He will say, “My Lord, no.”

He will say, “Today I will forget you just as you forgot Me.”

Then He will meet the second and say, “Did I not honour you? Did I not make you a leader? Did I not give you a wife? Did I not subject horses and camels to you, and leave you to rule and take a quarter of the spoils?”

He continued: He will reply, “Yes, my Lord.” He will say, “Did you think that you would meet Me?” He will reply, “My Lord, no.” He will say, “Today I will forget you just as you forgot Me.”

Then He will meet the third and say the same to him. He will reply, “My Lord, I believed in You, Your Book and Your messengers. I prayed, fasted and gave charity.” He will speak as highly of himself as he can. Then he will be told, “Shall We bring forth Our witness against you?” He will wonder to himself, “Who will testify against me?” His mouth will then be sealed, and his thigh will be told, “Speak!” His thigh, flesh and bones will speak of his deeds. This is done so that his own testimony leaves him without excuse. That is the hypocrite with whom Allah is angry.’”

Muslim’s narration ends here. In another narrator’s version—which matches Muslim’s narration and is likewise authentic—he said:

“Then a herald will proclaim, ‘Let every community follow what it used to worship!’ The allies of the devils will follow the devils, and the Jews and Christians will follow their allies into Hell. Then we will remain, O believers. Our Lord will come to us—and He is our Lord—and say, ‘Why are these people standing here?’ We will say, ‘We are Allah’s believing servants. We worshipped Him, and He is our Lord. He will come to us and reward us, and this is where we stand.’

“He will say, ‘I am your Lord, so proceed.’ Then the bridge will be laid down, with hooks of fire upon it that snatch people away. At that point I will be permitted to intercede: ‘O Allah, grant safety! O Allah, grant safety!’

“When they reach the bridge, everyone who has spent a pair of things from his possessions in Allah’s cause will be called by all the keepers of Paradise: ‘O servant of Allah! O Muslim! There is good here, so come! O servant of Allah! O Muslim! There is good here, so come!’

“Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, that servant has nothing to lose: he may leave one gate and enter through another.’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, tapped him on the shoulders and said, ‘By Him in whose Hand is my soul, I hope that you will be among them.’”

translated_text:
This is an authentic hadith. It states that the disbeliever and the hypocrite meet their Lord.

It may be said that its apparent meaning is that all creation will see their Lord, and Allah will meet each servant at that point. However, Ibn Khuzaymah, Judge Abū Ya‘lā and others said that the “meeting” mentioned in the report is distinct from seeing Him; it does not mean that Allah showed Himself to the one to whom He addressed these words. These scholars say that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stated that the believers would see their Lord, since they asked, “Will we see our Lord?” The pronoun refers to the believers. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then mentioned that the disbeliever would meet his Lord, who would rebuke him. After that, each community would follow what it used to worship, and only thereafter would the believers see Him.

This is clarified by the report in the two Sahīh collections, narrated by al-Zuhrī from Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib and ‘Atā’ ibn Yazīd, from Abū Hurayrah:

The people asked, “O Messenger of Allah, will we see our Lord on the Day of Resurrection?”

He said, “Do you have any doubt about seeing the moon on the night when it is full, with no clouds obscuring it?”

They replied, “No, O Messenger of Allah.”

He said, “Do you have any doubt about seeing the sun when no clouds obscure it?”

They replied, “No.”

He said, “You will see Him just as clearly. The people will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection, and He will say, ‘Whoever used to worship anything, let him follow it.’ Some will follow the sun, some will follow the moon, and some will follow false objects of worship. This community will remain, including its hypocrites. Allah will come to them and say, ‘I am your Lord.’ They will reply, ‘We will remain here until our Lord comes to us. When our Lord comes, we will recognize Him.’ Then Allah will come to them in His form which they recognize and say, ‘I am your Lord.’ They will reply, ‘You are our Lord,’ and recognize Him. The bridge will be laid across the midst of Hell, and I will be the first of the messengers to cross with my community; and no

They replied, “Yes.”

He said, “They resemble the thorns of the sa‘dān plant, but none knows their immense size except Allah. They will snatch people according to their deeds. When Allah wishes to show mercy to whomever He wills among the people of the Fire, He will command the angels to bring out those who used to worship Allah. They will bring them out, recognizing them by the marks of prostration, for Allah has forbidden the Fire to consume the marks of prostration. They will emerge from the Fire charred, and the water of life will be poured over them. They will then grow as a seed grows in the debris carried by a flood.

“Then Allah will finish judging between His servants, and a man will remain between Paradise and the Fire—the last of the people of the Fire to enter Paradise. Facing the Fire, he will say, ‘My Lord, turn my face away from the Fire! Its stench has tormented me, and its fierce heat has burned me.’

“He will say, ‘If this is done for you, can you be expected to ask for nothing else?’

“He will reply, ‘I will ask for nothing else, by Your might!’ He will give Allah whatever pledges and covenants He wills, and Allah will turn his face away from the Fire. When He turns him toward Paradise and he sees its beauty, he will remain silent for as long as Allah wills him to remain silent. Then he will say, ‘My Lord, bring me close to the gate of Paradise.’

“Allah will say to him, ‘Have you not already given pledges and a covenant that you would ask for nothing beyond what you had requested?’

“He will reply, ‘My Lord, let me not be the most wretched of Your creation.’

“He will say, ‘If I grant you that, can you be expected to ask for nothing else?’

Once the believers have been delivered from the Fire—by Him in Whose Hand is my soul—no one will plead more earnestly with Allah to secure a right in full than the believers will plead with Allah on the Day of Resurrection for their brothers who are in the Fire.’”

This hadith contains evidence that they saw Him the first time before He said, “Let every community follow what it used to worship.” This is the general “first vision” mentioned in the account of the “first vision” narrated from Abū Hurayrah. In that hadith, he related the vision and the meeting; only afterwards does He say, “Let every community follow what it used to worship.”

A similar account also appears in an authentic hadith narrated by al-‘Alā’ from his father, from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah will gather the people on the Day of Resurrection on a single plain. Then the Lord of the worlds will appear to them and say, ‘Will the people not follow what they used to worship?’ The cross will be made to appear to its worshipper, fire to its worshipper, and the image to its worshipper. They will follow what they used to worship.

“The Muslims will remain, and the Lord of the worlds will appear to them and say, ‘Will you not follow the people?’

“They will reply, ‘We seek refuge in Allah from You! Allah is our Lord, and we will remain here until we see our Lord.’ He will be commanding them and making them steadfast.

“Then He will withdraw from sight and appear again, saying, ‘Will you not follow the people?’

“They will reply, ‘We seek refuge in Allah from You! Allah is our Lord, and we will remain here until we see our Lord.’ He will make them steadfast.

“They asked, ‘Will we see Him, Messenger of Allah?’

“He replied, ‘You will have no doubt about seeing Him at that moment. Then He will withdraw from sight and appear to them again, making Himself known to them. He will then say, “I am your Lord, so follow Me.” The Muslims will rise, and the Bridge will be laid.’”

translated_text:
Clearer than all of this in showing that the “first vision” encompasses everyone at the gathering is the lengthy hadith of Abū Razīn al-‘Uqaylī. A number of scholars have narrated it, and most hadith scholars have accepted it. Ibn Khuzaymah narrated it in his Kitāb al-Tawhīd (The Book of Divine Oneness), stating that he relied in that book only on reliably established hadiths. In this report, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“You will emerge from the graves and from the places where you fell dead. You will look upon Him, and He will look upon you.”

He related: I asked, “Messenger of Allah, how can we look upon Him and He look upon us when He is one Person and we fill the earth?”

He replied, “Shall I tell you of something comparable among Allah’s wonders? The sun and moon are a small sign from Him. You see them simultaneously, and they see you, without your having any difficulty seeing them. By the life of your God, He is far more able to see you and let you see Him than they are to see you and let you see them.”

I asked, “Messenger of Allah, what will our Lord do with us when we meet Him?”

He replied, “You will be presented before Him, your faces laid bare before Him, and nothing about you will be hidden from Him. Your Lord will take a handful of water in His Hand and sprinkle it towards you. By the life of your God, not one of your faces will fail to receive a drop. As for the believer, it will leave his face like a white cloth; as for the disbeliever, it will mark his nose like black charcoal. Then your Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, will depart, and the righteous will follow in his footsteps—or he said, ‘The righteous will depart after him.’” He said, “They will then proceed along a bridge of fire.” He went on to relate the account of the Bridge.

The compilers of the Sunan collections have narrated a portion of Abū Razīn’s hadith with a good chain of transmission:

Abū Razīn said: I asked, “Messenger of Allah, will each of us see his Lord on the Day of Resurrection? What sign of this is there in His creation?”

He replied, “Abū Razīn, does not each of you see the moon as though alone with it?”

I said, “Yes.”

He said, “Allah is greater.”

Thus, this hadith shows that his words,

“You will look upon Him, and He will look upon you,”

apply generally to all creation, as the context indicates.

Ibn Khuzaymah also narrated from ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, may Allah be pleased with him, a report traced back to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“By Allah, there is not one of you with whom Allah will not be alone, just as one of you is alone with the moon on the night of the full moon—or he said, ‘on a night.’ He will say: ‘Son of Adam, what deluded you concerning Me? Son of Adam, what did you do with what you knew? Son of Adam, how did you respond to the messengers?’”

These are among the hadiths upon which those holding this view rely. Some of them have also appealed to His words, glorified and exalted is He:

“But when they see it close at hand,”

believing that the pronoun refers to Allah. This is mistaken, for Allah, glorified and exalted is He, says:

“They say, ‘When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?’ Say, ‘Knowledge of it is with Allah alone, and I am only a clear warner.’ But when they see it close at hand, the faces of those who disbelieve will be distressed, and it will be said, ‘This is what you used to call for.’”

This makes clear that what they see is the promise—that is, the punishment promised to them. Do you not see that He says:

“And it will be said, ‘This is what you used to call for’”?

They have also seized upon flimsy interpretations of the Quran that provide no evidence whatsoever.

As for those who restrict the vision to those who outwardly profess Allah’s oneness—both believers and hypocrites—they cite the previously mentioned hadiths of Abū Hurayrah and Abū Sa‘īd, as we have related them. Those who affirm that a disbeliever or hypocrite will see Him affirm this only once, or twice for hypocrites, as a “vision of recognition.” Thereafter, He will veil Himself from them on the plain of the gathering.

“Whoever is blind in this life will be blind in the Hereafter and even further astray.”

He also says:

“And We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind.”

Describing them without qualification as blind is incompatible with their “seeing Him,” which is the highest form of sight.

In short, my purpose in this treatise is not to discuss this question exhaustively, for the field of knowledge is vast. Rather, the aim is to explain that this “question” is not among the important matters that warrant extensive discussion and dissemination among the general public and the learned alike, until it becomes a rallying cry that divides hearts and sets people at odds.

Nor, to my knowledge, is this “question” one that warrants shunning one another and severing ties. Most of those before us who discussed it were people who adhered to the Sunnah and followed the transmitted teachings. People disagreed over it without shunning one another or severing ties, just as the Companions—may Allah be pleased with them—and those after them disagreed over whether the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saw his Lord in this world. They used strong language concerning it, as when the Mother of the Believers, ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: “Whoever claims that Muhammad saw his Lord has uttered a tremendous lie against Allah.” Yet this disagreement did not lead them to shun one another or sever ties.

Likewise, Imam Ahmad debated some people of the Sunnah over “the question of testifying that the ten will be in Paradise,” until voices were raised during the debate. Ahmad and others held that this testimony should be given, yet they did not shun those who refrained from giving it. There are many other comparable questions.

Those who differ over this “question” are more deserving of being excused than others. As for the “majority,” their excuse

is clear from what the Quran indicates and what has been transmitted from the early generations. Moreover, most hadiths concerning “seeing Allah” explicitly mention only the believers seeing Him; no explicit text stating that the disbeliever will see Him has reached them; and they have found that unqualified references to seeing Him have come to signify the utmost honour and the highest bliss.

As for those who affirm this vision, whether generally or with distinctions, I have already explained their grounds for being excused. They say that His words:

“No! Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day.”

refer to the veiling that follows the reckoning. For one may say, “I have barred so-and-so from my presence,” even though some form of seeing occurred before that exclusion. This veiling is general and uninterrupted, and it is this veiling that distinguishes them from the believers. For He, glorified and exalted, will manifest Himself to the believers on the gathering grounds of the Resurrection after the disbelievers have been veiled from Him, as the hadiths cited earlier indicate. Then He will manifest Himself to them in Paradise, both generally and particularly, continually, forever and without end.

They also say that the statements of the early generations accord with what is in the Quran. Furthermore, this form of “seeing,” which encompasses all creatures, may be a lesser form, unlike the “seeing” reserved exclusively for believers. For “seeing” takes forms so vastly different that its two extremes can scarcely be defined.

There are rules of conduct that must be observed here. Among them is that anyone who refrains from discussing this question and does not advocate any position may not lawfully be shunned, even if he holds one of the two views. For even with religious innovations graver than this, only those who promote them are shunned, not those who remain silent. This case is therefore all the more deserving of such restraint.

translated_text:
Another such rule is that scholars should not make this question a test and a badge of allegiance by which they judge the standing of their brethren and opponents. Such conduct is displeasing to Allah and His Messenger. Nor should they raise it with ordinary Muslims who are safe and free from discord. However, if someone is asked about it, or encounters a person suited to being informed about it, he should share whatever knowledge he possesses that he hopes will prove beneficial. This differs from believing that the believers will see their Lord in the Hereafter: belief in that is an obligatory duty, because of the mass-transmitted reports concerning it from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his Companions, and the early generations of the Muslim community.

Another such rule is that no one may state without qualification that the disbelievers will see their Lord, for two reasons.

First: an unqualified reference to “seeing Him” has come to convey honour and reward. To use it without qualification is therefore misleading and unsettling. No one may use wording that suggests something contrary to the truth unless it has been transmitted from the early generations, and this wording has not been transmitted from them.

Second: when a statement applies generally, but expressly singling out one of its instances would depart from propriety in speech, such singling out is forbidden. Allah is the Creator of everything and wills every event that occurs. Nevertheless, a person is forbidden to single out created things regarded as filthy, or events deemed reprehensible by the revealed law, by saying in isolation, “O Creator of dogs,” or “O One who wills adultery,” and the like. This differs from saying, “O Creator of all things, O You by whose will everything takes place.”

translated_text:
Likewise, in this case, if someone were to say, “There is no one with whom his Lord will not meet in private, with neither a gatekeeper nor an interpreter between them,” or, “All people will be gathered before Allah; He will look upon them, and they will look upon Him,” this wording would differ from the earlier wording in what it suggests.

Let no one, therefore, depart from the transmitted wording, even though disagreement may arise over some aspects of its meaning. Such disagreement is inevitable; the matter is as our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has told us. All goodness lies in following the righteous early generations, acquiring extensive knowledge of the hadith of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, understanding it deeply, holding fast to the rope of Allah, adhering to whatever fosters unity and harmony, and avoiding whatever leads to disagreement and division. The exception is a clear case in which Allah and His Messenger have commanded some form of avoidance: that command must be obeyed wholeheartedly.

But when it is unclear whether a statement or action warrants punishment, one must refrain from imposing it, because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Avert the prescribed punishments where there is doubt, for it is better for you to err in pardoning than to err in punishing.”

This was narrated by Abū Dāwūd. This applies especially when the matter leads to prolonged evil and division among Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah, for the harm arising from such division is many times greater than the evil resulting from a few people’s error on a subsidiary issue.

When someone is uncertain about a matter, let him offer the supplication narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh, on the authority of ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said:

Having said this, I ask Allah the Almighty, Lord of the mighty Throne, to guide us and you to the words and deeds He loves and is pleased with; to enable us to follow the guidance of His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, inwardly and outwardly; to unite us upon guidance; to bless our affairs with success; to make our hearts like those of the best among us; to protect us from Satan; and to grant us refuge from the evil within ourselves and from our evil deeds.

I have written this letter seeking what is right. I desire only to put things right as far as I can, and my success comes only from Allah. Even so, I do not fully know the reality of what has passed between you or the particulars of your circumstances. I have written only on the basis of what I understood from those who spoke to me. My foremost purpose is simply to reconcile you and bring your hearts together.

As for discussing “this issue” and others exhaustively, and clarifying the truth of the matter, I may speak or write about that at another time if I see a pressing need for it. At present, however, I consider restoring harmony among you to be the more urgent need.

Peace be upon you, and Allah’s mercy and blessings. All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds. May Allah bless our master Muhammad, his family, and his Companions, and grant them abundant peace. Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.

translated_text:
Shaykh Shams al-Dīn Ibn al-Qayyim said:

I heard Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah explain the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “Light—how could I see Him?” He said: “It means that there was light there, and light prevented me from seeing Him; so how could I see Him?”

He said: “This is supported by another wording in the Sahīh collection: ‘Did you see your Lord?’ He replied, ‘I saw light.’” (*)

This hadith has proved so perplexing to many people that some have misread it as “Nūran innī arāhu” (“A light—indeed, I see Him”), treating the yā as an adjectival suffix and the preceding expression as a single word. This is incorrect in both wording and meaning. What caused their confusion and error was that they believed the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had seen his Lord. Since his words, “How could I see Him?” amounted to a denial of having seen Him, they were bewildered by the hadith. Some rejected it on the grounds that its wording was inconsistent. All of this departs from what the evidence entails.

‘Uthmān ibn Sa‘īd al-Dārimī reported in his Book of Refutation that the Companions unanimously agreed that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not see his Lord on the night of the Ascension. Some, however, excepted Ibn ‘Abbās from this consensus.

Our shaykh says: “This is not, in reality, a disagreement, for Ibn ‘Abbās did not say
translated_footnote:
(*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd said (p. 58):
This quotation from Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, appears in Ijtimā‘ al-Juyūsh al-Islāmiyya, pp. 47–49.
It appears that the shaykh’s words, may Allah have mercy on him, end with “ra’aytu nūran” (“I saw light”) in the third line, and that the remainder, beginning with “wa-qad a‘dala” (“It has proved perplexing”), is Ibn al-Qayyim’s own wording, may Allah have mercy on him. And Allah Most High knows best.

The shaykh—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

Section

As for “seeing Him,” it is authentically reported from Ibn ‘Abbās that he said, “Muhammad saw his Lord with his heart twice.” ‘Ā’ishah, however, denied that he saw Him. Some reconciled their statements by saying that ‘Ā’ishah denied seeing Him with the physical eyes, while Ibn ‘Abbās affirmed seeing Him with the heart.

The wordings authentically reported from Ibn ‘Abbās either leave the manner of seeing unspecified or specify that it was with the heart. Sometimes he says, “Muhammad saw his Lord,” and sometimes, “Muhammad saw Him.” No explicit statement that he saw Him with his physical eyes has been authentically reported from Ibn ‘Abbās.

Likewise, Imām Ahmad sometimes leaves the manner of seeing unspecified, and sometimes says, “He saw Him with his heart.” No one has said that he heard Ahmad say, “He saw Him with his physical eyes.” However, some of his followers heard certain statements of his that left the manner of seeing unspecified and understood them to mean seeing with the physical eyes, just as some people heard Ibn ‘Abbās’s unqualified statements and understood them in that sense.

There is nothing in the evidence that entails that he saw Him with his physical eyes, nor has this been established from any of

the Companions, nor is there anything in the Quran and Sunnah that indicates this. Rather, the authentic texts point more clearly to its denial, as reported in Sahīh Muslim from Abū Dharr:

“I asked Allah’s Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), ‘Did you see your Lord?’ He replied, ‘Light—how could I see Him?’”

Allah Most High has said:

“Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed, to show him some of Our signs.”

Had He shown Himself to him, to be seen with his physical eyes, mentioning that would have been more fitting. Likewise, He says:

“Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?”

“He certainly saw some of the greatest signs of his Lord.”

Had he seen Him with his physical eyes, mentioning that would have been more fitting.

In the two Sahīhs, Ibn ‘Abbās is reported to have said concerning His words:

“We made the vision which We showed you only a trial for the people, as well as the accursed tree in the Quran.”

“It was a vision seen with the eyes, which Allah’s Messenger (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) was shown on the night he was taken on the Night Journey.”

This was a “vision of the signs,” for he told the people what he had seen with his physical eyes on the night of the Ascension. That became a trial for them: some believed him, while others disbelieved him. He did not tell them that he had seen his Lord with his physical eyes. Nor is there any mention of that in any of the authentic hadiths concerning the Ascension. Had it occurred, he would have mentioned it, just as he mentioned things of lesser significance.

The authentic texts and the agreement of the early generations of the Muslim community establish that no one sees Allah with his physical eyes in this world, apart from the disagreement some of them had concerning our Prophet Muhammad (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) alone. They agreed that the believers will see Allah directly on the Day of Resurrection, just as they see the sun and the moon.

translated_text:
He was asked:

About people who claim that they see Allah with their own eyes in this world, and that they obtain without asking what Moses obtained by asking.

He replied:

The “early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars” unanimously agreed that the believers will see Allah with their own eyes in the Hereafter. They also unanimously agreed that they do not see Him with their own eyes in this world. Their only disagreement concerned the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace).

It is established in the authentic hadith collection that he said:

“Know that none of you will see his Lord until he dies.”

Anyone who says that the friends of Allah or others see Allah with their own eyes in this world is a misguided innovator, opposing the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community. This is especially so if they claim to be superior to Moses. Such people are to be called upon to repent; unless they repent, they are to be put to death. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
The shaykh, imam and erudite scholar, Shaykh al-Islām Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-‘Abbās Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah be pleased with him—was asked:

What do the esteemed scholars and leading authorities in religion—may Allah be pleased with them all—say concerning the hadith that al-Bukhārī cited as supporting evidence in his Sahīh, namely the statement of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“Allah, Mighty and Majestic, calls out in a voice that those far away hear just as those nearby do: ‘I am the King; I am the Judge’”?

And concerning his statement (peace be upon him) in the well-known hadith:

“Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ‘O Adam, rise and send forth those destined for the Fire.’ Then comes a call in a voice: ‘Allah commands you to send forth those destined for the Fire.’”

Some people have said: “An attribute of Allah cannot be established on the basis of a single hadith.” What, then, is the answer to this question, drawing upon the Quran, the Sunnah, transmitted reports, reasoned argument, examples and analogous cases? Please explain this matter at length and give us a ruling. May you be rewarded.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. The fundamental principle in “this subject” is that a person must speak only with knowledge. Although this is commanded in all matters, it is even more obligatory in this subject. Allah Most High says:

“Say:

‘My Lord has only forbidden shameful deeds, whether open or secret, sin, unjust aggression, associating with Allah anything for which He has sent down no authority, and saying about Allah what you do not know.’”

Allah Most High also says:

“He only commands you to commit evil and shameful deeds, and to say about Allah what you do not know.”

And He says:

“Do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge.”

And He says:

“O People of the Scripture, do not exceed the bounds in your religion, nor say anything about Allah except the truth.”

And He says:

“Was not the covenant of the Scripture taken from them, that they would say nothing about Allah except the truth?”

Just as a person may not affirm anything without knowledge, neither may he deny anything without knowledge. Thus, the burden of proof rests upon the one who denies, just as it rests upon the one who affirms.

Another principle that must be understood is that “proofs of the truth do not contradict one another.” When Allah reports something—whether affirming or denying—it is impossible for another of His reports to contradict that first report. Nor can anything understood through reason independently of revelation contradict what that report conveys.

Proofs that yield knowledge cannot contradict one another, whether both are based on revelation, both are rational, or one is based on revelation and the other is rational. Contradiction may, however, arise between things that some people suppose to be proofs but are not. Someone may hear a report and suppose it to be authentic when it is not, or understand it to mean something it does not indicate. Or a specious argument may occur to him which he supposes to be a rational proof, though it is false: truth has become confused with falsehood in his mind, and on that basis he rejects what Allah and His Messenger have reported.

This is one of the reasons why those who reject the messengers go astray: either by rejecting them altogether, as did those who rejected all the messengers, such as the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd and others like them; or by believing in some and disbelieving

in others, such as those among the People of the Scripture who believed in some messengers but not others, and those among the philosophers who believed in some of what the messengers brought but not all of it. Some innovators within the religious communities—Muslims, Jews and Christians—have fallen into error in this way. Specious arguments arose in their minds which they thought disproved what the messengers had conveyed concerning Allah Most High’s names and attributes. They therefore supposed that they were obliged to give their own views precedence over the revealed texts. These specious arguments have been discussed at length elsewhere, where the errors of the philosophically inclined Jahmiyyah, the Muʿtazilah, and those misguided followers who agreed with them have been explained.

The guiding principle in affirming the divine attributes is to uphold the position of the early generations of this Ummah and its leading scholars: Allah is to be described as He described Himself and as His Messenger described Him, while safeguarding this description against distortion, likening Him to creation, specifying how His attributes are, or negating them. Nothing is like Allah in His essence, His attributes or His actions. Whoever denies His attributes negates them, and whoever likens His attributes to those of His creatures likens Him to creation. What is required is to affirm His attributes while denying that they resemble the attributes of created beings: affirmation without likening Him to creation, and declaring His transcendence without negating His attributes. As Allah Most High says:

“There is nothing like Him”

—this refutes those who liken Him to creation—

“and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing”

—this refutes those who negate His attributes. Thus, whoever likens Him to creation worships an idol, while whoever negates His attributes worships a nonentity.

“The way of the messengers”—may Allah’s blessings be upon them—is to affirm Allah’s attributes of perfection in detail and to declare, in general terms, that He bears no likeness to creation. Their way is therefore “detailed affirmation” and “general negation.” The heretics among the philosophers, the Qarāmitah, the Jahmiyyah and others like them follow the opposite course: detailed negation and general affirmation.

Thus Allah Most High states in His Book that He “has knowledge of all things,” “has power over all things,” and is “Most Forgiving, Most Merciful,” “Almighty, All-Wise,” and “All-Hearing, All-Seeing”; that He “created the heavens and the earth and everything between them in six days, then rose over the Throne”; that He “loves those who fear Him,” is pleased with the believers and angry with the disbelievers; and that He “does whatever He wills.” He also states that He spoke directly to Moses, called to him from the right side of the Mount, and brought him near for a private conversation; and that He will call to His servants, saying: “Where are My partners whom you used to claim?” There are many other such statements.

Allah Most High also says:

“There is nothing like Him.”

“Do you know of any equal to Him?”

“And there is none comparable to Him.”

He thereby makes clear that Allah has no likeness, equal or peer. Thus none of His attributes can resemble any attribute of created beings, nor can any created being equal or rival Him in any of His attributes—glorified and exalted is He.

The heretics, however, have reversed this approach, likening Him to nonexistent things, impossibilities and contradictions. Their extremists say: He is neither living nor dead, neither knowing nor ignorant, neither hearing nor deaf, neither speaking nor mute. Indeed, they may even say: He is neither existent nor nonexistent, neither something nor not something.

Others say: He is neither inside the world nor outside it, neither separate from the world nor indwelling within it. They use similar expressions to negate mutually opposed alternatives that cannot both be absent. Thus the leading exponents among them say that He is absolute existence.

translated_text:
Sīnā and his followers—even though they have established in “logic” what all rational people know: that what is absolute with absoluteness stipulated exists only in the mind, not in concrete reality. Their claim thus amounts to saying that the Necessary Existent does not exist in external reality, although they acknowledge what rational people do not dispute: that existence necessarily includes a being whose existence is necessary in itself.

Others say that He is absolute without any stipulation—as al-Qūnawī and others maintain. They identify Him with the “existence” predicated of the necessary and the contingent, the one and the many, the mental and the external, the eternal and the originated. He would therefore be either an attribute of created things, a part of them, or those very things themselves.

The former group identify Him with abstract “existence,” unrestricted by any qualification. This entails that He is neither necessary nor contingent, neither knowing nor ignorant, neither powerful nor powerless. Yet they also say that He is intellective and intelligible, lover and beloved. Thus they contradict themselves in their misguidance, making one into two and two into one. Likewise, they seek to affirm an existence stripped of every attribute and unrestricted by any qualification, yet they distinguish it by what belongs to no other existent.

For this reason, some of them say that the knower and knowledge are one, and that He is knowledge itself. They thus identify the knower by himself with the knower through another, and the bearer of an attribute with the attribute itself. Their contradictions are even greater than those of the Christians in their “Trinity” and “union,” through which they corrupted faith in divine oneness and the prophetic message.

translated_text:
The statements of Ibn Sab'īn, Ibn Rushd the Younger, Ibn al-Tūmart, Ibn 'Arabī al-Tā'ī, and others like them among the Jahmiyyah—those who deny the divine attributes—revolve around this principle, as has been explained at length elsewhere. Something approaching this union is also found in the statements of many speculative theologians and Sufis, into whose thought certain strands of the doctrine of union had entered without their realizing the corruption they contained.

The discussion of “the question of Allah Most High’s speech,” and people’s confusion concerning it, rest upon this principle, for it is one of “the questions concerning the divine attributes.” It has ramifications that distinguish it from all the other questions concerning the attributes. People have fallen into great confusion over it, as we have explained elsewhere. We have also explained that “the early generations of the Muslim community and its imams” adhered to the faith with which Allah sent His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They described Allah as He described Himself and as His Messenger described Him, without distorting or denying His attributes, specifying their modality, or likening them to those of creation.

They affirmed that the Quran is the speech of Allah Most High. They attributed to Allah the speaking, private discourse, and calling with which He described Himself, as well as what the Prophetic traditions and transmitted reports affirm in accordance with the Book of Allah Most High.

None of the Companions, those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment, or the other imams of the Muslims said that Allah’s speech is created—that He created it in something other than Himself, with no speech subsisting in Him—as the “Jahmiyyah” among the Mu'tazilah and others claimed. Rather, when they openly introduced this innovation, the early generations and the imams condemned it vehemently. They recognized that its true implication was that Allah neither speaks, commands, nor forbids, for speech, like every other attribute, is predicated only of the one in whom it subsists.

translated_text:
Thus, if He were to create speech in the tree—“Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me”—that would be the tree’s speech, and the tree itself would be saying, “Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me.” This would be like the speech uttered by people’s skins when their owners ask them, “Why have you testified against us?” They will reply, “Allah, who causes all things to speak, has caused us to speak.” Likewise, the Most High said, “And We subjected the mountains to glorify Us along with David.”

If His speaking meant that He created speech in something other than Himself, then all speech in existence would be His speech, since He is its Creator. Indeed, the proponents of divine indwelling among the Jahmiyyah explicitly stated this, as in the verse attributed to Ibn ‘Arabī, the author of al-Fusūs and al-Futūhāt:

All speech in existence is His speech;
Prose or verse—to us it is the same.

It is known that when Allah creates knowledge, power, movement, or will in a particular entity, that entity is the one that knows, has power, moves, or wills. Thus, if His speech were nothing but what He creates in something other than Himself, that other thing would be the one speaking it. This is discussed at length in its proper place.

The well-known specious argument of those who deny divine speech is that they believed “speech” to be an attribute that can exist only through an act subsisting in the speaker. Thus, if the Lord spoke, attributes and actions would subsist in Him, and they alleged that this was impossible.

They said: “For we inferred that the world came into being only by establishing that bodies came into being; and we inferred that bodies came into being from the accidents subsisting in them—that is, their attributes and actions. If attributes and actions subsisted in the Lord, it would necessarily follow that He too had come into being, and the proof by which we established that the world came into being and that the Maker exists would be invalidated.”

The adherents of the Sunnah who affirm the divine attributes replied to them:

“Your argument is an innovation in religion; none of the early generations of this community or its leading scholars used it. Indeed, al-Ash‘arī stated in his ‘Epistle to the People of the Frontier’ that this argument is forbidden in the religion of the Messengers and that the religion of the Muslims must not be founded upon it. Others stated that it is rationally invalid, just as it is religiously forbidden, and that when the early generations and leading scholars condemned the speculative theologians, the Jahmiyyah, and those who engaged in speculation about accidents and bodies, their foremost intention was to condemn arguments such as this. This has been discussed at length in its proper place.”

After “the doctrine of the Jahmiyyah” emerged, “Abū Muhammad ‘Abd Allāh ibn Sa‘īd ibn Kullāb” appeared, agreeing with the early generations and leading scholars in affirming “Allah’s attributes and His exaltedness above His creation.” He explained that His “exaltedness above His creation” is known through reason, whereas His “rising over the Throne” is known through revelation. Likewise, al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī, Abū al-‘Abbās al-Qalānisī, and other speculative theologians who affiliated themselves with the Sunnah and hadith came after him.

Then “Abū al-Hasan al-Ash‘arī” came and followed the approach of Ibn Kullāb and others like him. In his books, he outlined the doctrines of the adherents of the Sunnah and hadith, noting that Ibn Kullāb agreed with most of them. These men are called “the Sifātiyyah” (affirmers of the divine attributes), because they affirm Allah’s attributes, in opposition to the Mu‘tazilah. However, “Ibn Kullāb and his followers” did not affirm that acts connected to Allah’s will and power subsist in Him, nor did they affirm anything else connected to His will and power as subsisting in Him.

by “temporally originated occurrences” created things, or events that alter the subject in which they occur, or similar things that people mean by this expression. Rather, they mean to deny any acts or other matters connected to His will and power. They therefore deny that there can subsist in Him any act of creating, rising over the Throne, coming, arriving, speaking, calling out, speaking privately, or anything else that He is described as willing and having power to do.

Ibn Kullāb disagreed with their statement, “No accidents subsist in Him.” He said, “Attributes subsist in Him, but they are not called accidents.” Yet he agreed with what they intended by saying, “No temporally originated occurrences subsist in Him”: namely, that nothing connected to His will subsists in Him.

From the time he drew this distinction, those who affiliated themselves with the Sunnah and the community—who held that the Quran is uncreated, that Allah will be seen in the Hereafter, and that Allah is above His heavens, over His Throne, distinct from His creation—came to hold two positions, mentioned by al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī and others.

One group agreed with Ibn Kullāb, including al-Qalānisī, al-Ashʿarī, Abū al-Hasan ibn Mahdī al-Tabarī, and their followers. Many followers of the four imams and others agreed with these men, including adherents of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abū Hanīfah, and others.

Al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī used to agree with him, but it was later said that he withdrew his agreement. Ahmad ibn Hanbal had instructed people to shun al-Hārith al-Muhāsibī and other followers of Ibn Kullāb when they openly expressed this position, just as al-Sarī al-Saqatī instructed al-Junayd to beware of some of al-Hārith’s statements. This principle continued to be debated until it occasioned a dispute between Abū Bakr ibn Khuzaymah, known as the Imam of Imams, and some of his companions. He learned that they had agreed with Ibn Kullāb, so he forbade them from doing so, censured them, and criticized Ibn Kullāb’s doctrine on grounds well known among the imams of hadith and the Sunnah.

From that time onward, those who affiliated themselves with the Sunnah disputed whether Allah speaks with sound or not. Ibn Kullāb’s followers denied this, saying that speaking with sound entails an act subsisting in the speaker and connected to his will. In their view, nothing connected to Allah’s will and power can subsist in Him, whether an act or anything else. They therefore said:

“Allah does not speak with sound. Rather, His speech is a single meaning that is command, prohibition, and statement. If expressed in Arabic, it is the Quran; if expressed in Hebrew, it is the Torah; and if expressed in Syriac, it is the Gospel.”

We know that when the Torah is translated into Arabic, it does not become the Quran; indeed, its meanings are not those of the Quran. We know that when the Quran is translated into Hebrew, it does not become the Torah revealed to Moses. We also know that the meaning of the verse on debt is not the meaning of the Verse of the Footstool, nor is the meaning of “May the hands of Abū Lahab perish” the meaning of “Say, ‘He is Allah, One.’”

They said: Whoever regards commands and prohibitions as attributes of speech rather than types of speech holds a position whose falsity is self-evident. This is akin to the position of those who profess the unity of existence. Whoever holds that existence is one and the same entity, both necessary and contingent, makes a claim whose falsity is self-evident. The same applies to whoever regards the meanings of speech as a single meaning that is command, prohibition, and statement.

Rather, speech is divided into non-declarative utterances and statements. Non-declarative utterances are divided into requests to act and requests to refrain from acting; statements are divided into negative and affirmative statements. Likewise, that which exists is divided into the necessary and the contingent. The contingent is divided into a living entity subsisting in itself and an entity subsisting in another. What subsists in another is divided into that which requires life and that which does not require life.

Thus, the term “one” may signify oneness in kind or oneness as an individual entity. Saying “Speech is a single meaning” is like saying “Existence is one.” If the speaker means that it is one kind, one genus, one category, or the like, this is not the same as meaning that it is a single entity, a single essence, and a single individual. For this is a willful denial

of sense perception, reason, and revelation. As for the former, what is meant is that these things share something in common, just as existing things share in what is designated by “existence,” and the various types of speech share in what is designated by “speech.” All of this has been discussed at length elsewhere.

Then another group recognized the falsity of Ibn Kullāb’s position on speech, yet agreed with his fundamental premise that nothing connected with Allah’s will and power subsists in Him. They also held that the Quran is Allah’s uncreated speech. Since they recognized only two possibilities—something eternal, unconnected with Allah’s will and power, or something created and separate from Him—they were compelled to say that Allah speaks with a sound, or sounds, that are eternal and beginningless, unconnected with His will and power; and that He has always been, and will always be, characterized by those eternal, beginningless sounds inseparable from His essence.

This position is attributed to Abū al-Hasan ibn Sālim, the teacher of Abū Tālib al-Makkī—if the attribution to him is authentic. It is, however, the position of many followers of Ibn Sālim and those who agreed with them among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others.

The Karrāmiyyah, together with a large group among the Murjiʾah, the Shia, and others, said that Allah speaks with sounds that subsist in Him and are connected with His will and power, and that temporal occurrences connected with His will and power subsist in Him. However, they held that this comes into being after not having existed; that in pre-eternity Allah was not a speaker except in the sense of having the power to speak; and that He comes to be characterized by what occurs through His power and will after not having been so characterized. These people considered themselves to agree with the community that Allah has acts subsisting in Him which are connected with His will and power, and that, besides these, there subsist in Him volitions and speech connected with His will
