and power. But they said: A succession of temporal occurrences cannot take place in Him, for whatever is subject to such a succession must itself have originated. They agreed with the Muʿtazilah in using this argument to establish that the world had a beginning.

Just as Ibn Kullāb distinguished between accidents and temporal occurrences, these people distinguished between temporal occurrences arising anew and their being inseparable from Him. They denied that such occurrences were inseparable from Him, without denying that they arise in Him—just as they said that created things separate from Him come into existence, after not having existed, through His will and power.

The eternalist philosophers demand that all these groups explain what causes temporal occurrences to arise after not having existed. They argue that this entails giving one alternative precedence without a determining factor, and temporal occurrences arising without a newly occurring cause. They say that this is impossible according to clear reason. This is their most formidable specious argument for “the eternity of the world”—a thorny predicament and an overwhelming difficulty. These groups found themselves unable to answer them, to the point that they resorted to concessions.

We have discussed this at length elsewhere and set out “the decisive answers” to the philosophers’ arguments according to the approach of the early generations and the imams. We have explained that whoever affirms what the texts of the Quran and Sunnah entail can engage the philosophers in rational debate and decisively refute them, and will recognize that sound reason accords with authentic revelation.

We have also explained how “each of the groups within the Muslim community” can answer them. Since these groups are closer to the truth than the philosophers, they can answer them by showing what necessarily follows from the philosophers’ own premises, in a way the philosophers cannot evade. They can say to the philosophers: “Your position is more evidently false, according to revelation and reason, than the position of any Muslim group.” Thus, each Muslim group can say to them:

“If the only way we can give you a conclusive answer that dispels your specious argument—apart from an answer based on your own premises—is either to agree with you in something contrary to revelation and reason, or to agree with our fellow Muslims in something that does not contradict revelation—and may not contradict reason either—then the latter is preferable.”

The philosophers saw an opportunity to prevail over the various Muslim groups because of the innovations each group had introduced. They seized upon each group’s innovation and used it as an argument against them. Someone holding such an innovated position could therefore say:

“I would rather abandon this innovated position and agree with what the Quran, the Sunnah, and the statements of the early generations of the Muslim community indicate than agree with the philosophers on a position that I know constitutes disbelief according to revelation, and whose falsity reason also demonstrates.”

“As for the early generations and the imams,” none of them is reported to have held that the Quran is created; nor that it is a single meaning subsisting in His essence, which is at once command, prohibition, and statement, and which is what the Torah, the Gospel, the Quran, and other verbal expressions signify; nor that it consists of eternal, beginningless sounds unrelated to His will and power; nor that Allah did not speak until He brought speech into being for Himself, thereby becoming one who speaks.

As for the claim that people’s voices when reciting the Quran, or their utterances, are eternal and beginningless, this too is among the “newly introduced innovations” whose falsity is more evident than that of others. The early generations and the imams are among those furthest removed from this position. Sound reason recognizes that the claim that people’s voices are eternal and beginningless is self-evidently false.

However, this originated in their dispute over the “question of utterance.” The explicitly recorded position of Imam Ahmad and other scholars of his standing is that whoever says that uttering and reciting the Quran are created is a Jahmī, while whoever says that they are uncreated is an innovator. This is because “utterance and recitation” may mean the words uttered and recited, which are Allah’s speech. Whoever regards Allah’s speech, which He sent down to His Prophet, as created is a Jahmī. These expressions may also refer to the act itself and to human attributes. Whoever regards human actions and voices as uncreated is therefore a misguided innovator.

This is also how al-Ashʿarī reported the position of the people of the Sunnah and hadith in his book al-Maqālāt (Accounts of Doctrines). He said:

“They say that the Quran is uncreated speech, and that discussing the positions concerning suspension of judgment and utterance is an innovation. Whoever adopts either the position concerning utterance or that of suspending judgment is an innovator. According to them, one should neither say that uttering the Quran is created nor say that it is uncreated.”

None of the imams or the early generations said that Allah does not speak with a voice. Rather, it is firmly established from more than one of them that Allah speaks with a voice. This is conveyed in well-known reports from the early generations and the imams. They would relate the reports mentioning Allah’s speaking with a voice, and none of them rejected those reports. Indeed, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ahmad said:

“I said to my father, ‘Some people say that Allah does not speak with a voice.’ He replied, ‘My son, these people are Jahmīs; all their arguments revolve around denying the divine attributes.’”

He then mentioned some of the reports transmitted on this subject. Al-Bukhārī’s statements in The Creation of Actions explicitly affirm that Allah speaks with a voice and distinguish between Allah’s voice and human voices. He cited several hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on this subject. Likewise, in his Sahīh, he included a chapter on the words of the Most High:

“Until, when fear is removed from their hearts, they say, ‘What has your Lord said?’ They say, ‘The truth.’ And He is the Most High, the Most Great.”

He cited evidence that Allah speaks with a voice. That is the extent of the point. Just as this is the recognized position among the “people of the Sunnah and hadith,” it is also the position of the great majority of the Muslim community’s groups. Most of these “groups” affirm that Allah speaks with a voice, despite their disagreement over whether His speech is created or subsists in Him; whether it is eternal or originated in time; or whether He has always spoken whenever He wills.

This is the position of the Muʿtazilah, the Karrāmiyyah, the Shīʿah, most of the Murjiʾah, the Sālimiyyah, and others among the Hanafīs, Mālikīs, Shāfiʿīs, Hanbalīs, and Sufis.

Among the Muslim groups, none denied that Allah speaks with a voice except Ibn Kullāb and his followers. Likewise, none maintained that speech is a single meaning subsisting in the speaker except him and his followers. Nor did any Muslim group maintain that people’s voices when reciting the Quran are eternal and beginningless, that an eternal voice is heard from people, or that we ourselves hear “the Quran” from Allah, except a small group claiming affiliation with the people of hadith among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, Dāwūd, and others.

No Muslim maintains that the written letter formed by the ink in copies of the Quran is eternal and beginningless. Thus, affirming “letters and voice” in the sense that the ink and people’s voices are eternal is a false innovation that none of the imams espoused. Likewise, denying that Allah speaks with a voice and treating His speech as a single meaning subsisting within Him is a false innovation that none of the early generations or the imams espoused. What the “early generations and the imams” agreed upon is that the Quran is Allah’s speech, sent down and uncreated

In Arabic, a “call” is a raised voice. The term “call” is not applied to anything that is not a sound, either literally or figuratively. Since a call is a kind of sound, evidence establishing the particular kind necessarily establishes the broader category. Thus, if evidence indicates that a human being is present, one knows that an animal is present.

Similarly, when He states that He possesses knowledge and power, this indicates that He possesses an attribute, because knowledge and power are types of attribute—even if the wording of the Quran does not state that knowledge is an attribute or that power is an attribute. Likewise, when He states in the Quran that He creates, provides, gives life, and causes death, this indicates that He acts, since these are particular kinds within the broader category of action. If this attribute is established by what the Quran indicates in several places, then the hadiths concerning it accord with the Quran’s indication, and this attribute is not established solely on the basis of this report.

translated_text:
The fifth answer is as follows:

The evidence from revelation and reason establishing that Allah speaks also establishes that He speaks with a voice. There are four views concerning what the term “speech” denotes. Some say it denotes wording that conveys meaning. Others say it denotes the meaning conveyed by the wording. Others say it denotes each separately, with a distinct sense for each. Still others say it encompasses both together. This last view is that of the early generations, the jurists, and the majority of scholars.

Thus, when someone says, “So-and-so spoke,” the statement, without further qualification, is understood to refer to both wording and meaning together. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah has pardoned my ummah for the thoughts that occur within them, so long as they neither speak of them nor act upon them.”

He also said:

“Two phrases are light on the tongue, heavy in the balance, and beloved to the Most Merciful: Glory and praise be to Allah; glory be to Allah, the Magnificent.”

He also said:

“The truest words spoken by a poet are the words of Labīd: ‘Indeed, everything other than Allah is vain.’”

There are many similar examples. Thus, when used without qualification, “speech” encompasses both wording and meaning together. If meaning alone or wording alone is called speech, this is only with a qualification indicating that particular sense. This has been explained at length elsewhere, as has the fact that speech, when mentioned without qualification, comprises both wording and meaning together. The Quran and hadith abound in passages affirming the speech of Allah Most High; what is understood from them, therefore, is the affirmation of both wording and meaning for Allah.

translated_text:
The sixth answer is as follows:

Muslims agree that the Quran is Allah’s speech. If His speech consists only of meaning, while the Arabic wording that conveys those meanings is not His speech, then that wording must be something created by Allah in something other than Himself. It would therefore be the speech of that other entity, because, as explained earlier, speech created in a particular locus is the speech of that entity. Thus, the Arabic speech would not be Allah’s speech, but the speech of another. Yet it is known beyond doubt as part of the Muslim faith that Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, informed his ummah that the Arabic speech he conveyed from Allah was Allah’s speech, not the speech of another. If the Arabic wording were created, it would not be Allah’s speech, and what the ummah received from its Prophet would therefore be false.

This is one of the strongest arguments the Sunnis advance against the Jahmiyyah to establish that the Quran is not created. They argued:

“If Allah had created it in something other than Himself, it would have been an attribute of that other entity, just like all other created attributes: when Allah creates them in a particular locus, they are attributes of that locus.”

This very argument establishes that the Arabic Quran is Allah’s speech, not the speech of another. For if it were created in a particular locus, the Arabic speech would be the speech of the locus in which it was created. Yet it is known beyond doubt as part of the religion of Islam that the Arabic speech is Allah’s speech, not the speech of another.

This refutes the claim made by some later scholars that the term “speech” applies to wording and meaning in two distinct senses. They may be answered as follows:

“If each is literally called speech, neither can be created. For if either were created, it would be the speech of the locus in which it was created.”

translated_text:
For this reason, the early Kullābiyyah did not say that the term “speech” applies to wording and meaning in two distinct senses, because that would invalidate their argument against the Muʿtazilah and commit them to saying that Allah’s speech is created. Rather, they said that “speech” applies figuratively to wording and literally to meaning. Their later followers recognized that this was self-evidently false and that the term “speech” literally includes wording. They therefore assigned it two distinct senses, which committed them to holding that Allah’s speech is created. Thus, they face two unacceptable alternatives: either to say that Allah’s speech is created, or to say that the Arabic Quran is not Allah’s speech. Both positions are known to be false.

The discussion is not about people’s own vocal sounds and movements. Rather, it concerns the Arabic Quran itself, revealed to Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This becomes clear if we consider the Quran before it was sent down to him and he conveyed it to creation.

If it is said that all of it is Allah’s speech, that He spoke it, and that Gabriel conveyed it from Him to Muhammad—as is known from the religion of the messengers—then this explicitly establishes that there is no distinction between the letters and the meanings: the one is part of Allah’s speech just as the other is.

If, however, it is said that He created in something other than Himself an ordered sequence of letters indicating a meaning subsisting in His own essence, this explicitly declares that those combined letters are not His speech and that He did not speak them in any way.

If it is said that those letters are literally called speech, yet were created in something other than Him, it follows that they are the speech of that other entity, not Allah’s speech. This contradicts what is known from the religion of Islam. If it is said that they are not literally called speech, this contradicts what is necessarily known from language and revealed law.

translated_text:
speech; but the question concerns the Quran, which consists of “wording and meaning”: is all of it Allah’s speech? Or is its wording Allah’s speech, but not its meaning? Or is its meaning Allah’s speech, but not its wording?

It is necessarily known in the religion of Islam that all of it is Allah’s speech. Allah Most High has said:

“When We replace one verse with another—and Allah knows best what He sends down—they say, ‘You are only a fabricator.’ Rather, most of them do not know. Say, ‘The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth’”—up to His words—“We certainly know that they say, ‘It is only a human being who teaches him.’ The language of the one they allude to is foreign, whereas this is clear Arabic.”

Some of the polytheists used to say that Muhammad merely learned the Quran from a slave belonging to Banū al-Hadramī. So Allah Most High said that the language of the person to whom they attributed the Quran was foreign, whereas this was clear Arabic. This demonstrates that Muhammad conveyed the Quran in both its wording and its meaning; abstract meanings alone were not sent down to him. Had that been the case, it would have been possible to say that he received meanings from this foreigner and then expressed them in his own language. Thus, when Allah stated, “The language of the one they allude to is foreign, whereas this is clear Arabic,” after saying, “Say, ‘The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth,’” this indicated that the Holy Spirit brought it down in this clear Arabic language.

The Seventh Point

Allah’s speech, like all other speech, may be heard from the speaker himself, just as Moses heard Allah’s speech from Allah, and the Companions heard the speech of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, from him. At other times, it is heard from someone conveying it on the speaker’s behalf, just as the Muslims heard the Quran from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and from those who conveyed it on his behalf.

and an example of this is His statement, Most High:

“If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the speech of Allah.”

Likewise, the speech of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is heard from the Companions.

It is well known that when a hadith narrator relates his saying:

“Actions are only by intentions, and each person shall have only what he intended,”

the speech, in both wording and meaning, is that of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He uttered it in his own voice, while the narrator conveyed it through his own movements and vocal sounds. It is also well known that someone conveying speech from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and other speakers like him utters its letters and meanings, even though it is possible to narrate from him by meaning and to substitute some words for others. Thus, Allah recounts in the Quran the statements of peoples who spoke languages other than Arabic.

If it were supposed that the person whose speech was conveyed had spoken only the meaning of the speech, with someone else expressing it on his behalf, he would be like a mute in whom meanings subsist without his expressing them—until someone else expresses them in words of his own. It is well known that “speech” is an attribute of perfection incompatible with muteness.

If someone who says, “No speech subsists in Allah,” has thereby likened Him to inanimate objects, attributed deficiency to Him, and denied Him perfection, then someone who likewise says, “He expresses the meanings within Himself only through an expression that subsists in another,” has likened Him to a mute who expresses himself only through an expression that subsists in another. This view denies Him an attribute of perfection and makes other beings among His creation more perfect than Him.

It has been established elsewhere that the Creator is more deserving of every perfection possessed by a created being, and more deserving of being free of every deficiency from which a created being is free. This is among the proofs establishing His attributes of perfection, such as life, knowledge, and power, for these are attributes of perfection

They have also argued that, were He not to possess attributes of perfection, He would possess their opposites, which are attributes of deficiency—and Allah is far above such things. An inanimate object, however, is, according to them, described as neither blind nor sighted, because it lacks the capacity for either.

This objection has confounded many later scholars—even Abū al-Hasan al-Āmidī and other speculative theologians like him—and they thought that it could not be answered. The answers to it have been discussed at length elsewhere. Among the “answers” to this, he mentioned the following: this entails an even greater deficiency. For something capable of possessing sight or blindness, knowledge or ignorance, and speech or muteness is more perfect than something incapable of either member of these pairs, since an animal is more perfect than an inanimate object. The Eighth Argument

It may be said:

“Allah’s speech” is either something created and separate from Him, with no speech subsisting in His essence—as the Jahmiyyah, including the Muʿtazilah and others, maintain—or His speech subsists in Him. The first possibility is false by the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community, its leading scholars, and all Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah. There is abundant scriptural and rational evidence of its falsehood, as has been explained at length elsewhere.

If His speech subsists in Him, there are only two possibilities: either meaning alone subsists in Him, as Ibn Kullāb and his followers maintain, or both meaning and letters subsist in Him. The first possibility is false.

First, “a single meaning” cannot constitute command, prohibition, and statement, nor can it be what is signified by the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran.

Second, abstract meaning cannot be heard, whereas scriptural texts and consensus establish that Allah’s speech is heard from Him, as Moses son of ʿImrān heard it. For this reason, the more rigorous proponents of the view that speech consists solely of meaning maintain that it cannot be heard. However, “a group among them” claimed that it can be heard, basing this on their view that hearing can apprehend anything that exists, that sight can apprehend anything that exists, and that smell, taste, and touch can apprehend anything that exists. Most rational thinkers hold that the falsehood of this is rationally self-evident. This is one of the points for which the majority most strongly criticized Abū al-Hasan al-Ashʿarī and those who agreed with him among the followers of Ahmad and others.

Third, if speech were nothing but meaning, there would be no difference between Allah’s speaking to Moses and His revealing to others, nor between His speaking from behind a veil and His speaking through revelation. For all prophets share in having knowledge of abstract meaning conveyed to their hearts.

For this reason, those who built upon this false premise said that someone who practices spiritual discipline may hear Allah’s speech just as Moses son of ʿImrān heard it, as mentioned in “al-Ihyā’” and similar works. Such people came to imagine that the inspirations they received were like Allah’s speaking to Moses son of ʿImrān.

The “philosophers” entered through this door, claiming that Allah’s speaking to Moses was merely an emanation flowing into his soul from the active intellect, and that “Allah’s speech” is nothing but the addresses that arise within souls, just as “angels” are the images produced by the imagination that arise within hearts. Such things may occur both in wakefulness and in sleep. Thus, they made Allah’s speaking to Moses son of ʿImrān something of the same kind as a person seeing his Lord in a dream while He speaks to him, and similar experiences. This necessarily follows from the position of anyone who makes Allah’s speech an abstract meaning. If this entailment is necessarily known to be false in the religion of Islam, then what it entails is known to be false.

Fourth, if speech consisted solely of meanings, the created being would be more perfect than the Creator. Just as we know that the living is more perfect than the dead, the knowledgeable more perfect than the ignorant, the capable more perfect than the incapable, and one who speaks more perfect than one who is mute, we also know that one who speaks with both meanings and letters is more perfect than one who speaks only with meanings, without letters. And since

the Lord cannot be described by attributes of imperfection, must possess attributes of perfection, and cannot lack any attribute of perfection possessed by a created being, it is impossible for His speech to be imperfect or for a created being to surpass Him by possessing perfect speech. This is why Moses son of Imrān was favored above others by Allah’s speaking to him: He addressed him with speech that Moses heard from Allah. Thus, His addressing Moses with His voice was a greater distinction than having abstract meanings revealed to one’s heart without hearing them with one’s ears.

Fifth, if speech were nothing but abstract meaning, half the Quran would be Allah’s speech and half would not: its meaning would be Allah’s speech, but its words would not. This contradicts what is known in the religion of the Muslims. Hence, they distinguish between the Quran, which is Allah’s speech, and the abstract meanings He revealed to His Prophet. They know that Gabriel brought down the entire Quran to him, and that Gabriel and Muhammad had no part in it beyond conveying and delivering it. The former is His messenger from among the angels, and the latter is His messenger from among humankind.

For this reason, Allah sometimes attributes it to one and sometimes to the other, using the designation “messenger,” as He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger. And it is not the word of a poet; little do you believe.”

In this verse, the messenger is Muhammad. And He says:

“Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger, possessed of strength, held in honor by the Lord of the Throne, obeyed there and trustworthy.”

the other to have originated it. Since He attributes it sometimes to one and sometimes to the other, we know that He attributes it to each because he conveyed and delivered it, not because he originated or produced either its wording or its meaning. For this reason, He said:

“the word of a noble messenger,”

not “the word of an angel” or “a prophet.” He used the designation “messenger” to make clear that he conveys something from another, as the Exalted says:

“O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord.”

The Sunan collections report that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to present himself to the people during the pilgrimage season, saying:

“Will no man take me to his people so that I may convey the speech of my Lord? Quraysh have prevented me from conveying the speech of my Lord.”

Furthermore, His words, “Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger,” refer to the Quran and therefore encompass its wording just as they encompass its meaning. “Quran” is a name for both together. Thus, when a commentator explains it or a translator translates it, he does not call his commentary or translation “Quran.” Indeed, the Muslims agree that a person in a state of ritual impurity may touch books of Quranic commentary, and they agree that its commentary cannot serve as the recitation in prayer. The same applies to its translation into a language other than Arabic, according to the great majority of scholars. As for the view reported from Abū Hanīfa, it has been said that he retracted it, and it has also been said that it is conditional upon calling the translation “Quran.”

In any event, permitting a translation to take its place for certain rulings does not entail that the name “Quran” applies to it. Likewise, when the value of camels, cattle, or sheep is paid as zakat in their stead, what is paid is not called camels, cattle, or sheep; rather, it retains its own name, whatever it may be. Similarly, if the formula “Allah is Most Great” in prayer is replaced with “Glory be to Allah” or the like, and it is held that this validly commences the prayer—as Abū Hanīfa maintains—one would not say that the substitute is the formula “Allah is Most Great.”

Likewise, if we suppose that we translated the Quran in a permissible manner, one would not say that the translation is “Quran,” nor would we call it “Quran.” If, then, the Quran were Allah’s speech solely on account of its meaning, while its wording and composition were not Allah’s speech but were called such only because they signify Allah’s speech, anything conveying the same meaning as this wording and composition would share its designation and rulings. It would therefore have to be called “Quran” and be subject to the rulings governing the Quran. This matter is discussed at length elsewhere.

The Ninth Argument

This Quran, which the Muslims recite, is the speech of Allah that He sent down to His Prophet, as established by the revealed texts and the consensus of the Muslims. Allah has declared whoever says that it is the word of a human being to be a disbeliever, and has threatened to cast him into Saqar, saying:

“Leave Me with the one I created alone,”

—through His words—

“Indeed, he thought and deliberated.
So may he be destroyed—how he deliberated!
Then may he be destroyed—how he deliberated!
Then he looked;
then he frowned and scowled;
then he turned away and was arrogant,
and said, ‘This is nothing but magic handed down.
This is nothing but the word of a human being.’”

There is no doubt that, by saying, “This is nothing but the word of a human being,” he did not mean what Allah meant by saying, “Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger.” Had he meant that human beings conveyed it from someone else, just as people learn it from one another, this would not have been false. Rather, he meant that it had originated with human beings and been composed by them.

Thus, whoever holds that its “wording and composition” originated with Muhammad has made half of it the word of human beings. Whoever holds that they originated with Gabriel has made half of it the word of the angels; and whoever holds it to be

He declared whoever said, “It is the word of the angel, or the word of the air or trees,” to be a disbeliever; indeed, whoever said, “It is the word of a human being,” disbelieved. This shows that no part of the Quran—“neither its wording nor its meaning”—is the word or speech of any created being. Rather, it is the speech of Allah Most High. Moreover, the demonstrative “this” in His words, “This is nothing but the word of a human being,” refers not to the meaning alone, excluding the wording, but to both.

The Tenth Argument

Allah has stated that the Quran was sent down from Him, as He says:

“Those to whom We have given the Scripture know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth.”

And He says:

“Say, ‘The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth.’”

And He says:

“The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise.”

The pronoun encompasses both the wording and the meaning. This is especially clear in His words, “The revelation of the Book.” For those who say, “Allah’s speech is the meaning alone, not the letters,” use “the Book” to designate the Arabic composition, and “speech” to designate the meaning, while “Quran” is used for both. Thus, everyone agrees that the term “the Book” encompasses the Arabic wording. When He states that “The revelation of the Book is from Allah,” it is therefore known that the Arabic composition was sent down from Allah. This supports the statement of the early generations: “It originated with Him”—meaning that He is the One who spoke it.

This is a “brief answer” to the question posed, within the space this sheet allows, for the matter is discussed at length elsewhere. Allah knows best. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. May Allah bestow His blessings and abundant peace upon our master Muhammad, his family, and his Companions. Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.

The first is that one may say:

No reliable evidence—whether scriptural or rational—has established that the “Throne” is one of the round, spherical celestial spheres. This was asserted only by a group of later scholars who studied “astronomy” and other branches of philosophy. They held that there are nine celestial spheres, and that the ninth—al-Atlas—encompasses the others and is spherical like them. It imparts to them their eastern motion, although each sphere has its own particular motion besides this common motion.

Then, upon hearing mention in the accounts of the prophets—may Allah’s blessings and peace be upon them—of “Allah’s Throne,” His “Footstool,” and the “seven heavens,” they conjectured that the “Throne” was the ninth sphere. This was because they believed that beyond the ninth sphere there was either nothing whatsoever or, alternatively, nothing created.

Some of them then held that the “ninth sphere” sets all the other spheres in motion, so they made it the source of events. They claimed that Allah brings into being within it whatever He decrees for the earth, or brings it into being within the “soul” which they claimed was attached to it, or within the “intellect” from which they claimed this sphere had emanated. Some of them sometimes called this intellect the spirit; others sometimes identified the “soul” with the spirit. Some also identified the “soul” with the Preserved Tablet, just as they identified the “intellect” with the Pen. At other times, they identify the “spirit” with the tenth, active intellect associated with the sphere of the moon

“An example of this” is that they determined that one celestial body lies below another because the lower eclipses the upper, but not vice versa. From this they inferred that the upper body lies in a sphere above the lower one. Likewise, they inferred from differing motions that the spheres are distinct, even positing several spheres within a single sphere, such as the epicycle and others. As for anything existing above these for whose existence they have no evidence, their method gives them no knowledge of either its existence or its nonexistence.

Likewise, the assertion that the motion of the “ninth” sphere is the source of events is erroneous and misguided even according to their own principles. For they say that the “eighth” sphere, together with the fixed stars it contains, has a motion peculiar to it, and that this motion has two poles distinct from those of the “ninth.” The same applies to the “seventh” and the “sixth.” If each sphere has its own distinctive motion—and the differing motions cause the various celestial configurations that arise, while those configurations cause events in the lower world—then the motion of the ninth is only one component of the cause, just like the motion of any other sphere.

The configurations that arise in the heavens—a celestial body’s conjunction with another at the same degree; its opposition to it when they are separated by “half the celestial circle,” namely 180 degrees; its trine with it when they are separated by “a third of the celestial circle,” namely 120 degrees; its square with it when they are separated by “a quarter of it,” 90 degrees; its sextile with it when they are separated by “a sixth of the celestial circle,” 60 degrees; and other such configurations—arise only through differing motions, each distinct from the others. For the distinctive motion of the “eighth” is not the same as

translated_text:
the motion of the ninth, even though it follows it in the overall motion, like a person moving aboard a ship in the direction opposite to its movement. Likewise, the distinctive motion of the “seventh” does not arise from the ninth or the eighth. The same applies to all the other spheres: the distinctive motion of each does not arise from the spheres above it. How, then, can the motion of the ninth alone be made the source of all events, as claimed by those who suppose that the Throne is dense?

In their view, the ninth sphere is simple, with uniform parts and no variation whatsoever. How, then, could it cause diverse things independently of the things receiving its influence and of other causes? Yet these misguided people nevertheless divide it into three hundred and sixty degrees and attribute to each degree an effect different from that of another, without any difference in the things receiving those effects. This is like someone taking a single body of water and attributing to one of its two portions an effect different from the other’s—not according to the things receiving those effects. Rather, he makes one portion impart heat, another cold, another happiness, and another misery. They themselves, and every rational person, know that this is falsehood and misguidance.

Since these people have nothing that rules out the existence of something else above the nine spheres, to assert categorically that the Messengers’ reports mean that the Throne is the ninth sphere is to speculate about the unseen and speak without knowledge.

{وَهُوَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ فِي سِتَّةِ أَيَّامٍ وَكَانَ عَرْشُهُ عَلَى الْمَاءِ}

translated_text:
this assumption.

Furthermore, the spheres are all of the same kind in their shapes and in the way they enclose one another. The relation of the seventh to the sixth is like that of the sixth to the fifth. If there is a ninth sphere, its relation to the eighth is like that of the eighth to the seventh. As for the “Throne,” the transmitted reports indicate that it is distinct from other created things, and that its relation to some of them is unlike their relation to one another.

Allah Most High says:

“Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with praise and believe in Him”—to the end of the verse.

And He, glorified is He, says:

“And eight will bear the Throne of your Lord above them that Day.”

He thus states that the Throne has bearers both now and on the Day of Resurrection, and that its bearers and those around it glorify Him and seek forgiveness for the believers. It is known that each celestial sphere is sustained—by the power of Allah Most High—in the same way as all the other spheres; there is no difference in this respect between one sphere and another. Even if it is supposed that some of them actually have angels bearing them, the same would hold for their counterparts. Allah Most High says:

“And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne”—to the end of the verse.

Here He mentions that the angels surround the Throne. Elsewhere, He mentions that it has bearers, and in a third passage He mentions both its bearers and those around it together, saying:

“Those who bear the Throne and those around it.”

Furthermore, He has stated that His Throne was upon the water before He created the heavens and the earth, as Allah Most High says:

“And it is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water.”

It is also established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī and elsewhere, from ‘Imrān ibn Husayn, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah was, and there was nothing other than Him. His Throne was upon the water. He wrote everything in the Record and created the heavens and the earth.”

In another version recorded by al-Bukhārī:

“Allah was, and there was nothing before Him. His Throne was upon the water. Then He created the heavens and the earth and wrote everything in the Record.”

In an authentic version recorded by someone else:

“Allah was, and there was nothing with Him. His Throne was upon the water. Then He wrote everything in the Record.”

It is also established in Sahīh Muslim, from ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Amr, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah decreed the destinies of all creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, and His Throne was upon the water.”

This determination took place after the Throne had come into existence and fifty thousand years before the creation of the heavens and the earth.

He, glorified and exalted is He, praises Himself as the Owner of the Throne, as in His words:

“Say, ‘If there were other gods alongside Him, as they claim, they would surely have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne.’”

And His words, Most High:

“Exalted in rank, Owner of the Throne, He sends revelation by His command to whomever He wills of His servants, to warn of the Day of Meeting—the Day they will stand exposed; nothing about them will be hidden from Allah. To whom does sovereignty belong today? To Allah, the One, the All-Subduing.”

And He, Most High, says:

“And He is the All-Forgiving, the Most Loving, Owner of the Throne, the Glorious, Who does whatever He wills.”

The word “Glorious” has been read in the nominative, as an attribute of Allah, and in the genitive, as an attribute of the Throne.

And He, Most High, says:

“Say, ‘Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?’ They will say, ‘They belong to Allah.’ Say, ‘Will you not then fear Him?’”

Thus, He describes the Throne as glorious and mighty. And He says:

translated_text:
Most High:

“So exalted is Allah, the True King! There is no god but Him, Lord of the Noble Throne.”

Thus, He also describes the Throne as noble. Likewise, in the two Sahīh collections, Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would say in times of distress:

“There is no god but Allah, the Magnificent, the Forbearing. There is no god but Allah, Lord of the Mighty Throne. There is no god but Allah, Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth, Lord of the Noble Throne.”

Thus, in this hadith too, he describes the Throne as mighty and noble.

As for the disputant’s statement:

“The relation of the highest celestial sphere to what lies beneath it is like that of another sphere to what lies beneath it.”

If the Throne belonged to the same kind as the celestial spheres, its relation to what lies beneath it would be like that of another sphere to what lies beneath it. This would not warrant treating it as a distinct kind or singling it out for mention, just as it does not warrant singling out one heaven rather than another—even though, according to these people, the higher heaven relates to the lower as one celestial sphere does to another. It would differ from what lies beneath it only by being larger, just as the higher heaven differs from the lower.

Indeed, the relation of the heaven to the air, and that of the air to the water and the earth, is like the relation of one celestial sphere to another. Yet He has not singled out any of these kinds, as distinct from what adjoins it, either for mention or by describing it as noble, glorious, and mighty.

Moreover, it is known that it is not the cause of their existence or their motions. Rather, they have motions of their own. It is therefore impermissible to say that its motion is the cause of events. Indeed, if the motion of the celestial spheres causes events, the motions peculiar to the other spheres are more numerous. Nor does its encompassing them necessarily mean that it is larger than all of them combined, unless it has sufficient thickness to match their combined size. Otherwise, it is well known that

translated_text:
when the thicknesses are comparable, the combined bulk of what lies within is greater than that of what surrounds it; indeed, it may be many times as great. Moreover, the diverse motions that do not derive from its motion are more numerous, although its motion encompasses them all.

It is established in Sahīh Muslim, on the authority of Juwayriya bint al-Hārith:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came in to her while she was glorifying Allah using pebbles, as she had been doing from the dawn prayer until mid-morning. He said: ‘Since leaving you, I have uttered four phrases which, if weighed against what you have said, would outweigh it: Glory be to Allah, as many times as the number of His creatures; glory be to Allah, commensurate with the weight of His Throne; glory be to Allah, as much as pleases Him; glory be to Allah, to the extent of the ink for His words.’”

This shows that the weight of the Throne is the greatest of all weights. Yet they say that the ninth celestial sphere is neither light nor heavy. Rather, the hadith indicates that the Throne alone is the heaviest thing that can be invoked in such a comparison, just as the number of created beings is the greatest number that can be invoked.

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Sa‘īd reports:

“A Jewish man whose face had been slapped came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said: ‘O Muhammad, one of your Companions slapped my face.’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘Summon him.’ They summoned him, and he asked: ‘Why did you slap his face?’

“He replied: ‘O Messenger of Allah, I was passing through the marketplace when he was saying, “By Him who chose Moses above all mankind!” I said, “You wicked man! Above Muhammad too?” Anger seized me, and I slapped him.’

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘Do not rank the prophets above one another, for people will fall unconscious on the Day of Resurrection, and I shall be the first to regain consciousness. Then I shall find Moses holding one of the legs of the Throne. I do not know whether he regained consciousness before me or was recompensed for his swoon.’”

This makes clear that the Throne has legs. A supporting leg is also mentioned using the term sāq (leg), and the statements on this subject are similar.

The two Sahīh collections also report that Jābir said:

“I heard the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say: ‘The Throne of the Most Merciful shook at the death of Sa‘d ibn Mu‘ādh.’”

A man said to Jābir, “Al-Barā’ says that it was the bier that shook.” He replied, “There were grudges between these two tribes, al-Aws and al-Khazraj. I heard Allah’s Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say: ‘The Throne of the Most Merciful shook at the death of Sa‘d ibn Mu‘ādh.’”

Muslim also relates it in his Sahīh through Anas:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, while Sa‘d’s bier lay there: ‘The Throne of the Most Merciful shook for him.’”

Yet according to them, the motion of the ninth celestial sphere is perpetual and uniform. Anyone who interprets this as referring to the delight and joy of the bearers of the Throne must provide evidence for his claim, as mentioned by Abū al-Hasan al-Tabarī and others. Moreover, the context and wording of the hadith rule out this possibility.

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, Abū Hurayra reports that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever believes in Allah and His Messenger, establishes prayer, pays zakat, and fasts Ramadan, Allah has undertaken to admit him to Paradise, whether he emigrates in Allah’s cause or remains in the land where he was born.”

They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, should we not give people this glad news?”

He replied, “In Paradise there are one hundred degrees which Allah has prepared for those who fight in His cause. The distance between each two degrees is like that between heaven and earth. So when you ask Allah, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the most central and highest part of Paradise. Above it is the Throne of the Most Merciful, and from it the rivers of Paradise spring forth.”

said: ‘O Abū Sa‘īd, whoever is content with Allah as his Lord, Islam as his religion, and Muhammad as his Prophet is assured of Paradise.’ Abū Sa‘īd was amazed at this and said, ‘Repeat that for me, O Messenger of Allah.’ He did so, then said, ‘There is another deed by which Allah raises His servant one hundred degrees, the distance between each two degrees being like that between heaven and earth.’ He asked, ‘What is it, O Messenger of Allah?’ He replied, ‘Fighting in Allah’s cause.’”

Sahīh al-Bukhārī also relates:

“Umm al-Rabī‘ bint al-Barā’—the mother of Hāritha ibn Surāqa—came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said, ‘O Prophet of Allah, will you not tell me about Hāritha?’ He had been killed on the day of Badr, struck by a stray arrow. ‘If he is in Paradise, I shall bear it patiently; but if he is elsewhere, I shall weep bitterly for him.’ He said, ‘O mother of Hāritha, there are many gardens in Paradise, and your son has attained the highest Firdaws.’”

The first hadith thus makes clear that the Throne is above al-Firdaws, which is the most central and highest part of Paradise, and that Paradise contains one hundred degrees, the distance between each two degrees being like that between heaven and earth, with al-Firdaws the highest of them. The second hadith agrees with it in its description of the hundred degrees, and the third agrees with it that al-Firdaws is the highest of them.

If the Throne is above al-Firdaws, one may argue that, if this is so, it entails a height and elevation not established by astronomy. For calculation does not establish that the distance between the ninth sphere and the first is one hundred times the distance between heaven and earth; moreover, in their view, the ninth sphere is contiguous with the eighth. This has thus made clear that the Throne is above al-Firdaws, which is the most central and highest part of Paradise.

is greatest?’ He replied, ‘Āyat al-Kursī (the Verse of the Footstool).’ Then he said, ‘O Abū Dharr, the seven heavens compared with the Footstool are nothing but a ring cast into a vast wilderness, and the Throne’s greatness compared with the Footstool is like that of the wilderness compared with the ring.’” This hadith has several chains of transmission. It was related by Abū Hātim ibn Hibbān in his Sahīh, Ahmad in al-Musnad, and others.

Those who have argued that “the Throne is dome-shaped” have cited the hadith related in Sunan Abī Dāwūd and elsewhere from Jubayr ibn Mut‘im, who said:

“A Bedouin came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, people are exhausted, families are hungry, and wealth has been destroyed. Pray to Allah for us, for we seek your intercession with Allah, and Allah’s intercession with you.’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, kept glorifying Allah until its effect showed on his Companions’ faces. He said, ‘Woe to you! Do you know what you are saying? Allah is not sought as an intercessor with any of His creatures. Allah’s majesty is far greater than that. Allah is upon His Throne, and His Throne is over His heavens and His earth like this’—and he gestured with his fingers in the shape of a dome.”

Another wording reads:

“‘His Throne is above His heavens, and His heavens are above His earth, like this’—and he gestured with his fingers in the shape of a dome.”

Even if this hadith indicates a domed shape—as does his statement that al-Firdaws is the most central and highest part of Paradise, together with his statements that its roof is the Throne of the Most Merciful and that above it is the Throne of the Most Merciful, since what is most central can be highest only in something rounded—this does not indicate that the Throne is one of the celestial spheres. Rather, if it is assumed to be above all the celestial spheres, such a shape is possible for it, whether one says that it encompasses the spheres or that it is above them without encompassing them, just as the earth’s surface is above the earth’s upper half without encompassing it.

{لَا الشَّمْسُ يَنْبَغِي لَهَا أَنْ تُدْرِكَ الْقَمَرَ وَلَا اللَّيْلُ سَابِقُ النَّهَارِ وَكُلٌّ فِي فَلَكٍ يَسْبَحُونَ}

" الْقُبَّةِ "
 فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَتَعَرَّضُ لِهَذَا الْمَعْنَى؛ لَا بِنَفْيٍ وَلَا إثْبَاتٍ؛ لَكِنْ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الِاسْتِدَارَةِ مِنْ الْعُلُوِّ؛ كَالْقُبَّةِ الْمَوْضُوعَةِ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ.

 إنَّ الْأَفْلَاكَ غَيْرُ السَّمَوَاتِ لَكِنْ رَدَّ عَلَيْهِ غَيْرُهُ هَذَا الْقَوْلَ بِأَنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى قَالَ: 
{أَلَمْ تَرَوْا كَيْفَ خَلَقَ اللَّهُ سَبْعَ سَمَاوَاتٍ طِبَاقًا}
 
{وَجَعَلَ الْقَمَرَ فِيهِنَّ نُورًا وَجَعَلَ الشَّمْسَ سِرَاجًا}
 فَأَخْبَرَ أَنَّهُ جَعَلَ الْقَمَرَ فِيهِنَّ وَقَدْ أَخْبَرَ أَنَّهُ فِي الْفَلَكِ وَلَيْسَ هَذَا مَوْضِعَ بَسْطِ الْكَلَامِ فِي هَذَا. وَتَحْقِيقُ الْأَمْرِ فِيهِ وَبَيَانُ أَنَّ مَا عُلِمَ بِالْحِسَابِ - عِلْمًا صَحِيحًا - لَا يُنَافِي مَا جَاءَ بِهِ السَّمْعُ وَأَنَّ الْعُلُومَ السَّمْعِيَّةَ الصَّحِيحَةَ لَا تُنَافِي مَعْقُولًا صَحِيحًا؛ إذْ قَدْ بَسَطْنَا الْكَلَامَ عَلَى هَذَا وَأَمْثَالِهِ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ. فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ يُحْتَاجُ إلَيْهِ
translated_text:
Iyās ibn Mu‘āwiya said:

“The sky is like a dome over the earth.”

The celestial sphere is known to be rounded in this way. However, the word “dome” necessarily implies roundness from above, but does not necessarily imply roundness on all sides unless this is established by separate evidence. The word falak (celestial sphere), by contrast, denotes roundness without qualification, as in His words, Most High:

“It is He who created the night and the day, the sun and the moon; each floats in an orbit.”

And His words, Most High:

“It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; each floats in an orbit.”

This implies that they are in a sphere that is round without qualification, as Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: “In a circle like a spindle’s whorl.” As for the word “dome,” it neither affirms nor denies this meaning. Rather, it indicates roundness from above, like a dome set upon the earth.

Some have said that the celestial spheres are distinct from the heavens. Others, however, have refuted this view on the grounds that Allah Most High says:

“Have you not seen how Allah created seven heavens, one above another,”

“and placed the moon among them as a light and made the sun a lamp?”

He thus states that He placed the moon within them, while also stating that it is within the celestial sphere. This is not the place to discuss this matter at length, examine it thoroughly, or explain that what has been correctly established by calculation does not contradict what revelation has brought, and that sound knowledge derived from revelation does not contradict sound rational conclusions. We have discussed this and similar matters at length elsewhere. For this is needed

 .
translated_text:
in this and similar matters that have perplexed many people, who see what is said to be known through reason as conflicting with what is said to be known through revelation. This has led each group to deny what it does not fully understand. Matters reached the point where some speculative theologians opposed the philosophers concerning the “celestial spheres” with arguments for which they had no evidence, whether from revelation or reason. They thought these arguments defended the revealed Law, although what they denied was also established by scriptural evidence.

As for the “philosophizers and their followers,” the furthest they reach is to draw inferences from the sensory phenomena they have observed; they know nothing beyond that. They may know, for example, that rising vapour condenses into clouds, and that when clouds collide, a sound results, and so forth. Yet their knowledge of this is like their knowledge that semen enters the womb. But what brings it about that semen, whose constituent parts are alike, gives rise to these different organs and their different functions, in this precise and masterful arrangement, containing such wisdom and mercy as to astound the mind?

Likewise, what causes this air or vapour to condense into clouds of a particular measure, at a particular time, over a particular place, and then to rain down upon people when they need it, providing them with just as much water as they require—neither so much that they perish nor so little that they are left in want? And what causes water to be conveyed to barren land that receives no rain, or receives too little to sustain it—such as the land of Egypt, where a little rain is insufficient, while abundant rain demolishes its buildings?

Allah Most High says:

“Have they not seen that We drive water to barren land and bring forth thereby crops from which their livestock and they themselves eat? Will they not then see?”

translated_text:
The same applies to moving clouds. It is known that every motion is either “forced,” and thus dependent on the force acting upon it; “natural,” occurring only when a body has departed from its proper centre and tends to return to it; or “voluntary,” which is fundamental. All motions therefore depend upon the voluntary motion proceeding from the angels of Allah Most High, who are “those who administer affairs” and “those who apportion affairs,” alongside the other descriptions Allah has given of the angels. Reason also corroborates this. A discussion of this and similar matters belongs elsewhere.

Our purpose here is to show that the difficulty raised in the question is dispelled under every supposition, so that the answer rests on arguments grounded in knowledge, rather than uncritical acceptance or merely conceded premises. Once we have shown that the question can be answered under every supposition—as we shall explain—it will not matter which of these suppositions actually holds, even though we know which it is. However, formulating the answer on one particular supposition rather than another, and establishing that supposition, would require a lengthy discussion that is unnecessary here. An answer that holds under every supposition is both better and more concise.

The second point:

Whether the “Throne” is the ninth celestial sphere, a body encompassing the ninth sphere, something above it relative to the earth’s surface without encompassing it, or is described otherwise, it must be understood that the upper and lower worlds are exceedingly small in relation to the Creator Most High

as He Most High says:

“They have not accorded Allah His due measure. The entire earth will be in His grasp on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be rolled up in His right hand. Glory be to Him! Exalted is He above all that they associate with Him!”

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Hurayrah reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah, Blessed and Exalted, will grasp the earth on the Day of Resurrection and roll up heaven in His right hand. Then He will say, ‘I am the King! Where are the kings of the earth?’”

In the two Sahīh collections—with the wording given by Muslim—‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar reports that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah, Blessed and Exalted, will grasp the earth on the Day of Resurrection and roll up heaven in His right hand. Then He will say, ‘I am the King! Where are the kings of the earth?’”

In the two Sahīh collections—with the wording given by Muslim—‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar reports that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah will roll up the heavens on the Day of Resurrection, then take them in His right hand and say, ‘I am the King! Where are the tyrants? Where are the arrogant?’ Then He will roll up the earths in His left hand and say, ‘I am the King! Where are the tyrants? Where are the arrogant?’”

In another wording in the Sahīh, ‘Abd Allāh ibn Miqsam reports watching ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar recount how the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah takes His heavens and His earth in His hand and says, ‘I am the King.’” The Prophet clenched and opened his fingers, saying, “I am the King.”

“I watched the pulpit shaking from its very base, until I wondered, ‘Will it fall with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, upon it?’”

translated_text:
a Jewish man, who said:

‘O Muhammad, Allah places the heavens on one finger, the earths on one finger, the mountains on one finger, the water and moist earth on one finger, and the rest of creation on one finger. Then He shakes them, saying, “I am the King! I am the King!”’

He said: The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, laughed until his molar teeth showed, confirming the rabbi’s words. Then he recited:

‘They have not appraised Allah with His true appraisal, while the earth entirely will be within His grasp on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded in His right hand’—to the end of the verse.”

This verse and the authentic hadiths explaining it—widely transmitted reports whose authenticity the scholars have unanimously affirmed and which they have received with acceptance—make clear that the heavens, the earth, and everything between them are so small in relation to the greatness of Allah Most High that, when He grasps them, they are no more than a small object in the hand of one of us, such that He tosses them as a ball is tossed.

The imam ‘Abd al-‘Azīz ibn ‘Abd Allāh ibn Abī Salamah al-Mājishūn, a peer of Mālik, said in his well-known discourse in which he refuted the Jahmiyyah, those who opposed them, and those who reinterpreted his words:

“As for the one who denies what the Lord has said of Himself, out of excessive speculation and affectation, the devils have lured him away, leaving him bewildered on earth. He then proceeds, as he claims, to argue for denying the descriptions and names the Lord has given Himself, saying: ‘If He has such-and-such, He must necessarily have such-and-such.’

Thus, the obscure has blinded him to the clear. Because the Lord remained silent about attributes He did not name, he denied those that the Lord did name concerning Himself. Satan continued to lead him on until he denied the words of Allah Most High:

‘Faces that Day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.’

He said: ‘No one will see Him on the Day of Resurrection.’ By Allah, he has thereby denied the greatest honor Allah has accorded His close servants on the Day of Resurrection: beholding His Face, and His bestowing radiance upon

them,

‘In a seat of honor near a Sovereign, Perfect in Ability.’

He has decreed that they shall not die, and they grow radiant through looking at Him.”

He went on to say:

“He denied that Allah will be seen on the Day of Resurrection only to uphold his misguided and misleading argument. For it is known that, when He reveals Himself to them on the Day of Resurrection, they will behold of Him what they had previously believed in and he had denied.

‘The Muslims said, “O Messenger of Allah, shall we see our Lord on the Day of Resurrection?” The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, replied, “Do you have any difficulty seeing the sun when no clouds obscure it?” They said, “No.” He said, “Do you have any difficulty seeing the moon on the night of the full moon when no clouds obscure it?” They said, “No.” He said, “You will see your Lord in the same way.”’

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

‘The Fire will not become full until the Compeller places His Foot in it. Then it will say, “Enough! Enough!” and its parts will draw together.’

‘He said to Thābit ibn Qays, “Allah has laughed at what you did for your guest last night.”’

He also said—as has reached us from him:

‘Allah laughs at your distress and despair, and at the swiftness with which you are answered.’

‘An Arab man asked him, “Does our Lord indeed laugh?” He replied, “Yes.” The man said, “We shall never lack good from a Lord who laughs.”’

There are other similar reports that we have not enumerated.

Allah Most High said:

‘And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.’

‘And be patient with your Lord’s judgment, for you are under Our Eyes.’

He said:

‘So that you might be brought up under My Eye.’

He said:

‘What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two Hands?’

He said:

‘They have not appraised Allah with His true appraisal, while the earth entirely will be within His grasp on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded in His right hand. Exalted is He and high above what they associate with Him.’

فَوَاَللَّهِ مَا دَلَّهُمْ عَلَى عِظَمِ مَا وَصَفَ بِهِ نَفْسَهُ وَمَا تُحِيطُ بِهِ قَبْضَتُهُ إلَّا صِغَرُ نَظِيرِهَا مِنْهُمْ عِنْدَهُمْ إنَّ ذَلِكَ الَّذِي أُلْقِيَ فِي رُوعِهِمْ؛ وَخَلَقَ عَلَى مَعْرِفَتِهِ قُلُوبَهُمْ فَمَا وَصَفَ اللَّهُ مِنْ نَفْسِهِ وَسَمَّاهُ عَلَى لِسَانِ رَسُولِهِ سَمَّيْنَاهُ كَمَا سَمَّاهُ وَلَمْ نَتَكَلَّفْ مِنْهُ عِلْمَ مَا سِوَاهُ لَا هَذَا وَلَا هَذَا لَا نَجْحَدُ مَا وَصَفَ وَلَا نَتَكَلَّفُ مَعْرِفَةَ مَا لَمْ يَصِفْ انْتَهَى. وَإِذَا كَانَ كَذَلِكَ فَإِذَا قُدِّرَ أَنَّ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ كَالْكُرَةِ وَهَذَا قَبْضُهُ لَهَا وَرَمْيُهُ بِهَا وَإِنَّمَا بَيَّنَ لَنَا مِنْ عَظَمَتِهِ وَصْفَ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ بِالنِّسْبَةِ إلَيْهِ مَا يُعْقَلُ نَظِيرُهُ مِنَّا. ثُمَّ الَّذِي فِي الْقُرْآنِ وَالْحَدِيثِ يُبَيِّنُ أَنَّهُ إنْ شَاءَ قَبَضَهَا وَفَعَلَ بِهَا مَا ذَكَرَ كَمَا يَفْعَلُ ذَلِكَ فِي يَوْمِ الْقِيَامَةِ وَإِنْ شَاءَ لَمْ يَفْعَلْ ذَلِكَ فَهُوَ قَادِرٌ عَلَى أَنْ يَقْبِضَهَا وَيَدْحُوَهَا كَالْكُرَةِ وَفِي ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْإِحَاطَةِ بِهَا مَا لَا يَخْفَى وَإِنْ شَاءَ لَمْ يَفْعَلْ ذَلِكَ وَبِكُلِّ حَالٍ فَهُوَ مُبَايِنٌ لَهَا لَيْسَ بمحايث لَهَا. وَمِنْ الْمَعْلُومِ أَنَّ الْوَاحِدَ مِنَّا - وَلِلَّهِ الْمَثَلُ الْأَعْلَى - إذَا كَانَ عِنْدَهُ خَرْدَلَةٌ إنْ شَاءَ قَبَضَهَا فَأَحَاطَتْ بِهَا قَبْضَتُهُ وَإِنْ شَاءَ لَمْ يَقْبِضْهَا بَلْ جَعَلَهَا تَحْتَهُ فَهُوَ فِي الْحَالَتَيْنِ مُبَايِنٌ لَهَا وَسَوَاءٌ قُدِّرَ أَنَّ الْعَرْشَ هُوَ مُحِيطٌ بِالْمَخْلُوقَاتِ - كَإِحَاطَةِ الْكُرَةِ بِمَا فِيهَا - أَوْ قِيلَ إنَّهُ فَوْقَهَا وَلَيْسَ مُحِيطًا بِهَا؛ كَوَجْهِ الْأَرْضِ الَّذِي نَحْنُ عَلَيْهِ بِالنِّسْبَةِ إلَى جَوْفِهَا وَكَالْقُبَّةِ بِالنِّسْبَةِ إلَى مَا تَحْتَهَا أَوْ غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ.
 فَعَلَى التَّقْدِيرَيْنِ يَكُونُ الْعَرْشُ فَوْقَ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ وَالْخَالِقُ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى فَوْقَهُ وَالْعَبْدُ فِي تَوَجُّهِهِ إلَى اللَّهِ يَقْصِدُ الْعُلُوَّ دُونَ التَّحْتِ وَتَمَامُ هَذَا بِبَيَانِ:
translated_text:
So, by Allah, nothing has shown them the immensity of what He has described of Himself, and of what His grasp encompasses, except their awareness of how small its counterpart in themselves is. This is what has been instilled in their minds, and He created their hearts with knowledge of it. Whatever Allah has described of Himself and named through His Messenger, we name as He has named it, without presuming to know anything beyond it. We do neither of these two things: we neither deny what He has described nor presume to know what He has not described.” End of quotation.

That being so, if created things are assumed to be like a ball, and this is how He grasps them and casts them, then what He has explained to us of His greatness is simply how created things stand in relation to Him, in terms whose counterpart we can understand from ourselves. Moreover, what is in the Quran and hadith makes clear that, if He wills, He grasps them and does with them what has been mentioned, as He will do on the Day of Resurrection; and if He wills, He does not do so. He is therefore able to grasp them and cast them like a ball. The encompassing of them that this entails is evident. If He wills, however, He does not do so. In every case, He is distinct from them, not co-located with them.

It is well known that any one of us—and to Allah belongs the highest example—who has a mustard seed may, if he wishes, grasp it so that his grasp encompasses it. If he wishes, he may leave it ungrasped and instead place it beneath him. In both cases, he is distinct from it. Likewise, whether the Throne is assumed to encompass created things—as a sphere encompasses what is within it—or is said to be above them without encompassing them, like the surface of the earth on which we stand in relation to its interior, or a dome in relation to what lies beneath it, or otherwise:

On either assumption, the Throne is above created things, and the Creator, glorified and exalted is He, is above it. When the servant turns towards Allah, he directs himself upwards, not downwards. This discussion is completed by explaining:

translated_text:
the third point:

We say: either the Throne is spherical like the celestial spheres and encompasses them, or it is above them without being spherical. If the former is the case, it is well known—and agreed upon by those knowledgeable in this matter—that the celestial spheres are round and spherical in shape; that the upward direction is towards the outer surface, which is convex; and that the downward direction is towards the centre. The celestial spheres have only two directions: up and down.

The six directions, however, pertain to a living creature, which has six sides. It faces one direction, which is therefore in front of it, and leaves another behind, which is therefore behind it. One direction is to its right, another to its left, another towards its head, and another towards its feet. These six directions have no fixed character in themselves; rather, they depend on relative position and relation. Thus, what is to the right of one creature may be to the left of another; what is in front of one may be behind another; and what is above one may be below another.

The upward and downward directions of the celestial spheres, however, do not change: the outer surface is above, and the centre is below. This is so even though the face of the earth, which Allah has laid out for His creatures and made firm with mountains, is where people, beasts, trees, plants, mountains, and flowing rivers are found. As for the other side of the earth, the sea surrounds it, and there are no human beings there, nor anything associated with them. Were anyone assumed to be there, they would be on the surface of the earth and would not be

translated_text:
the case that those on this side were beneath those on the other, or that those on the other side were beneath them. Likewise, the celestial spheres encompass the centre, yet neither side of a sphere is beneath the other, nor is the northern pole beneath the southern pole, or vice versa. The northern pole is, however, the one visible to us above the earth, and its altitude depends on people’s distance from the equator. For someone thirty degrees from the equator, for example, the pole’s altitude is thirty degrees. This is what is called the latitude of a locality.

Just as the sides all around the earth and the rounded sides of the celestial sphere are not above or below one another, so too the living creatures, plants, and heavy objects upon the earth cannot be said to be beneath those on the other side. This is merely something a person imagines, involving a relative sense of “below.” Consider an ant walking beneath a ceiling: the ceiling is above it even though its feet face the ceiling. Likewise, someone suspended upside down remains beneath the sky even though their feet point towards it. Similarly, a person on one side of the earth or the celestial sphere imagines that the other side is beneath them. No two people who hold that the celestial spheres are spherical disagree on this matter.

The spherical form of the celestial spheres is not only the position of astronomers and mathematicians; it is also the position of Muslim scholars. Abū al-Hasan ibn al-Munādī, Abū Muhammad ibn Hazm, Abū al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzī, and others have stated that Muslim scholars agree on this. And He has said

, exalted is He:

“And it is He who created the night and the day, and the sun and the moon, each floating in an orbit.”

Ibn ‘Abbās said: “A whorl, like the whorl of a spindle.” In Arabic, *falak* means something round. Hence the expression *tafallaka thady al-jāriya*: “The young woman’s breast has become rounded.” Everyone who knows that the celestial spheres are round knows that the encompassing sphere is above its centre on every side. In their view, anyone who imagines that someone on one side of a celestial sphere actually has someone on its opposite side beneath him is mistaken.

Since this is so, if the Throne is assumed to be round and to encompass created things, it would be the highest of them and their roof—above them without qualification. A person could therefore turn towards it and towards what is above it only upwards, never in any other direction. Anyone who turned towards the ninth sphere, the eighth, or any other celestial sphere in a direction other than upwards would be ignorant, by the agreement of all rational people. How much more so when turning towards the Throne or towards what is above it! The most that can be supposed is that it is spherical. Allah Most High encompasses all created things in a manner befitting His majesty, for the seven heavens and the earth in His hand are smaller than a chickpea in the hand of one of us.

As for the statement: “If it is spherical, and Allah is beyond it, encompassing it and distinct from it, what is the point of a servant turning towards Allah when supplicating and worshipping Him, directing himself upwards rather than downwards? The reply is:

This question arises only from the mistaken supposition that half the celestial sphere lies beneath the earth and beneath the human beings and animals on its surface. This is a grave error. If the celestial sphere were beneath the earth on one side, it would be beneath it on every side. It would necessarily follow that the celestial sphere was beneath the earth without qualification. This reverses the facts, for the celestial sphere is above the earth without qualification.

The “astronomers” say: If a hole were bored through the earth in the direction of our feet, and a heavy object—such as a stone or the like—were dropped into it, it would come to rest at the centre. Even if another stone were dropped from that side, the two would meet at the centre. If two people, rather than two stones, were imagined meeting at the centre, their feet would meet, and neither would be beneath the other. Rather, both would be above the centre, and both would be beneath the celestial sphere.

The same applies to east and west. If one man were in the east, whether in the sky or on earth, and another in the west, whether in the sky or on earth, neither would be beneath the other. This would be so whether his head, feet, belly, back, or side faced the sky or the earth. If either sought what is above the celestial sphere, he would seek it only upwards, not in the direction of his feet, his right, or his left, for two reasons:

No rational person would say that he should bore through the earth and then ascend from the other side, or that he should go right, left, forwards, or backwards to some other place on earth and then ascend. Wherever he went would be equivalent to his present position or below it, and the celestial sphere would still be above him. Travelling in any of these five directions would therefore entail a longer journey and needless exertion.

If a man wished to address the sun or the moon, he would address it only upwards, even though the sun and moon rise and set, moving away from the point directly overhead. How much more, then, does this apply to Him who is always above everything, who neither sets nor disappears—glorified and exalted is He?

Just as motion, such as that of a stone, tends towards its centre by the shortest route—a straight line—how could the deliberate seeking that arises in the hearts of Allah’s servants turn away from the short, straight path to a long, winding route? Allah Most High created His servants with a sound and upright innate disposition, except for those whom the devils have led astray, taking them away from the innate disposition with which they were created.

It runs contrary to the innate disposition, for a person seeks his goal by the shortest route, especially when the One he seeks is the One he worships and relies upon. If he turns towards Him by a path other than the straight path, his journey is inverted and reversed.

Moreover, in his journey and intention, such a person combines negation with affirmation: drawing nearer to the One he seeks while moving farther away from Him, seeking Him while recoiling from Him. For if he turns towards Him by the most distant and remote route, abandoning the nearest and shortest one, he combines two contradictory intentions. His intention to seek Him is therefore not complete, since a complete intention excludes its contradiction and opposite. This is known through the innate disposition.

If someone loves the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with complete love and seeks him—or loves anyone else, whether that love is praiseworthy or blameworthy—then whenever his love is complete and he seeks his beloved, he takes the shortest route by which he can reach him.

This differs from the case in which his love is conflicted. For example, he may love something that religion disapproves of loving, so that his desire continues to urge him to seek it while his reason forbids him from doing so. You therefore see him approaching it by a roundabout route, as people commonly say: “One foot forward and one foot back.”

Likewise, if his religious commitment is deficient, and his reason bids him go to the mosque, undertake jihad, or pursue other goals that religion commends but the soul dislikes, he continues towards that goal by a roundabout route, moving slowly along the way. All this is known through the innate disposition.

Similarly, if someone does not intend to go in person, but wishes instead to address the one he seeks, call upon him, or the like, then, if his intention is complete, he addresses him from the nearest direction from which his call can be heard and his aim achieved. If a man were in a high place and another wished to call to him, the latter would turn towards him and call. If he lowered his head into a well and called in such a way that the other could hear his voice, this would be possible. Yet someone whose intention is to make himself heard would not naturally do this without some overriding benefit. Such conduct occurs only when the intention is weak or something similar.

As for the “hadith of lowering,” reported from Abū Hurayrah and Abū Dharr, may Allah be pleased with them both, al-Tirmidhī and others transmitted it through al-Hasan al-Basrī from Abū Hurayrah. Its chain is interrupted, since al-Hasan did not hear from Abū Hurayrah. However, it is strengthened by the report of Abū Dharr attributed to the Prophet. If it is authentic, its meaning agrees with this explanation, for his words:

“If one of you were lowered by a rope, he would descend upon Allah”

express only a hypothetical supposition: were such lowering to occur, what was lowered would come down upon Him. Yet no one can lower anything onto Allah, for He is high above in His essence. When something is lowered towards the earth, it stops at the centre and does not rise towards the other side. But if the lowering were hypothetically assumed, the stated consequence would follow.

The same applies to what the questioner mentioned: if it were supposed that a servant sought Him from that direction, He, glorified be He, would hear his words, and the servant would be turning towards Him with his heart. Yet the innate disposition prevents this, because a complete intention to seek something is incompatible with intending its opposite.
